# Authority, effects and publication

Status, 21 October 2026: normative reference. Code comments cite this
document by section number. It lands on main unchanged from revision
28, the revision in force (branch `request/authority-r20`, `8b1c3c9d`). Where the code
no longer follows a cited section, the citation check of request
`0270882b` lists it. `docs/scopes.md` is the reader's guide.

Date: 2026-10-04. Design only. Written for request R3
`f2d23e6fededcbeceba50574fbd2a9f2200588c7` under Hugh's direction
`d4e0706474be041d9657f5f8413f8bd9fdac24de` and plan 017 Draft 2.

Revision 28, on the adopted revision 26. Until revision 28 this line
read "Revision 27, on the adopted revision 26". Revision 2 applied the
planner's nine groups of corrections
in `f6c4d14bcfe0500cbad4c41764e866f92c0ec98d` to the first draft at
`43b68f5a`. Revision 3 applied the seven groups of
`5fd1047414dd8915d73d6323815aa3addc7cd2de` to revision 2 at `de9a1d64`.
Revision 4 applies the five corrections of the planner's reading
`def9c326` to revision 3 at `45727248`, answers R2's proposal R2-11,
and reads the founding and fork flows against R1 revision 5.
Revision 5 applies the four groups of the planner's reading `2dc1769b`
to revision 4 at `273125f2`, and answers R2's point R2-12. Its largest
change is a proposal, made with R2 revision 7, for reviewed adoption: a
change lane may hold its own integration work under the hold capability
that the `issue` definition declares (section 6.2).
Revision 6 answers the three contract findings of the independent
static assessment `4b275a9e` of revision 5 at `5ec08fab`, and the
follow-up `30a4d16a`. An export is dispatched only on a license that
the receiving lane records in its own history (section 4.2). A new
hold's fork is seeded from its own commitment (section 5.2). Every
time window names its clock, what a restart does to it and its
fail-closed rule, in one table (section 3.12). It also agrees with
R2 revision 8 on `cancel-merge` (section 6.4) and answers R2's point
R2-18 (section 6.2).
Revision 7 answers the independent static reassessment `fb0d5867` of
revision 6 at `da20beeb`, and the follow-up `ebeaddf0`. It makes six
changes, each with a witness table. The ancestry check keeps the
staged refs that it read, so a replay judges from them and never from
the refs as they are now (section 6.2). It also answers the
supplemental assessment `245c4031` and its follow-up `d31dfefa`: the
walk starts at the parents of the commit, and an own root stops it
only on an earlier admitted check (section 6.2). An entry records which read
of membership an observation came from, and whether it was reused;
what a replay still trusts is stated (section 3.3). The rule for a
clock that is behind is R1's, with no wider stop (section 3.12). A
pending answer to a withdrawal does not freeze a lane whose merge
item is final, and a refused withdrawal carries its own reason
(section 6.4).
Revision 8 answers the independent static reassessment `da88fb08` of
revision 7 at `524ba453`, and the follow-up `6a032249`. It makes one
change of substance. The ancestry check now inspects the commit it
starts from: a staged ref of other work that targets that commit is
judged, and the lane's own new root does not answer for it (section
6.2). Two wordings are corrected (sections 3.3 and 6.2).
Revision 9 answers the independent static reassessment `999c5262` of
revision 8 at `c9153f00`, and the follow-up `86e44a0a`. It makes one
change of substance. A commit that is reachable from the destination
branch's head, as the check read it, is published history. That now
holds for the commit the check starts from, as it already held for an
ancestor: no basis is asked for it, whether or not another commitment
still keeps a staged root on it (section 6.2). An unpublished commit
of other work is refused without a basis, as in revision 8.

- What a person's removal, or a revoked device, does to a hold that

- Each host and clock assumption as an operational obligation with

Revision 15 answers the independent review `14ad7c42` of revision 14
at `b3e55edb`, which requested changes. It keeps every rule and every
scope of revision 14, with the changes below. It adds no gate, no
timer and no second lifecycle. Each change uses the registration, the
control and the operation that the task definition already has. The
correction matrix has a row for each.

- A restore can be opened before a registration is `ready`. The order
  is the lane's step `instance`, then `register`, then `intend` for
  the restore, then its outcome. One registration admits at most 3
  restores. Every other operation of the worker stays behind `ready`
  (sections 5.9 and 12.1.7).
- A `pause` or a `cancel` that was admitted is applied by its own
  outcome entry, which needs no act of the worker. Every queued
  control has a stated end (sections 4.1, 5.8 and 12.1.7).
- A private stream records the key that opened it, and only that key
  continues it (sections 4.2 and 12.1.7).
- The scope contract's revision 12, as amended before its review, is
  adopted (`b2833098`). This note says so where it states the
  contract's standing. The count of 35 sends is now the contract's
  count as well (the status below; section 13.5).
- Three answers that the adopted contract asks of this note's owner:
  the genesis act of each platform definition, the item form of
  `hold@1`, and a scripted capability in a test (section 13.7).
- Eight rows of section 12.1.8 are marked as supplied by the I2 base,
  which is under review, and one more in part.

Revision 16 answers the independent review `60c940f3` of revision 15
at `8dfda899`, which requested changes: two findings on the task
definition, and one question of order that it did not make a
condition. It keeps every rule and every scope of revision 15, with
the changes below. It adds no gate, no timed rule and no second
lifecycle. Each change uses the control, the registration and the
operation that the task definition already has, and one new item that
records a failed recovery. The correction matrix has a row for each.

- An authorized `pause` or `cancel` is always admitted, or it is a
  repeat of one that is already `queued`. Revision 17 keeps the one
  exception beside this sentence: a `pause` while the task is `idle`
  or `paused` is new work (section 12.1.7). At most 62 controls of the
  six other kinds are `queued` at once, and at most one stop of each
  kind. So the last two places of the 64 are a stop's. A task also
  reserves the entries of its stops before any is signed (sections
  5.8 and 12.1.7).
- A restore that fails for a fault of the checkpoint stays closed
  until a person decides. The failure is an item of the task scope.
  The controller or an admin signs `decide-recovery`, which names
  that failure exactly and chooses to repair or to abandon the chain.
  One decision to repair admits one replacement restore. The first
  restore of a task, and a restore after a host is lost, need no
  decision (sections 5.9 and 12.1.7).
- The outcome of a `pause` makes every `start` and `resume` that is
  still `queued` `void`, as the outcome of a `cancel` already did. A
  `start` or a `resume` is not admitted while a stop is `queued`. So
  a task runs again only by a control that was signed after the last
  stop (section 12.1.7).

Revision 17 is written for the planner's request `f1142e84`, on the
adopted revision 16 at `7bc60cf6`. It is bounded: five decisions and
one coordination, and nothing else. It keeps every rule and every
scope of revision 16, with the changes below. It adds no gate, no
timed rule, no second lifecycle and no test quota. It changes no byte
of either pinned lane definition, and no pinned digest. The
correction matrix has a row for each change, and section 13.8 is the
index.

- What gives a hold a workspace. A hold has a fork, tokens and an
  instance exactly when its definition uses at least one guard or
  effect of `hold@1`. The rule is read from the definition's bytes
  alone. The scope's commit derives the three records, as platform
  code, at the entries that section 5.7 names. A definition that
  uses only the item form gets the item form and nothing more
  (sections 5.7 and 13.7; section 12.1.8, P9).
- Four answers that the adopted contract asks. A license request is
  bound by its source, its export and its number alone (section
  4.2). A `withdraw` is bound only when it is whole and comes from
  the lane that owns the operation, and the one entry that it may
  use is stated with its bound (section 5.8). Activation, and a
  creating directory's read of a definition, are one answer (section
  12.1.2). A save and a restore state what they reserve in each of
  the five dimensions, and a checkpoint's receipt states what it is
  evidence of (section 12.1.7).
- Where four forms stand that the contract's revision 13 adopts or
  leaves open: P19, P20, P21 and P23 (section 13.8).
- Two precisions that the approval `33787163` asks for. The sentence
  that an authorized stop is always admitted keeps its one exception
  (sections 4.1 and 12.1.7). The recovery design's revision 4 is
  adopted (the status below; section 5.9).
- The standing of the fence of section 6.8. It is proposed, and it
  is not adopted (sections 6.8 and 12, U2).

Revision 18 answers the independent review `545feb91` of revision 17
at `63409e73`, which requested changes: one finding, and three
clarifications that it did not make findings. It keeps every rule and
every scope of revision 17, with the changes below. It adds no gate,
no timed rule, no second lifecycle and no test quota. It changes no
byte of either pinned lane definition, and no pinned digest. The
correction matrix has a row for each change.

- A mint that is answered after its token's use has ended makes the
  token `revoking`, and never `live`, in the entry that records the
  answer. That one rule now holds for a hold's end, for a renewal
  that changes the holder, and for a new instance. Revision 17 had
  it for a hold's end only. Nothing is done to the mint at the entry
  that ends the use. Two late answers for a fork are closed in the
  same way (sections 5.3, 5.7 and 5.8).
- A stop opens its save only with places for the save's whole
  closure, and is applied without a save otherwise. What "stopped
  and not saved" then means is stated (section 12.1.7).
- The counts of a save and of a restore are conditional, and each
  place that states them says so (sections 5.8, 12.1.7 and 13.8).
- A scope's budget does not bound how many token records and
  revocations one entry may hold. That bound is owed before an entry
  that cannot be refused is built (sections 5.7 and 13.8).

- The three kinds of observation, member by member, with the subject

- One entry of the task scope records `dispatched`: the delivery of

Revision 20 is the successor of the adopted revision 18. Revision 19,
at `c3f2f103`, was reviewed, and the verdict `d2068c05` requested
changes: two custody findings, and points that do not block. Revision
19 is not adopted. Revision 20 holds all of revision 19's content,
with the repairs that the verdict asks, and three things more. It
keeps every rule and every scope of revision 19 otherwise. It adds no
gate, no timed rule, no suite and no test quota. It changes no byte
of either pinned lane definition, and no pinned digest.

- The verdict's first finding. A person may save the root of a
  `fenced` instance: a whole closure, with every fence kept. The
  claim that one more closure "is always admitted" is replaced by
  the states in which it is, and the states in which nothing can
  save are listed (section 12.1.7, "A save of a fenced root" and
  "Where nothing can save").
- The verdict's second finding. A committed save ends a host only
  when its cut was final: every writer stopped or frozen from the
  cut through the commit and the destruction. A checkpoint says what
  its cut held, and never that the present root is complete (section
  12.1.7, "The final cut").
- The verdict's other points: a cross-reference for `ended`; the
  size of a rules observation's `content`, counted again by a
  script; the composition of nine cuts against the `max` of 8, as
  unproved and owned; and the recovery design's questions B11 and
  B12 (sections 3.3, 5.8 and 12.1.7).
- What the I3 source asks about authority: its deltas ED1 to ED17.
  The largest is what `within` of a grant is (section 3.3, "What the
  I3 source asks of this section").

- How the code of a platform definition joins the data of its row.
  The I3 source asks it (its deltas note, entry EC6), and it stops
  that delivery. The rule is one: a mark stands in the data where a
  form of that kind would stand, and its rule is run where that form
  would be derived. The common part is the scope contract's revision
  15, a draft, in its section 6.1. This note states the rule as its
  own for the seven definitions, and lists each of the 57 cells that
  begin "Code" as a mark, or says why it has none (sections 12.1 and
  12.1.8). Three cells are corrected: the inbox's `source`, and the
  rows `join` and `enrol` of membership.
- The planner's answer on an overdue host. It is a policy answer. It
  is neither of the two custody repairs above, and it replaces
  neither. An installation may end an
  overdue stopped host by rule. The act is still `end-host`, signed
  by the installation's controller. It names the rule, it follows a
  notice window, and the saved state is kept for a restore for a
  retention period. The clock lets a controller act, and destroys
  nothing by itself (section 12.1.7).

Section 13.10 is the index.

- Which pin a `pin-release` with a commit alone releases: the one

Section 13.11 is the index.

Revision 22 is on revision 21, at `f9ec25e4`, which is adopted, as
the builder's instruction for this revision states. It is bounded to
four inputs, and it keeps every rule and every scope of revision 21
otherwise. It changes no row, no byte and no digest of either pinned
lane definition. It adds no gate, no timed rule, no suite and no test
quota.

- What the source that built the marks asks of this note (the I3
  deltas EJ1, EJ8 and EJ9). The requests that an outcome's rule
  sends are marks with their clauses. A mark states its refusals, its
  most and its use of the clock. A notice's `source` holds no kind
  (sections 12.1, 12.1.6 and 12.1.8).
- The recovery design's five asks, C1 to C5. A `register` and a
  restore are refused over a fenced registration that is unsaved and
  undecided. A stale host can be ended. A destruction carries its
  cut. One more state is listed in which nothing can save (section
  12.1.7).
- The capacity finding. As revision 20's rows were written, a task
  that runs held nine places of `cut` against a `max` of 8, so no
  task could run. One save of a task is open at a time, for every
  entry that opens one. So all the saves of a task need one place of
  `cut`, and a task can run (sections 5.8 and 12.1.7).
- Extents, for the planner's request `42de9e34`: the design side
  only. A repository's rules name extents by patterns of paths. Each
  carries its approvals, who may give them, its checks and a class.
  A change meets the obligations of every extent that it touches.
  The destination judges it at the reservation, so no lane row
  changes. What is missing is listed, with its owner (section
  12.1.4a).

Section 13.12 is the index.

Revision 23 answers the verdict `6f9cc0c7` on revision 22 at
`55e41dfc`, which requested changes: one finding, and one point that
does not block. It also applies three decisions of the planner on
extents. Revision 22 is not adopted, and revision 21 is the text in
force. Revision 23 holds all of revision 22, with these repairs and
nothing else.

- The finding. Revision 22 let a further operation that changes the
  root join a save that was open, and promised that the save's cut
  would name its attempt. A cut names at most 8 attempts, and nothing
  refused a ninth. That join is withdrawn. One operation that changes
  the root is open at a time, with its save, as the adopted recovery
  design has it. The attempts that a cut must name are bounded at 8,
  and the `intend` that would be the ninth is refused, named
  `cut-full` (section 12.1.7, "The attempts of one cut").
- The point. A stop that waits and the retry of a refused save are
  one successor save, and the order between them is stated (the same
  passage).
- The planner's decisions. A change to the rules extent is never
  reviewed by its own author, with one recorded exception for a
  repository that has one controller. The classes `deployment` and
  `authority` carry four obligations beyond review, each with the
  record that holds it. An approver is always a grant on a member
  (section 12.1.4a).

Section 13.13 is the index.

Revision 24 answers the verdict `546fa613` on revision 23 at
`d2639ad9`, which requested changes: one finding, one disposition on
the lane forms' successor, and two points that do not block. It also
names three rules that the I3 source found missing for membership.
Revision 23 is not adopted, and revision 21 is the text in force.
Revision 24 holds all of revision 23, with these repairs and nothing
else. The save admission of revision 23 is kept exactly: one
operation that changes the root is open at a time with its save, a
cut names every unsaved attempt, and the ninth is refused.

- The finding. Revision 23 let the single-controller exception hold
  whenever membership showed one controller. The planner's decision
  lets an installation with one controller declare the exception in
  its rules. A count is not a permission. The exception is now
  available only where the rules that the destination observes for
  the reservation declare it. With no declaration the change is
  refused as any unmet `rules` extent is. The record of a landing
  that uses the exception names the revision of the rules that
  declared it, and the head of membership that showed one
  controller. The declaration is a form that is not built: the
  missing form 14 (section 12.1.4a).
- The disposition. A merge is admitted, in the words of the request
  `fdc3d7e2`, only in the destination's entry that reserves it, under
  the rules observed for that reservation. The lane's own earlier
  judgment is advisory, and is named so. Three states are stated,
  with the scope that judges each (section 12.1.4a, "Three states of
  a merge").
- The two points. The present standing of each sibling text is in one
  place, "The standing in force", below. Every other sentence on a
  sibling's standing is dated. The witness that cited the contract's

- Part 1. A token whose write can no longer act. The rule `mint` read
  whether its own attempt had an outcome, and did not read whether the
  item that holds the slot `token` was already final. After a
  `resend-receipt`, an older read could make the receipt final before
  the new mint answered, and the rule then gave an effect on a final
  item, which the contract makes a fault. From revision 28 a mint whose
  target is closed records its own evidence and opens the revocation,
  and sets no slot. The first outcome of a write attempt opens the
  revocation of its own mint's token, and sets nothing on a target that
  is final. Each token's revocation is `for` the holder of its mint,
  which reserved it. Both orders are worked through as entries (section
  12.1.5, "A token whose write can no longer act, and who cleans it
  up"). - Part 2. The family of that fault, swept over sections 12.1.1,
  12.1.2 and 12.1.5: 30 rules and clauses, each with what it may set and

This note answers decisions D2 and D3 of plan 017: how a scope knows
that a signer may act now, and how an exact change is published to a Git
destination and recovered when the outcome is unknown. It also places
control of hosted agents, credentials and outside effects in the new
model, and says what must be settled before anything earlier is retired.

What the existing publisher and authority code established was read for
this note and is kept beside it, with file and line anchors, in
`notes/2026-10-04-authority-effects-and-publication/publication-and-authority-facts.md`.
"Facts" below names that file. It is a reading of an earlier candidate's
source and notes at `d691e6e9`. Its section 10, new in revision 14, is a
reading of the I1 source at `a3e5a77e` and of four sibling notes. Its
section 10.4, new in revision 15, is a reading of the adopted
contract's revision 12 and of the I2 delivery note. None
of it is verified deployment behavior, and none is a complete source
audit. Nothing was run. The earlier code is an
inventory of learned rules. It is kept only where it has been read
against this one model, and its earlier interfaces, schemas, writers and
adapters go as each successor lands.

## 1. Decisions

| ID | Decision | Choice | Left open |
|---|---|---|---|
| D2-1 | Where authority lives | One membership scope for each repository holds members, keys, roles and controllers. One rules scope holds branch rules, labels and active definitions. | Authority across repositories: section 12. |
| D2-2 | How another scope knows it | It **observes** the membership scope: a bounded read, made before its turn, of one key's standing at membership's head. It retains the whole observation. | None |
| D2-3 | Freshness | An observation may be used for a stated time, counted from the moment the read began on the observer's clock. The times are grace windows, a product and protocol choice: within one, an act by a key that was just revoked can still be admitted. Each is a bound in the time of the clock that section 3.12 names for it. | The numbers: R4. The clock assumptions: section 12, H5 and H6. |
| D2-4 | Revocation | Takes effect in every scope no later than the window after membership records it, in the observing scope's clock time (section 3.12). A `compromised` revocation is also sent to the destination. From revision 14 it is not sent to agent tasks: each sees it by its own observation (section 3.5; G11). | None |
| D2-5 | When membership cannot be reached | An act that needs a grant is refused `authority-unavailable` once the observation is older than its window. Deliveries, timed entries and outcomes still take effect. | None |
| D2-6 | No walk through parents | A scope observes membership directly, by the reference fixed in its genesis. | None |
| D2-7 | Delegation | Specified as a record, and deferred from the first delivery. No key acts for another member in the first version. | Owner: a successor of I3. |
| D2-8 | Sessions | A read session is a short-lived, read-only token bound to one repository. There are no acts by bearer token. | None |
| D3-1 | Who owns publication | One destination scope for each branch that is published to. It is the only writer of that branch. | Several destinations: not designed. |
| D3-2 | The linearization point | The destination's reservation. After it the operation is authorized by the destination's own record and needs no member's continuing authority. | None |
| D3-3 | What the source promises | The change lane's `merge` entry is a complete, pinned statement of what is live on the manifest, and a commitment to change none of it until the operation ends. | None |
| D3-4 | The messages | One request with one result, then destination-owned progress as relationship updates with revisions. | None |
| D3-5 | The write | Every send of one operation is the same compare-and-swap on one ref. | The host property it rests on: section 12, H1. |
| D3-6 | What decides an outcome | Reading the branch back. Never a push reply, a token's state or elapsed time. | The read's consistency: H2. |
| D3-7 | Releasing the slot | On `published`. Or on `aborted`, which needs proof that nothing sent for the operation can still land. | Until a fence contract is adopted, an abort with an unknown send holds the slot. |
| D3-8 | Objects and the receipt | The lane that owns the hold stages a commit's objects, as a numbered root with pins, before the act that needs them. That lane is an issue lane or, as section 6.2 proposes, the change lane itself for its own holds. No lane stages from another lane's hold. The destination writes a receipt ref after confirmation, named by the operation. | Section 6.2; section 6.10. |

## 2. Rules kept from the earlier code

Each was learned by building and measuring. Each is kept as a rule of
the new design. The anchor is the section of the facts file.

| Rule kept | Facts |
|---|---|
| Reservation is one transaction and the only linearization point. An act before it can stop the operation; an act after it cannot cancel it. | 1.4, 8 |
| The slot is released only by a read of the branch, never by time, token state or a lost container. | 1.1, 1.5 |
| Every send of an operation pushes the same integration under the same expected base. | 2.3 |
| A push's own report can show that nothing was applied. It never shows that something was. | 2.2 |
| In the earlier measurement, revoking or expiring a token did not stop a push whose body was already sent. No bound is known. | 5.1 |
| An attempt is recorded durably before its token exists. A token's record and a stored wake-up exist before its create is sent. | 1.7, 4.3 |
| An unknown provider effect is kept until that request's own answer. Elapsed time, a token's lifetime and an inventory do not settle it. | 4.2, 4.3 |
| An inventory counts only when it is complete and readable, and then only for resources whose creation is already answered. | 4.3 |
| The canonical ledger revokes only tokens it can match by ID to its own records. It never sweeps the canonical repository. | 4.3 |
| A fork or snapshot repository is used, changed or deleted only when its provenance is exactly the canonical repository. | 4.3 |
| A name is created at most once and never reused. | 4.3 |
| `retired` and `compromised` are different revocations. A compromised key's earlier evidence stops counting, always. | 6.3 |
| Evidence is judged against the authority recorded when it was admitted, and against the key's state now. | 6.3, 8 |
| An exact retry of an accepted act returns its receipt after the key is revoked. | 6.2 |
| No member ever holds a write token for the canonical repository. | 4.1 |
| A check is signed by the checker service outside the sandbox. The read token never enters the runner. | 6.8 |

Two things the earlier code left unsettled, which this note does not
paper over: the facts file's open items 6 and 7. The protocol text said
no evidence is established for "did not and cannot land", while the code
ended a publication as aborted from push reports. And an attempt whose
outcome is unknown after a crash can never be shown not to have landed.
Sections 6.6 and 6.8 answer both.

## 3. Authority

### 3.1 What the membership scope holds

| Record | Content |
|---|---|
| Member | A handle, a role, and its state: active or removed. A removed handle is never reused and a removed member is never restored. |
| Key | A device or agent key, the member it belongs to, a label, and its state: active, revoked as retired, or revoked as compromised, with the entry that did it. A device key is made on the device and is not extractable from it. |
| Controller | For an agent member: the person who controls it, fixed when the agent is created. |
| Invitation | Single use, short lived, for a new member or for a new key of an existing member. The scope holds a hash of its secret; the secret travels in the link the admin hands over. |
| Recovery key | One, enrolled at founding and held offline. It may issue an invitation when no admin can. It cannot do work. It is replaced by a rotation act, not revoked. |
| Role table | Which actions each role holds. |

Membership is a platform definition. Its own acts are judged locally,
with the guards the earlier roster had: a handle is unique and never
reused; an invitation is used once and not after its end time; the last
active key of the last admin cannot be revoked, and the last admin
cannot be removed, except by the recovery key.

**The length of a handle. New in revision 11. Its unit is corrected
in revision 12.** The scope contract bounds, at validation, the bytes
of every timed entry. An attention form in such an entry can name
members, so that bound needs a bound on one member's handle, and the
contract leaves the bound to this note (R1 section 6.4). Proposed
here: a handle is at most 256 bytes long, counted as the bytes of its
UTF-8 form. Quoting and escaping are not counted.

- **That is I1's unit and I1's temporary value.** At `97518f68`, I1
  compares the UTF-8 length of the handle with its bound
  `memberBytes` (`packages/derive/src/values.ts`, line 22). That
  bound is 256, and I1 marks it temporary
  (`packages/contract/src/bounds.ts`, lines 18 and 62). The
  contract's sentence gives the number, 256, and names no unit.
- **The canonical form is longer, and is counted apart.** A handle
  is written there as a quoted string. So a handle of 256 unescaped ASCII bytes
  takes 258 bytes there, and an escape can write one byte of a
  handle as six. I1's validator allows for that when it bounds a
  timed entry: six bytes for each byte of a handle
  (`packages/derive/src/validate.ts`, line 922). The bound on a handle and the bound on an entry are two
  counts, and this note proposes only the first.
- **What revision 11 said.** "At most 256 bytes in its canonical
  form", and that this was I1's value. It was not: that is another
  unit, and a stricter one. Revision 12 proposes I1's unit. So it
  changes no bound that I1 holds, and it asks for no migration.
- **Owed before any source depends on it.** R1 is asked to state the
  unit in its section 6.4, so that the contract, I1 and this note
  agree in words (section 13.4).

The number is a proposal and not a measurement, and R4 owns it.
Membership refuses, as `bad-field`, an act that would enrol a member
with a longer handle. So no scope ever holds a longer one in a party
slot.

**The characters of a handle. Decided in revision 14 (G12).** A
handle is `@`, and then at least one character. Each character after
the `@` is a lowercase ASCII letter, a digit or a hyphen. The first
and the last are not hyphens. The bound of 256 bytes above counts the
whole handle, with its `@`.

- Such a handle takes no escape in its canonical form, so its
  canonical form is its bytes and two quotes.
- Membership refuses any other handle `bad-field`, in `invite-member`
  and `add-member`. The register refuses a founding whose
  `founderHandle` is not one, so that no founding ends at a handle
  that membership cannot seat (sections 12.1.1 and 12.1.3).
- It is a proposal. It is narrower than the bound, so a later
  revision can widen the characters without changing a bound that I1
  holds. How a handle is shown is R2's.

**The recovery key is not a member's key. New in revision 10 (review
row L1).** The recovery key "cannot do work". The base did not list
the guard that keeps it out of the table of keys. This is that guard,
in both directions.

| Act | Guard, in the act's commit, from membership's own records | Refusal |
|---|---|---|
| `join` | The signing key is not the recovery key, and never was one. Membership keeps the ID of each recovery key that a rotation replaced. | `recovery-key`. The invitation is not used, and its secret is not compared: this guard comes before the secret check (section 3.6, check 5). |
| The rotation of the recovery key | The new key is not a member's key, active or revoked, and never was one. | `key-in-use`. The recovery key does not change. |

So no key is ever in both sets. What the recovery key may sign is
unchanged by this guard: the acts that this section and section 3.6
give it. It signs no join, and it does no work.

| Case | Outcome |
|---|---|
| The recovery key signs a `join` with a valid, unused invitation. | Refused `recovery-key`. The invitation stays unused, and another key may use it. |
| A former recovery key, replaced by a rotation, signs the same `join`. | Refused `recovery-key`. |
| The control: a new device key signs it. | Admitted, as section 3.6 says. |
| A rotation names a device key of a member. | Refused `key-in-use`. |

The two refusal names are proposals for the membership definition,
which this note owns. The review dispositions ask R4 for one case of
this guard under its variant V6 or V9.

### 3.2 Roles and actions

A proposed first table. It is a value of the membership scope, changed
by an admin's act. Actions are the names R2 uses.

| Action | Admin | Maintainer | Member | Agent | Checker |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `issue.open`, `issue.comment`, `issue.edit-own`, `issue.close-own`, `issue.revise`, `issue.judge` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| `issue.request`, `issue.promise`, `issue.work` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| `issue.plan`, `issue.triage`, `issue.edit-any` | Yes | Yes | No | No | No |
| `change.open`, `change.propose`, `change.comment`, `change.edit-own` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |

| `membership.*`, `rules.*` | Yes | No | No | No | No |

| `task.operate` | For a task whose worker they are | For a task whose worker they are | For a task whose worker they are | For its own task | No |
| `inbox.own` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

The three `change` work actions are proposed with section 6.2. Each is
held by exactly the roles that hold its `issue` counterpart. So a

**Three rows are new in revision 14.** The platform definitions of
section 12.1 name an action for each act, as every definition must.
`destination.adopt` is the grant of `adopt-head` (section 6.9), and
`ledger.retry` of an act or a step that opens one further attempt
(section 12, G3). `task.operate` is the worker's grant in its own

the role `agent` still holds no `task.control`. From revision 16

agent holds it. `inbox.own` lets a
member mark the notices of that member's own inbox. A name that ends

**The table, counted. New in revision 24 (the I3 delta EM6).** The

| Role | Actions | The list, in the order of the table |
|---|---|---|

### 3.3 The observation

A scope that must judge a signer does this, before its turn:

1. It notes its own clock. That is the observation's time.
2. It asks the membership scope, by the reference fixed in its own
   genesis, for the standing of one key.
3. Membership answers from its head.

```ts
interface Observation {
  of: ScopeRef;                              // the membership scope, with its incarnation
  head: { seq: number; hash: Digest };       // the membership head that was read
  key: KeyId;
  keyState: "active" | "retired" | "compromised" | "unknown";
  member: MemberId; memberState: "active" | "removed";
  role: string;
  actions: readonly string[];                // what the role holds, by the role table at that head
  within: ScopeFilter;                       // where: this repository, or one task
  controller: MemberId | null;               // for an agent
  controllerActive: boolean | null;
  notAfter: Timestamp | null;                // an end time on the grant, if it has one
  definition: PlatformDefinition;            // the membership definition's version
  at: Timestamp;                             // the observer's clock when the read began
}
```

The entry records the whole observation it used. It is a retained input
(R1 section 9.2), so a verifier has it.

**Which read, and whether it was reused. A proposal.** The value of an
observation does not show which read produced it. Two reads that begin
at the same clock reading, with membership's head unchanged, return
the same bytes. So an entry records, with the observation, which read
it came from and how the entry used it.

```ts
interface ObservationUse {
  observation: Observation;
  read: { run: RunId; n: number };               // the read: the scope's run, and the read's number in that run
  use: "fresh" | "reused";
  prior: { seq: number; hash: Digest } | null;   // for "reused": the last earlier entry of this scope that retains this read
}
```

- A **run** is one life of the scope's process. `run` is a random
  value chosen when the process starts. `n` counts the reads of
  membership, and of the rules scope, that the scope began in that
  run, from 1. Both are held in memory, like the observation, and are
  gone after a restart.
- `fresh`: no earlier entry of this scope retains this read. `prior`
  is null.
- `reused`: an earlier entry of this scope retains this read. `prior`
  names the latest such entry.
- **The last use of a read** is the latest entry of this scope that
  retains it. A commit that wrote nothing is not a use.

Guards in the commit, in this order, before the grant guard below:

1. `read.run` is the scope's present run. If not, the observation is
   discarded and read again.
2. For a ten-second kind, `use` is `fresh`.
3. If an earlier entry of this scope retains this read, `use` is
   `reused`, `prior` is the latest such entry, and the commit's
   reading is later than that entry's time. Otherwise `use` is
   `fresh`.
4. The age is inside the window: it is less than the window. An age
   that equals the window is outside it ("At the bound", below).

An entry that retains an observation judges freshness. An act does,
and so does a reservation. Such an entry is never written with a
clamped time (section 3.12). So each such entry's time is its commit's
reading.

**What a replay checks, and what it trusts.** Membership writes no
entry for a read, so no history but the observer's can show that a
read happened. A replay therefore checks the observer's record for
consistency. It does not prove that a read was performed.

| | A replay derives again | A replay trusts, and reports as `trusted: observation-read` |
|---|---|---|
| The value | That membership's history at `head` gives that key that standing. | Nothing. |
| `fresh` | That no earlier entry of this scope retains the same `read`. | That the scope performed that read, that it began at `at`, and that the value was not held from an earlier read under a new number. |
| `reused` | That `prior` is an earlier entry of this scope with the same `read` and byte-identical observation; that no entry between them retains that read; that this entry's time is later than `prior`'s; and that the kind of commit is not a ten-second kind. | That no restart came between the two entries. |
| A ten-second kind | That `use` is `fresh`. | As for `fresh`. |
| Runs | That the entries of one run are not separated by an entry of another run. A history where a run returns is invalid, `run-returned`. | That the process did not restart inside what it records as one run. |

Who vouches: the runtime of the observing scope, and so the operator
of the deployment. It is the same party that is trusted for `at`.
Membership vouches for nothing here. A replay reports each grant with
this label. It does not report "no cached value was reused".

| Case | Entry A | Entry B | Revision 6: the values alone | This revision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Two fresh reads at one clock reading, membership's head unchanged | Read (r1, 7), `fresh`, time 1002 | Read (r1, 8), `fresh`, time 1002. The observation's bytes equal A's. | "The same observation as an earlier entry, and the time is not later": reported as a prohibited reuse. None happened. | Valid. Two reads, each used once. Each is reported as trusted. |
| A reuse at an equal reading | Read (r1, 7), `fresh`, time 1002 | Read (r1, 7), `reused`, `prior` A, time 1002 | Not told apart from the row above. | Guard 3 fails in the commit: the observation is read again. A history that holds B is invalid, `observation-not-moved`. |
| A reuse at a later reading, inside the window | Read (r1, 7), `fresh`, time 1002 | Read (r1, 7), `reused`, `prior` A, time 1050 | Valid. | Valid. |
| A reservation that reuses | Read (r1, 7), `fresh`, time 1002 | A reservation: read (r1, 7), `reused`, time 1005 | Valid by the values. The rule that a ten-second observation serves one commit was not checkable. | Guard 2 fails. A history that holds B is invalid, `observation-reused`. |
| A runtime that reuses a value and records a new number | Read (r1, 7), `fresh`, time 1002 | Read (r1, 8), `fresh`, time 1002, with no read made | Not detected. | Not detected. This is the trusted claim, and the report says so. |
| A reuse across a restart | Read (r1, 7), `fresh` | Read (r1, 7), `reused`, written after a restart | Not detected. | Guard 1 refuses it in the scope. In a history it is found only if an entry of run r2 lies between A and B: `run-returned`. Otherwise it is trusted. |

**The freshness proof, as one retained input. New in revision 10.**
The record above is a grant's freshness proof. This table states each
property of it in one place, with the rule that gives it. It adds no
rule.

| Property | Rule | The guard, or what a replay finds |
|---|---|---|
| Authority | A proof is made only by the observing scope's runtime, from one read of the membership scope that the scope's genesis fixes. It authorizes the judgment of the one entry that retains it, inside its window, and nothing else. The retained copy is evidence for that entry. No scope reads it again as authority. | The first condition of the grant guard, below. |
| The read's identity | `read.n`, the number of the read in its run. | Guard 3. In a replay: two entries retain one read only when the later one is `reused` and names the earlier. |
| The run's identity | `read.run`, a random value chosen when the process starts and held in memory. | Guard 1. In a replay: `run-returned`. |
| Trust | That the read was made, that it began at `at`, and that a `fresh` value was not a held one. The observing scope's runtime vouches, and so the operator. | Reported as `trusted: observation-read`. Never derived. |
| Clock | `at` and the commit's reading are readings of the observing scope's clock. Age is their difference. An entry that retains a proof judges time and is never written clamped. | Guard 4; `clock-behind`. A bound in real time only under H5. |
| One commit | A ten-second kind is read for one commit, and its `use` is `fresh`. | Guard 2. In a replay: `observation-reused`. |
| Restart | A proof is not kept across a restart. The scope reads again. | Guard 1. In a history it is found only as `run-returned`. Otherwise it is trusted. |

**How R1 types it.** R1 revision 7 left this member to this note: its
`Grant` had `fresh: FreshnessProof`, with the comment "R3 defines
this member". This note's definition is `ObservationUse`, above. The
contract, adopted at revision 10, takes that definition:
`FreshnessProof` is that type, member for member (R1 section 16.1);
`prior` is typed `Head` there, the same pair of `seq` and `hash`; the
replay row is in R1 section 9.3; and its three mismatch names are
this note's. The windows are not adopted there and stay proposals of
this note. The contract says that the implementation of revision 7
judges freshness through a port (R1 section 11.8). This note read no
source for that, and it claims no source that holds the adopted type.

In the commit, the grant guard holds when all of these do:

- the observation is of this scope's own membership reference, with that
  incarnation;
- the key is the signing key, and it is active;
- the member is active;
- the actions include the act's action, and `within` covers this scope;
- `notAfter`, if set, is later than the commit's clock reading;
- for an agent, `controllerActive` is true, or the action is a comment;
- the observation's age is inside the window for this kind of commit.

**Age and clocks.** Age is the commit's raw clock reading minus `at`.
Both are readings of the observing scope's own clock. No reading of
membership's clock is used, so no two clocks are compared.

- `at` is the time the read began, so age is never understated by the
  time the read took. "Ten seconds" means at most ten seconds on that
  clock.
- A negative age proves nothing. If `at` is later than the commit's
  clock, the observation is discarded and read again.
- If the commit's clock is earlier than the previous entry's time, the
  clock has gone back. The act is answered `clock-behind` and its
  observation is read again before a retry.
- **An observation does not outlive its process.** A scope keeps an
  observation for reuse in memory only. After a restart it holds none,
  and it reads again before the next act that needs a grant. No age is
  computed from a reading taken before a restart. The copy that an
  entry retains is evidence for that entry. It is never used again as
  authority.
- **A reused observation needs a clock that has moved.** An
  observation may serve a later commit only when that commit's reading
  is later than the time of the last use of its read, as defined
  above. An equal
  reading shows no passage of time, so it cannot show that the window
  still holds. The observation is then discarded and read again. This
  catches a clock that has not moved at all since the last use. It
  does not catch a clock that moves too slowly: section 3.12.
- **A ten-second observation serves one commit.** It is read for that
  input and used by that commit only. It is never taken from an
  earlier input. Its entry records `use: "fresh"`. So a reservation,
  a mint, an export check, a private read, a new staging and the
  taking or renewal of a hold never rest on a standing that was
  cached.

| Kind of commit | Window proposed | What the window is |
|---|---|---|
| An ordinary act in a lane, the directory or an inbox | 300 seconds | A grace window. An act by a key revoked up to five minutes ago can still be admitted. |
| A reservation in the destination | 10 seconds | The same, for ten seconds. |
| Taking or renewing a hold; minting a workspace write token; a new staging; an export of private work; a private read | 10 seconds | The same. Taking and renewing a hold are ten-second kinds from revision 10 (section 3.5). |
| A control of an agent task; a tool dispatch by an agent | 60 seconds | The same. |

These windows are not "current authority at the instant". They are a
stated limit on how stale a judgment may be. The limit is in the time
of the observing scope's clock. It is the same length in real time
only under the operational assumption H5 (section 12). Section 3.12
gives, for each window, the clock, what a restart does and the
fail-closed rule. A shorter window costs more reads of membership.
The numbers are for R4 to measure and for review to choose.

**At the bound. Decided in revision 14 (G14).** An observation whose
age equals its window is outside it. The base used both wordings, and
R4 asks. One rule now covers every bound of section 3.12: a time at
the bound is past it. An intent is expired when the commit's reading
equals its `notAfter`. A hold is not held when its `ends` equals the
lane's reading (section 5.2). A stream sends nothing at its end time
(section 4.2). A license is used only while less than ten seconds
have passed. This is the stricter reading of each, so it admits
nothing that the base refused.

**After a revocation is seen. Decided in revision 14 (G10).** A scope
may hold, in memory, more than one answer about one key: a cached
observation, and a later read for a ten-second kind. Answers can also
arrive out of the order in which membership gave them.

- Made stricter in revision 19: this point yields to the contract's
  order of heads where the two differ. "The three kinds of
  observation", below, says in which one case.
- A scope keeps at most one observation of a key for reuse: the one
  whose membership head has the highest position. An answer from a
  lower head never replaces one from a higher head.
- A read that shows the key `retired` or `compromised`, or its member
  `removed`, is kept for the rest of the run, whatever its window. A
  key is never restored and a removed member is never restored
  (section 3.1), so that answer cannot become untrue. From that read
  on the scope uses no answer that shows the key active: not an older
  one that it still holds, and not one that arrives later.
- So a revocation that any read of this run has seen takes effect in
  that scope at once, for every kind of commit, and not at the end of
  a window.
- A refused act leaves no entry, so a replay cannot check this. It is
  part of what the observing scope's runtime vouches for, under
  `trusted: observation-read`.

- **Unavailable.** If membership does not answer, the scope uses the
  observation it holds until its age reaches the window. From then on an
  act that needs a grant is refused `authority-unavailable`.
- **Cost.** For the 300-second and 60-second kinds, a scope reads
  membership once for each acting key in each window, and again after
  a restart or when its clock has not moved since the last use. A
  ten-second kind costs one read for each commit. The read is off the
  scope's queue and is a read of membership, not an entry in it.
- **No parent walk.** A lane holds the membership reference from its
  genesis.
- **Rules.** The rules scope is observed the same way where its present
  content decides something: the destination observes the branch rules
  at reservation. That observation names the rules scope and its
  incarnation, the head read, the rules revision and content, and the
  time the read began, and is retained in the same way, with its read
  and its use.

**The three kinds of observation. Decided in revision 19** (the
contract's point R1-55, and the questions of its section 15.3d). The
contract's revision 14 gives one envelope, `ObservationUse`, for
three kinds, and one place for an observation that is not a grant's:
the member `observed` of an act, of an outcome and of a delivery of a
result. It adopts the envelope and the four common members `of`,
`head`, `definition` and `at`. It says that the other members of the
two new kinds are its reading of this note's prose, and that this
note may replace them. This is this note's statement of them. The
adoption of the envelope agrees no payload. Where this differs from
the contract's proposal, the contract's next revision is asked to
take it.

```ts
/** The standing of one key. Unchanged: as above, member for member. It has no `subject`. */
interface Observation { /* of, head, key, keyState, member, memberState, role, actions, within,
                           controller, controllerActive, notAfter, definition, at */ }

/** The standing of one member, whatever key acts. */
interface MemberObservation {
  subject: "member";
  of: ScopeRef;                                  // the membership scope, with its incarnation
  head: Head;                                    // the membership head that was read
  member: MemberId;
  memberState: "active" | "removed" | "unknown"; // "unknown": membership holds no such member at that head
  role: string | null;                           // null when the state is "unknown"
  activeKey: boolean | null;                     // whether the member has at least one active key at that head
  controller: MemberId | null;                   // for an agent
  controllerActive: boolean | null;              // for an agent: its controller is active and has an active key
  definition: PlatformDefinition;
  at: Timestamp;
}

/** What the rules scope holds at one head. */
interface RulesObservation {
  subject: "rules";
  of: ScopeRef;                                  // the rules scope, with its incarnation
  head: Head;
  revision: number;                              // the position of the latest `publish` at that head; 0 when there is none
  content: RulesContent;
  definition: PlatformDefinition;
  at: Timestamp;
}
type RulesContent =
  | { asked: "rules"; approvals: number; ownerMayReview: boolean;
      checks: readonly { name: string; configuration: Digest; required: boolean; checker: MemberId }[];  // at most 32
      labels: readonly string[] }                                                                         // at most 32
  | { asked: "definitions"; active: readonly { digest: Digest; name: string }[] };                       // at most 16
```

- *What differs from the contract's proposal.* One member is added
  to `MemberObservation`: `activeKey`. Two uses need it. A person
  whose last key is revoked is still an active member, and neither an
  export's authorizer nor a task's worker may act for that member
  then (section 3.5, rule 5). `content` has a type: one of two fixed
  records, by what the reader asked for. Every other member is as
  the contract proposes it.
- *The subject of each kind.* Two observations are of the same
  subject when they have the same `of`, which is one scope in one
  incarnation, and the same identity under it. For an `Observation`
  that is the `key`. For a `MemberObservation` it is the `member`.
  For a `RulesObservation` there is nothing more: the rules scope is
  one subject, whichever `content` was asked for. This is the
  contract's reading, and it is confirmed.
- *The bound on each.* An `Observation` and a `MemberObservation`
  are fixed records. Their one list is `actions`, which holds at
  most the actions of the table of section 3.2, each a name of at
  most 64 bytes. Stated in revision 24: that is 34 names, for an
  admin (section 3.2, "The table, counted"). `content` is bounded by
  the rules definition's own
  declared types (section 12.1.4): 32 checks and 32 labels, or 16
  definitions. Corrected in revision 20: revision 19 said here that
  a `content` is under 16 KiB by those types. That was false, as the
  verdict `d2068c05` found. "The size of `content`, counted", below,
  has the numbers. `content` still stays inside the entry: its
  largest value is far under the entry size. It needs no digest and
  no value in a domain, which the contract offered for a large one.
- *The size of `content`, counted. New in revision 20.* A script
  built the largest value of each record from the declared maxima,
  and counted the bytes of its canonical JSON. A check's name is a
  text of 128 bytes, a label and a definition's name a text of 64, a
  handle at most 256 bytes with its `@`, and a digest 71 characters.
  A handle takes no escape (section 3.1). A text may: a backslash is
  written as 2 bytes, and a control character as 6.

  | The value | Checker as a member ID | Checker as a member reference |
  |---|---|---|
  | The verdict's case: 32 names and 32 labels of backslashes, a handle of 2 bytes | 16,621 bytes | 21,421 bytes |
  | The same, with handles of 256 bytes | 24,749 bytes | 29,549 bytes |
  | The largest by the types: names and labels of control characters, handles of 256 bytes | 48,813 bytes | 53,613 bytes |
  | `asked: "definitions"`: 16 names of control characters | 7,538 bytes | The same |

  The first row is the verdict's count, and the script gives the
  same two numbers. `RulesContent` holds the checker as a member ID,
  so its largest value is 48,813 bytes, unless a rule that this
  revision did not read keeps control characters out of a text. The
  item `rules` holds a member reference, and the last column is that
  projection. Any number below these is a bound that something must
  enforce, and nothing does: `publish` has no guard on the size of
  what an observation of the rules would hold. So the bound of a
  `content` is a proposal for the proof plan, with no guard of its
  own yet: either R4 takes the size by the types, or `publish` gains
  a guard on the canonical size of its fields. No source may rely on
  16 KiB.
- *Two more members of the record that was asked as "rules".
  Stated in revision 25.* `singleControllerException`, which the
  contract's revision 19 has, and `extents`, which is asked of the
  contract (section 12.1.4). The listing above is as revision 19 of
  this note wrote it. The sizes of "The size of `content`, counted"
  include neither.
  Stated in revision 27: the contract's revision 21, which is not
  adopted, makes `extents` a digest, with the list as a retained value
  (section 12.1.4, "A second byte domain"). It counts the largest
  `content` with both members at 48,931 bytes, as a sum of 48,813, 34
  and 84.
- *Where an observation of the rules is `of`.* The directory holds
  the rules scope's full reference, from the `applied` clause of its
  own `create`. The destination is created beside the rules scope.
  It holds the rules scope's ID, from the directory's seed, and fixes
  the incarnation in the first entry that retains an observation of
  the rules, as it does for membership (section 12.1).

Which kind each entry retains, where, in which window, and how many
at most. Every window is on the observing scope's clock, and an age
that equals the window is outside it.

| The entry | Scope | Kind, and place | Window, and use | The most in one entry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| An ordinary act in a lane, the directory, an inbox, membership or the rules scope | That scope | `Observation` of the signing key, in the grant | 300 seconds (W1). May be `reused`. | 1 |
| A control of a task; `apply`; `intend`; `decide-recovery`; from revision 19, `save`, `end-host` and `extend-host` | The task scope | `Observation` of the signing key, in the grant | 60 seconds (W2). May be `reused`. | 1 |
| `take-hold`, `renew-hold`; the steps `instance`, `token`, `stage` and `job-read`; `authorize-export`; `start-export`, `ask-license`; `open-read`, `continue-read`, `close-read`; `register` | The lane, or the task scope | `Observation` of the signing key, in the grant | 10 seconds (W3). `fresh`, and it serves that one commit. | 1 |
| The outcome of `judge`: a reservation (section 6.5) | The destination | In `observed`: an `Observation` of the merger's key and of each key behind a counted verdict or result; one `RulesObservation`, `asked: "rules"` | 10 seconds (W3), each. `fresh`. | At most the bound on the foreign entries of one entry, which is the contract's ceiling. A reservation that would need more is `evidence-too-large` (G5). |
| The delivery of a license result, which records `dispatched` (section 4.2) | The task scope | In `observed`: a `MemberObservation` of the authorizer; and one of the former holder, when the authorizer is no admin, for its `controller` | 10 seconds (W3), each. `fresh`. The license has its own window: 10 seconds from the entry of `ask-license` (W5). | 2 |
| `publish` | The rules scope | In `observed`: a `MemberObservation` of each check's `checker` | 300 seconds (W1), as the act's own grant. May be `reused`. Revisions 14 to 18 said "at a stated head" and gave no window. | 32 |
| `open-issue`, `open-pr` | The directory | In `observed`: one `RulesObservation`, `asked: "definitions"` | 300 seconds (W1). May be `reused`. | 1 |
| `open-task` | The directory | In `observed`: a `MemberObservation` of the worker. It carries the worker's controller. | 300 seconds (W1). May be `reused`. | 1 |
| `compromised`, at the destination | The destination | None. It reads, as history, the observations that its own reservation entry retained. | None. | 0 |

Stated in revision 27: two rows of this table change when the contract's
form `observes` takes effect. The row of the outcome of `judge` gains
one observation of the holders of `rules.publish`, and one of each
author. The row of the license result reads the former holder always,
and no longer "when the authorizer is no admin". "The rows of
`observes`", below, has both, and says what is in force until then.

- *The three numbers.* 300, 60 and 10 seconds are the windows of an
  observation. 80 seconds is no window of an observation. It is the
  bound from a revocation to the close of a private stream: a stored
  end time of 70 seconds after the last check that passed, which was
  itself judged on a 10-second observation (W4; section 4.2).
- *An outcome holds its observations in `observed`.* Revision 17
  said that the outcome of `judge` holds them in its evidence, which
  this note types. The adopted contract puts every retained
  observation in a grant or in `observed`, so that a verifier finds
  each without the definition's code. This note takes that. The
  evidence of `judge` is the read of the branch and of the commit's
  closure, and no observation.
- *A settling entry with no observation.* The contract lets the
  definition choose. A reservation waits for a later reading, and the
  publication stays `queued`. The delivery of a license result is
  written without the observation and without the dispatch, and the
  release stays `intent` (section 4.2).

*The order of heads, and G10.* The contract adds one guard: of one
subject, the heads that the entries of a scope retain never go back,
also across runs. A history that breaks it is a `mismatch`,
`observation-older`. The contract says that this is stricter than
this note's rule G10 in one case, and asks whether G10 yields. It
does.

- *The one case.* A scope holds an observation of a key for reuse,
  read at head h1. A ten-second commit then retains a later read of
  that key, at a higher head h2, which shows the key still active.
  That read serves its one commit and is not kept. Under G10 the
  scope could then use the held observation, at h1, for the next
  ordinary act of that key, while it was inside its 300 seconds.
  Under the contract's guard it may not: h1 is lower than h2, which
  an entry retains. It reads again.
- *Why G10 yields.* The cost is one read of membership. The gain is
  that a replay can check, from the entries alone, that no entry
  judged on a standing older than one that the scope had already
  recorded. G10 alone left that to the runtime's word. Nothing that
  G10 refused is admitted. One act that G10 admitted is refused:
  when membership cannot be reached for that further read, the act
  is answered `authority-unavailable`, although the held observation
  is inside its window. That is the stricter side.
- *What of G10 stands.* All of it, as a rule of the runtime: the one
  held observation for a key, and a revocation that any read of the
  run has seen. A revocation that was seen in a read whose act was
  refused leaves no entry, so it stays `trusted: observation-read`.
- *One thing is asked of the contract's next revision.* The guard is
  by subject, and a key and its member are two subjects. So an entry
  may retain a `MemberObservation` that shows a member `removed`, at
  head h2, and a later entry an `Observation` of a key of that
  member, held from before at h1, that shows the member active. In
  the runtime, G10 refuses that: a read that shows a member removed
  stops every answer that shows a key of that member active, for the
  run. A replay cannot check it. Asked: that for the order of heads
  an `Observation` is also of its `member`, so that its head is not
  lower than the head of a retained `MemberObservation` of that
  member. It costs no read that G10 does not already cost.
- *Case.* The directory holds an observation of key K, read at
  membership's head 40, and used for an `open-issue`. The same
  member then takes a hold in a lane: that is another scope, with
  its own reads, and nothing of the directory's changes. In one
  scope: a lane holds K at head 40 from a comment, 100 seconds ago.
  K signs `take-hold`. The lane reads K for that commit, at head 44,
  and the entry retains it. K then signs a comment, 20 seconds
  later. The held observation is 120 seconds old, inside its window,
  and its head is 40. The guard discards it. The lane reads K again,
  at head 44 or higher, and the comment's entry retains that read.
  Under revision 18 the comment was admitted on head 40.

**What the I3 source asks of this section. Decided in revision 20**
(the I3 deltas note, entries ED1 to ED17, at `ae3ea555`). The source
built the grant guard and the read from the adopted texts, and found
them silent in these places. Each answer is this note's, or names
the contract's revision 15, where the form is the contract's.

*What `within` is (ED2).* Until now `within` had a comment, "this
repository, or one task", and no form. So no act could be authorized
on a real answer.

- *The set.* `within` names one set of scopes: the scopes of one
  repository. That set is the membership scope itself, and every
  scope whose genesis records that membership scope, with that
  incarnation, as its membership reference: the directory, the rules
  scope, the destination, each lane, each inbox and each task scope
  of that repository. The register is in no such set, and no act of
  the register is judged on a grant.
- *The form.* `within` is `{ membership: ScopeRef }`: the membership
  scope, with its incarnation. It is always equal to the
  observation's `of`. The contract's revision 15 types it so.
- *How a scope recognises itself.* By its own recorded membership
  reference, and by nothing in the request. "`within` covers this
  scope" holds exactly when `within.membership` is the reference
  that this scope records, with the same incarnation. The table
  below says where each kind of scope records it.
- *What the read's request carries.* `{ of, key }`, as the source
  built it (ED1), and no more. It does not say who asks. Membership
  could not check such a statement, and it needs none: it answers
  the same for every scope of its repository. So one answer can be
  held and compared whoever asked.
- *What the answer states.* The observation without `at`, which is
  the asking scope's own clock: the head, the key's state, the
  member and its state, the role, the role's actions at that head,
  `within`, the controller and whether it is active, `notAfter`, and
  the definition. An answer with a member missing, added or of
  another form is no answer.
- *"One task" is not in `within`.* Three cells of the role table
  hold a condition on one task: "for tasks they control", "for a
  task whose worker they are" and "for its own task". Membership
  does not know which member controls or works which task. The task
  scope knows it, from its own `worker` and `controller` slots. So
  each condition is a guard of the acting scope's own row, on its
  own items, and it is no part of the grant. `actions` lists such an
  action for every role that holds it under any condition.
- *The commit guard.* As written above: the action is in `actions`,
  and `within` covers this scope. Then the row's own guards judge
  the condition, where the table has one.
- *What a replay checks.* That membership's history at `head` gives
  that key that role, and that role those actions, by the role
  table at that head. That `within.membership` equals `of`, and
  equals the reference that the observing scope's genesis records.
  A difference is a `mismatch`.
- *One thing is open, and owned.* An admin holds the three task
  actions "for any task", so its row guard must pass a signer who is

- *Which acts of a declared definition are a ten-second kind (ED3).*
  It is read from the row's forms, and never from its name. An act
  is a ten-second kind when its row has a `hold` effect that opens
  or renews, or when its `grant` is `work.export` or `change.check`.
  The second is `authorize-export`. The third is the result of a
  check, which section 3.11 puts on a ten-second observation, and
  which the table of nine rows left out. Every preparation step is a
  ten-second kind. Every other act of a lane is ordinary.

- *What makes it fit: two rows that the second commit changes.* An
  observation of a key holds the 64 actions of a role, each a text of at
  most 64 bytes. By those types alone, with control characters, it is
  26,198 bytes, and then one key fits beside 65 authors. So a name of an
  action has a rule on its characters: lower-case letters, digits, a
  hyphen and a full stop (section 12.1.3, the mark `action-list`). With
  it an observation of a key is at most 5,718 bytes. And the evidence
  held the changed set, which this note bounds at 256 KiB, the size of a
  whole entry. The changed set is now kept under a digest, apart from
  the entry (section 12.1.5, "The changed set, kept under a digest").
  The observation of the rules is not what fails to fit: it is 49,505
  bytes, because the extents are a digest.
- *Why the authors are whole, and the keys are bounded.* The lane's type
  allows 64 authors, and the integrator is one more. A manifest cannot
  choose to have fewer. A repository's rules say how many approvals and
  which checks a reservation needs, so the keys are the number that a
  repository can plan for: the distinct keys behind its approving
  verdicts and its listed checks. With 32 authors, 14 keys fit, with a
  margin of 17,751 bytes. The planner is asked for the three numbers
  (section 13.17).
  Decided by the planner (the act `53ecfb42`, answer d): 65 authors and
  8 keys are accepted, and splitting the change is the stated way out.
  The numbers 14 and 17,751 are of revision 27's script. By the script
  of revision 28, 14 keys beside 32 authors give 233,304 bytes.
- *A row that is over.* A manifest with more than 65 authors, or a
  reservation that asks more than 8 distinct keys, makes row 4 or row 5
  over. The contract then reads nothing for that row, and tells the
  rule. The publication ends `not-reserved`, with the reason
  `evidence-too-large` (section 6.5). That is narrower than revision 26,
  which bounded the observations of one reservation by their number
  alone, at the contract's ceiling, and did not show that they fit an
  entry. Rows 1 to 3 have one subject each, and are never over.
  - *The way out, and where a member sees it. Stated in revision 28*
    (the planner's act `53ecfb42`, answer d). The way out is to split
    the change: a manifest with fewer authors, or a change that needs
    fewer distinct keys behind its approvals and its listed checks. A
    member sees it at the lane. The update `refused` carries the reason
    `evidence-too-large`, the lane's merge item becomes `refused` with
    that reason, and the read of the publication at the destination
    shows the same `reason`. The words that a page shows for that reason
    are the lane forms' to state, and this note asks that they say
    "split the change" (section 13.18). No reason name is added, and the
    text of `reason` does not change.
- *The count permits nothing (row 3).* The holders observation says how
  many members hold `rules.publish`, and who the first is. No rule lets
  anything take effect because that count is 1. The single-controller
  exception needs its declaration in the observed rules, and the rule
  `judge` reads the declaration and the count together (section
  12.1.4a). The subject of the row, for the order of heads, is the
  action.
- *Row 4 is the missing form 15.* A `MemberObservation` carries
  `controller`. So the outcome of `judge` retains, for each author, who
  controls it. From that record the rule shows the second clause of the
  exception's third condition. From the same record it refuses the
  review of a member who controls an agent among the authors, where
  `ownerMayReview` is false and for the extent `rules` always. Revision
  26 listed that second use as open: it found no retained record for it.
  This row is the record.
- *An author that is no member of this repository.* The contract leaves
  such a subject out, and the rule reads that it is absent. The rule
  then takes the controllers of the authors as not known. That fails
  closed: the second clause of the exception is not shown, and where the
  second point of independence is asked, no review counts.
- *Rows 6 and 7: the license result reads both members, always (the
  contract's point R1-69).* Revision 19 had the former holder read "when
  the authorizer is no admin". Whether the authorizer is an admin is
  what the authorizer's observation shows, and in a clause no subject
  may rest on an observation. So both are read for every delivery of a
  license result. The most in one entry stays 2. Where the two are one
  member, that is one subject. `authorizer` is a party slot of the
  release, and `also.task` is the one item `task`. The row is IA's to
  build. Which names of `also` the row `ask-license` binds was not read
  in a source, and what a clause may read is the contract's section 6.6,
  which was not read for this revision.
- *Row 8, and one answer that changes with it.* Revision 25 confirmed,
  as built, that a checker whom the field names in another membership
  scope than the recorded one is refused `not-a-checker` (section 12.1).
  Under the form, an act that gives a member of another repository as a
  subject is refused `bad-field`, before a guard runs. So from the
  adoption of the form that answer is `bad-field`. A checker of this
  repository whose role is not `checker` is still `not-a-checker`.
- *Rows 8 to 10, with an observation missing.* The rows of the rules
  `checkers`, `definition-active` and `worker-standing` say that the
  guard is not completed. Under the form the commit stops, the scope
  reads what is missing, and the turn starts again. After the contract's
  bound on restarts the act is answered `authority-unavailable`. A
  definition whose bytes are missing is still `dependency-unavailable`
  (section 12.1.2).
- *A subject that is the signer's own member.* Where the worker of row
  10, or a checker of row 8, is the signer's own member, the grant's
  observation serves it when it passes the row's window, and `observed`
  holds no record of it. That is the contract's rule.
- *The table of nine rows, from the day the form takes effect.* Its row
  for the outcome of `judge` gains the holders and the authors, and its
  most is the sum above. Its row for the license result reads the former
  holder always.

A competing choice, not recommended: membership pushes every change to
every scope and waits for acknowledgments. It gives a tighter limit and
costs a fan-out that grows with the number of lanes.

### 3.4 Delegation, deferred

A delegation lets one key act for another member. It is not delivered in
the first version. The reason is plan 005's own choice: each hosted
agent is its own member with its own key, and the checker signs as its
own member.

The record is stated so that a later delivery does not invent it:

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| Grantor | The issuing device key and its member. Both must be active when the delegation is used. |
| Grantee | One key. |
| Actions and where | A subset of what the grantor's role held when it was issued, never membership or rules actions, and never re-delegable. |
| End time | Required. |
| Ended by | Its end time; the grantee key's revocation; the grantor key's revocation, of either kind; the grantor member's removal; the grantor's role losing the action. |

Until it is delivered, `principal` in a grant is always empty, and an
intent that claims to act for another member is refused. Owner of the
later delivery: a successor of scope I3.

### 3.5 Revocation

| Revocation | New acts by the key | Earlier evidence by the key | A reserved publication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retired | Refused in each scope once its observation is renewed, so within that scope's window, in that scope's clock time (section 3.12). | Still counts. | No effect. |
| Compromised | The same. | Stops counting wherever evidence is counted again: section 3.10. | An abort attempt, if the key is behind it and the notice arrives: section 6.8. |
| Member removed | As retired, for every key of the member. | Still counts. | No effect. |

- A revocation is one entry in membership. It is not sent to lanes.
- A `compromised` revocation is also sent, as a request, to the
  repository's destination scope. This shortens the path to a stop. It is
  not what makes the revocation effective; the window is. If the notice
  is delayed, the destination acts on it when it arrives, by the state
  the publication is then in. If it never arrives, new acts are still
  refused within the window, and a reserved publication completes.
- **No notice goes to a task scope. Narrowed in revision 14 (G11).**
  The base also sent the notice to each task scope whose agent or
  controller the key belongs to. One person may control any number of
  agents, so no one entry can send that many requests inside the
  contract's bound on sends, and membership keeps no list of task
  scopes. A task scope sees a revocation by its own observation,
  within sixty seconds on its clock (W2), and a private stream ends
  within eighty (section 4.2). No rule of the base rested on a notice
  arriving. The notice to the destination goes through the directory,
  which holds the destination's reference: two requests in all
  (sections 12.1.2 and 12.1.3).
- Evidence is counted at a `merge` and again at reservation. At each,
  every key behind a live verdict or result is observed. So no lane has
  to be told that a key it once saw is now compromised.

**A person's revocation, and a hold that is already held. New in
revision 10 (review row M1; security detail 3).** The table above
says what a revocation does to new acts and to evidence. It did not
say what a person's revoked device, or a person's removal, does to a
hold that the person already holds, to that hold's workspace token,
or to duties in flight. Section 3.7 says it for the controller of an
agent, and section 4.3 for an agent's own key. This is the rule for a
person. It is stated by itself, and it is not the agent-key rule.

It rests on three facts.

- A hold's **holder** is a member, not a key (R2 sections 3.4 and
  4.3: `holder` is set from the signer's member). The member is a
  person or an agent.
- A hold ends only by an entry of its lane: its timed end, a
  `release-hold`, or the end of the commitment it is under (R2
  section 4.3, "Holds end with their commitment"). A revocation and
  a removal are entries of membership, and they are not sent to
  lanes.
- A workspace token's plaintext is in the lane's ledger and at the
  Git gateway of the hold's current instance, and nowhere else
  (sections 4.2 and 5.3). No device holds it, and this note defines
  no path by which it reaches one.

**The policy.**

1. *No revocation ends a hold.* A revoked key or a removed member
   changes no hold item. The hold stays `held` until one of the three
   entries above.
2. *A hold is taken and renewed only on a standing that was read for
   that commit.* `take-hold` and `renew-hold` are ten-second kinds
   (section 3.12, W3). So a key that membership has recorded as
   revoked cannot extend a hold inside the five-minute grace window
   of an ordinary act. The grace that is left is the ten seconds of
   W3. A hold's opening also starts the creation of its fork, which
   is an outside effect, and that now rests on the same standing. The
   cost is one read of membership for each taking and each renewal,
   for R4 to measure.
3. *One revoked device takes nothing from the member.* When the
   person has another active key, the hold, its token and its
   instance are unchanged. The other key may renew and release.
4. *With no active key, or after a removal, the hold runs out.*
   Nobody can renew it. It ends at its end time on the lane's clock
   (W10), or earlier when the commitment's requester signs `cancel`.
   Until then no other hold can be taken under that commitment (R2
   section 4.3: `take-hold` and `accept-handover`).
5. *The writer is fenced before the hold ends.* The runtime of the
   hold's instance checks the holder's standing before each tool and
   each push, by an observation within sixty seconds (section 5.2,
   part 2; W2). When the check fails it starts no tool and no push,
   closes its gateway's route for the workspace token, makes a last
   checkpoint, which stays private, and marks the instance fenced.
6. *The token is not revoked early.* The lane is not told of the
   revocation. It revokes the workspace token when the hold ends
   (section 5.3), and not before. Until then the host still honours
   the token. So this policy does permit the token to stay valid, for
