   at most the rest of the hold. What bounds its use is custody and
   rule 5, not the token's state: the hosted instance is the only
   holder of the plaintext, and it sends nothing new after its fence.
7. *Nothing in flight is settled.* A push that the gateway forwarded
   before the fence may still land in that hold's fork, at any later
   time (H3). A mint, a command or a deletion whose answer was lost
   stays unknown, under its own identity. The revocation settles none
   of them. Neither does the token's later revocation, its expiry or
   the hold's end (section 5.4, rules 2 and 4).

| Event, as membership records it | The hold already held | Its live workspace token | The hosted instance | What the revoked key can still have admitted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One device of a person is revoked as `retired`. The person has another active key. | Stays `held`. Another key of the member may renew or release it. | Unchanged. It was never on the device. | Continues. | Nothing after its windows: an ordinary act within 300 seconds (W1), a control within 60 (W2), and a ten-second kind only on a read that began before the record (W3). |
| The same, as `compromised`. | The same. | The same. | Continues. Controls that the key signed and the task scope admitted earlier stay entries, and what the instance did under them is not undone. An admin may stop the task (section 3.2, `task.control`). | The same windows. Its earlier verdicts and check results stop counting (section 3.10). The notice of this section goes to the destination. |
| A person's last active key is revoked, and that person is the holder. | Not ended by this. Not renewable. It ends at its end time, or when the requester cancels the commitment. | Not revoked by this. Revoked when the hold ends. | Fenced at its next check: within sixty seconds on the task scope's clock. | A `report` or a `propose-manifest` by reuse of a root that is already `live`, within 300 seconds (W1): the stated grace. No renewal, no mint and no new staging after ten seconds. |
| A person is removed, and that person is the holder. | The same. The removed member stays the commitment's recorded performer and can sign nothing. The requester may `cancel` it and make a new offer. | The same. | The same. | The same. A removed member is never restored. |
| The person controls an agent that holds the hold: one device, the last key, or a removal. | Section 3.7. With the controller's last key gone the agent cannot renew, so the hold runs out as rule 4 says. | As above. | Section 3.7: no new tool within sixty seconds. | Section 3.7. |
| The agent's own key is revoked. | The agent-key rule of section 4.3: the task stops. Its holds are not renewed, and each ends as rule 4 says. | As above. | Fenced, as rule 5 says. | Nothing after its windows. |

**What a later holder gets.** A new fork, seeded from the lane's own
records and never from the old fork (section 5.2). The private
checkpoint of the removed or keyless person stays private. An admin
keeps private read and export (section 4.2), and may sign
`authorize-export` to a hold of the same lane.

**What is not adopted.** The security review proposed that a removal,
or a `compromised` revocation, end the hold at once by an entry of
the service. That is not adopted in this revision. It needs a message
from membership to each lane in which that member holds a hold, and
membership keeps no list of those lanes. It stays a named option
(section 12, U20). Under the policy above, a keyless person's hold
blocks its commitment for at most the hold's remaining duration on
the lane's clock, and the requester can end it sooner.

**A hold whose holder is a person: what this note does not state.**
Sections 4 and 5 state the environment and the token request for a
hold whose holder is an agent. R2 lets a person take a hold. Rules 1
to 4, 6 and 7 are rules of the lane and hold for either kind of
holder. Rule 5 needs a runtime, and a check that the member is active
and has at least one active key. Which runtime runs a person's
environment, under which task scope, and the form of that check, are
not stated in this note (section 12, "Owned gaps"). Whatever is built
must meet rule 5 and the custody rule: no workspace token on a
device. Decided in revision 14 (G9): such a hold's environment runs
under a task scope whose worker is that person, and each operation is
opened by an act that a device key of that person signs (section
12.1.7). So rule 5 holds with no check of its own: nothing starts
unless a device with an active key signs for it. The runtime is IA's.

**Witness: a person's last key is revoked while the person holds a
hold.** P holds hold h in lane L, under commitment K. Instance i runs
it. Token 9 is live, and its plaintext is at i's gateway. Times are
seconds after membership records the revocation, with each clock
keeping real time (H5).

| Step | Time | What happens | Hold h | Token 9 | Recorded as unknown |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | Membership records that P's last key is revoked as `retired`. Nothing is sent to L. | `held` | Live | Nothing |
| 2 | 3 | The gateway forwards a push that the instance began before step 1. Its reply is lost. | `held` | Live | That push |
| 3 | 20 | P's key signs `report` of commit C, which was staged as root 4 before step 1. L holds an observation of the key from before step 1. Its clock has moved since the last use, and the age is inside 300 seconds. | `held`. The report is admitted. | Live | That push |
| 4 | 30 | P's key signs `renew-hold`. The observation is read for this commit, and shows the key revoked. | `held`, with its end time unchanged. The act is refused. | Live | That push |
| 5 | At most 60 | The runtime's check fails. No tool and no push is started. The gateway's route is closed. A last checkpoint is saved, private. Instance i is fenced. | `held` | Live at the host. Nothing uses it. | That push |
| 6 | 400 | P's key signs another ordinary act. L's observation is past its window and is read again. | `held`. The act is refused. | Live | That push |
| 7 | Later | The requester signs `cancel` on K. Or the hold's end time comes. | `ended`, in that entry. | A revocation by its ID is sent. Until its own answer, that revocation is a duty. | That push, still. The hold's end does not answer it. |
| 8 | Later | The push of step 2 lands in h's fork. | `ended` | As step 7 | That push stays unknown until its own answer. Nothing reads that fork, and nothing can be staged from it without a held hold (section 6.2). |
| 9 | Later | V takes a hold under a new commitment. | A new hold | A new token, for a new fork | The new fork's seed is from L's records (section 5.2), and not from h's fork. |

The report of step 3 is admitted. That is the five-minute grace
window of section 3.3. It is stated, and it is not closed. Step 4 is
the witness of rule 2: in the base `renew-hold` was an ordinary act,
and the same renewal at 30 seconds could have been admitted on the
held observation.

The control for rule 3: P has a second active key. Step 4, signed by
that key, is admitted, and the hold's end time moves. Steps 5 to 8 do
not happen.

The review dispositions ask R4 for one witness row of this policy
beside its variant V8. This table is that row's content. It adds no
gate and no number of runs.

### 3.6 Devices, enrollment and recovery

- Each device makes its own key and keeps it. A key is never copied
  between devices.
- **Enrolling a device** is an admin's act that issues an invitation for
  that member, and a join signed by the new key. The invitation is
  single use and short lived. A join with no invitation, an expired one
  or a used one is refused. "The join, in order", below, says which
  reason each gets, and when. A member who is not an admin asks an
  admin. There is no self-enrollment in the first version.
- **Disconnected is not revoked.** An offline device or a closed browser
  changes nothing in membership.
- **Revoking one device.** Its key is revoked. Its acts and controls are
  refused within the windows, each in the clock time that section 3.12
  states. Its read session ends at its own expiry.
  A private stream it had open ends within eighty seconds on the task
  scope's clock, under the timing assumption that section 4.2 names.
  Other keys of the same member are untouched.
- **An act that was never sent.** A signed act that waited on one device
  is that device's alone. Another device does not find it, send it or
  treat it as work that exists (R2 section 10.1.1).
- **Losing every device.** An admin invites a replacement key for the
  active member. With no admin able to act, the recovery key issues that
  invitation. A removed member is never restored. With no admin, no
  device and no recovery key there is no recovery, and nothing is
  invented.

**The join, in order. New in revision 10 (review rows M3, M4 and
Info 1; security detail 1).** Two things are kept apart.

- **Authoritative use.** An invitation is unused or used. Only the
  commit that admits a join changes that, in membership's one
  history. Nothing else counts against an invitation: this note
  defines no counter and no limit that is keyed by an invitation.
- **Serving protection.** Limits on unauthenticated work. They are
  held in memory, outside the history, and no guard reads them (R1
  section 8.2, row 26). They decide only whether to serve. They can
  never use an invitation up, expire it or lock it.

A join needs no grant. Its authority is the invitation. The join
names the invitation and carries its secret, and it is signed by the
new key. An invitation's secret is at least 32 bytes from a
cryptographic random source: a proposal. So no limit on guesses is
needed, and none is defined.

| # | Check | Fails with | Counted by the address limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The request's size and shape. The secret has at least 32 bytes. | `bad-intent` | Yes |
| 2 | The signature of the new key over the join's canonical bytes. | `bad-intent` | Yes |
| 3 | `to` is this membership scope, with its incarnation. | `misaddressed` | Yes |
| 4 | The index of accepted keys. | Not a failure. The exact signed bytes of an admitted join return its receipt, also after the invitation is used. The same key and actor with other bytes: `idempotency-mismatch`. | No |
| 5 | `notAfter`. Then the guards on the signing key: it is not, and never was, a recovery key (section 3.1) or a member's key. | `expired`; `recovery-key`; `key-in-use` | No |
| 6 | The secret check. An invitation with that ID exists, and the hash of the secret equals the hash it holds. An unknown ID and a wrong secret get one answer, after the same work. | `invitation-refused` | Yes |
| 7 | The invitation's state and end time. They are read only after the secret matched. | `invitation-used`; `invitation-expired` (section 3.12, W9) | No |
| 8 | The target. For a new member, the handle is unused. For a new key of a member, the member is active. | `handle-in-use`; `member-removed` | No |
| 9 | The join is admitted. One entry marks the invitation used and enrols the key. | | No |

- Checks 1 and 2 need no state and are made before the request
  reaches a scope. Checks 3 to 9 are membership's.
- This is the order of an act's checks in the adopted contract (R1
  section 4.2), with the signature first and the
  index of accepted keys before `notAfter`. Revision 10 of the
  contract adds that an accepted key is answered before anything is
  fetched (its section 5.2). That agrees with check 4: the exact
  bytes of an admitted join get their receipt, whatever can no longer
  be read. Checks 5 to 8 are guards of the membership definition,
  which this note owns.
- **What a reader of an invitation's ID learns: nothing.** Whether it
  exists, is used or has ended is answered only to a caller who holds
  the secret (check 7). Check 6 gives an unknown ID and a wrong
  secret the same answer.
- An admitted join's entry holds the secret of an invitation that is
  now used. It can admit nothing again.

**The limits. A proposal, with no number.**

| Limit | Counts | When it is reached | What it cannot do |
|---|---|---|---|
| The address limit | For each client address, in a window: the join requests that failed at check 1, 2, 3 or 6. | Further join requests from that address are answered `rate-limited`, before check 1, until the window ends. | Refuse another address. Change an invitation. |
| The table of address windows | It holds a bounded number of windows. A window is made when a request from an address with no window fails. | That request is answered as its check says, a window is made for its address, and the oldest window is dropped. No request is refused for lack of a window. | Lock out every new address when it is full. |
| The bound on waiting secret checks | For one membership scope: the joins that passed check 2 and wait for checks 3 to 9. | A further join is answered `busy`. The same signed bytes may be sent again until `notAfter`. | Refuse or delay a revocation, a removal, an invitation, a rotation or an observation read. None of those is counted in it. |

- `rate-limited` and `busy` are serving answers. Nothing was judged,
  nothing is recorded and no key is used up.
- **Dropping the oldest window was considered against its cost.** A
  caller with more addresses than the table holds is then not limited
  for each address. That caller is not limited for each address by
  any bounded table. Refusing new windows instead turns the same
  flood into a lock-out of every other caller, which is review row
  M4. The work of one request stays bounded either way: one size
  check, one signature check and one keyed read. The total rate of
  requests is a limit of the serving platform. This note claims
  nothing about it. I3 and the installation design N5 own it.
- **A window that was dropped decides nothing.** Stated in revision
  11, as the review dispositions now ask (rows M3 and M4, at
  `bd24f413`). A limit is temporary state and no authority. A window
  that was dropped, or lost in a restart, refuses nobody, admits
  nobody and changes no invitation.
- **A restart** empties both limits. More unauthenticated work is
  then served for one window. No invitation changes: its state is in
  the history.
- **What a valid invitation can still do.** It is never used up,
  locked or expired by a limit. It stays valid until its end time. A
  join that carries its secret is admitted whenever it is served.
  Under load it may be answered `rate-limited`, when its own address
  is over the limit, or `busy`. It can then be sent again. It is
  refused `scope-full` only when membership has no room for it, and
  an invitation reserves that room when it is issued (section 5.8).
- The window, the two bounds and the form of an address's key are
  configuration. I3 proposes them and R4 measures them. For an IPv6
  address the key is I3's to choose, so that one network is not as
  many addresses as it likes. None is proposed here.

| Case | Request | Answer | The invitation after | Counted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a | Many joins from one address that name a real invitation, each with a junk signature. | `bad-intent` for each, then `rate-limited` for that address. | Unused. | That address only. |
| b | During case a, the invitee joins from another address with the right secret. | Admitted. | Used, by the invitee. | Nothing. |
| c | A new key signs a join that names the real ID with a wrong secret. | `invitation-refused`. | Unused. | That address. |
| d | The same with an ID that does not exist. | `invitation-refused`: the same answer as case c. | None exists. | That address. |
| e | The right secret, after the invitation was used by another key. | `invitation-used`. | Used. | Nothing. |
| f | The reply to an admitted join was lost, and the same signed bytes are sent again. | The first receipt (check 4). | Used. | Nothing. |
| g | The address table is full. A join from a new address fails at check 6. Then the invitee joins from another new address with the right secret. | `invitation-refused` for the first, and the oldest window is dropped to count it. The second is admitted: a join that does not fail needs no window. | Used, by the invitee. | The first address. |
| h | The bound on waiting secret checks is reached. | `busy`. Sent again later: admitted. | Unused, then used. | Nothing. |
| i | During case h, an admin revokes a key. | Admitted. It is not behind the bound. | Unchanged. | Nothing. |

The review dispositions ask R4 for one witness row for these limits.
Cases a and b, and g, are its content: one address cannot block an
invitation, and a full table locks nobody out. R4's key O10 names a
limit "for each invitation". This note defines none, for the reason
above, and asks R4 to state the key without it (section 13.4).

### 3.7 Agents and their controllers

- A hosted agent is its own member with role `agent`, its own key, and a
  controller fixed at creation. The key is held by the task scope's
  signer, never by the coding environment.
- An observation of an agent's key carries `controllerActive`: the
  controller is an active member with at least one active key.
- When it is false, the agent is granted only the comment actions. It
  cannot promise, take or renew a hold, report or propose. The task
  scope also observes before each tool dispatch, with the sixty-second
  window, and starts no new tool. So when an owner's last key is
  revoked, or the owner is removed, new lane acts stop within five
  minutes and new tools within one, each on the clock of the scope that
  judges it (section 3.12, W1 and W2). What is already admitted stays,
  and effects already begun are reconciled, not undone.
- One revoked device of a controller who has another active key changes
  nothing for the agent.

### 3.8 Founding

The rule "every act needs a current grant" cannot admit the act that
creates the membership it would be judged by. Founding has its own rule,
part of the directory's platform definition, and it is pinned in the
directory's genesis.

**The register.** A deployment has one founding register. It is a scope
with its own history, so its claims are entries that a verifier can
read. It is used at founding only. No ordinary act touches it. It owns
one kind of outside effect: creating the repository at the Git host.

**The register must be the configured one.** The register's full
reference, with its incarnation, is a value of the deployment's
configuration. It is set when the deployment is installed (N5) and is
held outside the register's storage. That the configured value is kept
is an operational assumption. The founding service addresses the
register by that reference. A register store that is empty, or that
holds another incarnation, does not match it. Every founding is then
refused `register-unavailable` at step 1. No claim is written, so no
repository is created and no directory is written: the steps below do
not run. An empty register store never mints an incarnation in answer
to a founding. The ways forward are an operator's: a restore of the
register's retained bytes, which keeps its incarnation; or a new
register, with a new configured reference and a new namespace at the
Git host, after the settlement of section 8.2. This note designs
neither, and a founding performs neither.

**The order.** No transaction spans the register, the Git host and a
directory. The order is recoverable at each step.

| Step | Where | Recorded | Sent |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Register | A claim, `pending`: the founding intent's digest, the seed's digest, the namespace at the Git host, and the founding policy value used. Refused if the signer does not satisfy the policy. A repeat of the same intent returns the claim as it stands. The claim's fact is the identity of the creation operation. | Nothing. |
| 2 | Register's ledger | Creation attempt n of that operation, before its request is sent, with a wake-up. The attempt has its own name for the repository, made from the seed's digest and n. A name is used by one attempt only. | To the Git host: create an empty repository with exactly that name. |
| 3 | Register | The outcome entry of attempt n (R1 section 4.3). `created`, with the host's repository ID, only from that request's own authenticated answer. Or `refused`. Or `unknown`. The first `created` outcome that the register records while the claim has no repository **selects** that repository: the claim records it, by host, namespace, name and ID. It is the only repository the claim ever names. A later `created` outcome selects nothing: "First selection", below. | On the selecting `created` only: the request `found`, to the directory the seed names. It carries the claim's fact, the signed founding intent, the repository, and the register's reference. |
| 4 | Directory | Genesis, **provisional**: the seed, a new incarnation, the founder's signed intent, the policy value, the recovery key the founder supplied, the claim's fact, the repository, and the register's reference with its incarnation. The creations of membership, rules and destination, and the import if there is one, are sealed in this entry as duties and are held. | One message: the result of `found`. It names the claim's fact, this genesis's fact and this incarnation. Nothing else leaves the directory. |
| 5 | Register | The delivery of that result. The claim becomes `active`, with the directory's incarnation and genesis fact. | A `confirm` control that names that genesis. |
| 6 | Directory | The delivery of the confirmation. The directory is active for bootstrap. Its held duties are dispatched now: the creations of membership, rules and destination, and the import. Membership's genesis records the founder's key and handle and the recovery key, and the founder's first two acts there make that key the first key of the first admin (section 12.1.3; restated in revision 14, because a genesis opens one item). The destination is bound to the claim's repository, by its ID, and to one branch. It then gives that branch its first head (section 12.2). | The three creations. Each child is provisional until the directory confirms it (R1 section 7.2). |
| 7 | Directory | Admits ordinary acts only when it holds the confirmation and the confirmed creation results of the scopes the act needs: membership for any act; the destination for a merge. For a founding by import, also the import's confirmed outcome. | Ordinary sends. |

Corrected in revision 25 (the I3 delta EP5; the contract's revision
19). Steps 3 and 4 say that the request carries "the signed founding
intent", and that the directory's genesis holds it with "the policy
value". No field holds a signed intent. The request names the claim
by its fact. The directory's genesis fetches the claim's entry and
retains it. That entry holds the founder's signed intent, and the
policy value under which the claim was judged. The directory keeps
neither in a slot of its own, so a verifier reads both in the claim's
entry, which the genesis retains. Section 12.1.1 has the fields.

**Creating the repository is not claimed to happen once.** It is an
outside effect under the ledger rules of section 5.4. No idempotency
contract of the host is identified, so none is relied on. What is
claimed is narrower: the claim names at most one repository, the first
whose creation the register recorded as `created` from that request's
own answer. More than one repository may exist at the host.

| Attempt n's own answer | Recorded | Then |
|---|---|---|
| Received: created, and the claim has no repository | `created`, with the repository ID. The claim selects it. A credential the host returned with it is revoked by its ID, or that revocation is a duty. | Step 3 goes on. No further attempt is opened for this claim. Attempts already sent stay as they are. |
| Received: created, and the claim already has a repository | `created`, with the repository ID, on attempt n only. The repository is recorded as not selected. A credential the host returned with it is revoked by its ID, or that revocation is a duty. | Nothing else. The claim's repository does not change. No `found` is sent for this one. The directory is not told and does not change. |
| Received: refused, the name exists | `refused`. This register never used that name before, so the repository under it is not this founding's. It is not adopted, read or changed. Admins get an incident. | Attempt n+1, with its own name, if the bound allows. |
| Received: refused for another reason | `refused`. That request created nothing. | Attempt n+1, with its own name, if the bound allows. |
| Not received: a lost reply, a time-out, or a crash after the attempt was recorded | `unknown`. It stays unknown until that request's own answer. A listing of the namespace does not answer it, and neither does a repository found under its name. | Attempt n+1 may be sent. It is another step, with its own identity and its own name. It settles nothing about n. |

**Why a founding may go on while an attempt is unknown.** What attempt
n could have made is one empty repository under its own name. The
claim does not name it. No destination is bound to it. The service
holds no credential for it, because the answer that would have carried
one never arrived. So it cannot become a second writer of the founded
repository's branch, which is another repository with another ID. What
stays owed is that possible repository and any credential the host
made with it. The duty stays in the register's ledger and on the
operator's page. Its name is never used again, and the founding never
deletes or adopts what is under it. Proposed bound: three creation
attempts for a claim. After that the claim stays `pending` and an
operator decides. So one founding leaves at most three such duties.

**First selection, and a late answer.** The bound and the ledger let a
founding go on. They do not say which repository it uses when more than
one request is answered. This rule does.

- *The guard.* The claim has one slot for its repository. It is set in
  the register's commit that records an attempt's outcome `created`,
  and only if the slot is empty in that commit. The register has one
  history, so of two `created` outcomes one is recorded first. The
  order of the outcome entries decides. The attempts' numbers do not,
  and neither does the order in which the host made the repositories.
- *Correlation.* An answer belongs to an attempt by that attempt's own
  request: the operation, the number n and the name made for n. The
  register admits an answer for attempt n only when it authenticates as
  the host's answer to that request and names that name. A second copy
  of an answer already recorded returns the recorded outcome entry and
  writes nothing. An answer for an attempt recorded `unknown` settles
  that attempt and no other. An answer that contradicts a recorded
  `created` or `refused` of the same attempt is an incident and changes
  nothing.
- *A late `created`.* It settles its own attempt: the attempt becomes
  `created`, with the repository's ID. The repository is recorded as
  not selected, with its host, namespace, name and ID. The claim's
  repository is not replaced. No `found` is sent for it, and the
  `found` already sent is not sent again for another repository. The
  directory's genesis, its confirmation and its destination's binding
  do not change, before activation or after. A credential returned
  with it is revoked by its ID, or that is a duty.
- *What stays owed.* A repository that was not selected is an owned,
  unused, empty repository. It is on the operator's page with its ID.
  It may be deleted, as a ledger duty with its own attempts. A delete
  addresses the ID that this attempt's own answer returned. It never
  addresses a name alone, so it cannot touch a repository that merely
  occupies a name. An attempt that is still `unknown` gives no ID, so
  nothing is deleted for it.
- *A next attempt is another step.* Attempt n+1 is opened only while
  the slot is empty and the bound allows. It settles nothing about n.
  Once the slot is set, no attempt is opened. Attempts already sent may
  still be answered, and each answer is handled as above.
- *All three unknown.* The claim stays `pending` with an empty slot,
  and an operator is told. If one of those requests is answered
  `created` later, the same guard applies: the slot is empty, so that
  repository is selected and step 3 goes on. This note designs no act
  by which an operator abandons a claim.

This does not say that the host made one repository. It says that the
claim uses one. Unrelated work does not wait on any of it.

One order, as a witness. Attempt 1 uses the name N1 and attempt 2 the
name N2.

| Step | What happens | Attempt 1 | Attempt 2 | The claim's repository | Sent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Attempt 1 is recorded and sent. Its reply is lost. | `unknown` | None | Empty | The create for N1. |
| 2 | Attempt 2 is recorded and sent. It settles nothing about attempt 1. | `unknown` | Sent, no answer yet | Empty | The create for N2. |
| 3 | Attempt 2's own answer arrives: created, with ID R2. | `unknown` | `created`, R2 | R2, selected | `found`, carrying R2. |
| 4a | Attempt 1's own answer arrives before activation: created, with ID R1. The directory is provisional, or not yet written. | `created`, R1, not selected | `created`, R2 | R2 | Nothing to the directory. The credential returned with R1 is revoked by its ID. |
| 4b | Instead, the same answer arrives after activation. The claim is `active` and the destination is bound to R2. | `created`, R1, not selected | `created`, R2 | R2 | The same as 4a. The active directory and its destination do not change. |
| 5 | The same answer for attempt 1 arrives again. | Unchanged. The recorded outcome entry is returned. | Unchanged | R2 | Nothing. |
| 6 | Cleanup of R1. | R1 is deleted by its ID, as a ledger duty, or stays an owned and unused repository on the operator's page. N1 is never used again. | Unchanged | R2 | A delete that names the ID R1. |

If attempt 1's answer is recorded before attempt 2's, R1 is selected
and R2 is the one not selected. The rule is the same. A third attempt
adds a third column and no new rule.

**What links a result to a claim.** The register admits a result only
when all of these hold: the claim is `pending`; the result's `of` is
the `found` request sent by that claim's `created` outcome entry; the
result's source is the genesis of the scope whose ID is the claim's
seed digest; and that genesis names this claim's fact and the
repository of that outcome. The first such result fixes the directory's
incarnation in the claim. A result that arrives when the claim already
holds an incarnation, and carries another, is recorded
`incarnation-conflict`. It activates nothing and gets no confirmation.
That directory stays provisional for good. It has sent nothing but its
result.

The directory admits a confirmation only when: its source is the
register that the genesis names, with that incarnation; the source
entry is the delivery of a result whose source is this genesis; and
the control names this genesis. Any other confirmation is answered
`source-unverified` and records nothing.

**Before activation.** A provisional directory admits a repeat of
`found`, which it answers from its genesis, and the confirmation.
Every other input is answered `scope-provisional`. It creates no
scope, starts no import and admits no act. Between the confirmation
and step 7 it runs its own bootstrap duties and admits nothing else.

| What goes wrong | What happens |
|---|---|
| A crash after the claim and before any creation attempt is recorded | The claim stays `pending`. The same founding intent, sent again, returns it, and the register opens attempt 1. |
| A crash or a lost reply after a creation attempt is recorded | That attempt is `unknown`, as the table above says. The register may open the next attempt, under a new name. |
| A crash after `created` and before the genesis | `found` is a send of a sealed entry and is delivered again. The directory writes its genesis when its store has never been written, and answers a repeat from that genesis (R1 section 7.1). |
| The directory's result to the register is lost | It is a send of a sealed entry and is delivered again. |
| The directory's storage is lost before the register holds a result | The repeated `found` reaches an empty store, which writes a new provisional genesis with a new incarnation. Its result is the first the register records, and the register confirms it. The lost one was never confirmed and had sent nothing but its result. |
| The directory's storage is lost after the claim is `active` | A `found` that is delivered again makes a provisional directory whose result is an `incarnation-conflict`. It is never confirmed. A second founding from the same intent returns the same claim, which names the lost incarnation. The ways forward are a restore, which keeps the incarnation, or a new repository: a new intent, a new seed, and so a new repository at the host. The lost one's duties are settled as section 8.2 says. |
| The register's own storage is lost | Its absence proves nothing about earlier writers or credentials. Every founding is refused `register-unavailable`, as above, until an operator restores the register or installs a new one. Admins get the incident. |

So two founding intents, or two imports, cannot produce two writers of
one branch: each founding has its own claim, the claim names one
repository, selected once, and a destination is bound to exactly that
repository. A new founding never points at an old
repository whose duties are unresolved.

**Against R1's rule for a provisional scope.** R1 revision 5 section
7.2 says a provisional child dispatches only its creation result, and
holds its other genesis duties until the confirmation. This note
agrees, and applies the rule in three places.

| Flow | Under this note | Agrees with R1 |
|---|---|---|
| The directory | Provisional until the register confirms it. Its creations and import are held duties of the genesis. | Yes for the rule. One conflict: R1 section 7.1 gives the directory no creator and has its genesis send the three creations at once. Section 13 asks R1 to make the register the directory's confirmer. |
| Membership, rules, destination | Provisional children of the directory. Membership answers no observation while provisional, so no grant rests on it. The destination reads no head, takes no reservation and mints no token while provisional. | Yes. |
| A lane and its forks | A fork is created only for a hold. A hold is taken by an act, and a provisional lane answers every act `scope-provisional`. So a lane that is never confirmed creates no fork, mints no token and stages nothing. This holds for an issue lane and for a change lane. | Yes. |
| A task scope | Provisional until its creator confirms it. Starting compute and the first use of the agent's signer are held until then. | Yes. This note states it here because the task scope is this note's proposal. |

That table is the base's text, and its one conflict reads R1 as
revision 7 was. The conflict is closed (section 13.1, point O5): the
contract, adopted at revision 10, makes the register the directory's
creator and confirmer.

What a verifier sees: the register's claim, attempt and outcome
entries, with the outcome that selected the repository and each
repository that was not selected; the directory's genesis with the claim's fact, the policy
value and the recovery key; and the confirmation. What it trusts and
reports as trusted: the host's answer to the creation request, and that
the configured register reference is the one the deployment was
installed with.
Corrected in revision 25: the policy value is in the claim's entry,
which the directory's genesis retains. It is in no slot of the
directory.

**The definitions, and the first head. New in revision 14.** The
register, the directory and membership are written as definitions in
sections 12.1.1 to 12.1.3. The founder's intent is addressed to the
register, as the contract's section 7.1 has it, and the request that
this section calls `found` is the contract's `create`. A repository
that was just created is empty, so the destination gives its branch a
first head before it reserves anything (section 12.2). For a founding
by import, the import copies the objects and writes no branch: the
destination is the only writer of the branch from its first value on.

### 3.9 Read sessions

- A device asks membership for a read session with a signed request.
  The token names: the deployment; the membership scope and its
  incarnation; the member and key; what may be read, which is this
  repository's scopes that the member's role may read; and an end time
  at most ten minutes away.
- The token is authenticated with a deployment secret, so a scope
  checks it without a call. A scope accepts it only when the membership
  reference in the token is the scope's own. A token for one repository
  is refused by every scope of another.
- A session reads. It signs nothing, controls nothing and gets no
  credential.
- **After a revocation**, a session already issued is still accepted
  until it ends: at most ten minutes. An open stream is closed when its
  session ends, and is not renewed without a new signed request, which
  is refused for a revoked key. So a revoked device stops reading within
  ten minutes. What it already displayed cannot be recalled.
- **Whose clock.** The end time is written by membership, from its
  clock, when the token is issued. Each scope compares it with its own
  clock, at every read and before every send on a stream. Those are
  two clocks. So "ten minutes" is ten minutes plus the difference
  between the reading scope's clock and membership's (section 3.12,
  W6; section 12, H6). A scope whose reading is earlier than its own
  previous entry's time answers a session read `clock-behind` and
  sends nothing. A scope that restarts closes its open streams; the
  token itself is unchanged and is checked again on the next read.
- **A reader that went away. New in revision 11 (review row Info 6,
  as corrected at `bd24f413`).** A stream that its client cancels or
  disposes of is not left to run until its session ends. The rule is
  R4's key O12, in its table "Streams and waits", row "Cancel or
  disposal", as the review dispositions cite it: the pending read
  completes, the subscription that the stream owns is released once,
  and no reconnect follows. That cleanup is immediate. I5 owns it in
  the client, and I3 in the service. The end of a session is a
  separate bound, and it is no substitute for the cleanup. Ten
  minutes of session policy bound nothing in real time by
  themselves: that is "Whose clock", above. A private stream has its
  own bound (section 4.2), which is real time only under H5. This
  key O12 is R4's. It is not this note's point O12, which is about a
  token's end time (section 13.1).
- There is no token that lets the service sign acts for a caller.

### 3.10 Evidence and review independence

**Counting evidence.** A verdict or a check result counts for a manifest
when:

1. it is live on that manifest in the change lane's pinned eligibility
   statement (section 6.2);
2. its signer held the action when it was admitted, which its entry
   records with the observation used;
3. its signer's key is not revoked as compromised now, by an observation
   within the reservation window;
4. for a verdict, the reviewer is independent of the manifest's authors.

Verdicts are counted by member. Two keys of one member are one reviewer.

**Independence.** Let A be the manifest's `authors`: everyone whose work
is in a selected contribution, former performers and holders included;
every performer and holder of the commitment that the integration
commit was built under, with the authors of the inputs used under it
(section 6.2); the authors of each earlier version that the manifest
supersedes (R2 revision 8, section 5.4); and the integrator (R1
section 6.7). A reviewer r is independent when:

- r is not in A;
- when the rules value `ownerMayReview` is false: r is not the
  controller of any agent in A.

`ownerMayReview`, when true, lets a controller review their agents'
work. That is plan 005's choice and R0 keeps it. It is an exception for
the controller relation only. It never exempts a reviewer who is in A:
a person who contributed, integrated, or held a hold under a selected
commitment cannot give the counted review, whatever the value. When
delegation is later delivered, a principal behind a contribution is in A
too. The value is in the rules scope, on the rules page, and beside each
review it allowed.

### 3.11 Checks: jobs, origin and results

- A checker is a member with role `checker` and its own key, held by the
  checker service.
- **The job.** R2's `request-check` opens a job item in the change lane.
  The job's identity is that entry's fact. The job fixes: the manifest;
  the tree; the check's name; the digest of that check's configuration
  in the rules scope at the head the lane observed; and a deadline.
- **Origin.** The checker service receives the job over the deployment's
  service binding. Before it runs anything it reads the job's entry
  from the lane, through the scope namespace, and checks: that the
  entry is a `request-check` act; that the lane's definition is a
  `change` definition that the repository's rules scope has activated;
  that the tree and name are what it was given; and that the
  configuration bytes it will execute hash to the digest in the job. An
  entry that merely looks like a job, in a lane of another definition,
  is not run.
- **Keeping an outcome.** The checker service keeps each job's outcome
  durably, by the job's fact, until the lane has admitted it or the job
  is superseded. A result the lane refused for now, for example during
  a merge, is submitted again later. The computation is not run again.
- **The result.** The `check` intent, signed outside the sandbox, names
  the job fact, the tree, the configuration digest and the outcome, with
  a digest of the details. The lane admits it when the signer holds
  `change.check`, the job exists, and the tree and configuration digest
  equal the job's.
- **What the sandbox returns is data.** Only a well-formed result
  counts. Output is capped.
- **A run that could not check anything.** A runner that fails, times
  out or exceeds its limits, or a checkout that could not be confirmed,
  is an error of the run. It is not a failed check. The checker service
  signs a `check-error` for the job, with the reason. The lane records
  it and sets the job to `errored`, which is not a pass and not a
  failure, and tells the author and the integrator. A retry is a new
  job. If the checker service gives no answer at all, the job's deadline
  is a timed entry that sets it to `timed-out` and tells the same
  people. So a required check is never silently waiting, and no page
  rests on an agent's statement. R2 revision 5 has both states and the
  act `check-error`.
- **Retry and late results.** A retry is a new job (R2 section 7.2). A
  result names its job, so a late or repeated result is recorded on the
  job it answers and cannot count for another.
- **A late answer on a `timed-out` job: R2's proposal R2-11, accepted.**
  While a job is `timed-out` and no retry has superseded it, the first
  authentic answer for that exact job decides it: `passed`, `failed` or
  `errored`. The entry that admits that answer is from then on the
  job's deciding entry, in place of the deadline's timed entry
  (section 6.3; stated in revision 11). The reasons: the deadline
  ended the waiting and proved nothing about the run; the answer
  names the job's fact, tree and configuration digest, so it can
  count for no other job; and the
  checker service keeps an outcome for exactly this case, such as an
  answer the lane refused during a merge. The conditions are those of
  any answer, judged when it is admitted: the signer holds
  `change.check` and is the checker the rules name; the tree and the
  configuration digest equal the job's; and no merge is in progress.
  Once a retry has superseded the job, a late answer is history and
  decides nothing. A job decided late counts for a merge only through
  that merge's eligibility statement and G's own checks at reservation
  (section 6.5). This acceptance is part of this proposed note. It is
  adopted when the note is.
- **The length of a job's deadline: R2's point R2-12.** Accepted: one
  check duration for a `change` definition, in the first version. The
  reasons: R1's value form gives a deadline as the commit time plus a
  constant, so one duration can be written today; and a deadline only
  ends the lane's waiting, so one generous value loses no result,
  because a late answer still decides the job (R2-11). Proposed value:
  30 minutes, for R4 to measure against the slowest required check. The
  check read token ends before the job's deadline (section 5.3): its
  lifetime is at most the duration, less the time the service needs to
  mint it and start the run. A retry is a new job with its own deadline
  and its own token. Left open, and not accepted for the first version:
  a duration for each check, read from the rules. It needs a form that
  R1 does not have, and a rule for a configuration that changes while a
  job waits. It stays a point for R1 and R2 (section 12, U11). A check
  that cannot answer within the definition's duration times out and is
  retried. This note does not claim that such a check is served well.
- **A deadline** ends a job's eligibility to be waited for. It does not
  prove that the run stopped or that its read token is no longer in
  use. The token's duty stays in the lane's ledger. The deadline is
  measured on the lane's clock and the token's end on the host's:
  section 3.12, W11 and W12.
- The read token goes to the runner's gateway and never into the runner.

**Who fixes a required check's configuration. New in revision 10.**
R2 section 17.6 proposes, to this note and to R4, that a required
check's configuration is fixed by the rules and not by whoever
requests the job. That is accepted, and this is the rule in full.

A check's **configuration** is one value. It is identified by the
digest of its canonical bytes.

| Member | Is |
|---|---|
| `name` | The check's name in the rules. |
| `image` | The runner image, by its content digest. Never a tag alone. |
| `environment` | Every variable that the runner is started with, by name and value. None holds a credential. |
| `steps` | The commands, in order, each as a list of arguments. The last step judges. The names of the cases that must pass are arguments of that step (R2 section 17.5), so they are inside the bytes and the digest. |
| `judged` | For "passed" and for "failed": the exit status and the last line that the judging step must end with. |
| `limits` | The time and the output that one run may use. |

The members are a proposal for R2 and R4 to agree. The byte domain of
the digest is `artroom-check-configuration-1`. The rules definition
declares it, as the contract's revision 11 lets the owner of a
retained value do (R1 section 15.3a, row 8; section 12.1.4).

| Place | Who acts | Guard | Refusal, or what follows |
|---|---|---|---|
| The rules scope | A key that holds `rules.*`: an admin (section 3.2). The act publishes a rules revision that gives, for each check: its name, whether it is required, its checker, and its configuration's digest. The rules scope retains the bytes under that digest. | The bytes hash to the digest. `image` is a content digest. The checker is a member with the role `checker`, by an observation of membership at a stated head (R4's key O9). | The act is refused, and the rules do not change. A configuration is never edited: a change is new bytes, a new digest and a new rules revision. |
| The change lane, at `request-check` | A member with `change.propose`. | The job's `configuration` is the digest that the lane's copy of the rules holds for that name. The requester's intent cannot set another. | The adopted scope contract, revision 10 (`f52573e7`, adopted by `85c18b66`), requires it in its companion file's `request-check` row: the intent carries the digest, a guard compares the name and the digest with the lane's copy, and a difference is refused `guard-failed`, named `not-a-check-of-the-rules`. R2's revision 12 had the earlier form, in which the effect copies the digest and no field of the intent carries one. Stated in revision 14: R2's adopted revision 14 has the contract's form. The intent carries `name` and `configuration`, and a `has` guard finds that record in `rules.checks` (its section 7.2). |
| The checker service, before a run | Nobody signs. | "Origin", above. And the bytes are fetched from the rules scope by the job's digest. They are never taken from the tree, the requester or the lane. | No run. Bytes that cannot be fetched, or do not hash to the digest: `check-error`, `configuration-unavailable`. |
| The change lane, at `check` and `check-error` | The checker. | The signer is the checker that the lane's copy of the rules names for that check. The tree and the configuration digest equal the job's. | Refused. Nothing is recorded. |
| The destination, at reservation | G, under the rules it observed for this reservation (section 6.5). | For each check that those rules require: the statement lists a live job with that name, its state is `passed`, its configuration digest is the one those rules hold now, and the entry that decided it checks (section 6.5). | Not reserved: `rules-not-met`, or `evidence-invalid` when the deciding entry does not check. |

- **The authority is the rules scope, and the last row is what
  holds.** A lane's copy of the rules can be behind or wrong. A
  requester who got a lane to record a weaker configuration would
  still not merge: G compares each job's digest with the rules that G
  observed itself.
- **What a configuration does not fix.** The files of the tree that
  its commands run. That includes the script that judges the named
  cases, when that script is in the tree (R2 section 17.7). A tree
  cannot lower the names that are asked of it. It can change the
  program that judges them, and that is a change to the tree, under
  review like any other.
- The lane's copy holds, for each check, its name, its digest,
  whether it is required and its checker. R2's revision 12 held
  `requiredChecks`, a list of names. R2's adopted revision 14 holds
  `rules.checks`, the list of records that the contract's companion
  file writes (its note N15). The rules scope's side is section
  12.1.4.

**What the checker signs, by what happened.** R2 section 17.6
proposes this mapping, and R4 asks this note to classify an install
failure and a missing lock file. Both are answered here. The states
are R2's (its section 7.2). None is added.

| What happened | The checker service signs | Job state |
|---|---|---|
| The entry is not a `request-check` of an activated `change` definition. | Nothing. Nothing is run. | Unchanged |
| The configuration's bytes cannot be fetched, or do not hash to the job's digest. | `check-error`, `configuration-unavailable` | `errored` |
| The image that the runner started from is not the one the configuration names, or cannot be resolved ("What ran", below). | `check-error`, `image-mismatch` or `image-unresolved` | `errored` |
| The checkout cannot be confirmed as the job's tree. | `check-error` | `errored` |
| A step before the judging step ends with a status that is not 0. An install that fails is this case. So is a tree with no lock file, when the install step needs one. | `check-error`, naming the step | `errored` |
| The runner does not start, is lost, or passes its limits. A test helper cannot listen on a local port. The judging step ends with a status that `judged` does not name, or with a status and a last line that disagree, or leaves no complete report. | `check-error`, with that reason | `errored` |
| The judging step ends with the status and the last line of "failed". | `check`, outcome failed | `failed` |
| The judging step ends with the status and the last line of "passed". | `check`, outcome passed | `passed` |
| No answer reaches the lane by the job's deadline. | Nothing. The timed entry applies. | `timed-out` |
| A retry. | Nothing for the earlier job. `request-check` opens a new job. | The earlier job is `superseded`. |
| A late authentic answer on a `timed-out` job that no retry superseded. | As its own row above. | `passed`, `failed` or `errored` (R2-11). The entry that admits it becomes the job's deciding entry (section 6.3). |

So a judged pass and a judged fail come only from a judging step that
ended with a complete report. Every other end is an error of the run,
a wait that ended, or a retry. None of those is shown or counted as a
failed check, and none is a pass.

**What ran. New in revision 10 (review rows L11 and Info 7; security
detail 4).** The configuration's digest says what was asked for. It
does not say what ran. The checker service records what ran, and
signs it with the result.

```ts
interface RunProvenance {
  job: FactRef;                          // the `request-check` entry
  tree: TreeId;                          // as checked out and confirmed
  configuration: Digest;                 // the bytes that were executed
  image: { declared: Digest;             // what the configuration names
           resolved: Digest };           // the content digest of the image that the runner started from,
                                         // as the container platform reported it for that start
  environment: Digest;                   // of the list of variables that the runner was started with
  steps: readonly { name: string; status: number | null }[];   // null: the step did not end
  run: string;                           // the checker service's record of this run
}
```

- The record is part of the result's details. The `check` intent
  signs the digest of the details, so the checker's key signs the
  record.
- **The guard.** The service signs `check` only when `image.resolved`
  equals `image.declared`, and `environment` is the digest of the
  configuration's own list. Otherwise it signs `check-error`. A
  platform that cannot report the resolved digest gives
  `image-unresolved`. So no pass and no fail is signed for an image
  or an environment other than the one the rules name.
- **The environment is part of what ran.** The runner is started with
  exactly the variables of the configuration, and with no other. The
  variables that the service itself needs, such as a home directory
  or settings that harden Git, are written in the configuration like
  any other, so the rules show them and the digest covers them.
- **The gateway matches the path exactly.** The runner's gateway
  forwards a request only when its decoded path is the job's
  repository path with one of the Git protocol's own suffixes. A
  prefix match is not enough. The exact rule is an item of I3's
  review of the retained runner (section 11).
- **What this is worth.** It is the checker member's signed
  statement. A replay checks the signature, the grant and the
  digests. It does not derive what ran: the container platform's
  report is taken by the checker service, and the service's key
  vouches for it. Whoever relies on a check relies on that key
  (section 5.5).
- **Where the bytes are kept.** By the checker service, with the
  job's outcome. Decided in revision 14 (G6): the lane does not
  retain them. Its entry holds the `details` digest, which the
  checker signed, and no judgment needs the bytes. So they are no
  retained input, and they need no bound. A page reads them from the
  checker service, by the job's fact. R2's revision 14 has `details`
  on `check-error`.

| Case | `image.declared` and `image.resolved` | Signed | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| The image that the rules name ran. | Equal | `check`, passed or failed, by the judging step | `passed` or `failed` |
| The image setting is unchanged and another image ran. | Different | `check-error`, `image-mismatch` | `errored` |
| The platform reports no digest for the start. | No resolved value | `check-error`, `image-unresolved` | `errored` |
| The runner was started with a variable that the configuration does not list. | Equal; `environment` differs | `check-error` | `errored` |

**At most one run for a job.** R4 asks whether two deliveries of one
job that overlap may each run. They may not. Before it starts a
runner, the checker service makes a record that the job's run has
started, keyed by the job's fact, by one write that creates the
record only if it is absent. A delivery that finds the record, or
whose write does not create it, starts no runner. When the run's end
cannot be found, because the host or the runner's own record was
lost, the service signs `check-error`, `run-lost`, and still starts
no second run. A retry is a new job. `run-lost` does not show that
the run stopped, or that its read token is no longer in use. That
token's duty stays (section 5.4). The claim is "at most one", and it
rests on the service's own durable record. If that storage is lost,
a second run can start, and this note does not claim otherwise. A
job whose record was made and whose runner never started has no run:
that is also `run-lost`.

**How a job reaches the checker, and who holds its read token.
Decided in revision 14 (G4).** The contract has no form for a send
outside the application, and R2's `request-check` row sends nothing
(its gap G22). No form is needed.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What the job is | The `request-check` entry. Its fact is the job's identity. |
| How the checker service learns of it | By a notice over the deployment's service binding, or by reading the lane's bounded read of its jobs. Either is bookkeeping outside the history: no entry, no send of the definition, no operation and no reservation. A notice that is lost delays the run. The deadline's timed entry ends the wait, and a retry is a new job. |
| What gives the origin | The service's own read of the job's entry from the lane, as "Origin" above says. Nothing that a notice carries is trusted. |
| Who asks for the read token | The checker, with its own key: a signed request for the step `job-read` of `git-read@1`, which names the job's fact. The change lane records it as a `preparation` entry (section 5.7). |
| What the lane judges in that entry | The signature and `notAfter`. The signer holds `change.check`, on an observation within ten seconds, and is the checker that the lane's copy of the rules names for that job's check. The job is `requested`. It is the first such entry for that job: a repeat is answered with the first, and mints nothing. |
| What it opens | A `token` record with the purpose check read, and its mint, with 1 attempt. For a filtered check, a snapshot repository's record and its creation, with at most 3 attempts. The plaintext goes to the runner's gateway and never into the runner. |
| When the token ends | It ends before the job's deadline, by its own end time at the host. The entry that decides the job, a `check` or a `check-error`, opens its revocation. The deadline's timed entry opens nothing. |
| Custody of the snapshot repository | The change lane's ledger, as section 5.1 says: one for a job. Its deletion is opened by the entry that decides the job, or by a later `retry` step. |

So "at most one run for a job" has a second support: at most one
`job-read` entry exists for a job, and so at most one read token. A
required check's configuration is fixed as the table above says, and
this changes none of it. The step is a form of the contract's
section 6.11. No source has that capability: the I1 validator at
`a3e5a77e` refuses `git-read@1` (section 12.1.8, P9).

**The Node version, and where it is shown.** R2 sections 17.2 and
17.10 (choice T6) leave three things to this note and R4, with the
owners of the two places where code runs: one exact supported Node
version; that its test-discovery command finds the tests; and that a
test may listen on a local port. This note chooses no version and
shows none of the three.

| Thing | Assigned to |
|---|---|
| The choice of one exact supported version, the same in both places, and the record that R2 asks for: from each place, the version, the discovery command's report of one trivial test file, and one listening test that answered | The commissioning and evidence owner. R4 holds the record as evidence. The planner commissions the baseline's source request (R2 choice T1) only when the record exists. |
| The witness in the checker | I3 produces it, by a job on the real runner. The version is part of the runner image, so it is inside each configuration's `image` digest. |
| The witness in a hosted coding environment | IA produces it, by a command in a real hosted environment. |
| What cannot stand in for either | A run on a developer's own machine. It is neither place. |

Until that record exists, the mapping above is a design, and "the
pinned version" names nothing.

### 3.12 Time windows: the clock, a restart and the fail-closed rule

Every freshness window, grace window, end time and deadline in this
note is a row of the table below. Each place that uses one refers
here.

**What a bound means.** Each bound is a bound in the time of the clock
that its row names. It is the same length in real time only under two
operational assumptions, which section 12 states as H5 and H6.

- H5: a scope's clock does not advance by less than the real time that
  passed, between any two readings that a row uses, across a restart
  too.
- H6: two clocks that a row compares differ by no more than a stated
  amount.

This note detects a clock that goes back, and a clock that has not
moved at all between two uses. It does not detect a clock that moves
too slowly. Where H5 or H6 does not hold, a bound is longer in real
time by the shortfall. This note claims no real-time bound without
them, and no measurement by R4 turns either into a guarantee.

| # | Window, and where | Proposed | The readings, and whose clock | Across a restart | Clock behind; clock not moved; timer lost | In real time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| W1 | An observation for an ordinary act in a lane, the directory or an inbox (section 3.3) | 300 seconds | Start: `at`, when the read began. End: the commit. Both on the observing scope's clock. | Not kept. The scope holds no observation and reads again. If membership does not answer: `authority-unavailable`. | Behind the previous entry: the act is answered `clock-behind` and is not written, and the observation is read again. Not moved since the last use: read again. No timer is involved. | 300 seconds under H5. |
| W2 | An observation for a control of an agent task, for a tool dispatch, and for the runtime's check before a push (sections 3.7, 4.1, 5.2) | 60 seconds | The same, on the task scope's clock. | The same. No tool and no push is started until a new observation is read. | The same. A refused check starts no tool and no push. | 60 seconds under H5. |
| W3 | A ten-second observation: the merger's key, each evidence key and the rules at reservation (section 6.5); taking or renewing a hold (section 3.5); minting or renewing a workspace token; `authorize-export`; the start of an export's copy, its `intent` and each `dispatched`; a private read and each check of a stream (section 4.2); a new staging (section 6.2) | 10 seconds | The same, on the clock of the scope that commits: the destination, the lane or the task scope. | It serves one commit and is never kept. A retry after a restart reads again. | Behind: the commit that needs the observation is answered `clock-behind`. It is not written, and its outside write or send is not made. It is never reused, so "not moved" has no case: two such reads at one reading are two reads, each recorded `fresh` (section 3.3). No timer. | The real time from the start of the read to the commit: 10 seconds under H5. On a slow clock it is the real length of that one turn. |
| W4 | A private stream's end time: 60 seconds to the next check and 10 to pass it; 80 seconds from a revocation (section 4.2) | 70 seconds stored; 80 in all | The check's commit, the stored end time and the reading before each send. All on the task scope's clock. | The stream is closed. It is opened again only by a new signed request and a new check. | Behind the last passing check: closed at once, `clock-behind`. Not moved since the last passing check, when the next check runs: closed, `clock-stalled`. Wake-up lost: no later check passes, so the end time is not moved, and the reading before each send still stops the stream at that end time. | 80 seconds under H5. |
| W5 | An export license: from the entry that asked for it to the `dispatched` commit (section 4.2) | 10 seconds | The time of the task scope's entry that sent the request, and the `dispatched` commit. Both on the task scope's clock. | The license is not used. The task scope asks again, as a new numbered request. | Behind: `clock-behind`, and nothing is dispatched. No timer. A late result lapses the license; it does not dispatch. | 10 seconds under H5. |
| W6 | A read session (section 3.9) | 600 seconds at most | Two clocks. The end time is set from membership's clock. Each reading scope compares it with its own clock, at every read and before every stream send. | The token is unchanged. The scope's open streams are closed. | The reading scope behind its own previous entry: the read is answered `clock-behind`, and no stream byte is sent. Behind membership's clock without that sign: the session is accepted for longer, by the difference. No timer: the comparison is made at each read. | 600 seconds plus the difference between the two clocks: H6. The length on each clock is real only under H5: two clocks that agree and have both stalled satisfy H6. |
| W7 | A grant's `notAfter` (section 3.3) | Set in the grant | Two clocks. The time is a value in membership's history. The observing scope compares it with its commit's reading. | The value is part of the observation, which is read again. | Behind the previous entry: `clock-behind`. Otherwise the grant is accepted for longer, by the difference between the two clocks. | The stated time plus that difference: H6, and H5 for each clock, as for W6. |
| W8 | The `notAfter` of a signed intent or of a signed direct request (sections 4.1 and 4.2; R1 section 4.2) | 15 minutes at most, R1's point R1-9 | Two clocks. The signer's device sets it. The receiving scope judges it in its commit. | The value is in the signed bytes. | Behind: `clock-behind`. R1 owns this rule. | R1's. This note adds nothing to it. |
| W9 | An invitation's end time (section 3.6) | Short; set with N5 | Set at the issuing entry and judged in the join's commit. Both on membership's clock. | The end time is in the item. | Behind: `clock-behind`, and the join is not admitted. No timer is needed: an invitation ends by the comparison in the join's commit. From revision 14 a timed entry also marks an ended invitation `lapsed`, so that its place and its reservation are released (section 12.1.3). The comparison still decides, and a lost timer admits nothing. | The stated time under H5. |
| W10 | A hold's end time, the lease (section 5.2; R1 section 6.8) | The definition's hold duration | Set in the commit that takes or renews the hold. Judged by the timed entry, and by the lane's answer to every fence or mint check. Both on the lane's clock. | The deadline is in the hold item. R1's drain derives what is due from the items and applies it before any other input (R1 section 5.2). | Behind: nothing is written while a transition is due (R1 section 5.3). Timer lost: no act passes the due end, because the next turn drains first; and the lane answers a fence or mint check "not held" when `ends` is not later than its reading, or when its clock is behind, whether or not the timed entry is written. | Exact on the lane's clock. The stated duration under H5. |
| W11 | A job's deadline (section 3.11) | 30 minutes | Set in the `request-check` commit. Judged by the timed entry. Both on the change lane's clock. | The deadline is in the job item, and the drain applies it. | Timer lost: the job waits longer. Waiting licenses nothing, and a late answer still decides the job. | The stated duration under H5. |
| W12 | The end time of a token at the Git host: publication, staging, receipt, workspace, fork read and check read tokens (sections 5.3 and 5.4, rule 4) | As the host allows; a check read token ends before its job's deadline | Two clocks. The end time is the host's. The owning scope compares it with its own clock when it settles the token's duty. | The token's record, with its ID and end time, is in the ledger. | Rule 4 settles a token only when the scope's reading is later than the end time by a margin and the clock is not behind. Timer lost: the duty stays and the next pass finds it. Whatever this clock reads, the host honours a token until the host ends it. | H6, between the scope's clock and the host's. The margin is the stated allowance. |
| W13 | The retention deadline of private work (section 5.6) | 7 days | Set at pause, idle attention or completion. Judged by the expiry entry. Both on the task scope's clock. | The deadline is in the task scope's records. | Behind: the expiry is not written. Timer lost: the work is kept longer. Nothing is deleted without the expiry entry. | The stated time under H5. On a slow clock or with a lost timer, private work is kept longer than stated. |
| W14 | Wake-ups, backoffs and retry delays of a ledger or of publication (section 5.4, rules 1 and 7; section 6.6) | By the ledger | The owning scope's timer. | A stored wake-up is in storage. If one is lost, the next turn or pass finds the duty. | These license nothing and settle nothing. A late or lost one delays work. | None is claimed. |

**Rules for every row.**

- *No timer grants anything.* A timer ends something or starts a
  check. So a lost timer extends no authority. It can lengthen waiting
  (W11, W14) and retention (W13). For a lease it changes nothing that
  an act or a writer can use (W10). For a stream it changes nothing
  while a send still reads the clock (W4).
- *A clock that went back* is found by comparing a reading with the
  previous entry's time (R1 section 5.3), or with the last passing
  check of a stream. What is then stopped is what R1 stops, and no
  more: "The backward clock", below. Revision 6 said here that every
  row then writes and sends nothing. That was wider than R1 and is
  withdrawn.
- *A clock that has not moved* is found only where one cached value is
  used twice: W1, W2 and W4. The value is then read again, or the
  stream is closed.
- *A clock that moves too slowly* is not found by any rule here. That
  is H5.
- *After a restart* a scope trusts what its history and storage hold:
  a deadline in an item, an end time in a record. It does not trust an
  observation, a license or an open stream from before the restart.
- *Once the defined age has passed*, the answer is unchanged: an act
  that needs a grant is refused `authority-unavailable` until a new
  observation is read. Deliveries, timed entries and outcomes still
  take effect (D2-5).

**The backward clock: what is stopped, and what is not.** R1 section
5.3 is the authority. This note adds no stop to it and removes none.
A scope's clock is behind when its reading in a commit is earlier than
the previous entry's time. The scope then decides in this order.

1. **Is a transition due?** A transition is due if its deadline is not
   later than the previous entry's time (R1 section 5.3). If one is
   due, nothing is written: the selection is dropped, the drain stops,
   and the waiting input is answered `clock-behind`, whatever it
   judges. A turn that an alarm started ends with no answer. The next
   turn drains again. This stops an input that judges no time too. No
   input is written ahead of a due expiry (R1 section 5.2).
2. **Nothing is due, and the input judges a time condition.** It is
   not written. The answer is `clock-behind`, and it may be retried.
3. **Nothing is due, and the input judges no time condition.** It may
   be written, with the previous entry's time and `clamped: true`. Its
   effects and its sends follow as for any entry.

Which inputs of this note judge time:

| Judges a time condition: never written clamped | Judges none: may be written clamped when nothing is due |
|---|---|
| Every act. Each judges its intent's `notAfter`, and an act that needs a grant judges the observation's age. | An outcome entry from an attempt's own answer: the read after a push, a "refused" or "not sent" record, a `created` answer, a storage's answer to a dispatch, the read that shows a staged ref present or absent. |
| A timed entry: a hold's end, a job's deadline, a retention expiry. | The delivery of a result: of `reserve`, of `withdraw`, of a license request, of `unpin`. |
| A reservation in G. It judges ten-second observations. | The delivery of a `publication` update at P. |
| Minting or renewing a token; an export's `intent` and `dispatched`; a stream's check. | The delivery of `reserve` or `withdraw` at G, of `pin-confirm`, `unpin` or `export-settled` at a lane, and of a `compromised` notice. |
| The delivery of `export-license` at a lane. Its handler judges that the hold has not ended. | A diagnosis. A checkpoint. |
| Settling a host token's duty by rule 4 of section 5.4. It compares the clock with the token's end time. | |

Three answers are not entries, and R1 does not rule on them. This note
keeps them closed while the clock is behind, whether or not anything
is due: a session read or a stream send is answered `clock-behind`
and sends nothing (W4, W6); and a lane answers a fence or mint check
"not held" (W10).

A clamped time orders an entry and proves nothing (R1 section 5.3). No
window of the table above starts or ends at a clamped time: an
observation's `at`, a license request, a hold's end and a token's
settlement are each set or judged by an entry that judges time, and
such an entry is never clamped. Where a clamped entry sets a deadline
from its own time, the deadline is later than the clock's reading
would give, by the difference. That can lengthen waiting or retention.
It extends no authority.

**Witness: a clock that is behind.** The previous entry's time is
2000. Every reading below is 1990.

| Case | Due at 2000? | Input | R1 section 5.3 | Revision 6 | This revision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a | No. The earliest deadline is 2600. | In G: the read after a dispatched push shows the integration commit. | Written, with time 2000 and `clamped: true`. | Withheld: "every row writes and sends nothing". | Written clamped. The publication is `published`, the slot is free and the final update is sent. |
| b | No. | In P: that final update is delivered. Or the result of a `withdraw`. | Written clamped. | Withheld. | Written clamped. |
| c | No. | An act by key k. | `clock-behind`. | `clock-behind`. | `clock-behind`. The observation is read again before a retry. |
| d | No. | In G: the next queued publication could be reserved. | Not written: it judges freshness. | Not written. | Not reserved on this reading. It stays `queued` and is tried again on a later turn. |
| e | Yes. A hold's deadline is 1995. | The outcome of case a. | Nothing is written. The outcome is offered again. | Nothing is written. | Nothing is written. The attempt stays open, and its answer is offered again. No result is lost and none is inferred. |
| f | Yes. A hold's deadline is 1998. It is later than the reading and not later than 2000. | Any. | Nothing is written. The timed entry is not written either: it is never clamped. | Nothing is written. | Nothing is written until a reading is not earlier than 2000. The lane answers a fence check "not held" all that time. |
| g | No. | A session read; a send on a private stream. | Not an entry. | `clock-behind`. Nothing is sent. | The same. |

## 4. Hosted agents and private resources

### 4.1 The task scope

Each hosted agent task has a **task scope**, a platform definition. Its
history holds controls and their outcomes: start, steer, answer, pause,
resume, cancel, authorize a new attempt. It does not hold the
transcript, command output or files. Those are private resources of the
task, stored beside it.

- A control is a signed intent to the task scope, in R1's form: the
  scope, the acting key, the kind, the fields, an idempotency key and a
  `notAfter`. It is an entry when admitted, so its outcome is recovered
  like any act: the same signed bytes return the same receipt.
- A control needs `task.control` for that task, by an observation within
  the sixty-second window (section 3.12, W2), and it must be signed by a
  device key of the controller or of an admin. A read session never
  controls. When delegation is delivered, a delegated key still cannot
  control: this authority is direct.
- A control takes effect as an entry and is applied at the next tool
  boundary. "Accepted, queued, applied" on the page are that entry, its
  place in the queue, and the entry that applies it. Stated exactly in
  revision 15: a `pause` or a `cancel` is applied by its own outcome
  entry, which the task scope writes and no key signs. A control of
  another kind is applied by the worker's signed `apply`. The base
  called both "the runtime's outcome entry", and the definition of
  revision 14 had only `apply` (section 12.1.7, "What ends a queued
  control"). Stated in revision 16: a `pause` or a `cancel` by an
  authorized key is always admitted, or it repeats one that is
  already `queued`, however many other controls wait (section 12.1.7,
  "Room for a stop"). Made exact in revision 17: one case is outside
  that sentence. A `pause` while the task is `idle` or `paused` is
  new work, and a scope with no free room may refuse it `scope-full`.
  A `cancel` is reserved from the task's genesis and is admitted
  there. No task becomes `running` without the room of its `pause`.

**The definition. New in revision 14.** The task scope's definition
is section 12.1.7. It names the worker of a task beside its
controller. For a hosted agent the worker is the agent. For a hold
that a person holds, the worker is that person, and each operation is
opened by an act that a device key of that person signs (section 12,
G9). A control is still the only instruction, and the worker's own
acts are a second action, `task.operate`, which gives no control.

### 4.2 Private reads, export and the hold's credential

Two different authorities are at work here and must not be mixed.

**A person's direct authority over private resources.** Reading the
transcript, uncommitted files or command output, and authorizing an
export of private work, need the controller's or an admin's own active
device key, by an observation within ten seconds, read for that commit
(section 3.12, W3). A session is not enough. A member handle or a
delegation is not enough.

**The service's authority to keep an agent working.** A hosted agent
must keep working while every laptop is closed. Its hold's write token
is provisioned by the platform, not by a person.

| Request | Signed by | Received by | Authority checked | Custody of the result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read the transcript, uncommitted files or command output | A device key of the controller or an admin | The task scope | `task.read-private` for that task, observed within ten seconds. A stream is checked again every sixty seconds and holds a stored end time.
