Each of those needs a signature by a device key (sections 3.9 and 4.2). | Every session ends at once. What was read stays read. |
| A checker's signing key | A key pair that is made for that one member and is never derived from another secret. Membership refuses to enrol a key that it already holds for another member: `key-in-use`. | `check` and `check-error` results signed as that checker, in every repository whose membership enrols that key. Each must still name a job that exists, with its tree and its configuration digest (section 3.11). | A verdict, a merge, a rules change. A result for a check that the rules give to another checker. | The old key is revoked as `compromised`. Its results stop counting at each later merge and reservation (section 3.10). A publication that is already `published` is not recalled. A reserved one gets an abort attempt (section 6.8). |
| An agent's signing key | The same. | Every act that the role `agent` holds, as that agent, while its controller is active. A token request for its own hold, whose plaintext still goes only to the instance's gateway. | A review, a merge, a control, an export, a membership or rules act. A token's plaintext. | The agent-key rule of sections 3.5 and 4.3. Holds run out. Duties stay owed. |
| The host account's credential | As the host issues it, and limited to the one namespace that the deployment configures. The service cannot check its strength. | A token for any repository or fork of that namespace: a write to a published branch that does not pass through a destination, a read of a private fork, a deletion. Assumption H4 fails. | A signature of any member. An entry of any scope. | The operator replaces it at the host. A token that someone else minted with it is in no ledger, so no ledger can revoke it (section 5.4, rule 5). Finding and ending such tokens is the operator's incident work, under N5. Until it is done, H4 is not safe to assume. A destination finds a branch that has moved (section 6.9). It does not find a writer who has not written yet. |
| The credential of owned checkpoint storage. Added in revision 14. | As the provider issues it, and limited to the deployment's own storage prefix. The service cannot check its strength. | Every checkpoint, staged export copy and private journal of every task of the deployment: read, change and delete. | A signature of any member. An entry of any scope. A token at the Git host. | The operator replaces it at the provider. What was read stays read. A checkpoint whose bytes were changed fails its digest at the next restore, and that restore fails closed (section 5.6). A deletion is found only then: the recovery design names a periodic audit as an open choice and proposes none. |

- **One key for one member.** A deployment that enrols one key as the
  checker of several repositories exposes all of them to one leak.
  Membership's guard is inside one repository. Across repositories
  it is the operator's obligation.
- **Tools that carry a credential.** An operator's tool that holds a
  deployment credential is run at the version that the lock file
  pins. It is given a secret by a file or by standard input (section
  5.3).
- **A replacement accounts for the old credential.** The old one is
  listed as active until its end at its issuer is confirmed. An end
  that is not confirmed stays owed in the operator's record. A
  replacement settles no token, no mint and no write that the old
  credential made.
- **Owners.** N5 and the operator, for setting, replacing and the
  incident work. I3, for the guard on the session secret and the
  guard on a key's enrolment.

### 5.6 Retention of private work

What is retained, and by whom, is R0 section 4.1 rows 1 to 10. The
complete environment experiment is the staged successor of the recovery
request C2, not a claim of this note. R3 states the rules that bear on
authority and effects:

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| What a checkpoint covers | The task's records and conversation; modified, deleted, untracked and ignored project files with modes and link text; the prepared Git object closure; command intents, output and observed exits. "Saved" means all of it, acknowledged under the guarded receipt. |
| The deadline | Starts at pause, at idle attention or at terminal completion. Active work renews it. It is visible and can be extended before it ends. Seven days is the initial configurable default. It is measured on the task scope's clock, and a lost timer keeps the work longer (section 3.12, W13). |
| A failed or corrupt save or restore | The last good checkpoint stays current. A restore that cannot verify its closure is a recovery failure, shown as such. |
| A running process after a restart | Reattached only to the matching instance and job. If the host was lost, the process is gone and the command is interrupted or unknown. |
| Pins | Bytes needed to settle an unknown effect are pinned past the deadline, until that effect's own answer. |
| Expiry | An entry in the task scope that marks the roots expired and leaves a tombstone. |
| Deletion | An outside effect with its own outcome, retried durably when it fails. Only owned payload that nothing pins is deleted. |
| A retry of an old operation after expiry | Answers "expired" or "unknown". It never dispatches again. |
| What an export carries. Stated in revision 14. | One checkpoint's root: its manifest and its payload. The journal records under its positions stay with the task (section 5.9). |

### 5.7 The hold capability's records, steps and evidence

New in revision 10, and read again in revision 11 against the scope
contract's revision 10. That revision is adopted, and it is "the
contract" below. The contract gives a capability four kinds of
declared form: records, guards, effects and steps (R1 section 6.11).
It declares four records of `hold@1` itself: `root`, `pin`, `check`
and `receiver-pin`. It leaves to this note the capability's other
records, the steps that ask for a credential, and the evidence of
each outside effect (R1 sections 4.3, 6.9, 6.11 and 15.8, and the
contract's point R1-26). This section is that list. Everything in it
is written in the contract's forms, and those forms are adopted. The
list is this note's: its records, its steps and its table of evidence
are proposals of revisions 10 and 11, and they are adopted only with
this note. Revision 7 of the contract had none of these forms. Under
it these were the ledger records of sections 5.1 to 5.4.

**Records.**

| Record | Key | States (final in bold) | Values | Made and moved by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fork` | The hold's item ID | `creating`, `selected`, `deleting`, **`deleted`**, **`failed`** | The seed of section 5.2: `commit`, `from`, `fact`, `under`. The creation operation. Once selected: the fork's ID and name at the host. | The entry that opens the hold makes it `creating`. The first `confirmed` outcome of the creation that is recorded while the hold is `held` makes it `selected` (section 5.1). `failed`: every creation attempt that the bound allows has a `refused` outcome. Or, from revision 14, the read for a seed from the destination's head showed no branch: `no-head` (section 5.2). With one attempt still `unknown` it stays `creating`. `deleting` and `deleted`: the fork's deletion, after the hold has ended and nothing pins its bytes. |
| `token` | A number from the capability's counter. Never reused. | `minting`, `live`, `revoking`, **`ended`** | Its purpose: workspace, fork read, staging or, from revision 14, check read. What it is for: the hold, the root or the job. Its mint operation. Once known: the host's token ID and end time. Its revocation operation. | A step, below, makes it `minting` and opens the mint. The mint's `confirmed` outcome makes it `live`. The entry that ends its use opens the revocation: `revoking`. The revocation's `confirmed` outcome makes it `ended`. So does rule 4 of section 5.4, whose form is point O12. A mint whose outcome is `unknown` leaves it `minting`. Made exact in revision 18: a `confirmed` mint makes the token `live` only while its use has not ended. Otherwise it makes it `revoking`: "A mint that is answered after its use has ended", below. |
| `instance` | The hold's item ID, and the runtime's instance ID | `current`, **`past`** | The task scope's reference, with its incarnation. From revision 14: the hold's epoch at the entry that made it `current`, so that a task scope reads the epoch from that one entry (section 5.9). | The step `instance` makes it `current`, and makes an earlier instance of that hold `past`. The hold's end makes it `past`. |

- The seed is a value of the `fork` record, and not a record of its
  own.
- "The task scope's reference recorded on a hold with its instance"
  (section 13) is the `instance` record. It is not a slot of the hold
  item: the contract's companion file says so in its note N5.
- A job's read token and its snapshot repository are records of the
  same form, in the change lane. From revision 14 they belong to
  `git-read@1`, and the step `job-read` opens them (section 3.11).
- *Stated in revision 15.* The adopted contract asks whether these
  records add anything to an entry that uses only the item form of
  `hold@1` (its point R1-49). They do not. The three records are
  forms beyond the item form, and section 13.7 says how the two
  stand together.
- *Decided in revision 17.* A hold has these three records exactly
  when its definition uses a guard or an effect of `hold@1`: "When a
  hold has a workspace", below. Where the table above says "the
  entry that opens the hold" or "the hold's end", it speaks of a
  hold of such a definition.

**When a hold has a workspace. Decided in revision 17** (the I3
plan's question Q3; the contract's point R1-49). Revision 15 said
that the three records above are forms beyond the item form. It left
open how a definition states that it uses them, and said that no
source may derive them from the `hold` effect alone. This is the
rule. A workspace here is the fork, the tokens and the instances of
one hold.

- *The predicate.* The holds of a definition have a workspace
  exactly when both of these are true. The definition lists `hold@1`
  in `capabilities`. And at least one guard or effect of the
  definition is a capability form whose `name` is `hold`: a
  `capability: { name: "hold", guard, with }` or a
  `capability: { name: "hold", do, with }`. It may be in any act,
  receive handler, timed rule or result clause, at any depth of
  `each`, `has` and `anyOf`. The `hold` effect is the item form, and
  it does not count. A form of `git-read@1` does not count.
- *It is a fact of the definition.* It is true or false for a whole
  definition. So it is the same for every hold type, every hold and
  every scope that pins the definition. It reads the definition's
  bytes and nothing else: no state, no clock, no configuration and
  no option of a runtime. The validator already lists every
  capability form of a definition (R1 section 6.1, "The test"). The
  predicate is that this list holds a form of `hold@1`. The
  validator, the runtime and a replay compute it in the same way,
  and no entry records it.
- *Why the definition, and not the item type or the row.* The
  builder's proposal was this predicate, taken for one item type. No
  capability form names an item type. `staged` names a commit and a
  commitment. `pin` names a consumer and an intent. `pin-hold` and
  `pin-release` name a commit. Only `license` names a hold. So "used
  on that item type" cannot be read from the bytes, and the
  proposal is taken for the definition. A rule for each row fails
  too: no hold row of either lane writes a capability form, as the
  table below shows. The forms are on the rows that use what a
  workspace made.
- *Why this is the contract's own line.* Every guard and effect of
  `hold@1` reads or writes a `root`, a `pin`, a `check` or a
  `receiver-pin`. A root and a check name the instance that a commit
  was staged from. A pin names a root. A receiver pin names the
  receiving hold's instance (R1 section 6.11). An instance is made
  only by the step `instance`, and a new staging needs the hold's
  current instance (section 6.2). So a definition that uses one such
  form cannot run without the workspace records, and a definition
  that uses none can never reach them. The contract already asks a
  runtime for the code of "each record that a form reads or writes"
  (its section 6.1). The predicate draws no second line.

Checked against the two pinned lane definitions, read as data at the
commit that the opening names. The counts are by a script.

| Definition | Lists `hold@1` | Rows that write the `hold` effect, and no capability form | Rows that write a guard or an effect of `hold@1` | Forms of `hold@1` | The predicate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `issue` | Yes | `take-hold`, `renew-hold`, `release-hold`, and the timed rule `hold-end` | The acts `report` and `refuse-report`. The handlers `export-license`, `export-settled`, `pin-confirm` and `unpin`. | 11: 5 guards and 6 effects | True |
| `change` | Yes | The same four | The act `propose-manifest`. The handlers `export-license`, `export-settled` and `publication`. | 8: 3 guards and 5 effects | True |

- Each definition has one hold type, `hold`. In `issue` a hold is
  taken to work on a goal in a fork. In `change` it is taken for
  integration work in a fork (section 6.2). Neither has a hold that
  should have no workspace, and neither has a capability form that
  it could use without one.
- A definition that uses only the item form has no capability form,
  so the predicate is false for it. The I2 fixtures of that kind
  keep their entries as they are.
- *What the rule cannot say.* A definition with two hold types, of
  which only one should have a workspace. Under this rule both have
  one. Saying otherwise needs a member on the item type, which
  changes a definition's bytes. No pinned definition needs it, and
  it is not designed.

**What is derived, and at which entry.**

| Entry | When the predicate is true, the commit also derives | When it is false |
|---|---|---|
| Opening: an act whose effects hold `hold: { do: "open" }` | A `fork` record, `creating`, keyed by the hold's item ID, with the seed of section 5.2. One operation: the fork's creation, with attempt 1; or, when the seed is the destination's head, the read of that head. | The item form only. |
| Renewal by the holder: `hold: { do: "renew" }`, and the holder does not change | Nothing. No record moves, and no token is revoked or replaced (section 5.3). | The item form only. |
| A renewal that changes the holder, so that the epoch rises. Neither pinned lane writes one: both guard `renew-hold` on the holder. | The `instance` that is `current` becomes `past`. Each `token` of the hold that is `live` becomes `revoking`, with its revocation operation. From revision 18: a token that is `minting` stays so, and the entry that records its mint's own answer opens its revocation, as after an end. The `fork` record does not move. From this entry on no step `instance` and no step `token` is admitted for that hold: "A changed holder", below. | The item form only. |
| A handover of the commitment: `accept-handover` | Nothing at a hold. Both lanes admit it only when no hold under that commitment is `held`. The new performer takes a new hold, and that opening derives a new fork. | Nothing. |
| End: `hold: { do: "end" }` in an act; or a hold that ends with what it is under | The `instance` that is `current` becomes `past`. Each `live` token of the hold becomes `revoking`, with its revocation operation. A token that is `minting` stays so, and the outcome entry that records its mint's answer opens its revocation: "A mint that is answered after its use has ended", below. The fork's deletion follows as the table of records says. | The item form only. |
| Expiry: the timed entry of the hold's rule | The same as an end. A timed entry has no signer, and these effects need none. | The item form only. |
| The steps `instance` and `token` | Admitted, under the judgments of the table of steps. | Refused, `capability-refused`, named `no-workspace`. It is an answer and no entry. So no instance exists, no new staging passes (section 6.2), and no `root`, `pin`, `check` or `receiver-pin` is ever made. |

- *Who derives them.* The scope's commit, as code of the capability
  version `hold@1`. It runs after the entry's declared effects, over
  the folded state, the one input and the pinned definition. It
  reads no clock but the commit's reading, no storage and no
  network. Each change of a record is a `record` effect, and each
  opening is an `operation` effect. Both are members that an entry
  already has (R1 sections 4.1 and 6.11). The code adds no member to
  an entry, an input, a message or an envelope. It refuses nothing:
  the `hold` effects are total, and so are these. A replay that has
  the capability's code derives the same effects from the same entry
  and compares them. A runtime or a verifier that lacks the code
  answers `unsupported-definition` for a definition whose predicate
  is true (R1 section 6.1).
- *A changed holder.* The contract lets a definition write a renewal
  that another member signs, and the epoch then rises (its section
  6.8). The fork holds the former holder's pushed work, and that
  work moves only by `authorize-export` (section 5.2). So such a
  renewal closes the hold's workspace for good. The steps `instance`
  and `token` are judged with one condition more: the hold's `epoch`
  is 1. A hold is opened at epoch 1, and while it is `held` its
  epoch is above 1 exactly when a renewal changed its holder. The
  refusal is `capability-refused`, named `holder-changed`. The new
  holder takes a new hold to get a fork. First found in the
  adversarial reading of this revision: without the condition, a
  definition's author could hand one member's fork to another by
  how the renewal row is written.
- *A mint that is answered after its use has ended. New in revision
  18* (review `545feb91`). Revision 17 gave this rule for a hold's
  end, in one row of the table above. A renewal that changes the
  holder had no such rule. So a mint that the first holder opened,
  and that was answered after the renewal, made a token `live` that
  no entry then revoked. The rule is now one rule, stated once.
  - *When a token's use has ended.* The rule is for a `token` record
    that is for a hold: its purpose is workspace or fork read. Its
    use has ended, at a commit, when one of three things is true in
    the folded state. The hold is `ended`. Or the hold's `epoch` is
    above 1, which says that a renewal changed its holder. Or the
    instance that the token's request named is `past`.
  - *At the entry that ends the use.* Nothing is done to a token
    that is `minting`. Its mint is not settled, not sent again and
    not given to anyone. The record stays `minting`, and the
    operation keeps its one attempt as it is: unanswered, or
    `unknown`.
  - *At the entry that records the mint's own answer.* The answer is
    the attempt's own authenticated answer, as a first outcome or as
    a late answer after an `unknown` (R1 section 4.3). If it is
    `confirmed` and the use has ended, the commit derives three
    things in that entry: the host's token ID and end time, as
    values of the record; the state `revoking`, straight from
    `minting`; and the revocation operation for that ID, with
    attempt 1. The token is never `live`. If the use has not ended,
    the token is `live`, as before. If the answer is `refused`, the
    token is `ended`, and nothing is revoked because nothing was
    minted.
  - *The plaintext.* The driver that holds a mint's answer gives the
    plaintext to a gateway only after the outcome entry is sealed,
    and only when that entry made the token `live`. For a token
    that the entry made `revoking`, the plaintext is dropped. No
    entry holds it in either case.
  - *Who derives it.* The same code of `hold@1` that derives the
    table above, in the commit, from the folded state and the one
    outcome input. It reads the hold's state and epoch and the
    instance's state, and nothing outside the scope. A replay that
    has the code derives the same three effects from the same entry.
    An outcome entry cannot be refused, and this adds no refusal.
  - *Where its room is.* The step `token` is new work. Its
    `preparation` entry is admitted only with the room of the row
    "A `token` that is `minting` or `live`" of section 5.8: the
    mint's first outcome and its late answer, and the revocation
    with its 3 attempts. That row holds while the token is
    `minting`, whatever happens to the hold. So the entry of the
    late answer and the revocation that it opens were both reserved
    when the mint was opened. Neither is new work.
  - *What one such entry holds.* The effects of one token. It is not
    the fan-out of an end, which is the next point.
- *The same line for a fork. New in revision 18.* The reading for
  the finding above found two more late answers.
  - A creation that is answered `created` selects the fork only
    while the hold is `held` (section 5.1). From revision 18 that
    means `held` at epoch 1. After a renewal that changed the
    holder, a `created` answer selects nothing, as after an end. The
    fork of that answer is deleted by the ID that the answer
    returned, and a credential that came with it is revoked. Both
    were reserved at `take-hold` (section 5.8).
  - When the seed is the destination's head, the outcome of the read
    opens the creation. From revision 18 it opens none when the hold
    is not `held` at epoch 1 at that outcome. The `fork` record is
    then `failed`, named `hold-closed`. Revision 17 did not say
    this, also for a hold that had ended.
- *Each way that an instance closes, against what may be pending.
  Checked in revision 18.* "Continues" means that the operation
  keeps its own attempts and its own answer, and that no closure
  settles it.

  | The closure | In the lane | A mint that is not answered | A fork's creation that is not answered | The read of a head that is not answered | A revocation, or a deletion, that is not answered |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | The hold ends: `release-hold`, the timed `hold-end`, or the end of what it is under | The hold is `ended`. The instance is `past`. | The rule above. It was revision 17's. | A `created` answer selects nothing (section 5.1). | It opens no creation: `hold-closed`. Found in this reading. | Continues. A fork's deletion starts only after the end. |
  | A renewal that changes the holder | The hold is `held`, at epoch 2. The instance is `past`. | The rule above. This is the review's finding. | A `created` answer selects nothing. Found in this reading: "while `held`" would have selected it. | It opens no creation: `hold-closed`. Found in this reading. | Continues. |
  | A new instance of the same hold, by the step `instance`: a restore, or a host that was lost | The hold is `held`, at epoch 1. The earlier instance is `past`. | The rule above, for a mint whose request named the earlier instance. Found in this reading, and narrowed: under revision 17 that token became `live`, with a route to an instance that was `past`. | Not touched. The fork is the hold's, and it is selected as before. | Not touched. | Continues. A token that is `live` is not revoked by this step: rule 4 of section 5.3 stands. |
  | A closure in the task scope: a `fence`; the `abandon` of a failed recovery; a `cancel` or a `pause`; the runtime's own fence when a grant is lost | Nothing moves. The lane is sent nothing, and writes no entry. The hold is `held` at epoch 1, and its instance is `current`. | No rule of the lane can apply, because the lane has no entry at which to derive one. A mint that is answered then makes the token `live`, as before. Its route is the fenced instance's, which the runtime has closed (section 5.2). Its revocation comes with the hold's end, which is reserved and cannot be refused, or when a second token replaces it (section 5.3, rule 4). | Not touched. | Not touched. | Continues. |

- *The fan-out of one entry is not bounded by the budget. Stated in
  revision 18* (the head news that the review `545feb91` cites). The
  entry that ends a hold, and the renewal that changes its holder,
  change each `live` token of the hold and open a revocation for
  each. Each of those was reserved when its token was asked for, so
  the scope's budget covers them all. The budget does not bound how
  many of them fall in one entry. A hold's end and its expiry cannot
  be refused. So before such an entry is built, the proof plan and
  the common capacity work must bound the tokens of one hold that
  may be `live` or `minting` at once, and must count every `record`
  effect and every revocation that one such entry can hold against
  the bound on one entry. That is owed to R4 and to the capacity
  follow-through `cc570904`. It is the bound that revision 17 asked
  of R4, with its owner and its condition now stated. No number is
  proposed here.
- *No pinned digest changes.* The rule adds no member to a
  definition. `issue` and `change` keep their bytes and their
  digests, and I2 owes nothing for it. What changes is what an entry
  of those lanes holds once the capability's code exists. The entry
  of `take-hold` then holds one `record` effect and one `operation`
  effect more. An entry that ends a hold with an instance or a live
  token holds their `record` effects, and the revocations. No sealed
  entry of a deployed scope is changed by this. In a runtime that is
  not a test, neither lane definition runs today: both answer
  `unsupported-definition` until the capability's code exists, as
  the I2 source's own record says of its pinned definitions. An
  entry that a test wrote with a scripted capability is test data
  (R1 section 6.11).
- *Two forms that were not taken.* A member on the hold item type,
  such as `workspace: true`. Or a member of the definition's entry
  in `capabilities`. Each changes the bytes and the digest of both
  pinned lanes, and needs an I2 follow-up. Each is also a second
  statement of one fact. A definition could then say "no workspace"
  and use `staged`, and the validator would need a rule to refuse
  that. The predicate cannot disagree with the forms, because it is
  read from them.
- *For I3.* Step 18 of the I3 plan no longer waits on this. Its step
  1 needs no type for the rule: a declared definition is as it is.
  Its step 16b gains one pure function over a validated definition,
  which gives the predicate from the validator's list of capability
  forms. Its step 18 builds the table above in the commit, after the
  `hold` effect; the two refusals of the steps; and the
  reservations of the rows for a `fork` and a `token` in section
  5.8, which apply only where the predicate is true. Its step 22
  uses the same function in the replay. The lanes' scenarios for
  `take-hold`, `release-hold` and `hold-end` then expect the derived
  effects.
- *Case.* A definition lists `hold@1`, has the four hold rows of
  `issue` and no other row of the capability. A member signs
  `take-hold`. The entry holds the item form: the hold, its holder
  and epoch 1. It holds no `fork` record and opens no operation. The
  member's key then asks for the step `instance`. It is refused
  `capability-refused`, `no-workspace`, and nothing is written. The
  same `take-hold` under `issue` holds the `fork` record,
  `creating`, and the creation's attempt 1. The step `instance` is
  then judged as the table of steps says. Added in revision 18: the
  order in which a mint is answered after a renewal that changed the
  holder is steps 5 to 9 of the witness of section 5.3.

**Steps.** A step is asked for with a signed request, and the lane
records it as a `preparation` entry (R1 section 5.5).
The contract declares `stage` and `check`. The first two of this
table are this note's, from revision 10. Revision 14 adds `job-read`
and `retry`. They answer the contract's point R1-26: the entry form of a
credential request is a `preparation` entry.

| Step | Asked with | Judged in the entry's commit | Derives |
|---|---|---|---|
| `instance` | A signed request by a key of the hold's holder. It names the hold, the task scope with its incarnation, and a new instance ID. From revision 21 its form is stated: "What a step reads of its signed intent", below. | The signature and `notAfter`. The hold is `held`, and its `ends` is later than the reading. The signer's member is the holder. The grant, by an observation within ten seconds; for an agent, with `controllerActive`. From revision 17: the definition's holds have a workspace, or `no-workspace`; and the hold's `epoch` is 1, or `holder-changed`. | The `instance` record, `current`. The earlier one, `past`. |
| `token` | The signed token request of section 4.2, by a key of the hold's holder. It names the hold and its current instance. From revision 21 its form is stated, below, and it is refused `tokens-full` at the bound on a hold's tokens. | The same, with the two conditions of revision 17. And: the instance named is `current`; the `fork` is `selected`. | A `token` record, `minting`, and its mint operation with its one attempt. |
| `job-read`. Added in revision 14. | A signed request by the checker's key. It names the job's fact. | The signature and `notAfter`. The signer holds `change.check`, on an observation within ten seconds, and is the checker that the lane's copy of the rules names for that check. The job is `requested`. No earlier `job-read` entry exists for it. | A `token` record with the purpose check read, `minting`, and its mint. For a filtered check, the snapshot repository's record and its creation (section 3.11). |
| `retire`. New in revision 21. | A signed intent of the kind `hold@1:retire`, by a key that holds `ledger.retry`. It names one root by its number, or one fork by its hold. | The signature and `notAfter`. The grant `ledger.retry`, by an observation within ten seconds. For a root: it is `live`; no pin on it is `provisional` or `held`; and the retention that R4 sets has passed since the entry that made it `live`. For a fork: its hold is `ended`; the fork is `selected`; no token of that hold is `minting`, `live` or `revoking`; no `instance` of it is `current`; no root that was staged from it is `creating`; and no `receiver-pin` that is `standing` names it. Each refusal is `not-retirable`. | For a root: the root, `retiring`, and its delete, an operation with at most 3 attempts. For a fork: the fork, `deleting`, and its deletion, an operation with at most 3 attempts. "Which entry makes a token, a retirement and a deletion", below. |
| `retry`. Added in revision 14. | A signed request by a key that holds `ledger.retry`. It names one operation of this lane's ledger. | The signature and `notAfter`. The grant, on an observation within ten seconds. The operation's stated attempts are used, and it is not settled. It is a revocation, a delete, or the creation of a staged ref. | One new operation of the same kind and target, with 1 attempt. It settles nothing about the earlier one (section 12, G3). |

- **A repeat.** The lane indexes a preparation entry by the request's
  digest, the capability and the step. The same request again is
  answered with the first entry and writes nothing. That is the rule
  of section 4.2: the record of the token already minted, or its
  `minting` state while the mint is unknown. Nothing is minted again
  for that operation.
- **A refusal** is an answer and no entry. Nothing was caused, and
  nothing is charged: what was fetched for it is discarded, because
  the turn wrote no entry (R1 section 17.3).
- The plaintext is never in an entry. It goes from the mint's answer
  to the gateway of the instance that the request names (section
  5.3).

**How the base's steps become entries.**

| The base says | Entry, in the contract's forms |
|---|---|
| "The lane writes the fork's creation operation in its ledger before the first attempt", with the seed (section 5.2) | When the seed is a report or a manifest: the entry that opens the hold. It makes the `fork` record with the seed and opens the creation, with attempt 1. When the seed is the destination's head: that entry opens one read of the branch instead, and the outcome entry of that read fixes the seed and opens the creation. No act reads the host in its commit. |
| A `created` answer selects, or is recorded as not selected (section 5.1) | An outcome entry, with `selected` derived (R1 section 4.3, item 7). A late answer is one more outcome entry after an `unknown` (item 3). |
| "S records the staging operation in its ledger before any token is minted" (section 6.2) | The `preparation` entry of the step `stage`. R1 section 6.11 maps the seven steps of section 6.2 onto entries. |
| A token is revoked by its ID | A revocation operation, opened by the entry that ends the token's use. |
| A credential that the host returned with a creation is revoked by its ID, or that is a duty | A revocation operation, opened by the outcome entry that recorded the answer. |

**Evidence of each outside effect.** The contract types an outcome's
evidence by its basis: the attempt's own authenticated answer, or a
read that the effect's owner defines as decisive, or none (R1
section 4.3, item 4). This table says which basis each
effect of section 8.1 has. It restates the rules of sections 3.8,
5.4, 6.2, 6.6 and 4.2. It changes none.

| Effect | Shown to have happened by | An attempt is shown to have done nothing by | Otherwise | Selects one result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Creating the repository at founding; creating a fork | That request's own answer, with the ID that the host gave. | That request's own answer, refused. | Unknown. Never a listing, an inventory or an occupied name. | Yes |
| Reading the branch's head for a seed; the ancestry read | That read's own answer. For the ancestry read the evidence is the ancestry record, and a read that was cut short gives a record that is `too-large` and no judgment. | Not a case: a read changes nothing. | Unknown: nothing rests on it, and it is read again as a new attempt. | No |
| Minting a token | That request's own answer, with the token's ID and end time. | That request's own answer, refused. | Unknown. Nothing is minted again for that operation. | No |
| Revoking a token | That request's own answer for that ID. | That request's own answer that no such token is live. | Unknown. The duty stays. Rule 4 of section 5.4 can end the token's cleanup when its ID and end time are known. | No |
| Creating a staged ref | A read of the ref that shows that commit, with the three checks of "The root" (section 6.2). | The host's own answer that refuses the create. | Unknown. A read that shows another value is an incident. | No |
| Deleting a staged ref | A read of the ref that shows it absent. | The host's own answer that refuses the delete. | Unknown. | No |
| Updating the branch; a fence; the receipt ref | A read of the ref that shows the commit, or the content, that this operation sends. | The gateway's record that nothing was forwarded, or the host's whole answer that rejects that ref (section 6.6, step 4). | Unknown. | No |
| Releasing an export; saving or deleting private work; deleting a fork or a snapshot repository; the import at founding | That request's own answer. | That request's own answer, refused. | Unknown. It is not sent again as if nothing had happened. | No |
| The first head of a branch. Added in revision 14. | A read of the branch that shows the commit that this operation sends (section 12.2). | The gateway's record that nothing was forwarded, or the host's whole answer that rejects that ref. | Unknown. | No |
| A push to a hold's fork. Added in revision 14. | A read of the fork's ref that shows the prepared commit (section 5.9). | The same two. | Unknown. No push is sent that would return the ref to the expected old value of an unknown attempt. | No |

**Where the contract's forms and this note do not yet fit.** Each is
an owned gap (section 12). None is treated as decided.

- For five effects the read shows that the effect happened and not
  which attempt did it: the branch update, a fence, the receipt, and
  the creation and the deletion of a staged ref. This note leaves an
  attempt whose own answer was lost as unknown, for good, and still
  ends the publication or moves the root (sections 6.2 and 6.6). The
  contract calls an operation settled only when every attempt has a
  `confirmed` or a `refused` outcome (its section 4.3, item 8). Point
  O11.
- Rule 4 of section 5.4 ends a token's cleanup when its known end
  time has passed. That is neither the attempt's own answer nor a
  read. The contract has no basis for it. Point O12.
- The base retries a revocation, a delete, an unresolved push and a
  receipt write without a stated number of attempts. The contract
  reserves room for every attempt that may still be opened (its
  section 17.2), so it needs a number. Section 5.8 says what is
  reserved meanwhile. Point O13.
- New in revision 11. A receiver pin needs the highest license number
  that its lane has decided, so that a refusal can use a reserved
  entry once (section 4.2, "A reserved license decision"). The
  contract lists the pin's values without it, and gives a refused
  deciding entry no effect. Which form carries the number is asked of
  R1 (section 12, G15).
- Where each stands in revision 14. The first is the contract's point
  R1-38, and the second its point R1-39. Both are owed to its next
  revision (G1 and G2). The first now covers two more effects: the
  first head of a branch, and a push to a hold's fork. The third is
  decided: each operation states its attempts (G3). The fourth is
  answered by the contract's revision 11 (G15).

**What a step reads of its signed intent. Decided in revision 21**
(the I3 deltas note, entries EF2 and EH6). Section 6.2 says that an
intent names its source "in its `source` field". No act of either
lane has a field of that name. The lane forms state the source of a
manifest as four fields, and a report names its commitment and no
hold. So the rule is stated by the fields that the rows carry. It is
a rule of `hold@1`, and it reads names of fields, as the capability
already reads the names `holder` and `under` of a hold.

| The intent | What the steps `stage` and `check` read | Where it stands in the lane data |
|---|---|---|
| It is addressed to this scope, and has the field `integration`: a manifest from a hold of this lane | The commit: `integration`. The hold: the field `hold`, an item of this scope. The instance: the field `instance`. The commitment: the hold's `under`. | `propose-manifest` of `change`, in its first shape (the lane forms, section 5.4) |
| It is addressed to another scope, and has the field `integration`: a manifest from a hold of this lane, proposed elsewhere | The commit: `integration`. The field `lane` must be this scope's reference, with its incarnation. The hold: the field `foreignHold`, an item ID of this scope. The instance: the field `instance`. The commitment: the hold's `under`. This lane does not pin the other lane's definition, so it reads these four by name. | `propose-manifest` of `change`, in its second shape, staged by an issue lane |
| It is addressed to this scope, has the fields `commit` and `commitment`, and has no field `integration`: a report | The commit: `commit`. The commitment: `commitment`, an item of this scope. The hold: the one hold of this scope that is `held` and whose `under` is that commitment. The instance: the `current` instance of that hold. | `report` of `issue`. Both lanes guard `take-hold` with `hold-held`, so at most one hold under a commitment is `held`, and a hold has at most one `current` instance. |
| Any other intent | Nothing. The step is refused `not-staged`. | No row |

- *What `stage` then judges.* As before. The hold that was read is
  `held`, its end time is later than the reading, and its holder is
  the signer's member. The instance that was read is `current`. No
  `live` root holds the commit under that commitment. With no such
  hold, with a hold that another member holds, or with no `current`
  instance, the step is refused `not-staged`.
- *The signer's own hold, and no other.* The hold of a report is
  found by its commitment, and not by the signer. It is used only
  when its holder is the signer's member. A member who is the
  performer of a commitment and holds no hold under it stages
  nothing. So no reading gives a signer a hold that the signer does
  not hold.
- *What `check` reads.* The commit and the commitment, by the same
  table. It needs no hold that is `held`: it reuses a `live` root
  whose staging hold was the signer's (section 6.2).
- *An intent with both shapes, or with neither.* The lane's own
  guard `source-shape` refuses it at the act. At the step the first
  row that fits is read, in the order of the table.
- *The steps with no act.* The step `instance`, the step `token` and
  the step `retire` are asked with a signed intent of their own. Its
  form is the contract's `Intent`, with these members.

| The step | `kind` | `to` | `fields` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `instance` | `hold@1:instance` | The lane that holds the hold | `hold`: the hold's item ID. `task`: the task scope's reference, with its incarnation. `instance`: the new instance ID, a text of at most 128 bytes. |
| `token` | `hold@1:token` | The same | `hold`: the hold's item ID. `instance`: the hold's `current` instance. |
| `retire` | `hold@1:retire` | The same | Exactly one of `root`, a root's number, and `fork`, a hold's item ID. |

  `on` is null and `expected` is empty. A field that the table does
  not name, or a missing one, refuses the step `bad-field`. The kind
  has the form of a step kind, which no act of a definition may have
  (the contract's section 6.2). So such an intent can never be
  admitted as an act. The eight members of a direct request, in
  section 4.2, are those of a request to a gateway, and are no form
  of this intent. The step `job-read` is step 24's, and its form is
  not stated here.

**Which pin a commit alone releases. Decided in revision 21** (the
I3 deltas note, entries EF9 and EH7). The contract lets `pin-release`
be written with `commit` alone. Three rows write it so, each in an
entry that did not admit the act: `refuse-report` of `issue`, and
`propose-manifest` and the handler `publication` of `change`. A pin's
key is the consumer and the intent, and such an entry has no intent
at hand.

- *The rule.* In each of the three rows the argument `commit` is a
  slot of an item: the report, the previous manifest, or the merged
  manifest. That item was opened by the entry that admitted its act,
  and an item's ID is the position of that entry. The pin that is
  released is this scope's own pin that is `held`, whose `commit` is
  that value, and whose `admitted` is that entry.
- *At most one matches.* One entry admits one act, and one act has
  one pin. So no two pins have the same `admitted`. Two reports of
  one commit have two pins, and each `refuse-report` releases its
  own.
- *When none matches.* Nothing is released, and the entry is written
  as its row has it. This is where the default was changed: the
  smallest decision that was proposed refuses by name. A capability
  effect has no refusal in the contract's forms. One of the three
  rows is the handler of a `relate` from the destination, and a
  refusal there would lose the record of a publication over a pin's
  bookkeeping. A pin that stays keeps its root and its three
  reserved entries, which is the safe side. An act that must be
  refused for want of a pin writes the guard `pin` in its row, which
  refuses `no-pin`. No pinned row does.
- *Never by a guess.* The rule that the source holds meanwhile,
  "exactly one `held` pin on that commit", is replaced. It released
  the wrong pin in no case, and it released none after two reports
  of one commit. Under this rule the pin is found by the item, and a
  pin of another intent is never released: its `admitted` is another
  entry.
- *What the code is given.* The item that the argument was read
  from: the subject of the slot operand. That is a change of source,
  and of no form. A `pin-release` with `commit` alone whose argument
  is no slot of an item names no pin, and releases nothing.

**Which entry makes a token, a retirement and a deletion. Decided in
revision 21** (the I3 deltas note, entries EF14 and EH11). Three
records had a state that no entry made.

| The record | The entry that makes it, and by which input | What it reserves |
|---|---|---|
| The two tokens of one attempt of a staging: purpose fork read, and purpose staging. Each is for the root, and not for the hold. | The entry that opens that attempt of the operation `stage`. For attempt 1 that is the `preparation` entry of the step `stage`. For a later attempt it is the outcome entry that opens it. Each token is `minting`, with its mint, an operation with 1 attempt. The attempt's request is sent only when both are `live`. | Each as a token: its mint and its revocation (section 5.8, the row of a token). The step `stage` is admitted only with room for the two tokens of each of its 3 attempts, as the row of a root that is `creating` says. |
| The end of those two tokens | The outcome entry that records that attempt `confirmed` or `refused` makes each `revoking`, with its revocation. An attempt that is `unknown` leaves them, and they end by their own end time or with the late answer (section 5.4). | Nothing new. |
| A root that is `retiring` | The `preparation` entry of the step `retire`, which names the root. It also opens the delete, with its attempts. Each attempt of the delete has one staging token, made as the tokens of a staging are. The read that shows the ref absent makes the root `retired`. | The row of a root that is `retiring`, in section 5.8. The step is new work, and is admitted only with that room. |
| A fork that is `deleting` | The `preparation` entry of the step `retire`, which names the fork by its hold. It also opens the deletion. Its `confirmed` outcome makes the fork `deleted`. | The entries that a `selected` fork already reserved for its deletion (section 5.8). |

- *No entry that ends a hold makes any of these.* The end of a hold
  cannot be refused, and it already holds the revocations of the
  hold's tokens. A fork's deletion "follows" the end, in the table
  above. It follows by a later step, and never in the ending entry.
- *Who signs `retire`.* A key that holds `ledger.retry`, which is an
  admin's (section 3.2). It is the grant of the act `retry`, which
  opens a further attempt of a deletion. An operator's tool may sign
  it with such a key. No timed rule and no outcome retires a root or
  deletes a fork.
- *A root that no attempt created.* It stays `creating`, as the
  source has it. Once its operation `stage` is settled with no
  `confirmed` outcome it reserves nothing, no pin is taken on it,
  and the next staging of that commit gets the next number. No state
  is added.
- *A staging's tokens are not the hold's.* They are not counted in
  the bound on a hold's tokens, and the end of the hold does not
  revoke them: a staging that was opened under a held hold may still
  finish. They are bounded by the 3 attempts of one staging.

**The bound on the tokens of one hold. Stated in revision 21** (the
I3 deltas note, entries EF7 and EH10; this note's side). "The fan-out
of one entry", above, asked for this bound and stated none.

- *A bound exists.* At most a fixed number of tokens of one hold are
  `minting` or `live` at once. It is a value of the capability's
  version. The number is R4's, with the capacity work under
  `cc570904`. None is proposed here.
- *Its floor.* 2. Rule 4 of section 5.3 needs the old and the new
  workspace token side by side while a credential is renewed. A
  staging's tokens are not counted here, as the passage above says.
  If the proof plan counts them on the hold instead, the floor is 4.
- *The judges refuse at the bound.* The step `token` is refused,
  `capability-refused`, named `tokens-full`, when the hold already
  has that many tokens that are `minting` or `live`. It is an answer
  and no entry. The source refuses it today with no name.
- *What one ending entry then holds.* The entry that ends a hold,
  its expiry and a renewal that changes its holder each derive at
  most: one `record` effect for the instance, and for each `live`
  token one `record` effect, one `operation` effect and one
  `attempt` effect. With a bound of N that is 1 + 3N effects of the
  capability, beside the entry's written effects. A token that is
  `minting` does not move in that entry.
- *An entry that cannot be refused is never built past its bound.*
  The contract's revision 16 states the rule: a maximum that depends
  on the state is held by refusing the opening that would pass it.
  Here the opening is the step `token`. So N is chosen, with the
  bound on one entry's derived effects, such that 1 + 3N fits beside
  the largest ending row of a lane. A runtime whose N does not fit
  does not run the capability.

### 5.8 Capacity: what each pending duty reserves

New in revision 10. A scope that is at its budget refuses new work
and must still record what it already owes. The scope contract,
adopted at revision 10 and "the contract" below, gives the
accounting: each pending duty reserves, when it is created, what its
settlement needs, in entries, items, records, pending requests and
bytes; a settling input draws only on its own duty's reservation; new
work is admitted only if it fits with the reservations it creates (R1
sections 17.1 to 17.3). The contract leaves to this note the
reservations of the hold capability and of the platform definitions
(its sections 17.2 and 17.5). This section declares them. The
accounting is adopted. The reservations declared here, and the two
declarations on a written refusal, are this note's proposals of
revisions 10 to 12, and they are adopted only with this note.
Revision 7 said only that a budget reserves room to settle (its
section 9.2). R4 sets every number.

Revision 10 of this note wrote this section against the contract's
revision 9. Revision 11 read it again against revision 10, which
changed four things that this section uses. Each is marked where it
is applied: a reservation covers a duty's whole closure; an entry
that records a refusal is new work; the closing checkpoint has an
exact rule; and a temporary static rule follows the chains of timed
rules.

**Two classes, kept apart.**

- **Essential.** The first input that settles a duty which an
  admitted entry created: a hold's end; the first answer on a job
  that is `requested`, or that is `timed-out` and not superseded; the
  outcome of an attempt that was opened, and its late answer; the
  read that decides a publication, with its final update; a
  revocation of a key; the join of an issued invitation; the result
  of a request that was sent; the first decision on a license request
  that a receiver pin reserved (section 4.2), and on a publication's
  one `withdraw`; the scope's closing checkpoint. From revision 16:
  one `cancel` of a task that is not cancelled, one `pause` of a task
  that runs, and the decision on a failed recovery. Its room is
  reserved when the duty is created. It is never refused for
  capacity.
- **Optional.** Everything else is new work, bounded by the free
  budget: a new job; an answer on a job that is `passed`, `failed`,
  `errored` or `superseded`, which is history; a new hold, staging,
  export or publication; a comment; a further attempt that no
  reservation covers; an entry that records a refusal, apart from the
  two that "A refusal that is written" declares, below; a checkpoint
  that is written while another duty is pending.

So the first essential result stays recordable at capacity, also when
it needs a new item, a new entry and a send. Later history and new
jobs are bounded apart from it, by the budget that is free.

**What each duty reserves.** "An operation" reserves 2 entries for
each attempt that may still be opened or answered: its first outcome
and its late answer (R1 section 17.2, row 5). "A
request" is 1 pending request and reserves 2 entries: a diagnosis and
the result (row 1). It also reserves what its clauses can start. For
each request of this table that adds nothing: "The closure of each
duty", below. The counts follow from the bounds this note
already proposes: three creation attempts (U9), one mint for an
operation, three license requests (U15), and, from revision 14, the
stated attempts of section 12, G3. They are derivations from
proposals. None is a measured budget.

|---|---|---|---|

| A lane | A `fork` that is `creating` | `take-hold` | The creation: an operation with at most 3 attempts. For each of those attempts, because each may be answered `created`: a revocation, for a credential returned with it, and the fork's deletion, each an operation with at most 3 attempts (G3). When the seed is the destination's head: one read operation. |

Stated in revision 27: seven rows of this table are restated in the
contract's forms: the two of the destination, the one of the register,
the one of the directory, and the three of membership. "The reservations
of the platform definitions, in the contract's forms", below, has them,
with what stays in force until the forms take effect. The rows of a
lane, of a task scope and of every scope are not restated.

- **The closure of each duty. Stated in revision 11.** The
  contract makes a reservation cover a duty's whole closure: the
  duty, and every duty that one of its settling entries can start
  (its section 17.2). The table above was written that way for
  operations. A row names the revocation, the deletion, the tokens,
  the read and the pin that its settling entries open, and each is
  counted in that row. The contract's revision 10 writes out two more
  cases. This is what they give here.
  - *A chain of timed rules.* Each timed rule that this note names
    leaves its item in a state that no timed rule lists. A hold's end
    leaves it `ended`. A job's deadline leaves it `timed-out`. A
    retention expiry marks the roots expired. So every chain is 1,
    and each deadline reserves 1 entry, as the table has it.
  - *What a request's clauses start.* A request reserves its 2
    entries, and the largest closure that one of its clauses can
    start. For each request of this table that is nothing more than
    its row already counts. The clauses of a `publication` update, of
    a `compromised` notice and of `export-settled` set no state that
    a timed rule or a `settles` lists. T records the result of a
    license request, and what follows it, which is the dispatch, the
    entry F and `export-settled`, was reserved by the release's own
    row when the copy started. The `applied` clause of a creation
    records the child, and the confirmation that follows is a
    control, which is part of its entry.
  - Both statements are about the platform definitions. From
    revision 14 those are written (section 12.1), and each states
    its timed rules and what its clauses start. The statements are
    still conditions on them and not a derivation: no validator has
    read them. The contract's validator
    derives each reservation from the definition itself. A definition
    whose timed rule leads to another, or whose clause starts a duty,
    reserves that too, and one whose closure is not finite is refused
    `reserve-unbounded`.
- **A refusal that is written. New in revision 11.** Under the
  contract's revision 10, an entry that records a refusal keeps what
  was read before the refusal and is charged for it in its own
  transaction. It ends no duty. So it is new work, and it draws on a
  reservation only where the owner of the duty declares that the
  refusal uses the reservation up (R1 sections 6.5 and
  17.3; its witness 18.18). Revision 10 of this note did not say
  which of its reserved entries a refusal may use. This note declares
  two, and no more. Each is one entry that an admitted duty already
  reserved, for one request of a bounded number.
  - *A bound license request.* Section 4.2, "A reserved license
    decision": at most two for one export, numbers 2 and 3.
  - *The one `withdraw` of a publication.* A publication reserves 1
    entry for one `withdraw`. R2 admits `cancel-merge` while a
    merge is `intended` and its `withdrawal` slot is empty. So a lane
    sends one `withdraw` for an operation, or a second in another
    envelope after an `undelivered` diagnosis of the first (section
    12.1.5). G's first
    decision on a `withdraw` uses that entry when three things hold.
    The sender is the scope that the operation's fact is in. The
    message names a publication that G holds. That publication still
    holds the entry. The decision is `applied` while the publication
    is `queued`, and `refused`, with the reason `reserved` or
    `ended`, in every later state (section 6.4). Without this, a
    destination with no free room could not answer a withdrawal that
    it must refuse, and the lane's request would stay pending for as
    long as the destination is full. G records, with the
    publication, that its `withdraw` was decided, so that the entry
    is used once. For a refusal that mark is all that changes in G:
    the publication's state does not move. Its form is the
    value `withdrawDecided` of the destination definition (section
    12.1.5). A repeat of the envelope
    writes nothing. A `withdraw` that is `not-owner` or `malformed`,
    one
    that arrives before its `reserve`, and one that arrives after
    the publication's last duty ended, are not covered. No
    publication holds an entry for them, and their deciding entry is
    new work. The witness "a refused withdrawal at a destination
    with no free room", below, shows the covered case, a repeat and
    two cases that are not covered.
    Corrected in revision 25: no form lets a refused delivery set
    the mark. So until the contract has one, this declaration covers
    an applied `withdraw` only, and a refused one is new work
    (section 12.1.5, "A refused `withdraw` sets nothing").
    Stated in revision 27: the contract adds no such form, and this
    note's ask for it is withdrawn. The exception covers an applied
    `withdraw`, as the rule (section 13.17, Part D).
  - *Every other refusal is new work.* Among them: a refused first
    `export-license`; a `reserve` that G refuses; an `export-settled`
    that is refused `not-final`, which leaves the entry that the
    `export` item reserved for the one that applies; and the pin
    handlers' `no-pin`, `pin-mismatch` and `still-needed`. With no
    free room for it, such an entry is not written, the request is
    not decided, transport answers "retry", and the sender keeps the
    duty. A refused act and a refused step write no entry, and are
    charged nothing.
- **The room of a stop. New in revision 16** (review `60c940f3`).
  Revision 15 reserved the outcome of a stop that was already
  admitted, and nothing for a stop that was not yet signed. So a task
  scope with no free room, or with a full `control` type, could
  refuse a `cancel`. The two rows above close the first, and section
  12.1.7, "Room for a stop", closes the second.
  - *What is reserved, and when.* A task holds room for one `cancel`
    from its genesis until it is cancelled. A task that runs holds
    room for one `pause`, from the `apply` that made it `running`.
    Each is the control's entry, its item, its outcome and its save.
  - *How the entry of a stop is admitted.* That entry ends the
    standing room and creates the stop's own reservation, which is
    never larger. So used plus reserved does not rise, and the
    contract's rule for new work admits the entry at a scope with no
    free room (R1 section 17.3). Nothing is drawn from another duty.
  - *Why a `pause` is armed by the `apply`.* A task can be paused
    many times, and one standing room is used once. The `apply` of a
    `start` or a `resume` is the only entry that makes a task
    `running`. It is new work, so it is the place where the next
    `pause` is paid for. A task that has no room for a `pause` does
    not start. A `pause` of a task that is `idle` or `paused` stops
    no tool, because no `intend` is admitted in those states, and it
    stays new work.
  - *What is the contract's, and what is owed.* The contract lets a
    runtime reserve more than a duty's closure, and never less (its
    decision D11-3). Its row 3 reserves for an act that declares
    `settles` and that takes its subject out of the listed states in
    its own entry. The entry of a stop leaves the task's state to its
    outcome, so `settles` does not say this room as written. The room
    is this note's declaration, like the entry that an active key
    reserves for its revocation. Its form is owed with the row P11 of
    section 12.1.8. `decide-recovery` needs nothing more: it takes
    the failure out of `undecided` in its own entry, which is row 3.
  - Only entries and items are counted here. Bytes and pending
    requests are counted the same way. R4 owns every number.
- **The closing checkpoint. Added in revision 11.** Each scope
  reserves 1 entry, and the bytes of one checkpoint entry, once, from
  its genesis on (R1 section 17.2, "The closing
  checkpoint"). That holds for a lane and for every platform scope of
  this note. Only a checkpoint that is written when no other duty is
  pending, on a head that is not a checkpoint, uses the reservation.
  A checkpoint beside a pending duty is new work, and with no free
  entry it is not written. The next entry that is not a checkpoint
  arms the reservation again. The contract's revision 9 reserved "one
  closing checkpoint" and gave no exact rule. Revision 10 of this
  note left the entry out of this table and of the witness below.
- **A temporary static rule does not cover a hold with a fork or a
  token. New in revision 11.** The contract allows a reserve of one
  fixed size, as a temporary step, only for a definition that
  declares no send, no `settles` and no capability that opens an
  operation. It asks this note what `hold@1` does to records at a
  hold's end (its section 17.3a). This is the answer. The entry that
  ends a hold creates no record. It changes the hold's `instance` to
  `past` and each live `token` of the hold to `revoking`, and it
  opens that token's revocation (section 5.7). An opened operation is
  a duty that no static bound of a definition limits. So a scope
  whose holds have a fork or a token is outside the static rule's
  domain, and only the accounting of this section covers it. A
  fixture whose holds have neither is inside the domain, and needs no
  reserve of records. Made decidable in revision 17: the holds of a
  definition have a fork and tokens exactly when the predicate of
  section 5.7 is true. So the domain of the static rule is read from
  the definition's bytes.

- **Every chain of attempts is finite. Decided in revision 14 (G3).**
  The base retried a revocation, a delete, the push of an unresolved
  publication and a receipt write without a count, and revisions 10
  to 13 reserved the first attempt of each and called each further
  one new work that is opened "when the scope has room". The
  contract's revision 11 rules that out: nothing that a written entry
  holds may depend on the free room (R1 section 17.3). So each
  operation now states its most attempts, and the entry that opens it
  reserves for all of them, as the table says. After the last one the
  scope opens no attempt by itself. The duty stays as it is and stays
  visible. Nothing is released, dropped or inferred. A further try is
  a new operation, opened by an act or a step that is itself new work
  (section 12, G3).
- **Bytes.** A reservation includes the bytes of what its settling
  entry newly retains (R1 section 17.2). Two inputs
  that this note owns are kept under a digest, apart from their
  entry, and the contract asks for the bound on one of each (its
  point R1-28).

  | Input | Bound on one |
  |---|---|
  | A snapshot of staged refs (section 6.2) | From revision 14: the bound on one retained input, which is the contract's and R4's number (G6). No count of its own is proposed. Its size is the number of staged refs in the repository at the read. One pair has a bounded size, because a ref's name has a fixed form and its target is a commit ID. So a bound on the bytes is a bound on the count. Section 6.2, "Work, and what counts it", and U18. |
  | The details of a check's result, with the record of what ran (section 3.11) | None is needed. From revision 14 a lane does not retain them (section 3.11; G6). |

  With that bound the reservation of an ancestry read is finite, so
  the contract's validator has no reason to refuse the definition
  `reserve-unbounded` on its account. A read that returns more than
  the bound gives a `too-large` record, and the act is refused
  `ancestry-too-large`. The number is R4's. So is the retention of
  staged roots, which decides how soon a repository reaches the
  bound (section 12, G6).
  Every other piece of evidence that this note defines is inside its
  outcome entry, and the entry's size bounds it.
- **A request to a full scope.** A request whose deciding entry
  would be new work, at a scope with no room for that entry, is not
  decided. That includes an entry that would record a refusal.
  Transport answers "retry", and the sender keeps the duty (R1
  sections 7.4 and 17.3). So a `reserve` to a full
  destination waits, and its lane shows it as outstanding. A first
  `export-license` to a full lane waits in the same way, whether it
  would be applied or refused: no license exists, so nothing is
  dispatched. A later license request that is bound to a standing pin
  does not wait, because its entry was reserved (section 4.2). A
  `compromised` notice to a
  destination is recordable for a publication that is already
  reserved, because that publication reserved the room. For a key
  that is behind no reserved publication the notice is new work
  there, and nothing rests on it: the next reservation observes each
  key itself (section 6.5).

**Witness: a destination at its budget.** The budget is made up to
show the accounting. It is not a proposal. Entries only are counted
here: pending requests and bytes are counted the same way. G has a
budget of 500 entries. Publication 7 is `unresolved`. The three
attempts that a push may have are all opened (section 12, G3). Its
attempts 1 and 3 were refused and are fully answered. Its attempt 2
was sent, the reply was lost, and its first outcome, `unknown`, is
written. Each attempt's mint, and each token's revocation, is
answered. Its updates `reserved` and `unresolved` were sent and
answered. What publication 7 still reserves, by the two rows above:

| Still reserved for publication 7 | Entries |
|---|---|
| The late answer of attempt 2's push | 1 |
| The read that decides | 1 |
| The final update, a request | 2 |
| One `withdraw` | 1 |
| An abort | 1 |
| The first `compromised` notice | 1 |
| The receipt: three attempts of the write; for each a mint and three attempts of a revocation; and the read | 6 + 6 + 18 + 1 = 31 |
| Total | 38 |

G itself reserves 1 more entry, for its closing checkpoint: the row
"Every scope" of the table above. No other duty of G is pending. So
Reserved is 38 + 1 = 39. Used is 461, and Free is 500 - 461 - 39 = 0.

| Step | Input | Kind | Used | Reserved | Free | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The state before | | 461 | 39 | 0 | |
| 1 | `reserve` for another operation | New work. It needs 1 entry for its delivery, and the reservation of a publication that is queued and then reserved: 4 and 68. That is 73. The closing checkpoint is reserved already, so it adds nothing. | 461 | 39 | 0 | Not decided. Transport answers "retry". The other lane's merge stays `intended`, and its page shows the request as outstanding. |
| 2 | The read that shows the integration commit | Settling. It draws 1. The abort and the notice are no longer needed, and their 2 are released. | 462 | 36 | 2 | Written. Publication 7 is `published`, and the final update is sent. The slot is free. |

It decides nothing about the publication, which is already final. The 33 that stay are the receipt's 31, the `withdraw` and the closing checkpoint. |
| 5 | The `reserve` of step 1, delivered again | New work, needing 73 | 464 | 33 | 3 | Not decided. It is decided when room returns. No rule here makes room by dropping a duty. |

The 4 and the 68 of step 1 are the two destination rows of the table

30 is the push with its three attempts: 6 for the push, 6 for the
three mints and 18 for the three revocations. At every step used,
