**The reservations of the platform definitions, in the contract's forms.
New in revision 27** (the I3 deltas FA3, FC1 and FC2; the contract's
revision 21, its sections 17.2 and 17.2a; the row P11 of section 12.1.8,
which said of the form "No form says it"). That revision of the contract
is not adopted. Every row of this block is in one of its forms, and
takes effect only when a contract revision that carries the form is
adopted. Until then the rows of the table "What each duty reserves",
above, stand as revision 26 has them, and no runtime holds them for a
destination: the I3 source keeps the flag `covered`, counted at 71
entries of each publication that no admission reserves, and a
destination must not be deployed with a budget that its publications
could pass (the delta FC1).

No number of this block is measured. Each amount is a sum, made by one
script from the counts and from the attempts of each kind, and the proof
plan measures it.

*What the old two rows got wrong.* The delta FC1 found three things in
the rows of a publication, and each is corrected here.

| # | Found | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "1 entry for the read that decides" is no upper bound: the rule opened a read after each outcome of a push that decided nothing, and one more for an abort | A push operation opens at most one read (section 12.1.5). A publication holds 3 reads: one for its push, one for an abort and one for its receipt. Each counts 2 entries. |
| 2 | A `resend` had no row | It states `adds`. So does `resend-receipt`, and so does `adopt-head`. |
| 3 | The receipt was 31 of the 68 entries, and no rule drew on them | The rule `receipt` is stated (section 12.1.5). Its part is 32 entries, with 2 for its read. |

**What a publication holds, count by count.** The form is `holds` on the
item type (section 12.1.5). The column "Why no more" is the witness that
each count is an upper bound of what the rules open for one publication,
at the worst case. A reader checks it against the rows of section 12.1.5
that it names.

| Kind | Count | Opened by | Why no more |
|---|---|---|---|
| `judge` | 1 | The rule `open-judge`, or "The next `judge`" in an outcome | A publication is named in `branch.judging` once, while it is `queued`. Its outcome ends `queued` in every case. An outcome that waits for an observation is the same operation. |
| `push` | 1 | The outcome of `judge` that reserves | It reserves once. A further push is a `resend`, which adds its own. |
| `mint` | 6 | The entry that opens an attempt of a write | One for an attempt. The push has at most 3 attempts and the receipt at most 3. |
| `revoke` | 6 | The first of three entries, for one token ("Who opens a revocation") | The entry that opens it empties the slot `token`, so a mint gets at most one. 6 mints. |
| `read` | 3 | An outcome of the push; `abort-if-behind`; an outcome of the receipt | A push operation opens at most one, and a receipt operation at most one (section 12.1.5). `abort-if-behind` opens one, and yields once for a publication, because `aborting` is set once. |
| `receipt` | 1 | The entry that makes the publication `published` | A publication is `published` once. A further write is a `resend-receipt`, which adds to the branch. |
| Requests | 3 | The send `publication-update` | The updates are `reserved`, `unresolved` and one final one. `unresolved` is sent when the state changes to it, and no state leads back from it but a final one. Where the publication is not reserved, the one final update is the only one. |
| Items | 1 | The entry that makes it `published` | The item `receipt`, once. |

**What a branch holds.**

| Kind | Count | Opened by | Why no more |
|---|---|---|---|
| `first-head` | 1 | The genesis, held; or the delivery of `import`, state `done` | The directory's import selects one result, so one `done` arrives (section 12.1.2). The rule `open-first-head` opens one only while the branch is `empty` and no `first-head` was opened for it. |
| `mint` | 6 | As for a publication | 3 attempts of the first head, and 3 of its receipt |
| `revoke` | 6 | The same | One for a mint |
| `read` | 2 | An outcome of the first head; an outcome of its receipt | One for an operation |
| `receipt` | 1 | The entry that makes the branch `ready` by a first head | Once |
| Items | 1 | The same entry | The item `receipt` of the first head |

**What an act adds.** The form is `adds`. Each act is new work, and is
admitted only with room for what it adds.

| Act | On | `adds` | Why that much |
|---|---|---|---|
| `resend` | A publication that is `unresolved` | 1 `push`, 1 `mint`, 1 `revoke`, 1 `read` | The push that it opens has 1 attempt: one mint, one token, and at most one read. The final update and the receipt are in what the publication still holds. |
| `resend-receipt` | The branch | 1 `receipt`, 1 `mint`, 1 `revoke`, 1 `read` | The same, for a receipt's write |
| `adopt-head` | The branch | 1 `adopt-read` | Its one read. The next `judge` that its outcome opens is `for` a publication. |
| `add-room` | A publication that is not final | 1 of each of its six kinds, 1 request and 1 item | The way out of a draw past a count. Signed again if more is needed. |
| `add-branch-room` | The branch | 1 of each of its six kinds, and 1 item | The same |

**The amounts, as sums.** The contract gives one operation of a held
kind k the amount `one(k)`. In entries that is 2 for each attempt that
the kind states: a first outcome and a late answer. Every kind of this
definition is a held kind, and the definition has no timed rule and, as
revision 27 states it, no `settles`. So `one(k)` holds nothing more. A
request reserves 2 entries, a diagnosis and a result: the clauses of the
update are empty. In the table a row of counts gives numbers of
operations, of requests and of items, and a row of entries gives
entries.

| | `judge` | `push` | `mint` | `revoke` | `read` | `receipt` | `first-head` | `adopt-read` | Operations | Entries for them | Requests | Entries in all | Items | Pending requests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Attempts of the kind | 1 | 3 | 1 | 3 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 1 | | | | | | |
| `one(k)`, in entries | 2 | 6 | 2 | 6 | 2 | 6 | 6 | 2 | | | | | | |
| A publication, counts | 1 | 1 | 6 | 6 | 3 | 1 | | | 18 | | 3 | | 1 | 3 |
| A publication, entries | 2 | 6 | 12 | 36 | 6 | 6 | | | | 68 | 6 | 74 | | |
| A branch, counts | | | 6 | 6 | 2 | 1 | 1 | | 16 | | 0 | | 1 | 0 |
| A branch, entries | | | 12 | 36 | 4 | 6 | 6 | | | 64 | 0 | 64 | | |
| `resend`, entries | | 6 | 2 | 6 | 2 | | | | 4 | 16 | 0 | 16 | 0 | 0 |
| `resend-receipt`, entries | | | 2 | 6 | 2 | 6 | | | 4 | 16 | 0 | 16 | 0 | 0 |
| `adopt-head`, entries | | | | | | | | 2 | 1 | 2 | 0 | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| `add-room`, entries | 2 | 6 | 2 | 6 | 2 | 6 | | | 6 | 24 | 2 | 26 | 1 | 1 |
| `add-branch-room`, entries | | | 2 | 6 | 2 | 6 | 6 | 2 | 6 | 24 | 0 | 24 | 1 | 0 |

- *By part, for a publication.* The `judge`, 2. The push with its three
  mints and three revocations, 30. Its read and the read of an abort, 4.
  The receipt with its three mints, its three revocations and its read,
  32. The three updates, 6. That is 74 entries, 1 item and 3 pending
  requests. Records: none.
- *Against the rows of revision 26.* Those rows give 4 and 68, which is
  72. The two are not the same count. Revision 26 counts 1 entry for the
  `judge` and for each read, where the contract's row 5 counts 2. It
  holds 1 entry for an abort, which is an outcome entry of a push or of
  a read and is counted there. And it holds 1 entry for one `withdraw`
  and 1 for the first `compromised` notice, which are no operations.
- *The two entries that `holds` does not carry.* The entry for one
  applied `withdraw`, and the entry for the first `compromised` notice
  that names a key behind the publication. Their forms are the two that
  the verdict on the contract's revision 21 asked to change: the binding
  of a `withdraw`, and the settlement by a truth value. They are carried
  (section 13.17). Until a contract revision states them, each stands as
  revision 26's row has it, as this note's declaration with no form.
  With them a publication reserves 76 entries, and a new `reserve` needs
  77 with its own.
- *Bytes.* By the contract's three amounts, for each entry that is
  counted: its static size, with the rows of `observes` at their `max`;
  what it may newly retain; and nothing for what it starts, which the
  counts hold. For an outcome entry of `judge` the static size is at
  most 248,629 bytes (section 3.3).
  Corrected in revision 28: 236,087 bytes, and 193,612 for the entry
  that records a `reserve` (section 3.3). Of the kinds here only `judge`
  retains anything apart from its entry: for each of its 2 outcome
  entries, one list of extents and one changed set, each of at most
  262,144 bytes (sections 12.1.4 and 12.1.5). No outcome fetches an
  entry. No other number is given: the source counts entries only.
- *Checked in revision 28: no count of this block changes.* The rules T1
  to T8 of section 12.1.5 open one revocation for a mint at the most, as
  before, and each is `for` the holder of its mint. A `resend-receipt`
  still adds 1 `receipt`, 1 `mint`, 1 `revoke` and 1 `read` to the
  branch. The reports that `reserve` names are fetched at its delivery,
  which is new work, so they are in no reservation of a publication. The
  entry that records a `reserve` retains at most 128 entries of other
  scopes, each of at most 262,144 bytes: 33,554,432 bytes, admitted at
  their real size (section 3.3).
- *In the order of use.* The 3 attempts of a write are opened one after
  another. So at one time one mint and one revocation of a write are
  open, and the rest of the count is with the holder. Used and reserved
  together do not rise when an operation is opened: the amount moves
  from the holder to the operation.

**When it is released.** By the contract's rule (its section 17.2a,
"Release").

- *A publication that is not final* holds every count that is left.
- *A final publication* holds a kind only while an open operation of it
  can still reach that kind, and its requests and its item only while
  such an operation exists or an update of it is pending. So one that
  ends `not-reserved` holds nothing once its `judge` is settled. One
  that is `published` holds what is left of every kind that an open
  operation of its receipt can reach by the marks. The mark of the kind
  `read` lists what a read of the branch may open, so by the marks that
  is every kind. What is left by then is mints, revocations and reads:
  its `judge`, its `push` and its `receipt` are drawn. A definition that
  wants less for a receipt states a second kind of read, as the contract
  says. None is stated here.
- *An attempt that stays `unknown`* keeps 1 entry for its late answer,
  and the counts that an outcome of its kind can reach. Whether a read
  may settle such an attempt is the contract's point R1-38, which is
  open.
- *A branch is never final.* So it holds what its first head and its
  acts did not draw for as long as it exists. Where the first head and
  its receipt each succeed at the first attempt, that is 4 mints, 4
  revocations and 2 reads: 36 entries, by the script. It is finite, it
  is counted, and it is more than is needed. The contract has no release
  for a holder with no final state. That is asked (section 13.17).

adopted: `once` on a send mark, and the closure of an operation counted
by outcome entry (its section 17.2). They take effect with a contract
revision that carries them.

- *No rule of the four returns a change of state. Checked in the second
  commit.* The contract's revision 22 has a rule of a form that declares
  `settles` return no `state` effect, and set no slot that a timed rule
  names as its deadline, and the planner decided it so (the act
  `2d3fa911`). `revoke-key` and `remove-member` hold marks at their
  `grant` and among their guards, and none among their effects: each
  changes the state by a written effect. `join` and `enrol` hold one
  effect mark, `key-id`, which returns one `value` effect on the slot
  `id`. Their changes of state are written effects. So all four stand
  under that rule.
- *The names that a mark binds.* `also.member` of `join` and `also.key`
  of `enrol` are bound by the mark `invitation`. The contract's point
  DI17 asks that `of` is `on` or an `also` name, and does not exclude a
  name that a mark binds. The contract is asked to confirm it (section
  13.17). If it does not, the two rows wait, and an invitation reserves
  as revision 26's row says, with no form.
- *The register's closure is larger than revision 26's row.* That row
  counted a revocation and a deletion for each of 3 attempts: 6 + 18 +
  18, and 2 for the request, which is 44. The contract counts by outcome
  entry, a late answer too, at the worst case of the mark: 6 times 13,
  and 2, which is 80. The planner accepted that way of counting (the act
  `39749e26`, answer b). The rule opens no more than before.
- *An invitation reserves more than revision 26's row.* That row counted
  the join and the records of one key and one member. The contract's
  closure counts also what the new key and the new member then await,
  and the inbox's creation.
- *The task scope.* Its rows, with the room of a stop, are IA's. They
  are carried.

shows it and the two acts that end it.

**The sums prove no bound for a whole path. Stated in revision 19**
(the request `837943bb`). The table above gives each duty of a task
scope its own closure: 30 entries for a save, 9 for a restore, and
the rows that revision 19 adds. Each is a sum for one duty. None of
them, and no addition of them, is a capacity bound for a task from
its genesis to its end. Four things are missing, and each is owed.

- *How many closures are open at once.* Several operations may each
  hold a save, beside the rooms of two stops, of one `save` and of
  one host. The most at one time is not stated. Stated plainly in
  revision 20, as the verdict `d2068c05` and the recovery design's
  question B11 ask: the save of a `cancel`, the save of a `pause`
  and the save of one operation each hold 3 places of `cut`. That is
  9, and the `max` of `cut` is 8. The room of the standing `save`
  holds 3 more. This note does not show that those rooms fit side
  by side, or that they need not. It is unproved. The choices are
  open: a guard that keeps places, a larger `max`, rooms that share
  places, or fewer saves in a closure, each with its bytes, records,
  requests and fan-out. The owners are the common capacity work
  under `cc570904`, R4 and IA, with the recovery design for B11.
  Until it is settled, no source may promise an operation that
  cannot be refused: not a stop's save, not the standing `save`, and
  not a save of a fenced root.
  Decided in revision 22, for the places under a type's `max`: the
  rooms do not add. "One save at a time", in section 12.1.7, has the
  rule, the rows that it corrects and the arithmetic. What stays
  unproved is the rest of this point: the entries and the bytes of
  the closures, which are used one after another and do add, and the
  form of a held place.
- *The other four dimensions.* Items by type and by place under each
  `max`, bytes at the bound on one entry, records and pending
  requests are counted here in words. No validator has derived them
  from the definition.
- *What is new work inside the path.* A `retry`, a further `save`,
  an `extend-host`, a replacement restore and a deletion of a key
  that appeared again are each admitted from free room. A path that
  needs one of them at a full scope stops there, and section 13.9
  says where.
- *The fan-out of one entry* that cannot be refused (section 5.7).

The owner is the common capacity work, under `cc570904`, with R4 for
every number and IA for the task's rows. What is owed is one
composition: for the task definition, the most that is used and
reserved together in each of the five dimensions, derived from the
definition's rows and bounds, with each standing room and each place
counted once. Until it exists, a figure of this section is evidence
for its own row, and for nothing wider.

**The exception for one `withdraw`, stated exactly. New in revision
17** (the contract's section 6.11, "Bound means covered"; its section
15.10, seam 1). The contract reads this note's `not-owner` and
`malformed` cases as not bound, and asks for that reading to be
confirmed. It is confirmed. The contract's revision 13, which is
adopted, also names "the one `withdraw` of a publication" as one of
two refusals that draw on a reservation (its point DI21).
This block states that exception in the contract's terms. It changes
no outcome of revisions 11 to 16.

*The binding.* A `withdraw` is bound to a publication when all of
these hold, in G's commit.

| # | The request is bound when | Read from |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The message is whole. Its one field, `operation`, is present and of its type, and it has no other member. | The message. |
| 2 | The envelope's source scope, with its incarnation, is the scope that the operation's fact is in. | The envelope; the field. |
| 3 | G holds a publication for that operation, and that publication still holds its entry for one `withdraw`: `withdrawDecided` is false, and the publication's last duty has not ended. | The publication. |
| 4 | It is the first delivery of that envelope. | G's index of decided deliveries (R1 section 7.4). |

*What each kind of `withdraw` decides.*

| A `withdraw` | Bound | Decided | Capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whole, from the lane that owns the operation, for a publication that holds its entry | Yes | By the table of section 6.4: `applied` while `queued`; `refused`, with `reserved` or `ended`, in every later state. The mark is set. Corrected in revision 25: the mark is set where the `withdraw` is applied, and a refusal sets none. | Settling. It uses the 1 entry. It is never left undecided for capacity. Corrected in revision 25: that holds for the applied case. A refused `withdraw` is new work until the contract has a form (section 12.1.5). Stated in revision 27: that form will not come by this note's ask, which is withdrawn. The applied case is the rule (section 13.17, Part D). |
| Whole, from another scope than the one that the operation's fact is in | No | `refused`, `not-owner`. Nothing in G changes, and the mark is not set. | New work. With no free room it is not decided, and transport answers "retry". |
| Not whole. This is `malformed`, which is the contract's `bad-field`. It may come from any sender, the owning lane too. | No | `refused`, `bad-field`, before any handler runs. Nothing changes, and the mark is not set. | New work, in the same way. |
| Whole, from the owning lane, before its `reserve` has arrived | No: G holds no publication | `applied`. G opens the publication as `not-reserved`, "withdrawn". | New work. |
| Whole, from the owning lane, after the mark is set, or after the publication's last duty ended | No | `refused`, with `reserved` or `ended`. | New work. |
| A repeat of an envelope | | The first deciding entry is the answer. Nothing is written. | Nothing. |

*The exception, exactly.* Every entry of G that records a refusal is
new work, apart from one: the deciding entry of the first bound
`withdraw` of a publication, when it refuses. That entry is a
settling entry, as it is when it applies. It draws on what the
publication reserved for it at its `reserve`: 1 entry, with its bytes
and the bytes of the foreign entries that it retains. It opens no
item, changes no record and sends no request of its own. When it
applies, the final update that it sends is the one that the
publication already reserved.
Corrected in revision 25: "when it refuses" waits on a form of the
contract. Until then the settling entry is the one that applies, and
a `withdraw` that is refused is new work (section 12.1.5, "A refused
`withdraw` sets nothing").
Stated in revision 27: the contract adds no place for an effect of a
refused deciding entry (its revision 19, section 15.6s; its revision 21,
section 15.3g, which is not adopted). So this note's ask for that place
is withdrawn, and the exception covers an applied `withdraw` as the
rule, with nothing more awaited from that ask. Whether a refused
`withdraw` of the owning lane is settled from what its publication holds
is the contract's form `bound`, which is under repair. It is carried
(section 13.17).

*Why it is safe.* It meets the contract's five conditions (R1
section 17.3).

- An admitted duty made the room: the delivery of `reserve`, which
  is new work and was admitted only with that room.
- The requests are bounded and counted: one decision for one
  publication, counted by `withdrawDecided`.
- The covered decision sets the mark in its own entry. So the entry
  is used once, whatever is decided.
  Corrected in revision 25: a refusal cannot set the mark. So this
  condition holds for an applied decision only, and the exception is
  narrowed to it until the contract has a form (section 12.1.5).
  Stated in revision 27: the contract adds no such form, and this note's
  ask for it is withdrawn. The exception covers an applied `withdraw`,
  as the rule (section 13.17, Part D).
- The binding reads the verified envelope, the message's own field
  and the publication, and nothing else.
- A repeat uses nothing.

*Its bound.* One entry for each publication that G admitted, used at
most once. Over G's whole history that is at most the number of its
`reserve` entries. Only the lane that sent a publication's `reserve`
can be bound to it, because a `reserve` is refused `not-owner` unless
the operation's fact is in its sender (section 12.1.5). So no scope
uses an entry that another lane's publication reserved. And no
message makes G hold more than it held before the message came.

*Why a `withdraw` that is not whole is not bound, when a license
request may be.* A license request is bound by two of its five
fields, read by themselves, and that is the contract's standing form
(section 4.2). A `withdraw` has one field, and it is the field that
finds the publication. A message with no usable `operation` names no
publication, so there is nothing to bind it to. The only other
message that is not whole has a member that is not declared, beside
a good `operation`. A correct lane sends none: the row `cancel-merge`
builds the message. This note keeps the reading that the contract
already has, and covers the whole message only.

*Case.* G is as at step 0 of the witness above: no free room, and
publication 7 `unresolved`. P's runtime is faulty, and its `withdraw`
for publication 7 carries a second member. It is not bound. Its
deciding entry would be `refused`, `bad-field`, as new work that
needs 1 entry. G has none free, so it is not decided, and transport
answers "retry". Publication 7 keeps its entry, and its mark is not
set. When G has room, the entry is written from that room, and the
mark is still not set. Control: if that message were bound, a faulty
message would use the one entry and set the mark. A whole `withdraw`
that P sent later, after an `undelivered` diagnosis (section 12.1.5),
would then be new work.

### 5.9 The recovery design's cuts, aligned

New in revision 14. The recovery successor design, revision 2 at
`dafb5b0c`, states how a hosted coding environment is saved and
restored. It adds no rule of authority (its decision RS-17) and uses
this note's windows, controls, revocation rules and lifecycle as they
are. It read this note at revision 13. This section says where the
two fit, what this revision changes to make them fit, and what each
still owes the other. Its identifiers are as that design gives them.
It is a proposal, like the rest of revision 14.

Stated in revision 16. Revision 2 of that design is the adopted one.
Its revision 4, at `16777d97`, was approved by review on 2026-10-05
(verdict `d432a424`), and its adoption is pending. This section rests
on revision 2. The one rule that revision 16 takes from it, in
section 8.2, reads the same in both.

Corrected in revision 17 (the approval `33787163`). Revision 4 of
that design, at `16777d97`, is adopted, by the planner's act
`2621bc2f`. It is the text in force. By its own record it changes no
rule of its sections 5 to 10 and nothing of its stage two. So what
this section took from revision 2 stands under revision 4, under the
same section numbers. Revision 4 still reads this note at its
revision 13, and still lists the task definition as owed. Section
12.1.7 is that definition, and it was adopted with revision 16.
Where the two notes' records meet, what a save and a restore
reserve, and what a checkpoint's receipt is evidence of, are in
section 12.1.7, "What a save and a restore reserve".

| The recovery design's term | In this note | Aligned in revision 14 |
|---|---|---|
| Checkpoint: a manifest for which a receipt exists | A private resource of a task. Its receipt is the `checkpoint` item of the task scope (section 12.1.7). | The identity of section 5.1 gains two members that the design adds: the hold's epoch when the instance was registered, and the save job. |
| Task | The task scope: one worker, one lane, one conversation. | The definition is section 12.1.7. |
| Lane | The lane that owns the hold. It judges a tool dispatch and a push. It sends nothing to the task scope when a hold ends. | Unchanged. |
| Incarnation | Part of each scope reference: the task's and the lane's. | Unchanged. Both are in a checkpoint's identity. |
| Hold | An item of the lane. A new holder, and a holder that resumes after its hold ended, takes a new hold. | Unchanged. |
| Epoch | The hold's, in the lane (R1 section 6.8). It is counted for one hold. The epochs of two holds are not compared: a guard compares the hold and the epoch together. | The lane's `instance` record carries the hold's epoch at the entry that made the instance current, so that a task scope reads it from one fetched entry (section 5.7). |
| Instance | One start of an environment. A hold has one current instance at a time, and may have several over its life: a restore after a host is lost makes a new one. | Section 5.1 already says "new at each start". The order of a new instance is stated below. |
| Job | One dispatch of work to an instance. | Named `job` in the task definition's `cut` and `checkpoint` only. A check job of section 3.11 is another thing. |
| Journal | Two private resources of a task: the conversation and the commands. Never entries. | An operation's intent is an entry of the task scope, with a digest of its private record. A `cut` item holds the journal positions of one checkpoint. |
| Pointer, registration | Local state of the task scope. | `task.current`, and the `registration` item. |

**A new instance, in order.** The recovery design relies on the lane
knowing a hold's current instance, and does not say how the lane
learns of a restore's instance. This is the order.

1. The worker's key asks the lane for the step `instance`, with a
   new instance ID that the task's runtime minted, on an observation
   within ten seconds (section 5.7). The lane's entry makes that
   instance `current` and the earlier one `past`. From that entry
   on, the lane answers a fence check from the earlier instance "not
   this instance".
2. The task scope's act `register` presents that entry. It opens the
   registration, `starting`, with the hold, the hold's epoch at that
   entry, and the instance. The earlier registration is `stale` in
   the same entry. `register` needs no registration before it, so it
   is also the first step of a fresh task.
3. The worker's act `intend` opens the restore as an operation
   (section 12.1.7). It names the hold, the epoch and the instance,
   and they must be those of the registration of step 2. It is
   admitted while that registration is `starting` and has opened no
   restore, or is `restore-failed` and has opened fewer than 3. It
   needs no `ready` registration. From revision 16 it is admitted
   only while no failed recovery of the task is `undecided`: "A
   recovery that failed", below.
4. The restore's outcome. `confirmed` makes the registration
   `ready`. `refused` makes it `restore-failed`. With no answer the
   outcome is `unknown` and the registration stays `starting`: a
   further restore then needs a new instance, by steps 1 and 2.
   Changed in revision 16: after `refused`, step 3 may be taken again
   under the rule below, and at most 3 times for one registration.
   Revision 15 let the worker take it again at once.

**Corrected in revision 15** (review `14ad7c42`). Revision 14 put the
`intend` first, before any registration, and asked for a `ready`
registration before every `intend`. Only step 4 makes a registration
`ready`, so no restore could be opened, for a fresh task or after a
failed restore. The order above is the one that a replay follows:
`register`, `intend` for the restore, its outcome, `ready`. An edit,
a command, a commit preparation, a dissociation, a push and a save
all stay behind `ready`.

**A recovery that failed. New in revision 16** (review `60c940f3`).
The recovery design names five failures of a restore that are faults
of the checkpoint: `checkpoint-missing`, `checkpoint-corrupt`,
`git-mismatch`, `unsupported-checkpoint` and `expired` (its section
8.2). Each fails closed. What can follow is "a person's recorded
decision, never a default": an operator restores the stored bytes and
the restore is tried again as a new job, or the owner starts again
knowingly, which abandons the chain. Revision 15 let a worker open a
replacement restore from `restore-failed` with no such record. So an
agent with its own grant could sign a second restore at once. The
rule is now this, and section 12.1.7 has its rows.

- *The failure is a record of the task scope.* A restore's outcome
  that is `refused` with one of the five reasons opens an item,
  `failure`, in the state `undecided`. It holds the registration,
  with its hold, epoch and instance, the restore's operation, the
  reason, and the checkpoint that the pointer named.
- *Nothing is restored while it is `undecided`.* No `intend` for a
  restore is admitted, under that registration or under a new one.
  The refusal is named `recovery-undecided`. A new instance does not
  help the worker: `register` is admitted, and its first restore is
  refused in the same way.
- *Who decides.* The task's controller or an admin, by a device key,
  with `task.control` on an observation within sixty seconds (W2).
  That is the grant of every control (section 3.2). The role `agent`
  does not hold it, and the worker's `task.operate` does not admit
  the act. The recovery design says "an operator" and "the owner".
  In this note's roles both are the person who controls the task, or
  an admin. Restoring the stored bytes is an operator's work outside
  this scope, and no entry records it. The decision is what is
  recorded.
- *What the decision names.* The act `decide-recovery` names the
  failure, and repeats its hold, its epoch, its instance, its
  operation, its reason and its checkpoint. Each must equal what the
  failure holds. The task is the scope that the act is addressed to.
  It also names the choice: `repair` or `abandon`. So the entry says
  who decided, about which failed restore, and what.
- *Repair.* The failure is `repair`. The next `intend` for a restore
  is admitted, under that registration while it has opened fewer
  than 3, or under a new instance. That entry makes the failure
  `retried`. So one decision admits one replacement. If the
  replacement fails for a fault of the checkpoint, its outcome opens
  a new failure, and a new decision is needed. A restore of an
  `expired` checkpoint cannot be repaired by restoring bytes, and its
  replacement fails again.
- *Abandon.* The failure is `abandoned`. In the same entry the
  pointer is emptied, the checkpoint that it named is `kept`, and the
  registration is `fenced` when it was `starting` or `restore-failed`.
  The task keeps its state and is not ended. A new chain starts by
  steps 1 to 4 in a new instance: its restore starts the environment
  from the hold's fork alone, and its first save has no prior. The
  abandoned chain's receipts stay as records. Every pin on them
  stands, and so does every unsettled effect: abandoning settles
  nothing outside (section 5.6).
- *What needs no decision.* The first restore of a fresh task. A
  restore after a host is lost, when no restore has failed. A new
  instance after a restore whose outcome is `unknown`, as revision 15
  has it. A replacement after a `refused` outcome whose reason is
  none of the five, such as a host that could not be started: that
  names no fault of the checkpoint, and the bound of 3 for one
  registration is its only limit. The reason is the runtime's report,
  and it is trusted as every outcome's evidence is.
- *A late answer.* A restore whose registration was replaced or
  fenced may still answer. If it answers `refused` with one of the
  five reasons, it opens the failure all the same, unless an instance
  has become `ready` since, the pointer has moved, or a failure is
  already `undecided`. So a worker
  cannot avoid the record by registering a new instance, or by
  fencing, before the answer arrives.

If the lane refuses step 1, because the hold has ended, nothing is
registered. The worker takes a new hold first, and that is the
design's "the same holder resumes". Between steps 1 and 2 the earlier
instance can start no tool and no push, and it can still commit a
save in the task scope. That save is private work of the same task,
and it is the registration's own. From step 2 on it can commit none,
because its registration is `stale`. So the pointer does not move
between steps 2 and 4, and the checkpoint that step 3 names is the
one that step 4 restores.

**The cases.** Each row is a case that the recovery design or its
acceptance map names. The third column is what the two notes give
together.

| Case | This note | Together |
|---|---|---|
| One device of several is revoked | Section 3.5, rule 3; section 3.7. | Nothing changes for the task, the hold, the token or the instance. A control from the revoked key is refused within sixty seconds. |
| The last key is revoked, or the controller is removed | Sections 3.5, 3.7 and 4.3. | No `intend` is admitted, so no tool and no push starts. The gateway's route is closed. A save that was already opened may commit. The hold is not renewed and runs out. Work is kept. Admins keep private read, export and stop. From revision 15 an admin's `pause` or `cancel` is applied by its own outcome entry, and it waits for no act of the worker (section 12.1.7). |
| Recovery of an active member, and a resume | Section 3.6: an admin, or the recovery key, issues an invitation for a replacement key of the active member. Section 4.3: a restored controller key must resume explicitly. | Nothing restarts by itself. A signed `resume` control is applied by the worker's `apply`. If the hold ended, the worker takes a new hold. Then the four steps above, and a restore of the checkpoint that the pointer names. A removed member is never restored. |
| A private export | Section 4.2. | The export names one checkpoint by its ID. The copy to the transfer stage is checked against the manifest. The source pin is the `pin` item, `export-source`. It carries the root alone, and no journal (the design's RU-13; section 5.6). |
| A takeover in the same lane | Sections 4.3 and 5.2. | The new holder has a new hold, a new fork, its own task scope, its own pointer and a first checkpoint with no prior. The former holder's chain is untouched and private. A save from the former holder's old instance moves only the former holder's own pointer. |
| A restore fails for a fault of the checkpoint. New in revision 16. | "A recovery that failed", above; section 12.1.7. | The instance is `restore-failed` and runs nothing. The pointer does not move. No earlier checkpoint and no empty root is offered. No restore is admitted until the controller or an admin signs `decide-recovery`. `repair` admits one replacement. `abandon` empties the pointer and starts a chain with no prior. |
| An export to a hold of another lane | Not designed (U15). | Owed, by this note's successor. |
| A person holds the hold | G9: section 12.1.7. | The authority is decided. The runtime is IA's (the design's RU-19). |
| Own-device key custody | Section 3.6: a key is made and kept on its device. Section 3.7: an agent's key is held by the task scope's signer. | The command journal holds no device key and is no device's journal of unsent acts. A checkpoint holds no credential field. |
| A read session against a control | Sections 3.9 and 4.1. | A session reads the minimal projection and never controls. Neither journal is readable through a session. |
| An agent's own lifecycle | Section 3.7: an agent is its own member, with its own key and a controller fixed at its creation. | Closing a browser changes nothing. Another active device of the controller keeps the agent working. |
| Delegation | Section 3.4: deferred, with its record stated (decision D2-7; U6). | Not used by the recovery design. Its named later scope is kept. |

**What the recovery design asks of this note, and the answer.**

| Asked | Answer in revision 14 |
|---|---|
| RU-15: the forms of the receipt, the pointer, the registration, an operation and a save's frozen cut in the task definition | Section 12.1.7. The two byte-domain tags that it proposes, `artroom-checkpoint-1` and `artroom-checkpoint-node-1`, are declared by the task definition for its own private values. |
| RU-10: who may declare a command read-only | The controller, by a control (section 12.1.7). |
| RU-11: whether a pin for an unsettled effect may be released without that effect's answer | No. Section 5.6 stands. The cost is bytes kept without end for an effect that is never answered. A later choice is the planner's, with this note's successor. |
| RU-12: a restore from a named older checkpoint | Not offered in the first version. No control asks for one. |
| RU-13: what an export carries | The root alone (section 5.6). |
| RU-14: the fork push | Accepted, below. |
| RU-16: a custody row for the credential of owned checkpoint storage | Sections 5.3 and 5.5. |
| RU-19: the environment of a hold that a person holds | G9. |

**A push to a hold's fork.** The base said that a fork push is an
operation of the task scope and gave it no evidence row. The rule is
the publication's (section 6.6), stated for a fork.

- **Before dispatch.** The intent's private record holds the fork,
  the ref, the expected old value, the exact ID of a prepared commit
  that a checkpoint already holds, and the registration's epoch and
  instance. For the first push to a fork the expected old value is
  the fork's seed.
- **The send.** The fence check of section 5.2 comes first. The
  gateway records that it is forwarding before it forwards. Each
  attempt is recorded "not sent", "refused" or "unknown", as section
  6.6 classifies a send. At most 3 attempts, each the same
  compare-and-swap (G3).
- **What decides.** A read of the fork's ref. It shows the prepared
  commit: the effect is confirmed, and an attempt whose reply was
  lost stays `unknown` (G1). It shows the expected old value: a
  further attempt may be sent. It shows anything else: an incident.
- **One guard more.** While an attempt of a push is `unknown`, the
  runtime sends no push to that ref whose new value is the expected
  old value of that attempt. A fork has one writer by custody, but
  that writer may rewrite its own history, and a ref that returned to
  the old value would let a late send apply.
- It rests on H1 and H3, under the same owners as for the branch.

**What this note asks of the recovery design.** That its text take
the four differences of section 12.1.7: a signed check of a stream,
a signed license request, a signed `withhold`, and `fenced` as a
record. From revision 16: that it take the `failure` item and the
act `decide-recovery` as the record of the decision that its section
8.2 asks for, and say whether a `refused` restore can have a reason
outside its five. And that its assumptions A1 to A12 be read from primary
documentation together with what the Git host and the serving
platform document for H1, H2, H5 and H6 (section 12). From revision
17: the six things of section 12.1.7, "Asked of the recovery
design".
From revision 19: that design's revision 5, which is proposed and
under review (as it was in revision 19: the opening, "The standing
in force", has its present standing), answers the six and asks ten
things back. Section
12.1.7, "The recovery design's ten asks", answers each. What this
note now asks of that design is at the end of that block.

## 6. Publication

### 6.1 Parties and items

| Party | Holds |
|---|---|
| Change lane P | The `merge` item for one operation; the manifest it names; the verdicts and jobs on it. Also its own commitments and holds, when its integration work is held in it (section 6.2). |
| Destination scope G | The **slot**: free, or held by one publication. The recorded **head** of the branch. A **publication** item for each operation. A record for each **attempt**. The token ledger. |
| Publisher | A container with Git and nothing else, behind a gateway. |
| Gateway | For each attempt, one **grant**: this ref, from this old commit to this new one. It records, durably and before it forwards, that it is forwarding. It forwards one update for a grant and then closes it. |
| Git host | The repository. |

Corrected in revision 25 (the I3 delta ER5): "a record for each
attempt" and "the token ledger" are no items of the destination. The
record of an attempt is the ledger's own. The token ledger is the
operations of the kinds `mint` and `revoke`, with two slots (section
12.1.5).

G is the only writer of the branch. That rests on three things: only G
mints a write token narrowed to that ref; the founding register lets one
directory, and so one destination, exist for a repository; and the
repository at the host is created at founding under a name used once.

States of a publication in G: `queued`, `reserved`, `publishing`,
`unresolved`, and the final states `published`, `aborted`,
`not-reserved`.

States of the `merge` item in P (R2 section 4.1): `intended`,
`committed`, `unknown`, and the final states `published`, `refused`,
`aborted`. The item also has a `withdrawal` slot: empty or `asked`.
The outcome of a withdrawal is not in the slot. It is the lane's
recorded result entry for the `withdraw` request (R2 revision 9;
section 6.4).

### 6.2 Staging the objects

A commit can be reviewed, checked and published only if its objects are
in the canonical repository. Staging puts them there. It is a real
write to the canonical repository, and it happens before the act that
needs it is admitted. So it needs its own authority and its own record.

**Who stages.** Always the **staging lane**: the lane that owns the
hold whose fork holds the commit. That lane owns the hold item, the
fork, the fork read token and the record of what it staged. No lane
stages from another lane's hold, and nobody reads another lane's fork.

**A hold in a change lane. Proposed for reviewed adoption.** Revision 4
let only an issue lane own a hold. A person who wanted to change one
file then had to file an issue, and take a commitment and a hold in it,
before a pull request could have content. That was a prerequisite the
`change` form did not declare. This revision proposes, with R2 revision
7, section 4.3:

- The `change` definition declares the hold capability that `issue`
  declares, `hold@1`. It holds `commitment`, `hold` and `export` items
  with the same slots and guards as the ones in `issue`, less the parts
  that read a goal's conditions or a report. No second runtime is
  built: it is the declared capability, used by a second definition.
- A commitment in a change lane is a commitment to integrate that pull
  request. A hold under it has its own fork, token, environment and
  instance, by section 5.1 unchanged.
- A change lane stages only from its own holds, and only for its own
  manifests. For such a commit the staging lane is P itself.
- A hold in an issue lane stays a valid source. Work in an issue, the
  split of a goal into concerns, and the assembly of their accepted
  reports are unchanged. An issue is a choice. It is not a
  prerequisite.
- No check is lowered. Every row below that needs a commitment, a
  performer, a held hold, a current instance or a grant needs it in
  either kind of lane. The grant for work in a change lane is
  `change.work`, held by the roles that hold `issue.work` (section
  3.2).

This is permission to revise the design. It commissions no source. It
is adopted only when both notes are reviewed.

**Three sources.** A commit is staged for one of two acts, and an
integration commit has one of two homes. The three sources are stated
separately.

| | Report source | Integration source, a hold in an issue lane | Integration source, a hold in the change lane |
|---|---|---|---|
| The act that needs the commit | `report`, in an issue lane L | `propose-manifest`, in a change lane P | `propose-manifest`, in a change lane P |
| Who made the commit, and where | The performer of the commitment reported on, in the environment of a hold under it | The integrator, in the environment of a hold under the integrator's own commitment in L. Assembly is work (R2 section 5.4). | The integrator, in the environment of a hold under the integrator's own commitment in P |
| The source, exactly | L with its incarnation; the hold's item ID; the hold's current instance; the commit | The same four, for the integrator's hold. The intent names the first three in its `source` field. | The same four, with P's own reference as the lane. The intent names the hold and the instance in `source`; the lane is the one the intent is addressed to. |
| The staging lane | L | L. Never P. | P |
| Judged by the staging lane from its own state | The commitment is `accepted` and the signer is its performer. The hold is `held` under that commitment, its end time has not passed on the lane's clock, its holder is the signer's member, and the instance is its current one. | The same, for the integrator's commitment and hold in L. | The same, for the integrator's commitment and hold in P. |
| Grant, by an observation within ten seconds, read for that commit (section 3.12, W3) | `issue.work` in L | `issue.work` in L, observed by L. And `change.propose` in P, observed by P. | `change.work` and `change.propose` in P, both observed by P. |
| Judged by P from its own state | Nothing. P takes no part. | The signature and `notAfter`; the proposal is `draft` or `open`; no merge is in progress; and L's pin entry names this intent's digest, this commit, P, and the lane, hold and instance that `source` names. | The signature and `notAfter`; the proposal is `draft` or `open`; no merge is in progress; and the row "judged by the staging lane", because P is that lane. |
| How the act comes to rely on the commit | L's own record of the staged root, in the entry that admits the report | A pin that L records for P, below. P reads no fork and no present state of L. | P's own record of the staged root, in the entry that admits the manifest |
| What moves between lanes | Nothing | The commit's objects, once, from the fork to the canonical repository. Two messages about the pin, below. No file, token or environment moves. | Nothing |

**The `source` field.** A `propose-manifest` intent always names where
its integration commit was built. The field is signed with the intent.
It is preparation data and provenance. It is not something the manifest
selects.

| Part | Is | Authenticated by |
|---|---|---|
| The lane | The staging lane's full reference, with its incarnation. Left out when the hold is in the change lane that the intent is addressed to. | The signature over the intent. For another lane, also that lane's own pin entry, which names the lane it is an entry of. |
| The hold | The hold's item ID in that lane. | The staging lane's own state: the hold exists there, its holder is the signer's member, and it is under a commitment whose performer is the signer. |
| The instance | The runtime instance the commit was built in. | The staging lane's own state: it is the hold's current instance for a new staging, or the instance in the live root's record for a reuse. |

No part is taken on the client's word. A `source` that names another
member's hold, a hold of another lane as if it were local, or an
instance the hold never had, fails the staging lane's guards before
dispatch, and nothing is staged. The entry that admits the manifest
keeps the field, so a verifier reads where each version was built. A
manifest does not have to name an issue. A change with no goal, no
plan and no selected report names a hold of its own lane.

**What a one-person change costs.** In its change lane: `open`; `offer`
and `accept`, which one member may sign when they hold both grants;
`take-hold`; the work; and `propose-manifest`. Those are acts of that
pull request. No issue is filed. R2's page that proposes a version
names the commitment and the hold as steps (R2 section 10.4.1), so
nothing is described as free that is not. A member with no held hold
in any lane still has no fork and no source, and can stage nothing
new.

**Authors.** A manifest's `authors` take in the attribution of the
commitment that the source hold is under: every performer it ever had,
and every holder of a hold under it (R1 section 6.7). For a hold in P, P
derives that from its own history. For a hold in L, L's pin entry
carries the list, with the authors of the inputs used under that
commitment, and P copies it. R2 revision 8 adds the authors of the
manifest that this one supersedes, and this note agrees: an earlier
version's commit is staged where a later integrator can build on it. So
a former performer or holder of the integrator's commitment cannot give
the counted review, in either kind of lane (section 3.10).

**Work that no recorded fact names: R2's point R2-18. Accepted in
part, as a proposal for review.** A fork is made from the canonical
repository, so a holder can fetch a commit that another commitment
staged, build on it, and name no selection. The seed rule of section
5.2 does not put such a commit in a fork's starting point. It does not
stop a holder from fetching one. R2 asks for a check of the commit's
ancestry against the staged roots. This note proposes it, as a guard
of R1's `git-read` capability, with its limits stated. S is the
staging lane: the lane that owns the source hold.

*When.* In the preparation of every `report` and every
`propose-manifest`, for a new staging and for a reuse, after the root
is `live` and before the act is admitted or a pin is recorded for
another lane. "The order of steps", below, is the one order. The
check is not a condition of the root becoming `live`. A `live` root
proves that the objects are present. It proves nothing about their
ancestry.

*What is read.* Only the canonical repository, in one read step with
its own token duty in S's ledger. No other lane's state is read.

1. The destination branch's head.
2. The list of refs under `refs/artroom/staged/`, each with its
   target, as the host returns it then. This list is the **snapshot**.
   It is mutable state of the host: a later staging adds a ref, and a
   retirement removes one.
3. Commits by ID, which are immutable.

*The walk.* The commit that the act names is the **start**. The start
is never a stop. It is in F only by the rule "The start", below. S
visits each parent of the start, and walks on through parents. Every
parent of the start is visited, whatever S's ledger says about the
start.

The walk stops at three kinds of commit. Each rests on evidence that
exists apart from the staging being judged:

- **The branch.** A commit that is reachable from the destination
  branch's head, as read for this check. The evidence is the head.
- **A checked own root.** The commit of one of S's own roots under the
  source commitment, when an earlier entry of S is a **prior check**
  of that commit. A prior check is an entry that admitted a `report`
  or a `propose-manifest` for that commit under that commitment and
  retains its ancestry record; or a pin entry of S that carries the
  record, once S has recorded for that pin a `pin-confirm`, or an
  `unpin` with the record that the manifest was admitted. The
  evidence is that entry.
- **A selected report.** In an issue lane, the commit of a report that
  a `selected` input of the source commitment names. The evidence is
  the input, which names an admitted report. Its authors are already
  in that commitment's attribution (R2 section 3.4).

The branch is tried first. A commit that is reachable from the head
is published history. It is a stop of the first kind, whatever else
it is, and nothing is carried through it.

A root is not a stop because S's ledger records it, or because it is
`live`. So these are not stops: the root of the staging being judged;
any root in `creating`; a root whose act was refused or never
admitted; a root whose pin is still `provisional`. Revision 6 stopped
at any own root under the source commitment. The candidate was such a
root, so the walk could end at its start and find nothing. That rule
is withdrawn.

Of the other commits it visits, each one that is the target of a
staged ref goes into a list F. The walk does not go past a commit in
F.

**What a checked own root carries.** A stop at a checked own root
does not hide what lay under it. Each commit in the F of its prior
check is added to this check's F, marked as carried through that
stop. So what was named for the earlier act must be named again, or
be covered by the row below. A start that the prior check put in F is
carried like the rest. Its commit is then the stop's own commit. One
kind of commit is not carried: a commit of that F that is reachable
from this check's head. It is published history now.

*The start.* Revision 7 said that the start is never in F. Then a
holder could fetch a commit that another commitment had staged, stage
that same commit again as their own root, and propose it. Its parents
were clean, so F was empty, and its authors were in no record. That
rule is withdrawn. S's own root for the start shows that the objects
are present. It does not show who the work belongs to, and it cannot
answer for another staged ref on the same commit.

S takes from the snapshot every staged ref whose target is the start.
It sorts each one, by the ref's name and S's own ledger:

- **Own.** The ref names S and S's incarnation, and its root number is
  a root that S's ledger records under the source commitment. The root
  of the staging being judged is one. An earlier root of the same
  commit under that commitment is another.
- **Foreign.** Every other ref: of another lane, of another
  incarnation, of S under another commitment, or with a root number
  that S's ledger does not hold.

Each ref is sorted by itself. An own ref never hides a foreign one,
whichever comes first in the snapshot. No Git author text is read.

When no ref on the start is foreign, the start is not in F and nothing
more is asked. That is every ordinary case: a commit that the holder
built and staged, new or reused.

When a ref on the start is foreign, the start is a **foreign start**.
S then asks one question before any basis: is the start published?

*A published start.* The start is published when it is reachable from
the destination branch's head, as read for this check. This is the
test of the stop "The branch", applied to the start. It reads `head`
and commits by ID, and nothing else. A published start is published
history:

- It is not in F, and no basis is asked for it. Its work is on the
  branch, and the publication that put it there named its authors.
- A foreign ref on it changes nothing. How long another lane keeps a
  root is that lane's retention. It does not decide whether the
  published revision can be inspected, checked and reported.
- The refs on it are still sorted, each by itself, and the record
  still names the first foreign one. The record marks the start
  `published`.
- Every parent of a published start is on the branch. The walk stops
  at each one, and F is empty.

Revision 8 had no such test. A report of the current head, made while
another commitment's root on that head was still kept, reached the
basis `row` with F = [the head] and was refused. That contradicted the
rule that published history is never listed, and it is corrected
here.

The test uses the head that this check read and the record keeps. A
commit that was published after that read is not published for this
check. That fails closed: a basis is asked, and a later preparation
reads the head again.

When a foreign start is not published, one basis answers for it. They
are tried in this order:

| Basis | Holds when | The start | Why the work is named |
|---|---|---|---|
| `own-check` | An earlier entry of S is a prior check of the start under the source commitment, and that check's record has no foreign start. | Not in F. | The commit was judged as this commitment's own when no other staged ref targeted it. The other ref came later, from a fetch of the canonical repository. |
| `input` | In an issue lane, a `selected` input of the source commitment names an admitted report of the start. | Not in F. | The input's authors are already in that commitment's attribution (R2 section 3.4). |
| `row` | Neither holds. | In F, marked as the start, with the first foreign ref of the snapshot that targets it. | Only if the act's row, below, names it. |

A prior check here is the one defined for a checked own root, above.
It must be an earlier entry. The entry of the act being judged is
never its own basis. A prior check whose record has a foreign start
is no `own-check` basis, published or not.

*The judgment.* The lane that the act is addressed to judges F from
its own state and the act's fetched facts. For a manifest whose source
is a hold in an issue lane L, L's pin entry carries F and P reads it
there, as it reads the attribution list.

| Act | Admitted only when |
|---|---|
| `report` | F is empty, carried commits and the start included. |
| `propose-manifest` | Each commit in F, the start included, is the commit of a report that this manifest selects; or the integration commit of an earlier manifest of this change lane; or is carried through a stop whose commit is the integration commit of an earlier manifest of this change lane. This manifest takes in that manifest's authors (R2 section 5.4), and they include the authors of what it selected. |

A commit in F that fails its row refuses the act `unnamed-work`, with
that commit. A foreign start is refused by the same refusal. No new
one is named. The ways forward are the acts that name work and carry
its authors: `use-input` on an accepted report, or a selection. A
foreign start with no accepted report has no way forward by its ID,
until its work is reported and accepted, or is on the branch. Once it
is on the branch, and a check reads a head that holds it, it is a
published start and no basis is asked.

*The record.* F is a result. It is derived from the snapshot, which
changes later. So the entry keeps what the check read, and not only
what it concluded. Revision 6 kept F and the head, and said a verifier
could walk again "from the repository as read now". That is withdrawn:
the refs as read now are not the refs that were judged.

```ts
interface AncestryCheck {
  commit: CommitId;                              // the commit judged
  root: { number: number; state: "live" };       // S's root for that commit, as S's ledger held it at the check
  head: CommitId;                                // the destination branch's head, as read for this check
  snapshot: { digest: Digest; count: number };   // the staged refs as returned: { ref, target } pairs in byte order of ref, as canonical JSON
  start:
    | { foreign: null }                          // every staged ref of the snapshot that targets `commit` is own
    | { foreign: string; published: true }       // a foreign ref, and `commit` is reachable from `head`: published history, no basis
    | { foreign: string;                         // the first foreign ref of the snapshot that targets `commit`, which is not reachable from `head`
        basis:
          | { kind: "own-check"; checked: FactRef }  // an earlier prior check of `commit` whose `start.foreign` is null
          | { kind: "input"; input: FactRef }
          | { kind: "row" } };                   // `commit` is in F, marked `start`
  stops: readonly (
    | { kind: "own-root"; commit: CommitId; root: number; state: "live" | "retiring" | "retired"; checked: FactRef }  // the prior check
    | { kind: "selected-report"; commit: CommitId; input: FactRef }
  )[];
  F: readonly (
    | { commit: CommitId; ref: string }          // met by this walk, with the first ref of the snapshot that targets it
    | { commit: CommitId; ref: string; start: true }  // the start, on the basis `row`, with `start.foreign`
    | { commit: CommitId; via: CommitId }        // carried from the prior check of the own-root stop at `via`
  )[];
  visited: number;                               // commits the walk visited
}
```

- The snapshot's bytes are a retained input of S, kept by their digest
  for as long as S's history is kept (R1 section 9.2). The entry holds
  the digest and the count.
- A ref's name holds the lane, its incarnation, the commit and the
  root number (the table "The root", below). So each pair of the
  snapshot gives which ref, its value, and whose root it was.
- A stop at the branch is not recorded. It is derived from `head`,
  which is a commit ID.
- `published` on the start is recorded, and it is also derived from
  `head`. A guard and a replay derive it again. Neither reads the
  branch again.
- The record names one foreign ref on the start, the first. A replay
  finds the others in the snapshot.
- `stops` holds at most a proposed 64 records, and F at most 64 with
  the carried commits and the start. Past either the act is refused
  `ancestry-too-large` (section 12, U17).

*The record's fields, as retained inputs. New in revision 10.* Each
field is fixed when the check is made. None is read again from the
host. The table says why each is kept, which guard reads it, and what
a replay derives it from.

| Field | Kept because | Read by | A replay derives it from |
|---|---|---|---|
| `commit`, the start | It is what is judged. | Guard 1 | The act. |
| `head` | The branch moves. "Published" is judged against this value and never against the branch as it is later. | Guards 3, 4 and 5 | Nothing: it is trusted, as `staged-ref-read`. |
| `snapshot`: the digest and the count, with the bytes kept under the digest | The staged refs change: a staging adds one, and a retirement removes one. | Guard 3, to sort the refs on the start | The bytes hash to the digest. That the host returned them is trusted. |
| `start`: `foreign`, with `published` or a basis | It is the judgment of the commit itself. | Guard 3 | The snapshot, `head`, and S's history of roots, checks and inputs. |
| `stops` | Each names evidence that exists apart from this staging: a prior check, or a `selected` input. | Guards 4 and 6 | S's history. |
| `F`, with the carried set: each entry that has a `via` | It is the result that the act's row judges. A carried commit comes from the prior check's own record. This check's snapshot is not read for it. | Guards 5 and 7 | The walk, and the records of the prior checks. |
| `published`: the mark on the start, and the boundary for ancestors and for carried commits | It is never read again from the branch. | Guards 3, 4 and 5 | `head`, and commits read by ID. |
| `root` | It is what the act relies on. | Guard 2 | S's history. |
| `visited` | It is the count of the parent walk, against its bound. | The bound | The walk. |

In the adopted contract, this record, member for member, is the
evidence of the outcome entry of the operation `check`, and a member
of the `check` record that the entry holds (R1 sections 6.11 and
16.4). The snapshot's bytes are in the byte domain
`artroom-snapshot-1` (R1 section 2.1). The guard is the capability
guard `ancestry` of `git-read@1`, and the replay row is in R1
section 9.3. What this note calls the pin entry, when the staging
lane is not the lane the act is addressed to, is the contract's
check entry (section 13.3).

R2 section 5.5, adopted, sums up `start` as it was in revision 8 of
this note: with a basis, and without `published`. The rule of
revision 9 is the one in force for this subject: a foreign start
that is reachable from the recorded head carries `published` and no
basis. R2 is asked to state its summary so (section 13.4). No form
and no refusal changes.

*The order of steps.* There is one order, in preparation, in S. A new
staging runs all of it. A reuse starts at step 4.

1. The checks before dispatch: the signature, `notAfter`, the grant
   and S's own guards on the hold.
2. S records the staging operation in its ledger, with the root
   number. The root is `creating`. This record is not evidence of
   ancestry, and neither is anything that follows from it alone.
3. The ref is created. A read shows that it holds the commit, that
   the fork's provenance is the canonical repository and that the
   whole closure is present. The root is then `live`. The ancestry
   check is not one of these checks.
4. S records the read's token duty in its ledger. Then it reads the
   head, the snapshot, and the commits it needs.
5. S makes the walk, from the parents of the start. It sorts the
   staged refs that target the start. For a foreign start it tests
   whether the start is reachable from the head it read. If it is,
   the start is published and no basis is asked. If it is not, S
   finds the basis. It builds the record. Past a bound, the act is refused `ancestry-too-large`. A
   root that was staged for it stays, with its duties, as "after
   dispatch" below says.
6. S stores the snapshot's bytes under their digest. This comes before
   any entry that names the digest.
7. When S is the lane the act is addressed to, the entry that admits
   the act retains the record. When the source is a hold in an issue
   lane L, L's pin entry carries the record, and P reads F there.

A reuse makes the walk again from the parents of the start, though
the root may have a prior check of the same commit. The start is
never a stop. A reuse also sorts the refs on the start again, from
the new snapshot.

Guards in the commit of the entry that retains or reads the record:

1. `commit` is the act's commit.
2. `root.number` is the root that the entry relies on or pins, and that
   root is `live` in S's ledger.
3. `start` fits the snapshot and S's ledger: sorted at this commit,
   the staged refs on the act's commit give the same `foreign`. With a
   foreign ref, `published` is recorded exactly when the act's commit
   is reachable from the record's `head`, and a basis is recorded
   exactly when it is not. That is derived from `head` and the
   commits, which do not change. An
   `own-check` basis names an
   earlier entry of S that is a prior check of the act's commit under
   the source commitment, with no foreign start. An `input` basis
   names an input that is `selected` under the source commitment at
   this commit. A `row` basis has the start in F.
4. Each `own-root` stop names a root that S's ledger records under the
   source commitment, with that number and state. Its `checked` names
   an earlier entry of S that is a prior check of that commit. The
   stop's commit is not the act's commit, and is not reachable from
   the record's `head`.
5. Each carried commit of F is in the F of the prior check that its
   `via` stop names. Every commit of that F is carried, except those
   reachable from the record's `head`, and none of those is.
6. Each `selected-report` stop names an input that is `selected` under
   the source commitment at this commit.
7. F passes the row of its act, in the table above.

If any of guards 1 to 6 does not hold, what was read no longer fits
S's state. The act is refused `ancestry-stale` and may be prepared
again. Guard 6 is one of them: a `selected-report` stop whose input is
no longer `selected` refuses the act `ancestry-stale`. So does an
`input` basis of guard 3 in the same case. The next preparation walks
without that stop or that basis, and the commit then meets its row.
If guard 7 does not hold, the act is refused `unnamed-work`.

*Replay.* A replay never reads the staged refs as they are now. It
makes the judgment again from the record and the snapshot.

| | A replay derives again | A replay trusts, and reports as `trusted: staged-ref-read` |
|---|---|---|
| The snapshot | That its bytes have that digest and that count. | That the host returned exactly that list, and that head, when S read them (section 12, H2); and that S kept what was returned. |
| The walk | From `commit`, by parents, with commits read by ID. The stops: reachable from `head`, the recorded `own-root` stops, the recorded `selected-report` stops. That it gives the same F apart from the start, each with the first ref of the snapshot that targets it, and the same `visited`, inside the bounds. | Nothing. A commit is named by its content. |
| The start | The refs of the snapshot that target `commit`. Each one sorted, by its name and by the roots that S's history records under the source commitment. That `foreign` is the first foreign one, or null when there is none. With a foreign ref: that `published` is recorded exactly when `commit` is reachable from `head`, and a basis exactly when it is not. The basis: for `own-check`, that `checked` is an earlier entry of S which is a prior check of `commit` under the source commitment, with no foreign start; for `input`, the `selected` input in S's history; for `row`, that the start is in F with that ref. | Nothing more. The snapshot and the head are trusted as the first row says. |
| The stops | That the start is not a stop. Each `own-root` stop against S's history: that root, with that number, under the source commitment, in that state at that entry; that `checked` is an earlier entry of S which is a prior check of that commit; that the stop's commit is not reachable from `head`; and that the carried commits are exactly that entry's F, less the commits reachable from `head`. Each `selected-report` stop against the `selected` input in S's history. | Nothing here. The prior check has its own snapshot, trusted as its own report says. |
| The judgment | The row of the act, over F. For a manifest pinned by L: that L's pin entry, retained as a foreign entry, carries this record, and that P's row holds over its F. | Nothing. |

Who vouches for the snapshot: S's runtime, and so the operator of the
deployment, resting on the host's read. The host keeps no history of
its refs, so no later read can confirm or deny a snapshot. A
difference between the snapshot and the refs as they are now is
expected. A replay does not read them and reports no fault from them.

A replay answers `incomplete` for this check, and makes no claim, when
the snapshot's bytes are missing, when a commit the walk needs can no
longer be read, or, for P, when L's history or snapshot is not
available (R1 section 9.2).

*Witness: a candidate cannot certify its own ancestry. The case of the
assessment `245c4031`.* The destination's head is D. U is a commit
staged under commitment K2 in lane L2, as root 1, and not published.
V, the integrator under commitment K, builds I. I's first parent is D
and its second is U. V stages I from a held hold under K, as S's root
5, and signs `propose-manifest`. The manifest selects no report of U
and supersedes nothing.

| Step | What happens | Revision 6 | This revision |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The staging operation for I is recorded under K, with root 5. | Root 5 is an own root under the source commitment. | The same record. It is not evidence of ancestry. |
| 2 | Root 5 is `live`. | The walk may begin. | The walk may begin. `live` shows that the objects are present. |
| 3 | The walk starts at I. | I is the commit of an own root under K. The walk stops at once. No parent is visited. | The start is never a stop. Root 5 has no prior check in any case. Both parents are visited. |
| 4 | D is visited. | Not reached. | D is reachable from the head: a stop. |
| 5 | U is visited. | Not reached. | U is the target of `…/L2/…/U/1`. It is no stop: not on the branch, not an own root, not a selected report. F = [U]. |

*Bounds.* The walk visits at most a proposed 4,096 commits, and F
holds at most 64. Past either, the act is refused
`ancestry-too-large`. The numbers are for R4 to measure. The other
choice, to admit the act with a record that the check was not
finished, is not proposed (section 12, U17).

*Work, and what counts it. New in revision 10.* `visited` counts the
commits of the parent walk and nothing else. A check does other work,
and the record counts none of it. R4's revision 8 notes this and asks
for it to be made clear.

| Work | When | How much | Counted or bounded by |
|---|---|---|---|
| The parent walk | Every check | At most the proposed 4,096 commits. | `visited`, and its bound. |
| Reachability from the recorded head | Once for each visited commit, to find a stop at the branch. Once for a foreign start. Once for each commit of a prior check's F, at each own-root stop, before it is carried. | The number of questions is bounded by the walk's bound, plus one, plus the recorded stops times the bound on F. The work of one question is commits read from the canonical repository. It depends on the branch's history between that commit and the head, and this note sets no bound on that. | Not counted by the record. No bound is proposed. |
| The snapshot | Every check | One list of every staged ref of the repository: read, put in order, hashed and stored. | `snapshot.count`. No bound is proposed (U18). |
| A replay of one check | Each time that check is replayed | The walk, the reachability questions and the sorting again, from the retained snapshot and from commits read by ID. | Not bounded by R1's bounds on one read: a whole replay is many reads (R1 section 9.1). |

Where that work falls:

- **Shared.** Every check of every lane reads one canonical
  repository and one list of staged refs. The list's size is the
  repository's, not the lane's. It grows with each staging and falls
  only with a retirement. R4's proposal R4-11 keeps a root for as
  long as any history that names its commit is kept, so under it the
  list grows with all that the repository has ever staged.
- **A hot lane.** One check for each preparation of a `report` or a
  `propose-manifest`, for a new staging and for a reuse.
- **The destination.** It makes no ancestry check. At reservation it
  checks that each selected report's commit is an ancestor of the
  integration commit (section 6.5). That is reachability work of the
  same kind, once for each selection.
- **A whole replay.** Every check of every scope again. Each keeps
  its own snapshot, so the bytes kept for replay are the sum of the
  snapshots, one for each check.

What this revision decides, and what it does not:

- The record is unchanged. A count of commits read for reachability
  depends on the method, and two correct replays could differ in it.
  So it is not a field.
- A check that cannot be finished ends with no judgment: the record
  is `too-large` and the act is refused `ancestry-too-large`. That
  fails closed. It admits nothing.
- Whether reachability gets a bound of its own, counted in commits
  read, and whether the snapshot gets a bound on its count, are not
  decided: U17, U18 and U21. No number is proposed for either, and
  none is measured. R4 owns the measurement: commits read for
  reachability, the snapshot's count and bytes, and the cost of one
  replayed check, for the shared repository, for a hot lane and for
  the destination.

*What this does not close.* The check sees ancestry by commit ID and
nothing else.

- Content that was copied without its commits is not seen: a rebase, a
  squash, a cherry-pick or a patch. That stays with review. A Git
  author line is text and is never used (R1 section 6.7).
- A staged ref that the host's read does not return is not seen. The
  read is trusted, and reported as trusted (section 12, H2). The
  snapshot is what S recorded of that read, and is trusted with it.
- A ref that is created after the snapshot was read, and before the
  act's commit, is not seen. The snapshot is the state at the read.
- A commit whose every root has been retired is no longer the target
  of a staged ref, and is not seen. That holds for the start as for
  an ancestor: a foreign start is seen only while a foreign ref on it
  is in the snapshot.
- A commit that is reachable from the branch is published history and
  is never listed: not as the start, not as an ancestor and not as a
  carried commit. A staged ref that some lane still keeps on it does
  not change that. "The branch" is the head that the check read and
  the record keeps (section 12, H2).

So this is not a claim that every author of a commit's content is
named. It is a claim that no unpublished commit staged for other work
is carried in by its ID, as the commit proposed or as an ancestor of
it, without a fact that names it. R2 owns the two refusals
as forms, and R1 the guard's form (section 13, O9).

**A new staging, and the reuse of a completed one.** They are different
and have different conditions.

In the rest of this section S is the staging lane: L, or P for its own
holds.

| | New staging | Reuse |
|---|---|---|
| When | S holds no live root for this commit. | S holds a live root for this commit. |
| Outside write | A read of the fork and one new ref in the canonical repository. | None. No token is minted and nothing is copied. |
| The hold | Must be `held`, as the table above says. Its fork must hold the commit. | Not needed. It may have ended. |
| What is checked instead | Nothing instead. That the commit's objects are already in the canonical repository is not a substitute. | The root's record names a hold whose holder was the signer's member. The commitment that hold was under is `accepted` and the signer is its performer now. For `report`, that commitment is the one reported on. |
| The intent | Its signature, `notAfter` and digest. | The same. |
| The grant | Within ten seconds, because a write follows. | The act's own grant, in its ordinary window. Nothing is written outside. |
| The ancestry check | Made, on the canonical repository, from the parents of the commit. The new root is not a stop. The refs on the commit are sorted, and the new root does not answer for a foreign one. A published commit needs no answer. | Made again, from the parents of the commit, because what is named belongs to the act and not to the root. A prior check of the same commit is not a stop for it. The refs on the commit are sorted again. A prior check with no foreign start is the `own-check` basis for a foreign ref that came later. A published commit needs no basis. |
| A pin | Recorded when the root is `live`, by an entry of S. | Recorded on the live root, by an entry of S. |

So section 5.2 holds as written. After its hold ends, a performer may
report a commit that was staged while the hold was held, if that root
is still live. In a change lane it may likewise propose such a commit.
It may stage nothing new. After a handover the former
