performer is not the performer: it can neither report nor reuse, and
the new performer cannot reuse a root staged from the former holder's
hold.

**What happens when a check fails, and when.**

- *Before dispatch.* If the signature, `notAfter`, a grant or a local
  guard fails before the fork is read, nothing is staged, no token is
  minted and nothing is written. This is the only case with no outside
  effect.
- *After dispatch.* The checks can pass and the act can still not be
  admitted: the key is revoked, the intent expires, the lane's state
  moves, or the commit fails validation at the act's own commit. Then a
  real staging exists, with its root, its fork read token and its
  staging token. Each is a duty in S's ledger. Once the root is `live`
  it holds a pin in state `provisional` for that intent. Settlement
  releases that pin, and the ledger may then retire the root. A root
  that is still `creating` holds no pin: its own creation duty keeps
  it. Nothing here claims that a refused act left no effect.

S records the staging operation in its ledger before any token is
minted, with the intent's digest, the source and the root.

This is one kind of outside write before an act's entry. The base
asked R1 to decide whether the ledger rule covers it, or whether
staging must be an act of its own with an outcome entry.

**Where that stands in revision 12.** The contract, adopted at
revision 10, decides it: an effect before an act is allowed only as
an operation that a sealed `preparation` entry of the owning scope
opens (R1 section 5.5). This note accepts that form as its
disposition of point O1. Under it, "S records the staging operation
in its ledger" is that `preparation` entry, and each attempt's result
is an outcome entry (section 5.7). So the record comes first and is
an entry, nobody signs for staging apart from the act's own intent,
and the commit is judged again at the act's commit. Revision 7 had no
`preparation` input. The form is in force with the contract. How this
note's own steps map onto it is the proposal of section 5.7. It is
still not a claim that staging and admission are one atomic step.

**The root.** A staged root is one ref with one **root number**.

| Part | Is |
|---|---|
| The root number | r, from a counter in S's ledger. Never reused. |
| The ref | `refs/artroom/staged/<lane scope ID>/<lane incarnation>/<commit>/<r>`, created only if absent, pointing at that commit. |
| With what | A fork read token from S's ledger, and a staging token for the canonical repository, narrowed by the gateway to creating that one ref. Two separate duties. |
| Checked after | Three things: that the ref holds exactly that commit, that the source fork's provenance is the canonical repository, and that the commit's whole object closure is present in the canonical repository. The ancestry check, above, comes after the root is `live`. It belongs to the act and not to the root, and it is not one of these three. |
| States, in S's ledger | `creating`; `live`; `retiring`; `retired`. A root moves forward only. `retiring` never returns to `live`. |
| `creating` to `live` | By a read of the ref that shows the commit, with the three checks of the row above. The read settles the effect. An attempt whose answer was lost stays unknown, and so does its token's duty. |
| Present with another value | An incident. The root does not become `live`. |

**Two protections, which are not the same.**

- *The creation duty* protects a root that is being made. A root in
  `creating` is never retired: retirement starts only from `live`. Its
  staging operation, recorded before any token, names the intent's
  digest, the source and the root. That record is not a pin, and it
  makes nothing usable.
- *A pin* is a consumer's record, in S's ledger, on a root that is
  already `live`. It makes the root usable by that consumer and keeps
  the root from being retired. A pin is recorded only on a `live` root,
  in an entry of S. No pin exists on a `creating` root, provisional or
  otherwise. Revision 4 said a provisional pin was recorded "with the
  root". It is recorded by the entry that makes the root `live`, or by
  a later entry on a root that is already live.

Pins and retirement are entries of one history, so one is always
first.

**Pins.** A pin has three states: `provisional`, `held`, and the final
state `released`. A root with a pin that is `provisional` or `held` is
never retired.

| What relies on the root | Where the pin is recorded | `provisional` from | `held` from | Released only by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A report in L | L, locally | Preparation of the `report` intent, on a `live` root. | The entry that admits the report. Its guard is that the root is `live`. | The entry that refuses the report. Or, for an accepted report, an entry of L made after a read shows the commit is an ancestor of the branch head. |
| An input in another issue lane, or a selected report in a manifest | No pin of its own | Not applicable. | Each must name an `accept-report` entry (R2 sections 3.4 and 5.2). An accepted report is final and holds its own pin in its own lane, by the row above. | Nothing to release. |
| A manifest whose commit was built under a hold of P itself | P, locally | Preparation of the `propose-manifest` intent, on a `live` root. | The entry that admits the manifest. Its guard is that the root is `live`. | The entry of P in which the manifest stops needing it: the entry that makes it `superseded`, or the entry that records its merge `published`. No message is sent. |
| A manifest whose commit was built under a hold in an issue lane L | L, for P. The pin's key is P's full reference with its incarnation, and the digest of the `propose-manifest` intent. It names the root and the commit. | Preparation of that intent, as an entry of L, on a `live` root. P receives that entry as a retained input and admits the manifest only if it names this intent's digest, this commit and P. | P's `pin-confirm`, sent by the entry that admits the manifest. | P's `unpin`. The lifecycle is below, in both orders. |
| An intent that was prepared and never admitted | S: the `provisional` pin of one of the rows above | As that row says. | Never. | S, after the intent's `notAfter`, and only on the settlement answer of the scope the intent was addressed to: no entry exists for that intent and none can follow. For a report, and for a manifest staged by its own lane, that scope is S itself. |

- A manifest becomes usable only after the pin entry exists. S's own
  history is the authority. A cached list of owners in P, or a list
  that looks empty while a message from P is still on its way, decides
  nothing.
- If P cannot be reached, or P's storage is lost, a pin that L holds
  for P stays. A loss is not an `unpin`.
- That an accepted report's commit is on the branch does not shorten
  what R4 keeps for replay. Retention for replay and the object closure
  that a check or a restore needs are separate rules, and a root is
  retired only when they also allow it.

**A manifest's pin in another lane: the messages, in both orders.**
This applies only when the staging lane L is not P. A manifest staged
by its own lane has no messages.

*Identity.* A pin's key in L is P's full reference with its
incarnation, and the digest d of the `propose-manifest` intent. L holds
at most one pin for that key: preparing the same intent again finds it.
The pin records the root's number r, the commit c, and the source hold
and instance. When L learns that the manifest was admitted, it also
records the manifest's fact, the fact of P's entry M.

*The messages.* R1 lets different requests arrive in either order.

| Message | Class in R1 | Sent by | Names | L admits it only when all of these hold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pin-confirm` | Request, `tell` | M, the entry of P that admits the manifest | M's fact, as the envelope's source; the commit c | The envelope's source scope and incarnation are the P of a pin's key. M, read as R1 section 7.4 says, is a `propose-manifest` act whose intent has that key's digest d and whose integration commit is c. The pin names c. |
| `unpin` | Request, `tell` | E, the entry of P in which the manifest stops needing the pin: the `propose-manifest` entry that supersedes it, or the delivery entry that records its merge `published` | The manifest's fact; the commit c | The envelope's source is that P. E contains this send, and E's own effects make that manifest `superseded`, or make a merge of that manifest `published`. The manifest's fact, fetched, is a `propose-manifest` act of P whose intent has digest d and whose integration commit is c. The pin for that key names c. |
| The result of each | Result | L's deciding entry | The request, by its source fact and ordinal | R1 section 7.4. |

E is the evidence that P no longer needs the root. L does not take the
message's word. It reads E, a sealed entry of P, and E's own effects
show the manifest superseded or its merge published. R2's definition
admits a superseding manifest only when no merge is in progress, so a
superseded manifest is named by no merge that is `intended`,
`committed` or `unknown`.

*The pin's states.*

| State | Means | Leaves it by |
|---|---|---|
| `provisional` | Prepared for intent d. L does not yet know whether a manifest was admitted. | `pin-confirm`, or P's settlement receipt for d: `held`. `unpin`: `released`. P's settlement answer that no entry exists for d and none can follow: `released`. |
| `held` | L holds the manifest's fact. The manifest was admitted. | `unpin` only. Not time, not a cached list, not an unreachable P. |
| `released`, final | Released, with how: `unpinned`, by E; or `never-admitted`, by the settlement answer. | Nothing. No message restores it. |

*Both orders.*

| | `pin-confirm`, then `unpin` | `unpin`, then `pin-confirm` |
|---|---|---|
| The pin before | `provisional` | `provisional` |
| First arrival | `pin-confirm` from M. L's deciding entry is `applied`. The pin is `held`, with M's fact. | `unpin` from E. L fetches M's fact, which shows that the manifest was admitted, and reads E, which shows that it no longer needs the root. L's deciding entry is `applied`. The pin is `released`, `unpinned`, with M's fact and E. This is not a `never-admitted` release, and it does not say the manifest was never admitted. |
| Second arrival | `unpin` from E. L's deciding entry is `applied`. The pin is `released`, `unpinned`, with E. | `pin-confirm` from M. L's deciding entry is `applied`. It records the confirmation on the released pin, as history. The pin stays `released`. Nothing is restored. |
| The pin after both | `released`, `unpinned`, with M's fact and E | The same |
| Results returned to P | One for each request, each `applied` | The same |
| The same envelope delivered again | Answered with its first deciding entry. No new entry. | The same |
| L's settlement question for d, after `notAfter` | Not needed once the pin is `held`. If it is asked while the pin is `provisional`, P answers with M's receipt and the pin becomes `held`. The `pin-confirm` that follows is `applied` and changes nothing. | Not needed: the pin is `released`. P cannot answer that none can follow, because M exists. |
| The root | Kept while the pin is `held`. After the release it may be retired, when no other pin and the retention for replay allow. | The same, from the first arrival. The later confirmation does not stop a retirement and creates nothing again. |

So `unpin` on a `provisional` pin is applied and not refused. A refusal
there would leave the pin to a confirmation that then holds it for a
manifest nobody needs. And a confirmation never moves a `released` pin
back.

*Other answers.*

- A message whose source entry, or whose manifest fact, cannot be
  fetched is not decided. It is retried, as R1 section 7.4 says for a
  dependency that is unavailable. The pin does not change.
- An `unpin` that fails a check, such as a manifest of another lane or
  an entry E that does not end the need, is decided `refused`. The pin
  stays as it was. P's parties and admins are told.
- A `pin-confirm` for which L holds no pin is decided `refused`, and is
  an incident: P admits a manifest only with L's pin entry as an input.
- An `unpin` for a pin that settlement released as `never-admitted` is
  an incident: P's own answer said that no entry could follow. It is
  decided `refused` and creates nothing again. If that root has been
  retired, the destination's own check that the commit and its closure
  are in the canonical repository (section 6.5) refuses a merge of
  that manifest.

*A lost answer.* L applies `unpin` and its result is lost. The result
is a send of L's sealed entry and is delivered again. A repeat of the
`unpin` envelope is answered with the same deciding entry. Nothing is
applied twice. If L's storage is lost instead, P records
`delivery-unavailable` for that send (R1 section 7.4). The pin's state
is then unknown, not released. P concludes nothing from the missing
answer, and P deletes nothing: only L's ledger retires a root. P's
manifest is not affected by an unanswered `pin-confirm` or `unpin`. P
keeps no pin state, and the manifest was usable from the pin entry it
was admitted with.

*What stays kept.* A merge that is `intended`, `committed` or `unknown`
names a current manifest. No entry has superseded that manifest and
its merge is not `published`, so no `unpin` for it exists, and its pin
is `held` or still `provisional`. So an unresolved publication keeps
its root. After a release, the retention for replay still applies.

*Where these are declared.* `pin-confirm` and `unpin` are two `tell`
sends of the `change` definition and two receive handlers of the
`issue` definition: R2 revision 7, sections 4.2 and 3.8. They are not
part of the act kinds counted there. R2 section 13 counts each against
R1's bound on the sends of one entry.

**Retiring a root.** S may retire a root when it is `live`, no pin on
it is `provisional` or `held`, and the retention R4 sets for replay has
passed.

1. S records `retiring` in an entry. From that entry on, no pin is
   accepted on this root, ever.
2. Only then S records the delete as a ledger duty, with its own
   attempt, its own token and a wake-up, and sends it: delete this ref
   if it holds this commit.
3. A read of the ref that shows it absent makes the root `retired`.
   Until then it stays `retiring`. A delete whose answer was lost stays
   an unknown attempt of S's ledger, with its token's duty, whatever
   the read shows later.

A need for the same commit after step 1 is a new staging. It gets the
next root number, and so another ref name. The expected value in the
delete protects against another commit under the same name. The root
number is what protects a new owner: a late delete can match only the
old name.

| Order | What S does | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| A pin is recorded, then the last other pin is released | The root still has a pin. No `retiring` entry is written and no delete is sent. | Root r stays `live`. |
| `retiring` is recorded and the delete is sent, then a need for the same commit arrives | The pin on r is refused. If the signer has a held hold whose fork holds the commit, S stages root r+1 under a new ref name and pins that. If not, the act is refused `not-staged`. | With a hold, the new owner relies on r+1, and the delete can remove only r's ref. Without one, nothing new is written. |
| The delete for r is sent and its answer is lost, then a need for the same commit arrives | r stays `retiring`, with an unknown delete. With a held hold, S stages r+1 and pins it; without one the act is refused `not-staged`. The first delete arrives late and removes r's ref, or finds it gone. | r+1, if staged, is untouched, and its owner keeps its only root. The lost delete stays a duty of S's ledger under r. |
| A pin and `retiring` arrive together | They are two entries of S. One is first. | The first row or the second. |

**Root r+1 is a new staging, with no exception.** It creates a new ref
in the canonical repository and mints a staging token. So it is a new
write, and it needs what every new staging needs: the signer's own
hold, `held`, whose fork holds the commit; that hold's current
instance; and the grant, observed within ten seconds. A signer with no
held hold is refused `not-staged`. That holds whether or not another
live root, or the branch, still holds the commit's closure: bytes that
already exist grant nobody a write. So a former performer, and the
holder of an ended hold, can cause no new ref.

Revision 4 allowed r+1 without a hold when the closure was still in the
canonical repository. That exception is withdrawn. The other choice was
a separately authorized root-retention operation, with its own guards,
ledger and fence. It is not designed here, and nothing in this note
needs it (section 12, U13).

A root whose creation had an unknown attempt keeps that attempt's duty
after it is retired. A late create can make the name appear again.
Nothing relies on it, and removing it later is cleanup, not settlement.

Repeating a staging proves nothing about a token whose mint or
revocation is unknown, and does not make any deletion safe. Those stay
in the ledger under their own rules.

A contributor's commit is readable by the integrator from the canonical
repository, by its ID, once its report is admitted. Nobody reads
another lane's fork.

**How the guard finds a selected input, and where reachability is
judged. Decided in revision 21** (the I3 deltas note, entries EF10
and EH8). `report` of `issue` writes the guard `ancestry` with
`commit` and `row` alone. The lane forms leave out `selected` there
on purpose: that argument is the selected reports of a manifest, and
not the inputs of a commitment. Guards 3 and 6 read the lane's own
items. Two things were not said.

*By which names the guard finds an input.* A `selected-report` stop,
and a basis `input`, each hold `input`, a fact reference.

- The fact is a local fact of the staging lane: it names this scope,
  with its incarnation, and the hash of this scope's entry at that
  position. A fact of another scope fails the guard.
- The input is the item that this entry opened: its ID is the fact's
  position. The guard holds for it when the item exists, its state
  is the state named `selected`, and its reference slot named `for`
  holds the source commitment.
- `selected` and `for` are names that version 1 of `git-read` reads,
  as `hold@1` reads `holder` and `under`. The item's type is not
  named: it is whatever type the fact's entry opened. In `issue`
  that is `input`, opened by `use-input`. A definition with no such
  state or slot has no selected input, and a record that names one
  is refused `ancestry-stale`.
- The guard takes no argument for this. So `report` needs no
  `selected`, and no row changes.

*Where each part is judged.* A commit holds no commit object, so it
cannot walk.

| What | In the commit that admits the act | By the walk at the check, and again by a replay |
|---|---|---|
| Guards 1 and 2 | In full. | Again. |
| Guard 3 | That the staged refs on the commit give the same `foreign`, from the retained snapshot. That an `own-check` basis names an earlier entry of S that is a prior check of the commit under the source commitment, with no foreign start. That an `input` basis names a selected input, as above. That a `row` basis has the start in F. | That `published` is recorded exactly when the commit is reachable from `head`, and a basis exactly when it is not. |
| Guard 4 | That each `own-root` stop names a root that S's ledger records under the source commitment, with that number and state, and that its `checked` is a prior check of that commit. That the stop's commit is not the act's. | That the stop's commit is not reachable from `head`. |
| Guard 5 | That each carried commit of F is in the F of the prior check that its `via` names. | That every commit of that F is carried unless it is reachable from `head`, and that none of those is. |
| Guard 6 | In full, as above. | That the stop's commit is the commit of that input's report. |
| Guard 7 | In full. | Again. |

- *What the admitting commit rests on, for the right column.* The
  record. The walk made it at the check, from commits read by ID,
  and the check entry holds it as its evidence. At run time that is
  the staging lane's runtime's word, under the label that the
  snapshot has, `trusted: staged-ref-read`. A replay walks again
  from the same commits, which do not change, and a record that the
  walk does not give is a `mismatch` at the check entry.
- *No scope retains commit objects for this.* The other choice was
  to retain the objects that a walk read, so that a commit could
  judge reachability. It is not taken: the bound of a walk is R4's,
  and the objects are in the canonical repository under a pinned
  root for as long as the pin stands.
- *What changes for a source.* A record with a `selected-report`
  stop, or with the basis `input`, is no longer refused
  `ancestry-stale` because the commit cannot judge it. It is judged
  by the left column. So `use-input` gives a way forward again.

### 6.3 What the change lane states and promises

P's `merge` entry carries an **eligibility statement**, derived by P's
own fold and so derivable again by a verifier:

- the manifest's fact, with its base, integration commit, tree, goal,
  plan, selected facts and decisions;
- **every** live verdict on that manifest, approvals and requests for
  changes alike, each with its member;
- **every** live job on that manifest, with its name, state and the
  result that decided it;
- the set of links that are `set`.

It is complete by construction: the fold lists what is live, and the
merger does not choose a subset.

**Each job, with the entry that decided it. New in revision 10
(request `9d55ac57`).** "The result that decided it" is made exact
here. For each live job on the manifest the statement holds:

| Member | Is |
|---|---|
| The job | The fact of the `request-check` entry that opened it. |
| `name` | The check's name. |
| `state` | `requested`, `passed`, `failed`, `errored` or `timed-out`. |
| The deciding entry | The fact of the entry of P whose own effects gave the job that state: a `check` entry, a `check-error` entry, or the timed entry of the job's deadline. A job that is `requested` has none, because nothing has decided it. For a job that an answer decided after its deadline, it is that answer's entry and not the timed entry. |

- **Which entry decides. Corrected in revision 11 (review `74b21dc8`,
  second finding).** Revision 10 said here that a later answer on a
  job that is already decided is history, and never becomes the
  deciding entry. That was too wide. Read with the table above, it
  kept the deadline's entry as the deciding entry of a `timed-out`
  job for good, against section 3.11 and R2's adopted section 7.2.
  The rule is this.
  - A job that is `requested` is decided by whichever P writes first:
    the first authentic answer on it, or its deadline's timed entry.
  - A job that is `timed-out`, and that no retry has superseded, is
    decided once more, by the first authentic answer on it: `passed`,
    `failed` or `errored` (section 3.11; R2-11). From that entry on,
    the job's deciding entry is that `check` or `check-error` entry.
    It replaces the deadline's timed entry, which stays in P's
    history as it was written.
  - A job that is `passed`, `failed`, `errored` or `superseded` takes
    no further decision. A later answer on it is history only. So is
    a second answer after the one that decided it. Neither changes
    the job's state or its deciding entry (R2 section 7.2). The exact
    signed bytes of an answer that was admitted return its receipt
    and write nothing.

  So the deciding entry is always the entry whose own effects gave
  the job the state that the statement shows.
- A job that a retry superseded is not live and is not listed. It
  keeps its own entries in P's history, and the `request-check` that
  superseded it names it. So superseded history stays attributable.
- An answer names its job, so no entry can be the deciding entry of
  another job.
- R2 section 7.2, adopted, already says that the statement lists each
  live job "with its state and what decided it: a result, an error
  result, or the timed entry". The slot that carries it is not in
  R2's adopted item. The adopted contract has the form: `job` has a
  reference `decidedBy`; `check`, `check-error` and the timed rule
  set it from the entry's own position; and `merge` collects it into
  the statement (R1 sections 6.2, 6.4 and 6.6; the contract's
  witness 18.16; the companion file's note N21; point R1-30). R2
  decides the slot in its own item. Until R2's item has it, the
  statement's content is this section's and R2's sentence, and the
  slot in R2's item is owed (section 13.4). Stated in revision 14:
  R2's adopted revision 14 has the slot `decidedBy` on `job` (its
  section 7.2), so that is no longer owed.
- The contract's forms already have the rule of revision 11. The
  companion file's rows for `check` and `check-error` set the job's
  state, and `decidedBy` from `self`, when the job is `requested` or
  `timed-out`. Its witness 18.16 has the late answer as the entry
  P.22, which replaces P.21. Those rows are right and are not to
  change. The prose of its note N21 says that "a later answer on a
  decided job does not change it". That is right only when "decided"
  means `passed`, `failed`, `errored` or `superseded`. R1 is asked to
  say so in the note (section 13.4).

*Witness: a deadline, then a late pass. New in revision 11.* P is a
change lane. Manifest 7 is current, and the rules require the check
`combined`. The entry numbers P.20 to P.22 are those of the
contract's witness 18.16.

| Step | Entry | Input | Job 20 | Its deciding entry | What follows |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P.20 | `request-check`, `combined` | `requested` | None | |
| 2 | P.21 | Timed: the job's deadline | `timed-out` | P.21 | A `merge` written now would state `timed-out`, with P.21. G would not reserve it: check 2 of section 6.5 fails, `rules-not-met`. |
| 3 | P.22 | `check` on job 20, passed: the first authentic answer, late. No retry has superseded the job, and no merge is in progress. | `passed` | P.22, in place of P.21 | It is admitted against the job's own reservation (section 5.8). P.21 stays in the history. |
| 4 | P.23 | A second `check` on job 20, failed, as a new signed intent | `passed` | P.22, unchanged | Result 23 is history only. The exact bytes of P.22's intent, sent again, would write nothing and return its receipt. |
| 5 | P.24 | `merge`. Its statement lists job 20 as `passed`, with the deciding entry P.22. | `passed` | P.22 | `reserve` is sent to G. |
| 6 | An entry of G | The reservation. G fetches P.20 and P.22, by their hashes. | | | Checks 1 and 3 hold from the statement, P.20 and the observed rules. Check 2: the state is `passed`. Check 4: P.22 is a `check` entry of P whose own effects set job 20, and no other, to `passed`. Checks 5 to 8 read P.22, the observed rules and G's own observation of the signer's key. When they hold, this required check is met. |

| The same history | Deciding entry of job 20 after step 3 | Step 6 |
|---|---|---|
| Under this revision | P.22 | Met, as above. |
| The control: under the wording of this note's revision 10 | P.21. The late answer "does not become the deciding entry". | The statement would name a timed entry for a job that is `passed`. Check 4 asks for a `check` entry whose own effects set the job to `passed`, and P.21 is not one: `evidence-invalid`. A legal late pass could never support a reservation. |
| A retry supersedes job 20 before the late answer | P.21, unchanged | Job 20 is not live and is not listed. The answer is history of job 20. The new job has its own deciding entry, or none yet. |

The entry is also P's commitment for this operation. From `intended`
until a final state, P admits no act that changes any of that: a new
manifest; a verdict, its withdrawal or dismissal; a check request or
result; a link or unlink; draft; close. R2 section 7.4 is the list. A
comment changes no verdict in R2 revision 2, so comments stay open.

### 6.4 The messages

R1 allows one result for a request. So progress is not sent as results.

| Step | Message | From, to | Class | The receiver's deciding entry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `reserve`, naming the operation | P to G | Request | G records it: `applied`, and a publication item is `queued`; or `refused`, when the destination named is not G or the message is malformed. One result returns. |
| 2 | `publication`, a relationship G owns, about that operation | G to P | Request, a relationship update | P applies it only if its revision is higher than the one P holds for that publication. Updates: queued, reserved, unresolved, and a final one. |
| 3 | `withdraw`, naming the operation | P to G | Request | G records it: `applied`, when the publication is `queued` or not yet known; `refused`, with a reason, in every other state. The table "G's answer to `withdraw`" below gives each reason. |

**What each message is bound to.** The operation is P's `merge` entry.
Every message about it names that entry's fact, P's full reference and
G's full reference, each with its incarnation. G's publication item
keeps all three. G's updates also name that publication item, and their
revision is the position of the entry in G's sealed history that sent
them.

- G accepts `reserve` and `withdraw` for an operation only from the
  scope that the operation's fact is in. A lane cannot withdraw another
  lane's merge.
- P's handler admits an update only when the sender is the scope and
  incarnation in `proposal.destination`, the operation is one of P's own
  merge items, and the publication item is the one first named for it.
- An update is applied only if its revision is higher than the one P
  holds for that publication.
- A merge item in a final state takes no further update. A later one,
  whatever its revision, is recorded as refused and changes nothing.
- Identical bytes delivered again return the first answer.

**When P sends `withdraw`: R2 revisions 8 and 9, agreed.** R2 admits
`cancel-merge` only while the merge item is `intended` and its
`withdrawal` slot is empty. The act sets the slot to `asked` and sends
`withdraw`. The slot says only that a withdrawal was sent. The result
of that request, "applied" or "refused", is recorded in P as its own
entry, whatever state the merge item is in when it arrives, and the
page reads it from there (R2 revision 9, section 7.4). So a result
that arrives after the final update is still kept. R2 says the rule
needs this note's agreement. This note agrees, for three reasons.

- P becomes `committed` or `unknown` only by an update that G sends
  after it reserved. G refuses every `withdraw` from reservation on.
  So a `cancel-merge` in those states could never apply, and refusing
  it in the lane loses nothing.
- `withdraw` is a request with one result (R1 section 7.4). Until that
  result is delivered, P does not know what G decided. `asked` with no
  recorded result says exactly that. A lost or late result is not proof that the withdrawal
  failed, or that it worked.
- The merge item's state still changes only by G's `publication`
  update or by the result of `reserve`. The `withdrawal` slot is a
  record of the request. It frees nothing by itself.

P's state can be behind G's. So a `withdraw` that P sent while
`intended` can reach G after G reserved. It can also reach G after G
ended the publication without reserving it, for example as
`out-of-date`. Revision 6 gave no answer for that second case, and R2
revision 9 showed every refusal as "already reserved". G's answer now
carries its reason.

**G's answer to `withdraw`, by the state of the publication when G
decides it.** The reasons are proposed forms. They are values of R1's
`reason` on a result.

| G's publication | Result | Reason | What G changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Not yet known | `applied` | None | G records the operation as withdrawn. A later `reserve` is refused, "withdrawn". |
| `queued` | `applied` | None | The publication ends `not-reserved`, "withdrawn". The final update is sent. |
| `reserved`, `publishing` or `unresolved` | `refused` | `reserved` | Nothing. The publication goes on. |
| `not-reserved`, with a reason such as `out-of-date`, `authority-lost`, `evidence-invalid`, `rules-not-met`, `incomplete` or `integration-invalid` | `refused` | `ended`, with `not-reserved` and that reason | Nothing. G never reserved this operation. The final update that G already sent stands. |
| `published` | `refused` | `ended`, with `published` | Nothing. |
| `aborted` | `refused` | `ended`, with `aborted` | Nothing. |
| Any, when the sender is not the scope that the operation's fact is in | `refused` | `not-owner` | Nothing. |
| Any, when the message is malformed | `refused` | `malformed` | Nothing. |

**How a reason is carried. Decided in revision 14 (G8).** A result's
`Reason` is a code and one name (R1 section 4.1), and it stays so. The
result of a refused `withdraw` carries the one name: `reserved`,
`ended`, `not-owner` or `bad-field`. Where the table above says
"`ended`, with" a final state and its reason, those two values are
not in the result. They are in the final `publication` update. G sent
that update when it ended the publication, and so before it could
answer `ended`. The lane's page reads them from its merge item, which
that update set (R1 section 15.3a, row 13; R2 section 13.7, G21).
This note's reason `malformed` is the contract's `bad-field`: an
ill-typed message is decided before any handler runs (R1 section
6.4).

A final publication is never opened again. `ended` changes nothing in
G's publication: it reports the state that G already recorded. From
revision 11, the first decision on a lane's one `withdraw`, applied
or refused, uses the entry that the publication reserved for it, and
G records that the entry is used (section 5.8, "A refusal that is
written", and the witness of a refused withdrawal there). "Nothing",
in the table above, is about the publication's
state. A refusal alone does not show that G reserved. Only the reason
`reserved` shows that, and a reader of the result must use the
reason. R2 revision 10, section 7.4, shows each reason in its own
words.

**The freeze reads the merge item's state, and nothing else.** A
pending, late or lost answer to a withdrawal does not freeze a lane
whose merge item is final. It does not free a lane whose merge item is
not final. Revision 6 said "frozen" for a pending answer without that
condition. R2 revision 9, section 7.4, has the row where the merge
item is final and the lane is free, and this table now agrees.

| P's `withdrawal` slot and recorded result | What G did | P's merge item | P is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `asked`, no result yet | Not known to P | Not final: `intended`, or `committed` or `unknown` if G's update arrived first | Frozen, because the merge item is not final. Nothing is inferred about the withdrawal. |
| `asked`, no result yet | The final update says how the publication ended. The answer to the withdrawal is not known to P. | Final: `aborted`, `refused` or `published` | Free, by the final update. The answer is recorded when it arrives. It changes nothing then. |
| `asked`, result "applied" | Recorded the operation as withdrawn while it was `queued` or not yet known | `intended`, then `aborted` by G's final update or by the result of `reserve` | Frozen until that final update or result arrives, and free from it. The `withdraw` result alone frees nothing. |
| `asked`, result "refused", reason `reserved` | Had reserved, and had not ended the publication | Not final, then as the publication goes; or already final | Frozen until a final state. Free once the merge item is final. |
| `asked`, result "refused", reason `ended` | Had already ended the publication: not reserved, with its own reason; or published; or aborted | Not final until G's final update arrives, then the state that the update gives; or already final | Frozen until that final update arrives, and free from it. The result alone frees nothing and sets no state. |
| `asked`, and G's storage is lost | Not known | Unchanged | Frozen if the merge item is not final: nothing has released it. Free if it is already final. P records `delivery-unavailable` and concludes nothing about the withdrawal. |

**How each state of G's publication reaches P.**

| In G | Update sent | P's merge item becomes | P is then |
|---|---|---|---|
| `queued` | None. The result of `reserve` says "applied". | Stays `intended`. | Frozen. |
| `not-reserved`, with a reason such as `out-of-date`, `authority-lost`, `evidence-invalid`, `rules-not-met`, `incomplete` | Final | `refused`, with the reason. | Free. |
| `not-reserved`, "withdrawn" | Final | `aborted`. | Free. |
| `reserved` | Progress | `committed`. | Frozen. |
| `unresolved` | Progress, with what the read saw | `unknown`. | Frozen. |
| `published` | Final, with the commit | `published`. | Free; the proposal is `merged`. |
| `aborted`, the host kept refusing | Final, with the host's reason | `refused`. | Free. |
| `aborted`, after a compromised key or a fence | Final | `aborted`. | Free. |

Cases:

| Case | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `withdraw` arrives before `reserve` | G records the operation as withdrawn. The later `reserve` gets the result "refused, withdrawn", and P's result clause sets the merge `aborted`. |
| `withdraw` while `queued` | The publication ends `not-reserved`, "withdrawn". |
| `withdraw` after reservation | Its result is "refused", with the reason `reserved`. The publication goes on. P records the result; the slot stays `asked`. |
| `withdraw` reaches a publication that is already `not-reserved` for another reason | Its result is "refused", with the reason `ended`, `not-reserved` and that reason. G changes nothing. P's merge becomes `refused`, with that reason, by the final update that G already sent. |
| `withdraw` reaches a publication that is already `published` or `aborted` | Its result is "refused", with the reason `ended` and that state. G changes nothing. |
| The result of `withdraw` is late or lost | P's `withdrawal` stays `asked` with no recorded result. P infers nothing about the withdrawal. P is frozen while its merge item is not final, and free once it is final. The result is a send of G's sealed entry and is delivered again. |
| G does not reserve | A final update with the reason. Nothing was sent to the host. |
| P restarts and a result or update was lost | Each is a send of a sealed entry in G and is delivered again. P answers a repeat from its history. |
| G's final update is delivered and P's answer is lost | G delivers it again. P answers with the entry that recorded it. |
| An update names another lane's operation, another publication item, or comes from another scope or incarnation | Refused by P's handler. |
| G's storage is lost while P's merge is `intended` or `committed` | P writes R1's `delivery-unavailable` diagnosis. P's merge stays as it is and P stays frozen for that operation. It is unknown, not ended. Admins are told. Nothing is released. Other lanes are not affected. Stated in revision 11, from the contract's revision 10: after that diagnosis P sends the request no more. A late result still settles it. If G's history is restored and G had not recorded the request, only a new dispatch reaches G. From revision 14 an operator's instruction sends the same envelope again, as bookkeeping (section 12, "A request that waits"). |
| `reserve` was never received: every attempt to deliver it was a routing refusal, and P writes R1's `undelivered` diagnosis. New in revision 10. | P's merge becomes `refused`, with the reason `undelivered`, and P is free. R1 writes that finding only when every attempt was answered by a routing refusal (R1 section 7.4). So the scope that P addressed did not take the request, and it reserved nothing. The finding rests on P's own log of attempts, which a replay reports as trusted. This is not the row above: `delivery-unavailable` proves nothing and frees nothing. R2 is asked to write the clause (section 13.4). |

**Witness: a final merge item with a pending answer.** P.60 is the
`merge` entry and P.61 is `cancel-merge`.

| P's merge item | The answer to P.61's `withdraw` | Revision 6 | This revision, and R2 section 7.4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `intended` | None yet | Frozen. | Frozen: the merge item is not final. |
| `aborted`, by a final update that arrived first | None yet | "Frozen. Nothing is inferred." in one table, and "Free" in the table of updates. | Free. The answer is still owed, and is recorded when it arrives. |
| `published`, by a final update that arrived first | Lost: G's storage is lost | "Frozen." | Free. P records `delivery-unavailable` for the `withdraw` send and concludes nothing about it. |
| `intended` | Lost: G's storage is lost | Frozen. | Frozen. Unknown, not ended. Nothing is released. |

**Witness: a withdrawal that reaches an operation G never reserved.**

| Step | Entry | What happens | G's publication | P's merge item | P's record of the `withdraw` result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | P.60 | `merge`. `reserve` is sent. | None | `intended` | None |
| 2 | G.30 | `reserve` is delivered. | `queued` | `intended` | None |
| 3 | G.31 | Another publication is published. The head moves. | `queued` | `intended` | None |
| 4 | G.32 | G judges this publication. Its base is not the head. The final update is sent. | `not-reserved`, `out-of-date` | `intended`: the update is not yet delivered | None |
| 5 | P.61 | `cancel-merge` is admitted: the merge item is `intended` and the slot is empty. `withdraw` is sent. | Unchanged | `intended`, slot `asked` | None |
| 6 | G.33 | `withdraw` is delivered. | Unchanged. Not opened again. | `intended` | None |
| 7 | P.62 | The final update of step 4 arrives. | Unchanged | `refused`, `out-of-date`. P is free. | None: the answer is pending, and P is free. |
| 8 | P.63 | The result of step 6 arrives: "refused", `ended`, `not-reserved`, `out-of-date`. | Unchanged | Unchanged | "refused", `ended` |

Revision 6 did not classify step 6. Read with R2 revision 9, P.63
would have been shown as "the destination had already reserved". G
never reserved. With steps 7 and 8 in the other order, the result is
recorded while P is `intended` and frozen, and the final update then
frees P. Both orders end with the same records.

### 6.5 Reservation: the point of no return

Stated in revision 27: five passages of this section are rewritten in
"Section 6.5 in the contract's order of reads", at its end. They take
effect when a contract revision that carries the forms is adopted. Until
then the text here stands as revision 26 has it.

G reserves the oldest queued publication when the slot is free.
Reservation is one commit in G and the only linearization point for
publication. Before its turn G reads: P's `merge` entry and the entries
its eligibility statement names; an observation of the merger's key and
of each key behind a counted verdict or result; an observation of the
branch rules; and the branch's head from the host. In the commit it
judges:

| Check | Not reserved, with |
|---|---|
| The manifest's base equals the head just read, and equals G's recorded head. | `out-of-date`, or section 6.9 when the two differ. |
| The integration commit and its whole closure are in the canonical repository, as read from the host; its tree is the one named; the base is its first parent; each selected report's commit is its ancestor. | `integration-invalid` |
| The merger's key holds `change.merge`, by an observation within ten seconds. | `authority-lost` |
| From the complete eligibility statement: no live request for changes; approvals by enough different members, each independent of the authors and each by a key not compromised; every required check's live job passed, each result by a key not compromised and for the configuration the rules name. | `evidence-invalid` or `rules-not-met` |
| The manifest is complete (R2 section 5.2). | `incomplete` |

Every observation that G uses here is read for this reservation, and
serves this one commit (section 3.12, W3). None is taken from an
earlier reservation.

G does not take a list of "counted" facts on trust. It counts from the
complete statement, under the rules it observed itself.

**What G checks of each required check. New in revision 10 (request
`9d55ac57`; R1's point R1-30).** A job's opening fact and a stated
`passed` are not the proof. For each check that the observed rules
require, G does all of this, in the commit of the reservation. Before
its turn it fetches each entry that the statement names for that job,
by its hash, and it retains them.

| # | G checks | From | Fails with |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The statement lists exactly one live job with that check's name. | The statement. P's definition admits at most one live job for a name and a manifest. | `rules-not-met` |
| 2 | That job's state is `passed`. A job that is `requested`, `failed`, `errored` or `timed-out` does not meet a required check. | The statement | `rules-not-met` |
| 3 | The job's opening entry is a `request-check` entry of P, for this merge's manifest, with that name. Its tree is the manifest's tree. Its configuration digest is the one the observed rules hold for that check now. | The fetched opening entry; the observed rules | `rules-not-met` for another configuration. `evidence-invalid` when the entry is not that. |
| 4 | The deciding entry is an entry of P, with P's incarnation. It is a `check` entry. Its own effects set that job, and no other, to `passed`. | The fetched deciding entry | `evidence-invalid` |
| 5 | The deciding entry's intent names that job, the job's tree and the job's configuration digest, with the outcome passed. | The same entry | `evidence-invalid` |
| 6 | Its signer's member is the checker that the observed rules name for that check now. | The same entry; the observed rules | `evidence-invalid` |
| 7 | Its signer held `change.check` when the entry was admitted, by the observation that the entry retains. | The same entry | `evidence-invalid` |
| 8 | Its signer's key is not revoked as compromised now, by an observation read for this reservation (section 3.12, W3). | G's own observation | `evidence-invalid` |

- **States that are not a decision by a result.** A `requested` job
  has no deciding entry. A `timed-out` job names its timed entry,
  which is not a result. Neither meets check 2, so neither reaches
  check 4. A job that an authentic answer decided after its deadline
  is not `timed-out` any more. Its state is the answer's, its
  deciding entry is the answer's entry, and it is checked like any
  other job (section 6.3, "Which entry decides"; stated in revision
  11).
- **A job that is not required** blocks nothing. G checks nothing of
  it beyond the statement's completeness.
- **A result cannot count for another job.** Checks 4 and 5 tie the
  deciding entry to the one job, by the entry's own effects and by
  the job that its intent names.
- **Custody and replay.** The entries that G fetched are retained
  inputs of the reservation entry (R1 section 9.2). A replay judges
  checks 1 to 8 again from them, from the observations that the
  reservation entry retains, and from the rules and the membership
  histories at the observed heads (section 10).
- **Cost.** One reservation fetches P's `merge` entry, the manifest's
  entry, each verdict's entry, and two entries for each required
  check. With v live verdicts and c required checks that is 2 + v +
  2c entries. The contract's bound on the foreign entries of one
  entry is 128, as its proposal for R4, where revision 7 had 64. R2's
  `review` type allows 256 live items, so the count can pass it.
  Decided in revision 14 (G5): G computes the count from the
  `reserve` message and from the rules that it observed, before it
  fetches anything. When the count is over the bound, the publication
  ends `not-reserved`, with the reason `evidence-too-large`. Nothing
  is fetched, and nothing is sent to the host. A replay derives the
  same refusal from the message and the observed rules. The way
  forward is in P: a new manifest version, whose verdicts are counted
  afresh, or fewer live verdicts.
- **What this is not.** It is a rule of this design. It is not a
  statement that any destination built today refuses a forged
  result. That source is owed by I3.

Then G takes the slot and sets the publication `reserved`.

**From this entry on, the publication is authorized by G's own record.**
Sending it, reading it back, writing its receipt and settling its
tokens are the service's acts under that record. They need no member's
continuing authority. So a retired revocation of the merger after
reservation does not stop the send. The only thing that affects a
reserved publication is a `compromised` revocation of a key behind it
(section 6.8).

Revocation against reservation, in both orders: recorded in membership
before G's observation began, the publication is not reserved; recorded
after, even one second after and before G's commit, it is reserved and
goes on. That second case is the ten-second grace window, stated. It is
ten seconds on G's clock (section 3.12).

**Section 6.5 in the contract's order of reads. New in revision 27**
(the planner's act `39749e26`, answer a; the contract's revision 21, its
section 16.1, "The order of the reads, and the judge of a destination";
the I3 deltas FA9, FC5 and FC6). The contract's revision 21 lets an
outcome fetch nothing: the entries that an outcome reads are those that
an earlier entry of the scope retained. It asks three changes of this
section, and the planner accepted them: every entry that the `reserve`
message names has a written type of fact; the count of entries is made
when the `reserve` is delivered; and the entries of a job that is not
required are fetched and retained with the rest. That revision of the
contract is not adopted. So the five passages below take effect only
when a contract revision that carries `origin`, `observes` and `second`
is adopted. Until then the text above stands as revision 26 has it. From
then on these passages replace five of it: the opening paragraph; the
sentence "Before its turn it fetches each entry that the statement names
for that job"; and the points "A job that is not required", "Custody and
replay" and "Cost".

*The opening, rewritten.* G reserves the oldest queued publication when
the slot is free. Reservation is one commit in G and the only
linearization point for publication. What G judges on is at hand in this
order.

| When | What G does | Its bound, and what follows past it |
|---|---|---|
| At the delivery of `reserve`, which is new work and can be refused | G fetches every entry that the message names as a fact: P's `merge` entry, which is also the source entry of the delivery; the manifest's entry; the entry of each listed verdict; and for each listed job its opening entry and, where the job states one, its deciding entry. G retains each, read or not. From revision 28: and the `report` entry of each selected report ("`reserve` names each selected report", below). | The contract's bound on the foreign entries of one entry, 128 as proposed. A message that names more is decided `refused`, `bad-field`. From revision 28 the count holds the reports. Nothing is fetched, and no publication is opened. |
| Before the turn of the outcome of `judge` | Nothing is fetched. The entries are at hand: the outcome's `uses` is a copy of the `uses` of the entry that recorded the `reserve` (section 12.1.5, the `origin` of the kind `judge`). | None of its own |
| The first step of reads | An observation of the branch rules, with the list of extents as a retained value; of the merger's key; of the holders of `rules.publish`; and of each author as a member (section 3.3, rows 1 to 4) | The `max` of each row. A row that is over: `not-reserved`, `evidence-too-large`. |
| The second step of reads | An observation of each key behind an approving verdict, and behind the deciding entry of a passed job of a check that the observed rules list (row 5) | The same |
| The evidence of the outcome | The branch's head, the integration commit's closure and the changed set, as the host answered | Section 12.1.5. A changed set past its bound: `not-reserved`, `evidence-too-large`. |
| In the commit | G judges the first table above, and "What G checks of each required check" | |

Every observation is read for this reservation, serves this one commit
and is `fresh`, as before. With no observation of a row the outcome is
not written, and the publication stays `queued`.

*The fields of `reserve`.* The types of two lists change, so that the
contract fetches what they name.
From revision 28 the message has a sixth field, `reports`: "`reserve`
names each selected report", below.

| Field | Type | What is fetched |
|---|---|---|
| `operation` | `{ type: "fact", kind: ["merge"], under: "change" }`, required. As revision 25. | P's `merge` entry. It is the source entry of the delivery. |
| `manifest` | `{ type: "fact", kind: ["propose-manifest"], under: "change" }`, required. As revision 25. | The manifest's entry |
| `verdicts` | `{ type: "list", max: 64, of: { type: "record", of: { review: { type: "fact", kind: ["review-verdict"], under: "change", required: true }, reviewer: { type: "member", required: true }, verdict: { type: "enum", of: ["approve", "request-changes"], required: true }, extent: { type: "text", max: 64 } } } }`, required. Changed: it had the mark `collect-list`. | The entry that each `review` names: the entry that opened the review |
| `jobs` | `{ type: "list", max: 64, of: { type: "record", of: { job: { type: "fact", kind: ["request-check"], under: "change", required: true }, name: { type: "text", max: 128, required: true }, state: { type: "enum", of: ["requested", "passed", "failed", "errored", "timed-out"], required: true }, decidedBy: { type: "fact", kind: ["check", "check-error", "timed:job-deadline"], under: "change" } } } }`, required. Changed in the same way. | The entry that each `job` names, and the entry that each `decidedBy` names |
| `links` | The mark `collect-list`, as revision 25: at most 32 records, each with `link` and `issue` | Nothing. A field whose type is a mark names no fact to fetch, and the rule `judge` reads nothing of a link's entry. |

- *Where the kinds come from.* `review-verdict`, `request-check`,
  `check`, `check-error` and `timed:job-deadline` are the kinds of the
  pinned `change` lane, read as data in the I3 worktree: the act that
  opens a `review`, the act that opens a `job`, and the three kinds of
  the job's reference `decidedBy`. If a row of the lane changes, this
  row changes with it, in a revision of this note. A sender writes a
  local item as a fact of the entry that opened it, so `review` and
  `job` arrive as facts (the contract's section 6.6).
- *A list of at most 64 verdicts. Narrower than revision 26.* The
  contract fetches a fact only where a written type names it (its
  revision 21, section 6.1, "What an entry of another scope must be to
  be at hand"). A written list type states a `max` of at most the
  contract's bound on the elements of a list, which is 64 as proposed
  (its section 6.1, adopted in its revision 19). The lane's type
  `review` allows 256 live items. So a `reserve` that lists more than 64
  verdicts is refused `bad-field`. Under revision 26 a reservation could
  count up to 126 verdicts, less 2 for each required check. No number is
  chosen here: the 64 is the contract's bound, and the row follows it. A
  list type that may be as long as its sender's `collect` allows is
  asked of the contract, and the bound is put to the planner (section
  13.17).
- *The member `extent`* is a text of at most 64 bytes. A verdict that
  states a name which is no extent of the observed rules counts for none
  (section 12.1.4a).
- *The mark `collect-list` stands on one field now,* `links`, where it
  stood on three.

*The count, rewritten.* Replaced in revision 28 by "The count, with
reports", below: at most 2 + v + 2j + r. As revision 27 wrote it: The
message names at most 2 + v + 2j entries,
for v listed verdicts and j listed jobs: P's `merge` entry, the
manifest's entry, one for each verdict, and for each job its opening
entry and its deciding entry. A job that is `requested` states no
deciding entry, and names one. The count is made when the `reserve` is
delivered, from the message alone. No observation is read for it, and no
rule of this note makes it: it is the contract's check of a message
against the bound on the foreign entries of one entry (its section 6.4,
point DH4). A message that names more than the bound is decided
`refused`, `bad-field`. Nothing is fetched, and no publication is opened
for it.

- So the reason `evidence-too-large` has no case left for a count of
  entries, and the evidence `{ over: "entries" }` of revision 25 is
  withdrawn. The reason stays for a changed set past its bound, and for
  a row of observations that is over.
- *What P is told.* The result of its `reserve`: `refused`, `bad-field`.
  Its merge item becomes `refused` with that reason, by the clause that
  it has. Under revision 26 it learned `evidence-too-large` from an
  update of a publication. The way forward is the same: a new manifest
  version, whose verdicts are counted afresh, or fewer live verdicts.
- *Two cases, by a script.* 64 verdicts with 31 jobs name 128 entries,
  and are fetched. 64 verdicts with 32 jobs name 130, and are refused.
- *One entry is named twice.* The field `operation` names the delivery's
  own source entry. This note counts it once: 2 + v + 2j holds one for
  it. Whether the contract's check counts a field that names the source
  entry again is asked (section 13.17). The two readings differ by one
  entry.
  Stated in revision 28: every other repeat has a rule: "One entry that
  is named twice", below.

*A job that is not required, rewritten.* It blocks nothing, and G checks
nothing of it beyond the statement's completeness, as before. Its
opening entry and its deciding entry are fetched and retained at the
delivery of `reserve`, as every listed job's are. That is what the count
above counts.

*Custody and replay, rewritten.* The entries that G fetched are retained
inputs of the entry that recorded the `reserve` (R1 section 9.2). The
outcome of `judge` names the same entries in its `uses`, as a copy, and
retains no entry of its own. A replay finds the origin again, compares
the `uses`, and judges checks 1 to 8 from those entries, from the
observations that the outcome retains, from the list of extents that the
rules observation names, and from the rules and the membership histories
at the observed heads (section 10).
From revision 28: the `report` entries of the selected reports are among
those retained entries, and a replay derives each report's commit from
them.

*Each reason, with what it reads.* Checked for this revision: each
reason of the first table still has its inputs, and one input was
missing before.

| Reason | What decides it | Where it is at hand |
|---|---|---|
| `out-of-date` | The head that was read is not G's recorded head, or is not the manifest's base | The evidence; `branch.head`; the manifest's entry, in `uses` |
| `integration-invalid` | The closure, the tree, the first parent, and the selected reports as ancestors | The evidence; the manifest's entry. One input is at hand in no entry: below. Changed in revision 28: the commit of each selected report is read from its `report` entry, in `uses`. Every input is at hand. |
| `authority-lost` | The merger's key does not hold `change.merge`, by an observation within ten seconds | Row 2 of section 3.3. The key is the signer of P's `merge` entry, in `uses`. |
| `evidence-invalid` | An entry is not what the statement says of it; a key behind a counted verdict or result is compromised | The entries in `uses`; row 5. From revision 28: or the named reports are not the manifest's selections. |
| `rules-not-met` | A request for changes; approvals; required checks; extents; the single-controller exception | Row 1 with its retained list of extents; rows 3, 4 and 5; the statement; the evidence's changed set |
| `incomplete` | The manifest states that it is not complete | The manifest's entry |
| `evidence-too-large` | The changed set is past its bound; or row 4 or row 5 is over | The evidence; what the contract tells the rule of a row |

- *One input that no entry at hand holds: the commit of a selected
  report.* Check 2 asks that each selected report's commit is an
  ancestor of the integration commit. The manifest's entry names each
  selected report as a fact of an issue lane. The commit is in that
  lane's `report` entry, which the `reserve` message does not name and G
  does not fetch. The evidence's member `ancestors` lists commits that
  the runtime found to be ancestors. The rule cannot derive, from an
  entry at hand, which commits the reports name. This was so in revision
  26, and the delta FA9 says that the evidence names no commit. It is
  not decided here. To name each report in `reserve` would add up to 32
  entries to the count that the planner accepted. It is carried, with R2
  (section 13.17).
  Decided in revision 28, by the planner's answer (the act `53ecfb42`,
  answer c): `reserve` names each selected report, and the rule derives
  the commit from the entry. "`reserve` names each selected report",
  below. Nothing of this point is carried.

*Which member of which entry holds each fact (FC5).* The delta asks.
This table is this note's reading of the pinned `change` lane, as data,
in the I3 worktree. R2 owns those rows, and nothing here changes one.

| What the rule reads | The entry at hand | Where in it |
|---|---|---|
| The merger's key | P's `merge` entry, which the field `operation` names | The `actor` of its signed intent |
| The manifest that the merge is of | The same | The intent's field `manifest`, which is the position of the manifest's entry |
| The base, the integration commit, the tree and the completeness | The manifest's entry: a `propose-manifest` entry | The intent's fields `base`, `integration`, `tree` and `complete` |
| The integrator | The same | The member of the entry's grant: its signer |
| The authors | The same | What the entry's recorded effects put in the party list `authors`. How an `attribute` effect is recorded is the contract's section 6.7, which this revision did not read. Owed, with R2. |
| That a verdict is that reviewer's, on this manifest, with that verdict | The entry that `review` names: a `review-verdict` entry | The member of its grant; the intent's fields `manifest` and `verdict` |
| The key behind a verdict | The same | The `actor` of its signed intent |
| A job's opening | The entry that `job` names: a `request-check` entry | The intent's fields `manifest`, `name` and `configuration`; the tree in its recorded effects |
| A job's deciding entry | The entry that `decidedBy` names: a `check` entry | The intent's fields `job`, `tree`, `configuration` and `outcome`; its recorded effects on the job; the `actor`, and the grant with the observation that the entry retains |

- *Is a verdict's entry fetched at the reservation?* No. It is the entry
  that the fact in `review` names, and it is fetched at the delivery of
  `reserve`. Revision 25 said in section 12.1.5 that nothing in the
  three lists is a fact that the destination fetches, and in this
  section that one reservation fetches each verdict's entry. The two did
  not agree, as the delta says. From this revision the lists `verdicts`
  and `jobs` name facts, and `links` names none.

**`reserve` names each selected report. Decided in revision 28** (the
verdict `af0d0a5e`, its second finding; the planner's act `53ecfb42`,
answers a to c). Revision 27 left one input of check 2 in no entry at
hand: the commit of each selected report. It asked the planner whether
`reserve` should name each report. The planner answered that it does,
with up to 32 entries more, so that the destination judges from entries
at hand and a replay derives the same. This block states it. It is in
the forms of the contract's `origin` and of a written type of fact, as
the block above is, and takes effect with it. Where the block above and
this one differ, this one is the rule.

*One more field.* The fields of `reserve` are six.

| Field | Type | What is fetched |
|---|---|---|
| `reports` | `{ type: "list", max: 32, of: { type: "fact", kind: ["report"], under: "issue" } }`, required. New in revision 28. | The entry that each element names: a `report` entry of an issue lane. It opened the report, and its recorded effects hold the report's commit. |

- *Where the type comes from.* The pinned `change` lane, read as data:
  the field `selected` of `propose-manifest`, and the slot `selected` of
  the item `manifest`, are a list of at most 32 records `{ accepted,
  report }`, and `report` has exactly this type of fact. If that row of
  the lane changes, this row changes with it, in a revision of this
  note. - *Only the report is named, and not its acceptance.* The lane
  judged the acceptance when it admitted the manifest (R2 section 5.2).
  The destination needs the commit, which the `report` entry holds. To
  name both would add 64 entries, where the planner decided 32. - *The
  list may be empty, and is still present,* as the other lists are. A
  `reserve` with no field `reports` is `bad-field`. So this row and the
  lane's row that sends the field take effect together ("What the lane
  must send", below).

*The reports are bound to the manifest's selections, exactly.* The rule
`judge` reads the manifest's entry, which is in `uses`: the field
`selected` of its signed intent. It asks two things. The list `reports`
has as many elements as `selected` has records. And for each place i,
the element i of `reports` is the same fact as the member `report` of
the record i of `selected`: the whole fact reference, compared by its
text, byte for byte. Where either fails, the publication ends
`not-reserved`, with the reason `evidence-invalid`: the statement is not
what the manifest says. No name is new.

- *Why in the outcome, and not at the delivery.* A written guard of a
  handler compares operands, and no operand reads a list inside a
  fetched entry beside a list of the message. The rule of `judge` is
  given each entry in `uses` by its bytes. So the check stands with the
  other checks of the statement against its entries, under the same
  name, and no mark is added. - *The commit of a report.* For each
  element, the rule reads the entry that it names, in `uses`: the commit
  that the entry's recorded effects set in the slot `commit` of the
  report that the entry opened. The lane's own guard reads the same
  value, by the part `{ opened: "commit" }`. An entry that opened no
  report, or that set no commit, makes the publication `not-reserved`,
  `evidence-invalid`. Section 12.2 says why a report with no commit does
  not arise in the first version. - *Check 2, its last clause.* Each of
  those commits is in the member `ancestors` of the evidence. Otherwise:
  `not-reserved`, `integration-invalid`, as before. - *What the evidence
  still gives, and what it no longer gives.* The commits are no longer
  the runtime's word: the rule derives them from retained entries. That
  a commit is an ancestor of the integration commit is the host's answer
  to this attempt's read, as `present`, `tree` and `firstParent` are.
  The member `ancestors` holds those of the reports' commits that the
  host showed to be ancestors, and no other commit: one that no named
  report holds makes the outcome `bad-input`. - *A replay* finds the
  origin, compares the `uses`, derives the binding and each commit from
  the same entries, and reads the host's answer from the evidence. It
  takes the ancestry on the evidence, as it takes the closure and the
  tree.

*The count, with reports.* It replaces "The count, rewritten", above. A
message names n entries:

n = 2 + v + j + d + r

for v listed verdicts, j listed jobs, d of those jobs that state
`decidedBy`, and r reports. The 2 are P's `merge` entry and the
manifest's entry. By the types v is at most 64, j at most 64, d at most
j and r at most 32. So n is at most 2 + v + 2j + r. Revision 27 wrote 2
+ v + 2j, and revision 26 wrote 2 + v + 2c.

*The ceiling on the foreign entries of one entry.* The contract's
ceiling is 128 (its section 7.5, as proposed). It is not raised. So a
`reserve` is taken only where

2 + v + j + d + r is at most 128, which is: v + j + d + r is at most
126.

Each report takes one of the 126 places, as a verdict does, and a job
that was decided takes two. A message over the ceiling is decided
`refused`, `bad-field`, at its delivery, by the contract's check of a
message against that bound (its section 6.4, point DH4). Nothing is
fetched, and no publication is opened. The lane's merge item becomes
`refused` with that reason.

| Verdicts | Jobs that state `decidedBy` | Jobs that state none | Reports | Entries named | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 31 | 0 | 0 | 128 | Taken |
| 64 | 32 | 0 | 0 | 130 | `refused`, `bad-field` |
| 64 | 15 | 0 | 32 | 128 | Taken |
| 64 | 16 | 0 | 32 | 130 | `refused`, `bad-field` |
| 30 | 32 | 0 | 32 | 128 | Taken |
| 31 | 32 | 0 | 32 | 129 | `refused`, `bad-field` |
| 64 | 0 | 62 | 0 | 128 | Taken |
| 0 | 63 | 0 | 0 | 128 | Taken |

Each row is a sum by a script. With 32 reports, and with each of the 32
checks that the rules may list decided, 30 verdicts fit. The way forward
for a lane is as before: a new manifest version, whose verdicts are
counted afresh, fewer live verdicts, or fewer selections.

- *64 verdicts. Decided by the planner* (the act `53ecfb42`, answer a):
  the bound is acceptable until the contract has a longer list type. Ask
  1 of section 13.17 stays asked.

*One entry that is named twice.* The count is by naming: each fact that
a field names counts 1, a repeat included. So the count is never under
the number of entries that are fetched.

| The repeat | What follows |
|---|---|
| The field `operation` names the delivery's own source entry | Counted once: the 2 holds it. Whether the contract's check counts it again is still asked (section 13.18). The two readings differ by one entry. |
| Two records of `verdicts` with one `review`, or two records of `jobs` with one `job` or with one `decidedBy` | The lane's `collect` gives one record for an item, and a deciding entry sets one job. So the statement is not the lane's. The publication ends `not-reserved`, `evidence-invalid`. |
| One fact twice in `reports` | Taken only where the manifest's `selected` holds it twice at the same places, by the exact binding. It counts 2. |
| One entry in two fields | It cannot be: each field's type states its own kinds, and no kind is in two of them. |

Whether one entry that is named twice has one record in `uses` or two is
the contract's. No rule here reads the number of records.

*Where each named entry must come from.*

| Field | The scope of the entry | Checked by | A failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `operation` | The sender, which is P | The written guard of `reserve` on the part `scope` | The delivery is `refused`, `not-owner` |
| `manifest`; each `review`; each `job`; each `decidedBy` | P, in P's incarnation: the scope of `operation` | The rule `judge`, as checks 3 and 4 have it for a job | `not-reserved`, `evidence-invalid` |
| Each element of `reports` | The issue lane that the manifest's selection names: the scope is part of the fact, and the binding is exact | The rule `judge` | `not-reserved`, `evidence-invalid` |
| Every one of them | A scope that pins a definition with the name that the field's type states as `under`: `change`, or `issue` for a report | The contract, when it fetches a fact under a written type | The delivery is `refused`, `bad-field` |

The destination does not judge that an issue lane is of its own
repository. No form lets it, which is the part of G7 that is asked of
the contract. The lane judged the selection when it admitted the
manifest.

*What the lane must send.* This is asked of the lane forms note. One row
changes: the act `merge` of the `change` lane, in the first of its
sends, which is the `tell` named `reserve` to the destination. That send
gains one field, `reports`: the member `report` of each record of the
slot `selected` of `also.manifest`, in the slot's order. No row of the
lane's handler `publication` changes, and no update carries a report.
The source of the field needs one form: a send source that gives one
member of each record of a list. The contract has that form for an
argument of a capability, `{ each, as, value }`, and not for a send. It
is asked of the contract (section 13.18). The change moves the bytes and
the digest of the pinned `change` definition, which is R2's to do.

*The five passages of the block above, as they read from revision 28.*

| Passage | It gains |
|---|---|
| The table of when: at the delivery of `reserve` | G fetches the `report` entry of each selected report too, and retains it, read or not |
| "The fields of `reserve`" | The row `reports`, above. The message has six fields. |
| "The count, rewritten" | Replaced by "The count, with reports" and the ceiling |
| "Custody and replay, rewritten" | The `report` entries are among the retained inputs of the entry that recorded the `reserve`, and the outcome of `judge` copies them in `uses`. A replay derives the binding and each commit from them. |
| "Each reason, with what it reads", and the point under it | `integration-invalid` reads the reports' commits from entries in `uses`. `evidence-invalid` has one more cause: the named reports are not the manifest's selections. Every input of every reason is at hand in an entry. |

| What the rule reads | The entry at hand | Where in it |
|---|---|---|
| The selections of the manifest | The manifest's entry | The intent's field `selected`: a list of records `{ accepted, report }` |
| The commit of a selected report | The entry that an element of `reports` names: a `report` entry of an issue lane | The slot `commit` that its recorded effects set on the report that it opened |

### 6.6 Publishing: complete forward

Each step is an entry in G or a record in G's ledger, in this order.

1. **Open attempt n.** An entry records the attempt: the operation, n,
   the ref, the expected base and the integration commit.
2. **Mint.** The ledger records the token's duty, then asks the host. A
   mint whose answer is lost leaves the token's duty unknown; if nothing
   was sent with it, the attempt itself is "not sent".
3. **Grant and send.** The gateway opens one grant for attempt n. It
   records "forwarding" before it forwards the one update, and closes
   the grant after. A closed grant forwards nothing more, whatever
   process asks.
4. **Record what is known about the send.** One of:

| Evidence | Meaning | Requires |
|---|---|---|
| Not sent | No update of attempt n reached the host. | The grant is closed and its record shows nothing was forwarded. |
| Refused | The host answered that update and did not apply it. | The grant shows one forward; the host's answer was received whole; Git reports a rejection of that ref by the remote. |
| Unknown | The update may have been applied, or may still be. | Anything else: a forward with no whole answer; a timeout; a lost container or callback; a token revoked meanwhile; an error after sending. |

5. **Revoke the token.** A failed revocation is a duty. It decides
   nothing.
6. **Read back.** G reads the ref. The read, the route it used and the
   time are kept as evidence. That, and only that, decides:

| The ref holds | Then |
|---|---|
| The integration commit | `published`. G's head becomes that commit. The slot is free. |
| The expected base | `unresolved`. After a backoff, open attempt n+1: the same compare-and-swap. From revision 14 a publication's push has at most 3 attempts (section 12, G3). After the third, a further send is opened only by an admin's `resend`. |
| Anything else | Section 6.9. |
| The read failed | Nothing is decided. Read again. |

**Why sending again is acceptable.** Every send of this operation asks
for the same thing: move this ref from this base to this commit. If an
earlier send is still on its way, whichever arrives first moves the
ref, and the other is refused because the ref no longer holds the base.
This needs no recognition of a repeat by the host. It needs the host to
refuse an update whose old value is wrong (section 12, H1).

**What `published` settles and what it does not.** The read shows the
operation's effect: the branch holds the commit. It does not say which
attempt did it. Attempts whose evidence was unknown stay recorded as
unknown; they are not given an answer. Their tokens' duties stay in the
ledger. The slot is released because no send of this operation can
change the ref again: each expects the base, and under exclusive
ownership the ref does not return to it.

**What is never done.** G does not release the slot, or reserve another
publication, while this one is `reserved`, `publishing` or `unresolved`.

**A lost reply**, R0's step 14, is step 4 with "unknown", then step 6.

### 6.7 What P is told

G's relationship update is sent at each change: reserved; unresolved,
with what the read saw; and one final update. On `published`, with the
commit, P's proposal becomes `merged` and P sends each linked issue
"merged" (R2 section 8).

### 6.8 A publication that does not publish

After reservation a publication ends without publishing only as
`aborted`, and only with proof that **nothing sent for it can still
land**.

**The host keeps refusing.** If every attempt's evidence is "refused" or
"not sent", and the read shows the base, nothing is in flight. After
three such attempts G records the abort itself, with the host's reason.
P's merge becomes `refused`.

**A compromised key.** When membership's notice reaches G, and the key
is behind the held publication, G records an abort attempt at once. It
opens no further attempt and revokes the live token. In the earlier
measurement that stopped a push whose body was still uploading and did
not stop one whose body was sent; no guarantee is known either way.
Then the read decides:

| The ref holds | Evidence so far | Then |
|---|---|---|
| The integration commit | Any | `published`. The change is in the branch. P's parties and admins are told that it rested on compromised evidence. A reversal is a new pull request. |
| The base | Every attempt "refused" or "not sent" | `aborted`. |
| The base | At least one attempt unknown | Not provable. **The slot stays held.** The publication is `unresolved`, the page says the outcome is not known, and G keeps reading. |

That last row is the rule until something better is adopted. It is
honest and it can hold a branch for a long time.

**A fence, proposed for this design review.** G itself moves the ref
off the base, so that no send of the aborted operation can ever apply.

| Part | Specified as |
|---|---|
| The commit | Tree: the base's tree. One parent: the base. Author and committer: a fixed platform identity naming G's scope ID. Both times: the time of G's abort entry. Message: a fixed sentence and the operation's fact. So the commit ID is the same on every retry. |
| The operation | "Fence for" the aborted operation, with its own identity in G, its own attempts, grants, tokens and ledger duties, exactly as section 6.6. Its fact is G's abort entry. |
