| Authorized by | G's abort entry. No member's key, compromised or not, is involved. |
| The read shows the base | Send the fence again. Neither operation is final. |
| The read shows anything else | Section 6.9. |

The read decides which of the two operations landed. Every result
below depends on that.

| | The read shows the fence commit | The read shows the integration commit |
|---|---|---|
| What happened | The fence arrived first. | The original arrived first. |
| The original operation, in G | `aborted` | `published`, with the notice that it rested on compromised evidence |
| The fence operation, in G | `published` | `aborted` |
| The commit the branch holds, and G's head | The fence commit. Its content is the base's. | The integration commit. |
| G's final update to P (section 6.4) | `aborted` | `published`, with the integration commit |
| P's merge item | `aborted` | `published` |
| P's proposal | Not merged. It stays open, and its manifest is out of date. No linked issue is sent "merged". | `merged`. Each linked issue is sent "merged". |
| What P's parties and admins are told | The merge was stopped after a key behind it was revoked as compromised. The branch holds a fence commit that changes no content. | The change is in the branch. It was published before it could be stopped, and it rested on evidence by a key revoked as compromised. A reversal is a new pull request. |
| The receipt owed (section 6.10) | One, for the fence operation. It is named by the digest of the fence operation's fact, and holds G's final fact for the fence, the aborted operation's fact and the fence commit. None for the original. | One, for the original operation, as for any publication. None for the fence: it did not land. |
| Other open pull requests on that branch | Out of date. Each needs a new manifest. | The same, as after any publication. |
| Sends of the other operation that arrive later | The original's are refused by the host: the ref no longer holds the base. | The fence's are refused by the host, for the same reason. |
| Attempts with unknown evidence, and token duties | Those of both operations stay recorded as unknown, after both are final. They are not given an answer. | The same. |
| The slot | Free. | Free. |

In both columns the losing operation ends `aborted`, and that needs
proof that none of its sends can still land. The proof is that each
expects the base, and the ref does not return to the base. It rests on
H1 and H4, which are operational assumptions (section 12). It is not a
guarantee, and a finite set of races does not make it one.

A fence does not end by itself. It needs the host to answer and the
read to work. While either is unavailable the publication stays
`unresolved` and visible. And if something else could move the ref
back to the base, an old send could land after all.

**The standing of this section. Stated in revision 17** (the I3
plan's question Q12). Revision 16 is adopted as it is written. As
written, this section has two parts, and they stand differently.

- *Adopted.* Everything above the heading "A fence, proposed for
  this design review". An abort needs proof that nothing sent can
  still land. The host that keeps refusing. A compromised key, and
  its table of three rows. And the rule of that table's last row:
  while a send is unknown and the read shows the base, the slot
  stays held and the publication is `unresolved`. That is "hold". It
  is the rule in force (decision D3-7; section 12, U2).
- *Proposed, and not adopted.* The fence: its commit, its operation,
  the table of two columns, and the two paragraphs after that table.
  The text offered it "for this design review". The reviews of
  revisions 14 to 16 did not rule on it, and the approval
  `33787163` does not name it. The adoption of the note adopts this
  part as what it says it is, which is a proposal. Both rows for U2
  in section 12 say the same.
- *For I3.* Build the hold. Build no fence commit, no fence
  operation and no write of the branch that is not a publication's,
  and reserve nothing for one. The I3 plan's step 28 has it so. The
  proof plan's case for a fence is not run: the I3 plan cites it as
  F16, and section 12 as HS3. The words "a fence" in the evidence
  table of section 5.7, and in the destination's row of outcomes
  (section 12.1.5), describe the proposal. No source implements
  them.
- *What would adopt it.* A review that is asked about the fence by
  name. It would need H1 and H4 read for the chosen host (section
  12), and the fence operation's own reservations declared in
  section 5.8, which has none for it today. Until then an abort with
  an unknown send holds the slot.

### 6.9 Another writer

If a read shows a commit that is not the base, the integration commit,
or a fence G sent, something else wrote to the branch.

- G stops sending, keeps the slot, and records the incident with what
  it saw.
- Nothing is concluded from "the ref is different now". A writer that
  moved it could move it back, and a send still in flight would then
  apply.
- An admin's act, `adopt-head`, may record the observed commit as G's
  head only when every earlier operation of G is final, or fenced. It
  records who adopted what and why. Unknown duties stay in the ledger.
- A reset of the destination is section 8.3.

G reads the host's head before each reservation. That detects another
writer before the slot is taken.

### 6.10 The receipt in the repository

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is the receipt written in the same push as the branch? | No. Whether the host updates two refs atomically is not established (facts 5.2). |
| How is it written? | After `published`, by a second write: create a ref expected to be absent, pointing at a commit whose one file is the receipt. Its own grant, token and attempts. |
| What is its name? | `refs/artroom/receipts/<digest of the operation's fact>`. The operation's fact names P's scope, incarnation, position and hash, so the name is never reused, even if a destination's numbering starts again. |
| What does it hold? | G's final publication fact, with G's scope, incarnation and hash; the operation's fact; the manifest's fact; the integration commit. |
| What does a crash between the two writes leave? | A published branch with no receipt yet. The receipt is a ledger duty that survives the publication's final state and never holds the slot. Readback tells the cases apart: absent, write it; present with this content, done; present with other content, an incident. |
| What is it worth to a verifier? | It is an anchor the caller may choose to trust. It names facts. It does not derive the result. A replay still needs G's and P's histories and what they used, or it reports what is missing (R1 section 9.4). |

Stated in revision 27: "digest of the operation's fact" in the name is
the 64 lower-case hexadecimal characters of that fact's `hash`, with
nothing before or after them, in a form of the contract's revision 21,
which is not adopted. The receipt's file and its commit are stated byte
for byte in section 12.1.5. "A ledger duty that survives the
publication's final state" is an item of its own, `receipt`, because a
`published` publication is final and takes no effect (section 12.1.5,
"Where a receipt's records stand").

### 6.11 What is not claimed

- No transaction spans P and G. P's statement and G's reservation are
  two local commits joined by messages.
- No transaction spans G and the Git host.
- The compare-and-swap is the documented behavior of a Git push with an
  expected old value. That is the Git command's contract. It is not a
  statement by this host about its server, its reads or how late a sent
  update can apply.
- Nothing is published across two repositories or two branches as one
  operation.
- No timing or throughput is claimed.

## 7. Races, in both orders

Each row is one distinct pair. R4 chooses compact witnesses.

| Pair | First, then second | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| A retired revocation of the merger, and reservation | In membership before G's observation began | Not reserved, `authority-lost`. |
| | After G's observation began, before G's commit | Reserved. The grace window. |
| | After reservation | The publication goes on, under G's own record. |
| A compromised revocation of a reviewer, and reservation | Before G's observation began | Not reserved, `evidence-invalid`. |
| | After reservation, no attempt yet, notice arrives | Abort; nothing was sent; `aborted`. |
| | After reservation, an attempt unknown, notice arrives | Section 6.8: published, or held, or fenced if that is adopted. |
| | Notice delayed until after `published` | The branch is unchanged. P's parties and admins are told. |
| | Notice lost | Membership sends it again; it is a request with a result. Until it arrives, as "delayed". |
| P's `withdraw`, and G's reservation | Arrives while `queued`, or before `reserve` | Ended, "withdrawn". |
| | G reserves first | Refused, `reserved`. The publication goes on. |
| P's `withdraw`, and G's decision not to reserve | `withdraw` arrives first, while `queued` | Ended, "withdrawn". |
| | G ends the publication first, for example `out-of-date` | Refused, `ended`, with `not-reserved` and that reason. G never reserved, and the publication is not opened again. |
| A clock that is behind, and an outcome that judges no time | No transition is due by the previous entry's time | The outcome is written with a clamped time (section 3.12; R1 section 5.3). |
| | A transition is due | Nothing is written. The outcome is offered again. |
| A staging's own record, and its ancestry check | The record and the `live` root are first, as they always are | The walk still visits every parent of the commit. The candidate's root is not a stop (section 6.2). |
| A lane's own root on a commit, and another commitment's staged ref on the same commit | The other ref is in the snapshot of the first check of that commit | A foreign start. If the commit is not published, and no input or selection names it, the act is refused `unnamed-work` (section 6.2). If it is published, no basis is asked. |
| | The lane's check was admitted first, with no foreign start, and the other ref is staged later | The later ref takes nothing from the lane. A reuse finds a foreign start on the `own-check` basis and is admitted. |
| The publication of a commit that another commitment staged, and a check that starts from that commit | The publication is first: the head that the check reads holds the commit | A published start. No basis is asked, and F is empty, while the other root is kept and after it is retired (section 6.2). |
| | The check's read of the head is first | Not published for this check. A basis is asked, and without one the act is refused `unnamed-work`. A later preparation reads the head again. |
| The retirement of a staged root, and a replay of an ancestry check that listed its commit | The replay is first | F is derived from the snapshot. |
| | The retirement is first | The same F, from the same snapshot. The refs as they are now are not read (section 6.2). |
| A rules change, and reservation | In the rules scope before G's observation began | Judged under the new rules. |
| | After | Goes on under the rules G observed. |
| Another publication, and this one's reservation | The other publishes first | This one is not reserved, `out-of-date`. |
| | This one reserves first | The other waits `queued`, then is not reserved. |
| A new verdict in P, and P's merge | The verdict first | It is in the eligibility statement. |
| | The merge first | The verdict is refused: a merge is in progress. |
| A hold's end, and a report | The hold ends first | The report is admitted if its commit was already staged and that root is still `live`; it needs the commitment, not the hold. A new staging needs a held hold, and so does a new root for a commit already in the canonical repository. |
| | The report first | Nothing to decide. |
| A hold's end in a change lane, and `propose-manifest` from that hold | The hold ends first | The manifest is admitted only by reuse of a root that is still `live`. A new staging is refused `not-staged`. |
| | The manifest first | Nothing to decide. The hold's end changes nothing the manifest rests on. |
| A handover, and the former performer's report | Handover first | Refused: the signer is not the performer. |
| | The report first | Admitted. The handover follows. |
| Revoking device A, and a control from A | The revocation is observed first | Refused. |
| | The control is recorded first | It stands. The next is refused within sixty seconds on the task scope's clock (section 3.12, W2). |
| The controller's last key revoked, and an agent's push to its fork | Observed before the token is minted | No token. |
| | The push is in flight | It may arrive in that hold's fork, which nothing else uses. It cannot be staged without a hold, so no report of it can follow. Within the five-minute window the agent could still report a commit staged earlier. |
| A lost push reply, and the read | The update applied | The read shows the integration commit: `published`. |
| | It did not apply | The read shows the base: the same update is sent again. |
| The original update, and a fence | The original arrives first | The fence is refused. The original is `published` and P's merge is `published`. The fence operation is `aborted` and owes no receipt. |
| | The fence arrives first | The original is refused whenever it arrives. The original is `aborted` and P's merge is `aborted`. The fence operation is `published` and owes its receipt. |
| A pin on a staged root, and its retirement | The pin is recorded first | The root stays `live`. No delete is sent. |
| | `retiring` is recorded first, with the delete's answer lost or not | The pin is refused. A signer with a held hold whose fork holds the commit gets a new root under a new name. A signer without one is refused `not-staged`. The late delete can remove only the old root. |
| `pin-confirm` and `unpin` for one manifest, at the staging lane | `pin-confirm` first | The pin is `held`, then `released`. |
| | `unpin` first | The pin is `released`, with the record that the manifest was admitted. The later confirmation is recorded and restores nothing. |
| An `unpin` applied, and its result | The result is delivered | P records it. |
| | The result is lost | It is delivered again. If the staging lane's storage is lost, P records `delivery-unavailable` and concludes nothing. |
| Two `created` answers for one founding claim, or for one hold's fork | Attempt a's answer is recorded first | a's repository or fork is selected. b's is recorded as not selected, whenever it arrives, and replaces nothing. |
| | Attempt b's answer is recorded first | The reverse. The attempts' numbers decide nothing. |
| The directory's result, and the claim | The first result for a `pending` claim | The claim is `active` with that incarnation, and that genesis is confirmed. |
| | A later result with another incarnation | `incarnation-conflict`. Nothing is activated or confirmed. |
| A revocation, and a private stream's check | Recorded before the check's read began | The check fails. The stream closes at once. |
| | Recorded after the read began | The check may pass. The stream ends within eighty seconds of the record, as the task scope's clock measures it (section 12, H5). |
| The task scope's clock, and an open stream | A reading earlier than the last passing check, before a send | The stream is closed at once, `clock-behind`. No byte is sent on that reading. |
| | A clock that has not moved since the last passing check | Found when the next check runs. The stream is closed, `clock-stalled`. |
| | A clock that runs slow, or stalls between two checks | Not detected. The bound is then eighty seconds on that clock and not in real time (H5). |
| A revocation, and an act on a cached observation | The scope's clock has moved since the observation's last use, and its age is inside the window | Admitted. The grace window, in that scope's clock time. |
| | The scope's clock has not moved since the last use, or the scope restarted | The observation is read again. The act is refused if the read shows the revocation, and `authority-unavailable` if membership does not answer. |
| The end of the receiving hold, and an export's license request, in the lane | The hold ends first | The request is refused `target-not-held`. Nothing is dispatched. The release is `withheld`. |
| | The license entry is first | The task scope holds a license. A dispatch inside the license window is authorized, though the hold has ended. The bytes can reach only the instance the license names, which is fenced. |
| An export's license result, and the license window | The result is delivered and `dispatched` is committed inside ten seconds of the request's entry | Dispatched. |
| | The result is late, or the task scope restarted | Not dispatched. A new numbered request is sent. After three, `withheld`. |
| `export-settled`, and a dispatch | The final entry F is first | No dispatch follows: the release is final. The receiver pin is released on F. |
| | A dispatch is unanswered | No F exists, so no `export-settled`. The receiver pin stays `standing`, also after the hold ends. |
| Two commitments in one issue lane, and a new hold's seed | The other commitment reported first | The seed is the destination's head. The other commitment's report is not seeded. |
| | The hold's own commitment reported first | The seed is that report's commit. |
| A revocation of the authorizer, and an export's release | Observed before the commit that records `dispatched` | Not dispatched. The release is `withheld`. The receiver has no byte. The staged copy is deleted. |
| | Recorded in membership after that observation's read began, or after `dispatched` is recorded | The dispatch is authorized and is not recalled. A recorded `intent` or `dispatched` is not a delivery: the bytes may become readable at any later time, also after the revocation. The release is `confirmed` only by the storage's own answer, and `unknown` until then. |
| A dispatch of a release, and its answer | The answer is received | `confirmed`, or refused with nothing made readable. |
| | The answer is lost, or the runtime restarts first | `unknown`. The source pin, the receiver pin, the staged copy and the named hold and instance are kept. It is not dispatched again. |
| A person's last key is revoked, and that person's `renew-hold` | Recorded in membership before the read for that commit began | Refused. The hold keeps its end time and runs out (section 3.5). |
| | Recorded after that read began | Renewed: the ten-second grace window of W3. No later renewal is admitted. |
| A person's last key is revoked, and a push from the hold's instance | The runtime's check fails first | No push is started. The gateway's route is closed. |
| | The gateway forwarded the push first | It may land in that hold's own fork, at any later time. It stays unknown until its own answer. The token's later revocation does not answer it. |
| A hold's renewal, and its live workspace token | The renewal is admitted while the token is live | The token is not revoked and not replaced. |
| | A second token is asked for after the renewal | It is a separate request, with its own observation. The first token is revoked only after the gateway confirms the second (section 5.3). |
| A flood of joins that fail, and a join with the right secret | The flood comes first, from other addresses | The join is admitted. No limit is keyed by the invitation (section 3.6). |
| | The flood comes first, from the invitee's own address | `rate-limited` for that address until the window ends. The invitation is unchanged, and the same signed bytes are sent again. |
| The image that a runner started from, and the image the rules name | They are the same | `check`, by the judging step. |
| | They differ, or the first cannot be resolved | `check-error`. The job is `errored`. It is not a pass and not a failure (section 3.11). |
| A destination's first head, and a hold's seed from the destination's head | The read for the seed shows the first head | The fork is seeded there. |
| | The read shows no branch | The `fork` record is `failed`, `no-head`. No fork is created. A later hold reads again (section 12.2). |
| A first `withdraw` that is diagnosed `undelivered`, and a second in another envelope | The first never arrived | The second is the bound one. It uses the entry that the publication reserved. |
| | The first did arrive, and was decided | The mark is set, and the second is new work. Each has its own result, and neither settles the other (section 12.1.5). Corrected in revision 25: the mark is set only where the first was applied. Where it was refused, both are new work. |
| A read that shows a key revoked, and an observation of that key that the scope still holds | The read is first | The older observation is not used again in that run (section 3.3). |
| | An answer that shows the key active arrives after that read | It is not used. |

## 8. Outside effects and what must be settled

### 8.1 Every kind of outside effect in the new model

| Effect | Owner scope | Unknown outcome is kept as | Settled by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Update of the branch | Destination | An unresolved publication holding the slot | A read of the ref, for the operation's effect |
| A fence, a receipt | Destination | An attempt with unknown evidence; a duty | A read of that ref |
| The first head of a branch. Added in revision 14. | Destination | An attempt with unknown evidence. The branch stays `empty`. | A read of the branch, for the effect (section 12.2) |
| Creating a staged root | The staging lane | A ledger duty; a root that is `creating` | A read of that ref, for the effect. An attempt stays unknown until its own answer. |
| Deleting a staged root | The staging lane | A root that is `retiring`, with an unknown delete | A read of that ref, for the effect. The attempt and its token stay duties. |
| Creating the repository at founding | Founding register | A creation attempt, `unknown` | That request's own answer. A later attempt has its own name and settles nothing. An answer that arrives after another repository was selected settles its own attempt and selects nothing (section 3.8). |
| Mint or revoke of a token | The scope that asked | A ledger duty | That request's answer; or, for a token whose ID and end time are known, that time |
| Create or delete of a fork or snapshot repository | Lane | A ledger duty | That request's answer. A late `created` answer for a hold that already has a fork selects nothing (section 5.1). |
| A manifest's pin in another lane | The staging lane | A pin that is `provisional` or `held` | `pin-confirm`, `unpin`, or the settlement answer for the intent. Never a lost message, and never time. |
| Import of a repository at founding | Directory, after its confirmation | A retained attempt | That attempt's answer |
| A check job sent to the checker service | Change lane | A job with no result | A `check` or a `check-error` act. A deadline ends waiting; it does not prove the run stopped. |
| A check's run | The checker service, in its own durable record. It is not a scope. | A run that started and whose end was not found | That run's own end, as the service observed it. Otherwise `check-error`, `run-lost`, and no second run for that job (section 3.11). |
| An agent's command, edit, commit preparation or fork push | Task scope | An interrupted or unknown operation | Observation of that operation. A new attempt has its own identity. |
| A push to a hold's fork, as an effect. Stated in revision 14. | Task scope | An attempt that is `unknown` | A read of the fork's ref, for the effect. The attempt stays unknown until its own answer (section 5.9). |
| Save and delete of private work | Task scope | A duty | The storage's answer |
| Release of an export | Task scope | A release `dispatched` and not answered: `unknown` | The storage's own answer to that request. Until then the bytes may be readable, now or later. It is not dispatched again. A recorded `intent` alone is no effect. |
| An export's receiver pin | The lane that owns the receiving hold | A pin that is `standing` | `export-settled`, read against the task scope's final entry. Never the hold's end, a handover, elapsed time or an unreachable task scope. |
| A send outside the application, if ever adopted | Inbox | A send that is accepted, unknown or expired | Section 9 |

An inventory settles none of these when the request was sent and not
answered.

### 8.2 Before an earlier deployment is retired or reset

R0 scope E1 owes a settlement plan and ledger. This is what it must
contain. Nothing here is run by this note.

1. **Stop new effects first.** Before anything is counted, the earlier
   deployment stops admitting ordinary acts and starting new outside
   effects. Otherwise a clean count can be made wrong before it is used.
   What stays running is what settles: the alarms that read back
   publications, deliver and retry cleanup, and the storage and readers
   they need. They stay until their duties settle.
2. **Count what is in flight.** Dispatches recorded and not answered;
   open gateway routes; runner and publisher containers still running;
   outboxes; cleanup actors. Work that was prepared and never
   dispatched is cancelled by a recorded fence: its route is closed with
   nothing forwarded.
3. **Inventory Artroom's resources.** In each namespace and binding the
   configurations name: Workers and their versions; Durable Object
   storage; container applications and images; repositories, forks and
   tokens that the ledgers or provenance identify as Artroom's;
   secrets; and, at the source host, the repository's variables,
   secrets, deploy keys and workflow runs. A resource in the same
   account that nothing identifies as Artroom's is not treated as owned
   and is not touched. A missing registry entry or missing storage is
   not proof that a resource does not exist.
4. **For each Room found:** every landing not in a final state; the
   publication slot; every workspace, fork, snapshot repository and
   token duty; every mint record that is sent or unknown.
5. **Settle publications** only by a read of the branch, under the same
   host and exclusive-writer assumptions as section 12. A Room with an
   unresolved publication is not deleted.
6. **Settle tokens.** A token with a known ID is revoked, or its known
   end time has passed. A mint or create whose answer was never
   received stays unknown. It is not closed by a listing, and it is not
   closed because the publication it served became final.
7. **Settle repositories.** A fork or snapshot repository is deleted
   only when its creation was answered, its tokens are settled, and its
   provenance is exactly the canonical repository it was made from.
8. **Record.** A ledger row for each resource: settled with what
   evidence, or still owed and by whom.
9. **Then retire** what the ledger shows as owned and settled. The
   storage, reader and owner needed for a duty that is still unknown
   are kept.

An item that cannot be settled stays in the ledger. It does not block
the new model's work, which uses new storage, new names and a new
repository at the host. The earlier engine and its formats are not kept
running as a product; only what settles is.

### 8.3 Before a new-model deployment is reset

New acts and new outside effects are stopped first, as in section 8.2.
Then: no destination has a publication that is `reserved`, `publishing`
or `unresolved`; no gateway grant is open; no scope's ledger has a duty
that is sent or unknown; no scope has a request at
`delivery-unavailable`; no task scope has an unknown operation. The
founding register keeps its claims, so that a reset repository is
founded as a new one, on a new repository at the host.

## 9. A send outside the application

No channel is adopted. If one is, it must meet this contract, which
keeps the planner's corrections `7318cd52`.

- **Who sends.** The member's inbox scope. It alone holds that member's
  subscriptions and consent. A send is an outside effect of the inbox,
  with a ledger: prepared, in flight, accepted by the provider, unknown,
  expired.
- **What authorizes it.** The member's own signed act that registers a
  device subscription, by that device's key. A subscription has a
  generation.
- **What it carries.** A generic first payload, with no content of any
  lane.
- **Opening it.** The application then reads the item with the member's
  current authority. A revoked device's session is accepted until it
  ends, at most ten minutes (section 3.12, W6), and not renewed.
- **What cannot be promised.** That a delivery already accepted by a
  provider can be recalled. That an alert is displayed for a set time.
- **Budgets.** Reserved in the same commit that records the send.
- **Endpoints.** Validated as secure addresses of supported providers.

## 10. What a verifier can check

| About | Derived again from history | Trusted, and reported as trusted |
|---|---|---|
| A grant | That membership's history at the observed head gives that key those actions under that definition version. That the commit's time minus the observation's time is inside the window and not negative. That the entry's record of its read and use is consistent with the scope's history: section 3.3, "What a replay checks, and what it trusts". Equal values in two entries show nothing, and are not compared. | That the observation was made when stated. That each recorded read was performed, and that a read recorded as `fresh` was not a held value: `trusted: observation-read`, vouched for by the observing scope's runtime. That the scope's clock kept real time (H5). |
| An ancestry check | The walk, the sorting of the staged refs on the start, whether the start is published, F and the judgment, from the retained record and the retained snapshot, with commits read by ID: section 6.2, "Replay". Never from the staged refs as they are now. | That the host returned that head and that list of staged refs when the staging lane read them, and that the lane kept what was returned: `trusted: staged-ref-read`, vouched for by the staging lane's runtime, on H2. |
| A clamped entry | That its input judges no time condition, that its time is the previous entry's, and that no transition was due at that time (R1 section 9.3). | That the clock was right. |
| Independence | From the manifest's authors and the reviewer's observation. | Nothing further. |
| A reservation | Each check of section 6.5, from P's `merge` entry and the entries it names, the rules scope's history at the observed head, and membership's. | The observation times; the head read from the host. |
| An attempt | That it was opened before its evidence; that every attempt names the same base and commit; that "not sent" and "refused" have the evidence they require. | The gateway's record and the publisher's report. |
| An export's dispatch | That the `dispatched` entry retains the lane's license entry, that the license names the same export, digest, hold and instance, and that the entry's time is less than ten seconds after the entry that sent the request. | The authorizer's observation time; the task scope's clock. |
| A fork's seed | That the seed record's report or manifest has the same `under` as the hold. | The host's read of the branch, for a seed from the destination's head. |
| A join | That the hash of the secret in the join equals the hash that the invitation holds; that the invitation was unused at that entry and had not ended; that the signing key was not a recovery key or a member's key (sections 3.1 and 3.6). | Nothing further. The limits of section 3.6 are not in the history, and no judgment rests on them. |
| A check's result | The signature and the grant; that the job exists; that the tree and the configuration digest equal the job's; that the digest of the details is in the signed intent (section 3.11). | What ran: the image, the environment and each step's end. That is the checker member's signed statement, and a replay does not derive it. |
| `published` | That the integration commit is reachable from the branch as read now, and the receipt if present. | When it happened; the host's read. The report names the host and route. |
| `aborted` | That every attempt's evidence is "refused" or "not sent"; or, for an original operation, that a fence commit follows the base in the branch as read now; or, for a fence operation, that the integration commit does. | The evidence records; the host's read. |

**What no source may take as settled.** An unknown attempt, a token's
duty and a writer's duty each stay under their own identity until
that request's own answer, or until the rule that section 5.4 names
for it. None of these settles one: a restart; a listing or an
inventory; a scope that replaces another, or a new incarnation; the
removal of a staged root; a new ref. That holds in I3 and IA, and in
E1 for the earlier deployment.

**Later components and applications.** Each is retargeted or removed
by the owner that R0 names for it. Sections 8.2 and 11 give the order
for what this note covers. Revisions 10 to 12 remove nothing from
that work and stop none of it.

### 11.2 Revision 14: each disposition and definition, by delivery

New in revision 14. Section 11.1 is kept. This section maps what
revision 14 adds to the deliveries of R0 section 8: who builds it,
what it needs first, what cannot run before that, what source is
removed when it lands, and where it is accepted. Nothing here
commissions source, and nothing is built by being written. Removal
belongs to the delivery that replaces a thing. No earlier path is
kept running beside its successor, and no adapter is built between
the two models.

**What the I1 source is, for this map.** I1 at `a3e5a77e` is a
substrate. It has the commit protocol, the fold, delivery, timed
rules, a validator for revision 7's forms with some later ones, and a
replay of one scope. It has ports for what another owner decides,
and each production default refuses: no grant is current, nobody may
read, and no platform definition can be pinned
(`packages/scope/src/ports.ts`). Founding there asks no grant and
judges nothing about who signs (`packages/derive/src/genesis.ts`).
So an accepted review of I1 implements no grant, no observation, no
platform scope, no outside effect and no capability record. It also
implements none of the eight rows that R1 section 11.9 marks "must
change", which are I1's own later work. This note read that source,
as its opening says. It reads none of it as evidence that a rule of
this note is built.

## 12. What is not resolved

Host properties the design rests on. Each is an operational
assumption at the chosen host, reported as such. A finite run of races
or reads shows those cases. It does not establish a guarantee. Where an
assumption fails, the protocol's conclusions that rest on it are not
safe, and this note does not claim otherwise.

| # | Property | Evidence today | If it does not hold |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | The host refuses a ref update whose stated old value is not the ref's present value. | The Git push command's documented contract for an expected old value. Measured on this host in the earlier work: 20 of 20 races, and one winner in a 10-way race (facts 5.2). Not stated by the host as a guarantee of its server. | Two sends of one operation still give the same commit. But a late send could land after a later publication. Slot release and the fence would be unsound. |
| H2 | A read of the ref through the host's binding returns the ref's present value. | Used by the earlier code. Its consistency after a write is not documented. | A stale read of the base causes a harmless repeat. A stale read that shows the integration commit or a fence when the ref does not hold it would record a final state that is wrong. Finding a different head at the next reservation stops further publication but does not make that recorded result right; it is an incident. A replay reports that it trusted the host's read. |
| H3 | Nothing bounds how late a sent update can apply. | Stated as absent (facts 5.4). | The design assumes no bound. |
| H5 | The clock of each scope that judges a time does not advance by less than the real time that passed, between any two readings that one row of section 3.12 uses. That includes two readings on either side of a restart, for a deadline or an end time that is stored. | None. It is an assumption about the runtime's clock. This note detects a clock that goes back (R1 section 5.3; section 4.2), and a clock that has not moved between two uses of one cached observation or between two checks of a stream (sections 3.3 and 4.2). It does not detect a clock that moves too slowly. | Every bound of section 3.12 is a bound on that clock, and may be longer in real time: the grace windows, the license window, the private stream's eighty seconds, a hold's duration, a job's deadline and the retention deadline. The fail-closed rules of section 3.12 still hold. R4 measures boundaries. No measurement establishes this assumption. |
| H6 | Two clocks that one rule compares differ by no more than a known amount: a reading scope's clock and membership's, for a read session and for a grant's `notAfter`; a scope's clock and the Git host's, for a token's end time. | None. No amount is measured or proposed, except the 60-second margin of section 5.4, rule 4. | A read session, or a grant with an end time, is accepted for longer by the difference. A token's duty could be settled while the host still honours the token, if the difference is more than the margin. |
| H4 | The branch is written only by the destination. | Token custody and the founding register. Nothing at the host enforces it against another holder of a write token for the same repository. | Section 6.9. An old send could land if another writer returns the ref to an old base. |

**Each assumption as an operational obligation. New in revision 10.**
The table above says what each property is and what follows if it
fails. This one says what it rests on and who is answerable. Stating
an assumption does not prove it. Neither does a witness in a fixture,
or any finite run at the real host.

| # | The property | The contract it rests on | Who decides to rely on it | Who owns the evidence | The source boundary |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | The host refuses a ref update whose stated old value is not the ref's present value. | The Git push command's contract for an expected old value, as the chosen host's server carries it out. The host states no guarantee. | The operator who chooses the Git host for a deployment, recorded under the installation design N5. For this design, this note's review. | R4: cases HS1, HS2, HS3 and HS7 of its host session, at B5, when it is commissioned. I3 runs it. The earlier record is in the facts file, section 5.2. | The destination's publisher and its gateway. Every update is sent with its expected old value, through one grant, and no path sends one without it (sections 6.1 and 6.6). |
| H2 | A read of a ref through the host's binding returns the ref's present value. | The host's read interface, as the destination and a staging lane use it. Its consistency after a write is not documented. | The same. | R4: case HS6. It shows its reads and no rate. | One reader: for the readback (section 6.6), for the head before a reservation (section 6.9) and for the ancestry read (section 6.2). It records the route and the time. A replay reports what it read as trusted. |
| H3 | Nothing bounds how late a sent update can apply. | No contract. The host states no bound, and this design assumes none. The obligation is on this design: no elapsed time settles a send. | This note. | R4: case HS5 shows one case. Either result fits the design. | The ledger: no rule settles a send by time. Rule 4 of section 5.4 is the one rule that reads a time, and it ends only the cleanup of a token whose ID and end time are known. |
| H4 | The branch is written only by the destination. | Three things. Only the destination mints a write token for that ref, through its gateway (section 5.3). The host account's credential is in the deployment's custody (section 5.5). The operator keeps the host's own access to the repository closed to every other writer. Nothing at the host enforces the third. | The operator, under N5: who has access to the host account and to the repository. | The operator's record of that access. No run shows it. The destination's read before each reservation finds a branch that has moved (section 6.9). | The gateway is the only path by which a write token for the branch is used. The founding register allows one destination for a repository (section 3.8). |
| H5 | No scope's clock advances by less than the real time that passed, between two readings that one row of section 3.12 uses. | The clock that a scope's runtime reads, as the serving platform supplies it. The platform's statement of that clock was not read for this note, and none is cited. | The operator, under N5. | R4's clock table measures boundaries. No measurement establishes the property. | One clock port for each scope's runtime. Every reading that section 3.12 names is taken through it. |
| H6 | Two clocks that one rule compares differ by no more than a known amount. | For a read session and a grant's end time: the platform's clocks for two scopes. For a token's end time: the Git host's clock. Neither party states an amount. | The operator, under N5. | R4 measures the difference, and with it the margin of U16. | The check of a read session (section 3.9). The settlement of a token by rule 4, with its margin (section 5.4). |

**H1 to H6 at revision 14.** No row of the two tables above changes.
Each assumption keeps its evidence owner. This paragraph says how
that evidence is gathered, so that no second probe is commissioned
for the same host.

- **Documented properties first.** The recovery design lists twelve
  assumptions about its execution host and its storage, A1 to A12,
  and assigns their confirmation to the builder, from each provider's
  primary documentation, before its probe is commissioned (its
  section 4.2 and its dependency table). The same reading covers what
  the Git host and the serving platform document for H1, H2, H5 and
  H6: the push command's contract for an expected old value, the read
  interface's consistency after a write, and the clock that a runtime
  reads. One reading, by the builder, in the preparation for the
  recovery design's first stage. This note commissions no probe and
  asks for none.
- **What stays a run.** H1, H2 and the receipt: the cases HS1 to HS7
  of R4's host session, which I3 runs when the session is
  commissioned. The first head of section 12.2 is one more write of
  the kind that case HS7 already has: a ref created only if absent.
  It asks for no new case.
- **What no document and no run gives.** H3 and H4. H3 is assumed
  absent, and the design depends on no bound. H4 is the operator's
  record of access (N5).
- **A fork's ref.** The recovery design uses H1 and H3 for a push to
  a hold's fork (its section 12.3). That is the same property at the
  same host, under the same owners. A fork has one writer by custody,
  and section 5.9 states the one extra guard.
- **What a pure evaluator shows.** A derivation that is run again
  over recorded inputs, in a fixture or in a replay, shows that the
  entries follow from those inputs. It shows nothing about the host,
  the provider, a clock or a credential. Every label
  `trusted: observation-read` and `trusted: staged-ref-read`, and
  every row of section 10's last column, stays as it is.

Design choices left open:

| # | Choice | Options | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| U1 | The grace windows of section 3.3 | As proposed; from measurement | As proposed until R4 measures the cost of observations. They are a product choice as well as a cost. Each is a clock-time bound, under H5 (section 3.12). |
| U2 | An abort with an unknown send | Hold; the fence of section 6.8 | Hold is the rule. The fence is proposed for adoption by this design's review. Stated in revision 17: revision 16 was adopted with the fence still proposed. The fence is not adopted (section 6.8). |
| U3 | A controller and independence | By the rules value; always; never | By the rules value, as plan 005 chose, for the controller relation only. |
| U4 | Authority across repositories: collections and firm authority | Not designed | An alignment record only: a collection would be several repositories whose membership scopes accept grants from a common issuer. It is not narrowed out; it has no runtime and no delivery here. **Owner, from revision 10:** the planner, who files it as its own request, as an all-application successor after I3. What it would change here is named: a second source of observations (section 3.3), and a founding policy across repositories (section 3.8). Nothing in the first delivery waits on it. |
| U5 | The number of clear refusals before G aborts by itself | 3; 10 | 3. |
| U6 | When delegation is delivered | With I3; later | Later, as its own request. **Owner, from revision 10:** a successor of I3 (decision D2-7), on a request that the planner files. The record of section 3.4 is its starting point. Until it is delivered, `principal` is empty, and an intent that claims to act for another member is refused. |
| U7 | Where a change's own integration work is held | `change` declares the hold capability that `issue` declares, with `commitment`, `hold` and `export` items (section 6.2); or a separate work scope attached to the change; or every change is built under a hold in an issue lane, as revision 4 recommended | The first, proposed for reviewed adoption. It shares the declared capability, lowers no check and makes no issue a prerequisite. A separate work scope would need a new definition and a creation exchange for each change. The third is withdrawn: it made an unrelated issue an undeclared prerequisite of a one-person change. R2 revision 7 states the forms. Both notes return for review. |
| U8 | How a manifest's pin is recorded before the manifest is usable | In preparation, as section 6.2 proposes; or the manifest is admitted and is not usable until the pin's result returns, which costs R2 a manifest state | In preparation, for a hold in another lane. A manifest staged by its own lane is pinned in its own admitting entry. R1 decides, with its answer on staging. |
| U9 | The bound on creation attempts for one founding claim, and for one hold's fork | 3; 1 | 3 for each. The bound permits progress. The first-selection guard of sections 3.8 and 5.1 is what fixes which result is used. |
| U10 | The numbers behind the private stream's bound | 10, 60 and 10 seconds, so 80 on the task scope's clock, under H5; from measurement | As proposed until R4 measures. |
| U11 | The length of a job's deadline (R2-12) | One duration for a definition; one for each check, from the rules | One for a definition, 30 minutes proposed, accepted in section 3.11. One for each check stays open, with R1 and R2. |
| U12 | Where an export's authorization becomes irreversible | The `dispatched` record, with the pending delivery disclosed; or a fenced release operation in the storage that enforces the present target and authority | The `dispatched` record. A fenced operation would need a property of the storage that is not established, and none is asserted. |
| U13 | A new root for a commit already in the canonical repository | A held hold is required, as for any new staging; or a separately authorized root-retention operation with its own guards, ledger and fence | A held hold. No new authority is needed, and no ended hold gains a write. |
| U14 | An `unpin` that reaches a `provisional` pin | Applied, with the record that the manifest was admitted; or refused until the confirmation arrives | Applied. A refusal can strand the pin behind a late confirmation. |
| U15 | What licenses an export's dispatch, about the receiving hold | A license entry of the receiving lane, used inside a window on the task scope's clock, with a receiver pin that only the task scope's final entry releases (section 4.2); or a bounded observation of the lane's hold, like the observation of membership; or a release fenced by the storage, as in U12 | The license entry. It is a commitment of the scope that owns the hold, which is what R1's point R1-5 allows. An observation of a lane would be a second kind of observation that R1 does not have. Proposed: a 10-second window and at most three requests. An export to a hold of another lane is not designed. **Disposition and owner, from revision 10:** it is not delivered in the first version, and it is not a gate of the first Jam release. The design is owed by this note's successor, with R2 for the forms and IA for the source. The planner files that request when a chosen milestone has a journey that hands private, unreported work from one lane to a hold of another. The table "U15: the boundary of a cross-lane export", below, gives the dependency. |
| U16 | The margin after a host token's end time before its duty is settled | 60 seconds; none; from measurement | 60 seconds, until R4 measures the difference between the clocks (H6). |
| U17 | The ancestry check of section 6.2 (R2-18), when the walk passes its bound | Refuse the act `ancestry-too-large`; admit it with a record that the check was not finished | Refuse. Proposed bounds: 4,096 commits walked and 64 listed, for R4 to measure. A record of an unfinished check would let unnamed work through on size alone. Revision 7 adds a proposed bound of 64 recorded stops, with the same refusal. Revision 10 names the work that these bounds do not count: reachability from the head (section 6.2; U21). |
| U18 | What an ancestry check keeps for replay (section 6.2) | The whole snapshot of staged refs, by digest, with the record; or only the refs that the walk met, with the digest of the whole; or F alone, disclosed as a trusted result | The whole snapshot. A replay then derives F and the judgment again, and trusts only the read. Its size is the number of staged refs in the repository at the read. No bound on it is proposed, and R4 measures it. Keeping only the refs met would make the absence of the others a second trusted claim. Revision 10: the scope contract's candidate asks for a bound on one snapshot, so that the room for it can be reserved (its point R1-28). None is proposed here (section 5.8; G6). |
| U19 | What an entry keeps about the read behind an observation (section 3.3) | The read's identity and its use, with the trusted claim stated; or a read recorded by membership, as an entry or a counter there; or no record, and a narrower claim | The read's identity and its use. A record in membership would make every read a write of membership. With no record, a replay cannot tell two reads from a reuse at an equal reading. |
| U20 | Whether a `compromised` revocation, or a removal, ends that member's holds before their end time (section 3.5) | No: the hold is fenced and runs out. Or a notice from membership to each lane that holds one, whose handler ends the hold. Or an admin's act that ends any hold. | The first, for the first version. The second needs a list of those lanes, which membership does not keep, and a handler in both lane definitions. The third needs an act kind in both. Owner of a later choice: this note's successor, with R2. |
| U21 | A bound on the reachability work of an ancestry check, and on the count of its snapshot (section 6.2) | None. Or a count of commits read, with the refusal `ancestry-too-large`. Or a bound on the snapshot's count, with the same refusal. | Not chosen. If one is set it is a count and not a time, so that it is the same in a replay. No number is proposed until R4 measures. |

**U15: the boundary of a cross-lane export. New in revision 10.**

| Question | In one lane, which is designed | To a hold of another lane, which is owed |
|---|---|---|
| Where the `authorize-export` entry X is | In L, which holds the ended hold and the receiving hold. | In L. The receiving hold is in another lane, L2. |
| Who licenses a dispatch | L. | L2, because it owns the receiving hold. Its handler must check X as a fetched fact of L, and that X names a hold of L2. |
| Where the receiver pin is | In L. | In L2. |
| Who is told `export-settled` | L. | Both: L for the `export` item, and L2 for the receiver pin. That is two sends from one final entry. |
| Attribution | The receiving holder works under a commitment of L. A handover within one commitment already puts the former holder in its attribution. | Not designed. Exported work that enters a hold of another lane needs a recorded fact there that carries the former holder as an author, as `use-input` does for a report. Without one, unreported work would cross lanes with no author. This part is designed first. |
| What happens today | Complete: sections 4.2 and 4.3. | R2's `export` item names a member as `to`, and the license needs a held hold of the same lane whose holder is that member. A request that names no such hold is refused `target-not-held`. That refuses that one request. It denies nothing in one lane, and a handover with an export in one lane works as designed. |

**Owned gaps. New in revision 10. Disposed in revision 14.** Revision
10 listed fourteen things that it did not decide, and revision 11
added G15 to G18. Revision 14 gives each a disposition, against R1
revision 11, R2 revision 14, R4 revision 9 and the recovery design's
revision 2. Three kinds of disposition are kept apart.

- **Decided here.** The subject is this note's own. The rule is in
  the section named, as a proposal of revision 14.
- **Closed by a sibling.** An adopted sibling now holds the form.
  This note takes it.
- **Owed.** The seam belongs to another note, most often to the
  contract's next revision. It is named, with exactly what is asked,
  and nothing is decided here. No source may act as if it were
  decided.

A row that is decided or closed still has no source. An unknown
attempt keeps its own identity in every row. No read, no expiry, no
later attempt that succeeds and no new ref settles an earlier duty
whose outcome is unknown.

**Incidents. Decided in revision 14 (G13).** An incident is a finding
that contradicts what a scope recorded, or an input that the platform
built wrongly. The base says in several places that admins "get an
incident" or "are told". This is what that means.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is one | An answer that contradicts a recorded outcome (`outcome-conflict`). A ref that holds another value than the one a scope wrote. A second incarnation for one seed (`incarnation-conflict`). A `pin-confirm` with no pin, and an `unpin` for a pin released as `never-admitted`. A token that no ledger owns. A branch that another writer moved (section 6.9). A malformed input that the platform itself built (`bad-input`). |
| Where it is kept | In the entry that found it, when the finding writes one: a deciding entry that is `refused`, an outcome entry with its evidence, a clause that ran. And always in one operator's record, written by the runtime that found it: the time, the scope, the kind, and references to the facts in conflict. It holds no credential and no private text (R4's key O3). |
| What reads it | No guard, effect, send or clause. Losing the operator's record loses a notice and no fact. |
| Where it is shown | On the operator's page. And on the repository's admin page, for the incidents of that repository's scopes, to a read session of a member whose role holds `membership.*`. |
| Who is told | In the first version nobody is sent a notice. The contract has no form that tells a member who is in no party slot (its point R1-24). Where the base says that a lane's parties are told, the lane's own `notify` applies, and R2 owns that row. |

**A request that waits. Decided in revision 14 (G17).** Two cases
are listed for an operator and for admins, by the sending scope's
own bounded read of its sends: a request with a
`delivery-unavailable` diagnosis, and a request that transport
acknowledged and that has no result. Nothing is inferred from either,
and nothing is released on either (section 6.4).

- **Sending again.** An operator's instruction names one such duty by
  its entry and ordinal. The runtime dispatches the same envelope
  again, once. It is bookkeeping: no entry, no reservation and no
  second diagnosis (R1 section 7.4). It is written to the operator's
  record. The request keeps its identity, and a late result settles
  it.
- **Who notices.** Nobody by a timer. The lists above are read, and
  an age beside each row is display only. No state changes because a
  request is old.
- **What is not designed.** An automatic policy for sending again.
  R4 owns it, if a measurement shows a need.

### 12.1 The platform definitions

New in revision 14. This section answers gap G12. A platform
definition is code with one fixed meaning for each version (R1
section 6.1). This section is that meaning for version 1 of each of
the seven. It is written in the contract's own forms wherever a form
exists, so that source can hold as much of it as data as it can, and
so that what is left as code is listed and owned. Everything here is
proposed, and is adopted only with this note.

**How to read the tables.**

- They follow the contract's companion file. A literal in code type
  is a form of R1 revision 11, sections 6.2 to 6.6, as it would stand
  in a `DeclaredDefinition`. A final state is in bold.
- A cell that begins "Code" is a rule that the platform's code holds
  because no form says it. The key after it, P1 to P25, is a row of
  section 12.1.8, which gives the owner. From revision 20 each such
  cell is a mark in the data, with a rule: "Platform code: marks and
  rules", below. Section 12.1.8 lists them all.
- Every `max`, text length and integer range is an example, as in the
  companion file. R4 owns each number.
- Nothing here was validated. No validator, no script and no source
  read these tables. They were checked by reading against R1 revision
  11 and against the I1 validator at `a3e5a77e`
  (`packages/derive/src/validate.ts`). Section 12.1.8 says what that
  validator refuses today.

**The canonical form.** A platform definition is pinned by its name
and version, and not by a digest (R1 section 6.1). So its meaning is
this text, and no canonical bytes identify it. Where source holds the
declarable part of one as data, that value is a `DeclaredDefinition`:
`{ format: "artroom-definition-1", name, profile: { name: "restricted", version: 1 }, capabilities: [], genesis, items, acts, receives, timed, rules: {} }`.
Its `name` is the platform name without the version, which is what
`under` compares. None of the seven lists a capability, and none
declares a `rule`. From revision 20 the value is the contract's
`PlatformData`: it also holds `outcomes`, which names the rule for
the outcome entries of each operation kind that the definition owns,
and it holds a mark at each place that is code.

**Platform code: marks and rules. New in revision 20.** Until now a
cell that begins "Code" said that a rule exists, and no text said how
the rule joins the row's data. So no judge could run one, and the I3
source stopped there (its deltas note, entry EC6). The common rule is
the scope contract's, in its revision 15, a draft: its section 6.1,
"Platform code: a mark, and its rule", with the order of checks in
its section 4.2 and the replay in its section 9.3. This passage
states the rule as this note's, for the seven definitions. If that
draft changes, this passage follows it.
Stated in revision 24: "a draft" was the standing in revision 20.
The contract's revision 18 is adopted, and it keeps that passage of
its section 6.1 under the same name (the opening, "The standing in
force").

- *One rule.* A mark stands in the data where a form of the same kind
  would stand, and its rule is run where that form would be derived.
  A rule replaces no written form, and removes none.
- *A platform definition is data and rules.* The data is the value of
  "The canonical form", above, with one more member, `outcomes`, and
  with marks. The rules are a table of pure functions, one for each
  name that a mark states. Both parts belong to the one name and
  version. A runtime or a verifier that lacks one rule of a version
  does not have the version.
- *A mark.* `{ code, row }`. `code` names the rule. `row` is the key
  of section 12.1.8 that the cell gives. So the data itself says
  which places are code, and which gap each answers. A reader of the
  data cannot take a row with a mark for a row whose data gives all
  of its behaviour.
- *Seven places.* The table gives each, with the check of the
  contract's section 4.2 at which its rule is run.

| # | The place of a mark | The check | The rule returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The `grant` of an act | 9, in place of the grant check | That the signing key may act; or `unauthorized`. Narrowed in revision 22, with the contract's revision 17: it passes with no member. Every rule of this note already did. |
| 2 | A name of `also` | 8 | One local item of the stated type, or none |
| 3 | The type of a field, or of a slot | 7 for a field; 11 for a slot | Whether the value is of the type; or `bad-field` |
| 4 | A guard of the written list | 10, at its position | That it holds; that it does not, with a name; or that it is not completed |
| 5 | An effect of the written list, also in a result clause | 11, at its position | Effects, in the contract's forms |
| 6 | A send of the written list | 12, at its position | No request, or one. Its clauses are data. |
| 7 | `outcomes`, by operation kind | The judgment of each outcome entry of that kind | What the contract's section 4.3 leaves to the owner, with the entry's effects and sends |

- *What a rule reads.* The folded state before the entry; the entry's
  input, with the signing key as the intent's `actor`, the grant and
  `observed`; the commit's one reading; the entry's retained inputs;
  this scope's own earlier entries; and what the judge resolved
  before the rule's place. It reads no detached text's bytes, no
  storage, no network and no other scope's present state. So a
  verifier with the same version derives the same bytes.
- *What a rule writes.* Effects and requests in the contract's forms,
  and nothing else. No entry gains a member, and nothing in an entry
  says that a rule ran.
- *A version with a rule missing runs nothing.* A scope is not
  founded or created under it, and a scope that exists under it
  admits nothing. This is the I3 builder's decision EC4, which the
  planner confirmed, and the contract's revision 15 states it.
- *No declared definition holds a mark.* The validator refuses one
  unless its platform option is set, and no input reaches that
  option. A lane definition reaches a platform scope by a request or
  by reading a sealed entry, as before.
- *The names of the rules.* Each name in section 12.1.8's table is a
  name of version 1, proposed in this revision. A name is used once
  in a definition, and one rule may stand at several rows.

**What a mark states, and what an outcome sends. Decided in revision
22** (the I3 deltas EJ1 and EJ8, with the contract's revision 17, its
section 6.1).

- *The form.* A mark states three things in the data: `refusals`,
  the names with which its rule may refuse; `most`, the most that it
  returns; and `clock`, when it reads the commit's reading. The rule
  table states none of them apart from the data. So the form in
  which a version states them is the mark itself.
- *The values.* For each mark of section 12.1.8's table, `refusals`
  is the column "Refusals". `most.effects` is the count that the
  column "It returns" states, where it states one: one `value`
  effect, two, or an `operation` effect with its `attempt` effect.
  `most.operations` is each operation kind that the column names.
  `clock` is set for one rule, `dispatch`, of row 56. Where the
  column states no count, the number is owed before that rule is
  built: rows 12, 33, 35, 44, 45, 46, 49 and 50, and each rule of an
  outcome. For rows 45 and 46 the count is bounded by the 62 queued
  controls, which the refusal `controls-full` holds.
- *A request that an outcome sends.* An outcome's mark may hold one
  `send`: a send mark with its clauses. Three rows of this note have
  an outcome send a request, and section 12.1.8's table of further
  marks now lists them: the register's `create` of a directory, the
  directory's `relate` of an import, and the destination's `relate`
  of a publication.
- *Their clauses.* An outcome has no subject. So each effect of such
  a clause is an effect mark, whose rule finds its item. The row
  "The result of the `create`" of section 12.1.1 writes three
  effects on the claim as data. They are the effects of one rule,
  `claim-active`, in the clause `applied` of that send mark. The
  clause `conflict` has no effect, and `refused` has none and is an
  incident, as that row says.
- *The cause.* The directory's seed has the cause that section 3.8
  and the contract's section 7.2 give it: the digest of the
  founder's `found` intent, which opened the operation. The source
  found no cause for it. The contract has had one since its revision
  8, and its revision 17 says so.

**The acts that no grant judges (P13).** Ten cells have a mark at
`grant`. Any key may send such an act: nothing is read about a signer
before check 9. So the rule at `grant` is the whole of the act's
authority, and each one checks a thing that the scope's own history
holds. None passes a key on nothing.

| The act | The authority that the rule checks | What it reads | A pass |
|---|---|---|---|
| `install` | The intent is the one whose digest is the cause of this scope's seed. The genesis judge has checked the signature and the seed. Who may sign an install is N5's, and no rule of this note checks more. | The founding intent; the seed | Founds the one register of a deployment. No member. |
| `found` | The founding policy: it is `open`, or the signing key is one of `founders`. | `register.policy`, `register.founders`; the intent's `actor` | No member. The claim holds the key as `founder`. |
| `seat`, `first-key` | The signing key is the founding key that the genesis recorded. | `roster.foundingKey`; the `actor` | No member. The written guards let each act be admitted once. |
| `join`, `enrol` | The invitation: the signing key is not, and never was, a recovery key or a member's key; and the invitation that the act names exists and holds the hash of the act's secret. These are checks 5 and 6 of section 3.6, in that order. | `roster.recoveryKey`, `roster.formerRecovery`; the `key` items; the `actor`; whether the mark of `also` bound the invitation | No member. Refused `recovery-key`, `key-in-use` or `invitation-refused`. |
| `invite-member`, `invite-key`, `remove-member`, `revoke-key` | A current grant of the stated action, which is judged as written, and then the rule is not run. Otherwise: the signing key is the recovery key. | `roster.recoveryKey`; the `actor` | With a grant: the member of the grant, and the entry records it. By the rule: no member, and `authority: []`. |
| `rotate-recovery` | The signing key is the recovery key. | The same | No member. |

- *One thing that the rule cannot check.* The row `invite-member`
  says "the recovery key when no admin can act". The records do not
  show that no admin can act: an admin who has lost every device
  still has active keys. So the rule checks the key alone. Whether
  a further condition is wanted, and what record would show it, is
  open, with the planner.
- *An entry of such an act.* Made exact in revision 21, by branch,
  as the row of `invite-member` has it. Where the rule passed the
  key, the entry records `authority: []`. Where a current grant of
  the row's stated action was judged, the entry records that grant,
  and the rule was not run. A replay judges the grant, or runs the
  same rule on the same input, so an entry that no authority covers
  does not verify.

The folded state holds a head for each subject that an entry observed, with its `of` (the contract's section 16.1), so the incarnation is a function of the folded state from the first such entry on. | The same, for membership and for the rules scope, each by its own ID. |

    other observation in its window is answered

#### 12.1.1 The register

**The register, decided in revision 25** (the I3 deltas EP3, EP4, EP5
and EJ1; the contract's revision 19, its sections 6.1 and 15.6s).
Each point says whether it confirms what the I3 source built, or what
that source must change. The rows above are kept as they were
written, and where a row and this block differ, this block is the
rule.

- *Where `claim.policy` comes from (EP3). Confirmed as built.* It is
  a written effect of `found`:
  `{ value: { slot: "policy", from: { slot: "policy", of: "also.register" } } }`,
  with `also: { register: { item: "register", one: true } }`. So the
  claim keeps the policy value under which it was judged, which is
  "the founding policy value used" of section 3.8, step 1. The act
  names the register as a subject, so the founder's intent states its
  revision in `expected`, as the contract asks for each subject that
  no mark selects. No row changes the register item after its
  genesis, so that revision is 1.
- *The `create` of the directory carries no signed intent (EP5).
  Corrected.* The contract's revision 19 confirms that no field type
  holds a signed intent. The table "Messages between scopes" gave the
  `create` a field `founding`. That field is withdrawn. The fields of
  the `create` are six: `claim`, `repository`, `branch`,
  `founderHandle`, `recoveryKey` and, for a founding by import,
  `import`. `claim` is the fact of the `found` entry, and that entry
  holds the founder's signed intent. The directory's genesis fetches
  it as it fetches every fact that a creation names, and retains it in
  `uses`. A `create` that carries a field `founding` is refused
  `bad-field`, as for any field that the row does not declare.
  Confirmed as built.
- *The two fixed slots that no field gives (EP5). Confirmed as
  built.* `repository.register` is the scope of the claim's fact:
  `{ ref: { slot: "register", from: { field: "claim", part: "scope" } } }`.
  `repository.founder` is the value that the claim's entry set as the
  claim's `founder`, read by the part `set`. Both are written forms
  of the contract's section 6.5. Neither needs a rule.
- *What the selecting outcome sends, in place of a signed intent.*
  The fact `claim`. A reader who wants the founder's intent reads the
  claim's entry, which the directory retains from its genesis on. The
  policy value is in the same entry, as the claim's `policy`. The
  directory keeps no slot for the policy, and none is added.

**The rule `create-repository`, whole (EJ1). Decided.** The plan's
step 9c waited on the question EJ1: where the clauses of a request
that an outcome sends are written, and what the cause of the scope
is. Both are answered. The form is the contract's: an outcome's mark
may hold one `send`, a send mark with its clauses
(`outcomes[kind].send`, in the contract's `PlatformData`). The cause
is the contract's fourth cause. Revision 22 stated both for this
note. What was still missing is the rule's own row, and this is it.
Nothing outside this note is waited for. The source's judge of an
outcome must let a rule return the one request of the mark's `send`,
a `create` among them, which it did not when the deltas note was
written.

| Part of the rule | What it is |
|---|---|
| Name, place and row | `create-repository`, at place 7, for the kind `create-repository`. Row P16. Its `attempts` is 3. |
| Whether the kind selects | It selects one result (the contract's section 4.3, point 7). |
| The owner's local guard | The claim's `repository` is unset. The claim is the item that the opening entry opened: the `found` entry at the position that the operation's ID states. |
| Whether a read is decisive | Never. Only the request's own answer settles an attempt. A listing of the namespace and a repository found under a name decide nothing (section 3.8). |
| Whether another attempt is allowed | Yes, after `refused` or `unknown`, while fewer than 3 attempts are opened and nothing is selected. The ledger checks the last two. |
| The evidence, for `confirmed` | Basis `own-answer`. The body is `{ name, id }`, or `{ name, id, credential }`: each a text of at most 256 bytes. `name` is the attempt's own name. `id` is the host's ID of the repository. `credential` is the host's ID of a credential that the answer returned, and never its secret. |
| The evidence, for `refused` | Basis `own-answer`. The body is `{ name, nameExists }`, where `nameExists` is a truth value: the host answered that the name is taken. |
| The evidence, for `unknown` | Basis `none`. The body is `{ name }`. |
| An outcome that does not follow | `bad-input`: a body with another member or a missing one; a `name` that is not the attempt's own name; a basis `read`. |
| The attempt's own name | The 52 characters of the directory's scope ID after its prefix `sc_`, a hyphen, and the attempt's number in decimal. The scope ID is that of the seed whose digest the claim holds as `seed`. So the name is a function of the claim and the number, and a replay derives it. Whether a host takes such a name is the operational assumption of section 3.8. |
| What it reads | The outcome, with its evidence; the opening entry, by its position; the claim; `register.host` and `register.namespace`; the operation's attempts and its selection, in the folded state. |
| What it yields, on the selecting outcome | One `value` effect: the claim's `repository` is `{ host, namespace, name, id }`, with `host` and `namespace` from the register item and `name` and `id` from the body. And the one request of its `send`: the rule `create-directory`, below. |
| What it yields, on each `confirmed` outcome whose body holds `credential` | An `operation` effect, `revoke-credential`, with 3 attempts, and the `attempt` effect that opens its attempt 1. |
| What it yields, on each `confirmed` outcome that is not selected | An `operation` effect, `delete-repository`, with 3 attempts, and its attempt 1. |
| What it yields, on a `refused` outcome with `nameExists` | Nothing of an entry. The incident of section 3.8 is the operators' record, which N5 owns. |
| `most` | 5 effects: one `value`, and two operations with one attempt each. Operations: `revoke-credential`, `delete-repository`. |
| Refusal names | None. An outcome entry is never refused. |

**The send `create-directory`, and its clause.** Row k of the table
of further marks, made exact.

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Name and place | `create-directory`: the `send` of the mark of `create-repository`. Row P16. |
| When it gives a request | On the selecting outcome, and on no other. |
| The seed | `{ v: 1, kind: "directory", definition: "platform:directory@1", creator, cause, ordinal: 0 }`. `creator` is this register's reference. `cause` is the digest of the founder's `found` intent, which the claim holds as `intent`. The digest of this seed is the value that the rule `claim-seed` gave the claim as `seed` (row 5), so the two agree by construction. |
| The fields | `claim`: the fact of the `found` entry, which is the opening entry. `repository`: the record that the same outcome sets. `branch`, `founderHandle`, `recoveryKey` and, when the intent holds it, `import`: from the fields of the `found` intent, which the opening entry holds. |
| What it reads | The opening entry, by its position, with its signed intent; the outcome's body; the register item; this scope's own reference. |
| The clause `applied` | One effect mark, `claim-active`. |
| The clauses `refused` and `conflict` | No effect. Each is an incident, as the row "The result of the `create`" says. |
| The control | `confirm`, on `applied`, by the platform. |

**The effect mark `claim-active`.** It had a name in revision 22 and
no row. It is at place 5, in the clause `applied` of the send above.
Row P16. A clause of a request that an outcome sent has no subject,
so a rule finds the item. It reads the result's `of`, which names the
request by the outcome entry that sent it; that outcome entry, by its
position, for the operation that it belongs to; and the claim that
the operation's opening entry opened. It yields three effects on that
claim: `{ state: "active" }`; the reference `directory`, which is the
result's sender; and the reference `genesis`, which is the result's
source entry. `most`: 3 effects. It names no refusal. A clause never
refuses: where the claim is not `pending` the state effect is one
that the checks on effects refuse, the clause changes nothing, and
the result is recorded (the contract's section 6.1, the point on
EN8).
Stated in revision 28: the sweep of section 12.1.5, "The family of this
fault, swept", read each rule of an outcome and each clause of this
section, rows 22 to 25. None sets a slot of a claim that can be final
when it arrives. A late or an unselected answer of `create-repository`
sets nothing of the claim, and its cleanup is in the closure that
`found` reserved. For the clause above, the rule of the contract is that
an effect of a result clause on a final item is not applied. Nothing
changes here.

**The outcomes of `revoke-credential` and `delete-repository` (EP4).
Decided.** A read is not decisive for either. No statement of a host
is identified that an ID which answers "not found" was never usable,
so only the request's own answer settles an attempt. That confirms
the source. The bodies are new, and the source must check them.

| Kind | What the operation is for | `confirmed`, basis `own-answer` | `refused` and `unknown` | An outcome that does not follow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `revoke-credential`, 3 attempts | The credential that the body of its opening entry names. The opening entry is a `confirmed` outcome of `create-repository`. | `{ credential }`: the ID that the host answered as revoked | `{ credential }` | `bad-input`: another member, or a `credential` that is not the opening entry's |
| `delete-repository`, 3 attempts | The repository that the body of its opening entry names by `id` | `{ id }`: the ID that the host answered as deleted | `{ id }` | `bad-input`: another member, or an `id` that is not the opening entry's |

Each rule selects nothing and derives nothing. Another attempt
follows a `refused` or an `unknown`, to 3. After the third, the duty
stays in the ledger and on the operator's page. The register has no
act that opens a further one, and none is added here.

#### 12.1.2 The directory

One for a repository. It creates the repository's scopes and its
lanes, allocates numbers, and keeps one index row for each lane. It
orders no ordinary act of a lane.

| Item type | `many`, `max` | States (final in bold), `initial` | Parties | References | Values |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
