| `lane` | true, 100000 | listed; `listed` | `author`<br>`assignees` (list, max 10) | `scope` `{ type: "scope", kind: "lane" }` | `number` `{ type: "int", min: 1, max: 1000000000 }`<br>`kind` `{ type: "enum", of: ["issue", "pr"] }`<br>`title` `{ type: "text", max: 256 }`<br>`state` `{ type: "enum", of: ["open", "closed"] }`<br>`draft` `{ type: "bool" }`<br>`merge` `{ type: "enum", of: ["committed", "unknown", "published", "refused", "aborted"] }`<br>`labels` `{ type: "list", of: { type: "text", max: 64 }, max: 20 }`<br>`first` `{ type: "time" }`<br>`latest` `{ type: "time" }`<br>`seen` `{ type: "record", of: { title: { type: "int", min: 0, max: 1000000000, required: false }, state: { type: "int", min: 0, max: 1000000000, required: false }, draft: { type: "int", min: 0, max: 1000000000, required: false }, merge: { type: "int", min: 0, max: 1000000000, required: false }, labels: { type: "int", min: 0, max: 1000000000, required: false }, assignees: { type: "int", min: 0, max: 1000000000, required: false } } }` |

Code P17: `number` is `lastNumber` plus 1, and `lastNumber` rises. | For `open-pr`: `{ set: "destination", of: "also.repository" }` and `{ set: "rules", of: "also.repository" }`. Code P19 and P21: the definition that the field `definition` names is `active` in the rules scope, by an observation of the rules that this entry retains; and its bytes, with their named closure, are retained, read from the rules scope by that digest before the turn (G7, G16). Corrected in revision 25: that sentence is no check of the row (below, EP16). | None: a handler of class `advisory` sends nothing. |

- **What the directory admits, and when.** Before the register's
  `confirm`: a repeat of its creation, and the `confirm`. After it,
  an act is admitted only when its grant can be observed, which needs
  membership's reference. That is step 7 of section 3.8, with no
  second rule.
- **Activation and bytes, in one place (G7, G16).** The rules scope
  is the one authority for which definitions a repository may create
  lanes under, and the one holder of their bytes. The directory
  observes it as section 3.3 says for the rules, in the ordinary
  window. A definition that is retired there creates no new lane. A
  lane that exists keeps its pinned definition.
- **A concern.** Its parent creates it, under the parent's own
  definition, so the directory judges nothing. Its row and its number
  come with its first index row (R2 section 2).
- No timed rule exists. A `task` row that is `creating` is settled by
  its creation's result.

**Activation and the creator's read, as one answer. Stated in
revision 17** (the contract's points R1-22 and R1-35; its section
15.10, seam 4). Revision 14 decided the parts, in the rows G7 and G16
of section 12 and in the point above. The contract asks for them as
one answer. This is the same rule in one place, with each question
that the contract puts. No rule changes.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Who retains a lane definition's bytes | Three holders, each under the digest in the byte domain `artroom-definition-1`. The rules scope, from the entry of `activate`, with the named closure: it is the source for the repository. The directory, from the first `open-issue` or `open-pr` entry that names the digest, as a retained input of that entry. Each lane, from its genesis: its creator supplies the bytes with the whole named closure (R1 section 7.2). |
| Who activates a digest | A member who holds `rules.activate`, by the act `activate` in the rules scope (section 12.1.4). The entry opens a `definition` item, `active`, with the digest and the name that the bytes state. `retire-definition`, under the same grant, makes it `retired`. Nothing else activates: not the definition's author, not the directory and not a lane. |
| What the directory reads when it creates a lane | Two things, both before the turn. The observation of the rules, which says which digests are `active` at a stated head. And, the first time that a digest is named, the definition's bytes with their named closure. |
| From whom | The rules scope of its own repository, by the reference that the `applied` clause of its own `create` recorded in `repository.rules`. Never from the act's signer, from a lane or from another repository. The digest in the act's field `definition` says only which definition is asked for. |
| By digest | The bytes are checked against the digest that the act names, in that byte domain, and are then validated. Each definition of the closure is checked against its own digest. Bytes that do not hash to their digest are not used. |
| With what freshness | For activation: the observation is used within 300 seconds of the moment its read began, on the directory's clock (W1), as the act's own grant is. So a retirement takes effect at the directory no later than that window after the rules scope records it, and within the window a lane may still be created under a digest that was just retired. That is the grace of a window, as for a grant (decision D2-3). For the bytes: none is needed. A digest names one value for good, and bytes that the directory retained once are not read again. |
| The digest is not `active` in the observation | The act is refused `guard-failed`, named `not-activated`. No entry is written, no number is used and no lane is created. That holds for a digest that was never activated and for one that is `retired`. |
| The observation cannot be read, or is older than its window | The act is answered `dependency-unavailable`. No entry. The signer may send the act again. |
| The digest is `active`, and its bytes cannot be read or do not hash to it | The act is answered `dependency-unavailable`. No entry. `activate` retains the bytes in its own entry, so no act can make a digest `active` without its bytes. This case is a fault of storage or of reach. |
| Room for the bytes | The first act that names a digest is new work. It is admitted only with room for what it newly retains: that definition and its closure, at the bound on a closure (R1 section 17.2, the row "Definitions" of its table of retained inputs). Without that room it is refused `scope-full`. A later act under the same digest retains nothing new. |
| What a lane then knows of activation | Nothing of its own, and it reads nothing for it. A lane exists only by a `create` of its repository's directory. The directory sends one only under a digest that was `active` in the observation that its entry retains. A concern is created by its parent, under the parent's own definition. So "created under an activated definition" is a fact of a lane's genesis. The directory's entry shows it, and it never changes. A later retirement creates no new lane and changes no lane that exists (R1 section 6.1). |

- *What this answers of R1-22.* The contract asks how a lane learns
  its repository's activations without reading the rules scope's
  present state. It does not learn them, and it does not need to.
  Activation is judged once, by the directory, at the creation. What
  a `fact` guard still cannot check is that the source lane is of
  the judging lane's repository. That is the part of G7 that stays
  asked of the contract: the directory that a fetched entry's scope
  recorded at its genesis, as a member of the entry's use.
- *What this answers of R1-35.* A platform scope whose code takes a
  definition's digest from an input reads the bytes from the rules
  scope of its own repository, by that digest. The directory is the
  only such scope in this note.
- *What waits on a form.* The rule is whole. Two of its forms are
  the contract's and are still open there: the observation of the
  rules that an act entry retains (P19), and the bytes beside the
  intent of `activate` (P21). Section 13.8 says what I3 does meanwhile.

| Case | Input | What is written, or answered |
|---|---|---|
| a | Any act before the register's `confirm` is recorded | `scope-provisional`. |
| b | `open-pr` before the destination's applied result is recorded | Refused `guard-failed`: no destination. |
| c | `open-issue` under a digest that the rules scope does not hold as `active` | Refused `guard-failed`, named `not-activated`. No lane, and no number is used. |
| d | Two index rows of one lane arrive in the other order | The same row. The row from the lower position changes no field that the higher one set. |
| e | The first index row of a concern, and then the same row again | The row is opened, with the next number. The repeat is the same advisory, and opens nothing. |
| f | New in revision 17. An admin activates the digest D of `issue`. A member signs `open-issue` under D. An admin then retires D. 400 seconds later a member signs `open-issue` under D, with D's bytes supplied in the request. | The first `open-issue` is admitted. The directory read D's bytes from the rules scope before the turn, checked them against D, and retains them with that entry. The lane is created under D. The second is refused `guard-failed`, named `not-activated`: the observation read for it shows D `retired`. The bytes in the request are not read, because the directory takes bytes from the rules scope alone. The first lane keeps D and goes on. |

**The directory, decided in revision 25** (the I3 deltas EP6 to EP9,
EP11 to EP13 and EP15 to EP17, and EX4; the contract's revision 19,
its sections 6.1 and 15.6s; the lane forms' revision 15, its section
18.9). Each point says whether it confirms what the I3 source built,
or what that source must change. Where a row above and this block
differ, this block is the rule.

**The two creation rules of the genesis (EP6, EX4).** The contract
decided the form: a written list of sends may hold several marks when
at most one does not state `always`, and no operand gives a sibling's
scope ID. So the genesis `establish` holds three sends, in this
order: a written `create` of membership, the mark `create-rules`, and
the mark `create-destination`. Both marks state `always: true`. Their
names are those that the source's data already holds.

| Part | `create-rules` | `create-destination` |
|---|---|---|
| Place and row | Place 6, in the list of sends of `establish`. Row P20. `always: true`. | The same. |
| What it reads | The genesis input, which holds this scope's own seed; this scope's own reference; the field `branch`, as read. | The same, with the fields `repository`, `claim` and `import`, as read. |
| The seed that it sends to | `{ v: 1, kind: "rules", definition: "platform:rules@1", creator, cause, ordinal: 1 }` | `{ v: 1, kind: "destination", definition: "platform:destination@1", creator, cause, ordinal: 2 }` |
| The fields of the `create` | `branch`: the field. `directory`: this scope's own reference. `membership`: the scope ID of the sibling of creation 0. | `repository`: the field. `branch`: the field. `import`: a truth value, true when the creation's field `import` is present. `claim`: the field. `directory`: this scope's own reference. `membership`: the scope ID of the sibling of creation 0. `rules`: the scope ID of the sibling of creation 1. |
| What it yields | Exactly one request, in every genesis. | The same. |
| The clauses, as data | `applied`: `{ ref: { slot: "rules", from: { sender: true } } }`. `refused` and `conflict`: none. | `applied`: `{ ref: { slot: "destination", from: { sender: true } } }`, and the effect mark `open-import` of row 7. `refused` and `conflict`: none. |
| `most` | One request, with 3 fields. | One request, with 7 fields. Both are under the bound on the fields of one send. |
| Refusal names | None. Place 6 never refuses. A rule that gives no request has a fault, because the mark states `always`. | The same. |

- *`creator` and `cause`.* In each seed, `creator` is this scope's
  own reference, with its incarnation. `cause` is the digest of this
  scope's own seed, in the byte domain `artroom-seed-1`: the
  contract's third cause, for a scope that a genesis creates.
- *How a sibling's scope ID is derived.* The sibling's seed is built
  from the same four values and the sibling's own kind, definition
  and ordinal: for membership,
  `{ v: 1, kind: "membership", definition: "platform:membership@1", creator, cause, ordinal: 0 }`.
  Its scope ID is the contract's `ScopeId` of that seed: the text
  `sc_` and the 52 base32 characters of the seed's digest. It is not
  the bare digest. The deltas note says "the digest of the seed" for
  short. The source's stand-in builds the ID with the same function
  that names a scope at its genesis, so it is the contract's ID, and
  it is confirmed as built. The seed of membership that the rule
  builds must be the one that the judge builds for the written
  `create` of the same entry. It is, because both use the ordinal 0
  and the same `creator` and `cause`.
- *Two ordinals.* A seed's `ordinal` counts the creations of the
  entry from 0: membership 0, rules 1, destination 2. That is the
  "creation 0, 1 and 2" of the table "Names, creation and
  activation". The three sends are at the ordinals 1, 2 and 3 of the
  entry, because a child's genesis sends its own result first, at 0.
- *No member `membership` in these two creations.* The platform puts
  the member `membership` in the body of a `create` from what the
  creating scope records. At its genesis the directory records none:
  the slot `repository.membership` is set later, by the clause
  `applied`. So the body of each of these two creations holds
  `{ fields, directory }` and no member `membership`, and the field
  `membership` holds the ID. A created scope of the kind `rules` or
  `destination` reads its membership scope from that field ("Where
  the rules scope and the destination record their membership
  reference", in section 12.1).
- *The fields, each confirmed.* For the rules scope: `branch` names
  the branch that the rules are for; `directory` is the fixed
  reference of the item `rules`; `membership` is the ID. For the
  destination: `repository` binds it to the claim's repository by its
  ID (section 3.8, step 6); `branch` is its `name`; `import` decides
  whether its genesis declares `first-head`; `claim` is named in the
  founding commit and in the first receipt (section 12.2);
  `directory` is the sender that its handlers `import` and
  `compromised` accept; `membership` and `rules` name the two scopes
  that it observes. None is left out and none is added. The build
  found the same seven.

**The guard of `retry-import` (EP7). Decided.** It is a rule of
version 1.

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Name, place and row | `import-spent`, at place 4, the one guard of `retry-import`. Row P29: no guard form reads an operation. |
| What it reads | The `import` operations of this scope and their attempts, in the folded state; `repository.import`; `repository.imported`. |
| It holds when | `repository.import` is set; `repository.imported` is unset; at least one `import` operation exists; and every attempt that each `import` operation states is opened and has an outcome. |
| Refusal | `guard-failed`, named `import-not-spent`. |
| Not completed | Never. It reads this scope's own state only. |

- *An `unknown` attempt counts as used.* The row's words are "the
  import's stated attempts are used, and none is `confirmed`". An
  attempt whose outcome is `unknown` is used: its request was sent,
  and its outcome is recorded. The source's stand-in waits until
  every attempt is `confirmed` or `refused`. It must change to this
  row: with the stand-in, one lost reply that is never answered ends
  a founding by import for good.
- *Why a new import beside an unknown one is safe.* Every attempt of
  every `import` operation writes the same one ref,
  `refs/artroom/import/<digest of the claim's fact>`, and no branch.
  The destination reads the commit and its closure from the host
  itself before it writes the branch (section 12.2). And one import
  is used, as the next point says.
- *A read of operations by kind.* The folded state has none, so the
  source walks the scope's own entries. A bound or an index for that
  read is asked of the proof plan, with the request `cc570904`.

**The outcomes of `import` (EP9). Decided.**

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Name, place and row | `import`, at place 7, for the kind `import`. Row P16. Its `attempts` is 3, and a `retry-import` opens an operation with 1. |
| Whether the kind selects | It selects one result. The owner's local guard: `repository.imported` is unset. So one import is used, also when a late answer or a retried operation is `confirmed` after another. New in revision 25: the row above said only "`confirmed`: sets `imported`". The source must add the selection. |
| Whether a read is decisive | Never. |
| Whether another attempt is allowed | Yes, after `refused` or `unknown`, while the stated number allows and nothing is selected. |
| The evidence | `confirmed`, basis `own-answer`: `{ commit }`, a commit ID of 40 or 64 hexadecimal characters: the imported head. `refused` and `unknown`: an empty record. Any other body is `bad-input`. Confirmed as built. |
| What it yields, when `selected` | One `value` effect: `repository.imported` is the commit. And the request of its send, `import-update`: a `relate`, `import`, of the `repository` item, to `repository.destination`, state `done`, with the detail `commit`. |
| What it yields, on the last `refused` | The same `relate`, state `failed`, with no detail. |
| "The last `refused`" | The `refused` outcome after which every attempt that the operation states is opened and each has a `refused` outcome. An `unknown` attempt keeps the operation open, and no `failed` is sent for it. Confirmed as built. |
| What it yields otherwise | Nothing. A `confirmed` outcome that is not selected derives nothing and sends nothing. |
| `most` | 1 effect, and the one request. |
| Refusal names | None. |

**The fields of `open-issue` and `open-pr` (EP8). Decided, with the
lane forms' revision 15** (its section 18.9, the row EP8). The two
acts declare the fields that a requester supplies to the genesis act
of each pinned lane.

| Act | Its fields | What the rule `create-lane` adds to the lane's `create` |
|---|---|---|
| `open-issue` | `definition`, a digest; `title`; `body`, a detached text; `conditions` | `opener`: the signer, as the directory judged it. `number`: the number that `next-number` gave. |
| `open-pr` | `definition`; `title`; `body`, a detached text; `draft` | The same two, and `destination` and `rules` from the repository item. |

`kind` and `state` of the index row are constants of each row:
`issue` or `pr`, and `open`. The field `origin` of the `issue` lane's
genesis belongs to `add-concern`, and `open-issue` does not declare
it. A lane definition whose genesis takes other fields is not created
by these two rows. Confirmed as built.

**The rule `worker-standing` (EP11). Confirmed as built, with one
addition.**

| The rule finds | Its answer |
|---|---|
| No observation of the worker at hand, or one whose `of` is not `repository.membership` | Not completed, `dependency-unavailable`. The second is guard 1 of an observation, which discards it. |
| The worker's `memberState` is not `active`; or its `activeKey` is false; or the worker is a member of another membership scope | Refused `guard-failed`, named `worker-not-active` |
| The worker is an agent, its `controller` is not the signer, and the signer's role is not `admin` | The same refusal |
| Otherwise | It holds. |

The signer's role is read from the observation in the grant that was
judged. The addition is `activeKey`: a member whose last key is
revoked cannot work (section 3.5, rule 5). Whether the source reads
that member of the observation was not checked.

**The rule `index-row` (EP12). Confirmed as built.** `kind` and
`author` have no position in `seen`, and need none: a lane's kind and
its author are fixed at its genesis, so every index row of one lane
carries the same two. The rule takes each when the row holds none,
and keeps it. `number` is never taken from a lane: a row has the
number that the directory gave. `first` and `latest` are the earliest
and the latest of the source entries' times. `assignees` is set
whole, under the position in `seen.assignees`.

**One lane for each revision of the repository item (EP13).
Confirmed as built, and not wanted as a limit.** `next-number`
changes `repository.lastNumber`, so each opening moves the revision
of the item that the three acts name. Of two acts that were signed on
one revision, the second is answered `revision-moved` and is signed
again. That is what the forms give, and it is correct: no number is
used twice. It is a cost where many signers open lanes at once. The
smallest change that removes it is a counter item of its own, which a
mark of `also` selects, so that no act states its revision. It is not
made here. The proof plan is asked to measure the cost before a row
changes.

**The refusals of `definition-active` (EP15). Decided: the source
must change.** The rule states two refusal names.

| The rule finds | Its answer |
|---|---|
| The digest is not `active` in the observation | Refused `guard-failed`, named `not-activated` |
| The bytes of the definition, or of one of its closure, hash to their digest and do not validate in this runtime; or the closure names more definitions than the bound | Refused `unsupported-definition`, with that name. This is new. The contract's place 4 lets a specification state it, and the contract's section 7.2 gives the same bytes the same answer at a creation. It does not pass with time, so "unavailable" would tell the signer to send the act again for nothing. |
| No observation at hand, or one whose `of` is not `repository.rules`; or bytes that cannot be read, or that do not hash to their digest | Not completed, `dependency-unavailable`. Confirmed as built. |

**An advisory from a lane of another repository (EP16). Narrowed.**
The row `index` says "An advisory from a scope whose recorded
directory is not this scope changes nothing". No form lets the
directory check that: a guard reads the source entry, and not the
seed of the scope that sent it. So the sentence is no check of the
row, and it is withdrawn as a claim of this definition. What holds is
the platform's address rule: a lane's runtime sends an `index` row
only to the directory that the lane records, and the receiver checks
that the source entry holds that send to this scope. A lane records
the directory that its creator set, and a concern records its
parent's. So an honest runtime lists a lane only in its own
repository. A lane-kind scope that records this directory and was not
created by it, or by a lane of it, would be listed. Closing that
needs the form that gap G7 asks of the contract: the directory that a
fetched entry's scope recorded at its genesis, as a member of the
entry's use. An index row grants nothing: it is a row of a list.

**The row `open-task` (EP17).** The row is data, whole, and this note
asks nothing more of it. Whether a directory may be created while the
runtime lacks `platform:task@1` is the contract's section 7.2, with
the builder and IA. When the task's creation is answered
`unsupported-definition`, the clause `refused` of the row makes the
`task` item `refused`.

Stated in revision 28: the same sweep read each rule of an outcome and
each clause of this section, rows 26 to 30. The items `repository` and
`lane` have no final state, and a `task` leaves `creating` only by the
one result of its creation. A late or a retried answer of `import` is
not selected and derives nothing. Nothing changes here.

the member or of the key that it is for, with the hash of its secret
and its end time. So a join opens at most one item. The invitation's
ID, which a join names, is that item's ID.

- **Two things that are answers and no entries.** An observation
  (section 3.3) and a read session (section 3.9). Membership answers
  an observation from its head: the key's item, its member's item,
  the role's list of actions, and for an agent whether its controller
  is an active member with an active key. A provisional membership
  answers neither.
- **The founder, in two acts.** The base said that membership's
  genesis makes the founder's key the first key of the first admin. A
  genesis opens one item, so that takes two acts after it, `seat` and
  `first-key`, which the founder's client signs in turn. Between them
  the founding key can sign only `first-key`.
- **A timed end of an invitation.** The base needed no timer for
  one: the comparison in the join's commit decides (section 3.12,
  W9). That still decides. The timed entry only moves an ended
  invitation out of the live items, so that its reservation and its
  place under `max` are released. A lost timer admits nothing. Each
  chain is 1.
- **Reservations.** As section 5.8: one entry for the revocation of
  an active key, with one request for its `compromised` notice; one
  entry for a removal; and for an invitation one entry for its join,
  one for its timed end, and for a new member the creation of an
  inbox, which is a request.
  From revision 27: four rows declare `settles` for these, `revoke-key`,
  `remove-member`, `join` and `enrol` (section 5.8, "`settles` on the
  rows of membership").
- **Characters of a handle.** Section 3.1.
- **Three rules that the rows need. New in revision 24** (the I3
  deltas EM6, EM7 and EM8). The rows above state three things that
  no form says and that the table of marks did not list: the role
  table as five lists, the party `member` of a member that is opened
  from a handle, and the form of a handle. Each is now a rule of
  version 1, with its place, what it reads, what it returns and its
  refusals: `role-table`, `member-of` and `handle-form` (section
  12.1.8, rows o to q). So the table of marks gives membership ten
  rules, where it gave seven.
  Stated in the second commit of revision 27: eleven, with `action-list`
  (section 12.1.8, row aa).

|---|---|---|
| a | A `join` with the right secret, signed by a new key | One entry: the key is `active`, the member is `active`, and a `create` of the inbox is at ordinal 0. The same signed bytes again return its receipt. |
| b | The recovery key signs a `join` | Refused `recovery-key`, before the secret is compared. The invitation stays `invited`. |
| c | An admin revokes the last active key of the last admin | Refused `guard-failed`, named `last-admin`. |
| d | `revoke-key` with `as: "compromised"` | One entry. The key is `compromised`. One `tell` to the directory at ordinal 0, which the entry that enrolled the key reserved. |
| e | An observation is asked of a membership that its directory has not confirmed | No answer: `scope-provisional`. No grant rests on it. |

- **No fan-out (G11).** The base had the rules scope reach every
  open change lane, and no entry can do that within the contract's
  bound on sends. A lane asks instead. R2's adopted `rules` handler
  takes the update as it is. What R2 is asked for is the lane's side:
  one `tell`, `rules-wanted`, in `open`, addressed by the slot
  `rulesScope`, and one act that asks again. The revision rule of a
  relationship orders the updates. A lane whose copy is behind can
  refuse a `request-check` that the rules would allow. It can admit
  nothing that the destination then reserves, because the destination
  observes the rules itself (section 6.5).
- **An observation of the rules** is an answer and no entry, like an
  observation of membership. It gives the head, the revision and the
  values, and for the directory which definitions are `active`.
- **A founding starts with no active definition.** The first admin's
  acts keep the configurations, publish the rules and activate the
  two lane definitions. Until then the directory creates no lane.
- **Byte domain.** This definition declares
  `artroom-check-configuration-1` for a check's configuration, as the
  contract lets the owner of a retained value do (R1 section 15.3a,
  row 8).
- **A second byte domain. New in revision 27** (the contract's revision
  21, which is not adopted: its section 16.1, "The extents, in an
  observation of the rules", and its section 2.1, "A domain that an
  owner declares"). This definition declares `artroom-rules-extents-1`.
  A value in it is the canonical JSON of the list of extents as the slot
  `extents` holds it: 1 to 8 records, each with the six members of "An
  extent, with its bounds", below. Before the first `publish` it is the
  list of the three extents of the first definition, as "Before the
  first `publish`" computes them. The bound on one value is 262,144
  bytes, which is the contract's proposed entry size. The reason: a list
  is set only by a `publish`, whose entry holds the list in its field
  `extents`, and a `publish` whose entry would pass the entry size is
  refused `entry-too-large`. So no list that a rules scope holds is
  larger. By the bounds of the types alone a list could be 330,929
  bytes, as revision 25 counted. Such a list is never set. The number is
  the proof plan's to measure. It takes effect with a contract revision
  that carries the form.
- No timed rule exists. No entry starts a duty beyond its own
  request and result.

| b | `publish` names a configuration that was not kept | Refused, named `configuration-unknown`. |
| c | `activate` with bytes that do not validate | Refused `unsupported-definition`. Nothing is retained. |
| d | `rules-wanted` from a change lane | One deciding entry, `applied`: the `rules` update at ordinal 0 and the result at ordinal 1. The lane applies the update only if its revision is higher than the one it holds. |
| e | The destination observes the rules for a reservation | An answer: the head, the revision and the values. No entry is written here. |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

It is always completed: it reads the act alone. | None of its own | `rules-extent-required`, `catch-all-required` and `extent-check-unknown`, each under `guard-failed` |
| `rules-update` | 6: the one send of `rules-wanted` | The item `rules`; the delivery's `from` | One request, in every entry of the row: the `rules` update, below | One request, with 6 members of `detail` | None. Place 6 never refuses. |

*An extent, with its bounds.* The rule `extent-list` holds when the
value is a list of 1 to 8 records, and each record has exactly these
six members.

| Member | Bound |
|---|---|
| `name` | A text of 1 to 64 bytes. Each byte is a lowercase ASCII letter, a digit or a hyphen. No two extents of the list have the same name. |
| `patterns` | A list of 0 to 32 texts, each of 1 to 256 bytes. No byte is below 0x20, and none is 0x7F. A pattern does not begin or end with `/` and holds no `//`, so no name of a pattern is empty. |
| `approvals` | An integer from 0 to 64, as the value `approvals` of the rules |
| `approver` | A text of 1 to 64 bytes: the name of an action. Each byte is a lowercase ASCII letter, a digit, a hyphen or a full stop. |
| `checks` | A list of 0 to 32 texts, each of 1 to 128 bytes, with no name twice |
| `class` | `content`, `deployment` or `authority` |

- *Why a name has those characters.* A publication's `reason` names
  an unmet extent, in a text with separators ("The exact text of
  `reason`", in section 12.1.4a). A name of those characters needs no
  escape there.
- *An `approver` that is no action of the role table.* The rule does
  not check the name against the table of section 3.2. No member
  holds an unknown action, so such an extent is never met. That fails
  closed.
- *Why the type is a mark.* The record holds two lists. Whether a
  `list` may be a member of a `record` is asked of the contract by
  the lane forms' revision 15 (its section 20.2, ask 6), and is not
  answered. And no written type states the characters of a text. Row
  P28 of section 12.1.8.
- *One of the two reasons falls away. Corrected in revision 27.* A
  `list` may be a member of a `record`: the contract has said so since
  its revision 13 (its section 6.2, point DF1), and its revision 21
  answers the question in those words (its section 15.3g, "A list inside
  a record"). So the first reason above does not hold, and revision 25
  was wrong to call the question unanswered. The second reason stands
  alone: no written type states the characters of a text, and an
  extent's `name`, its `approver` and its `patterns` each have a rule on
  their bytes. The type stays the mark `extent-list`.

*The three checks of `extents-hold`*, in this order. The first that
fails gives its name.

| # | The check | Refusal name |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The fixed minimum of the `rules` extent: `extents` holds an extent named `rules` with the four patterns of "The first definition", at least 1 approval, the approver `rules.publish` and the class `authority` (section 12.1.4a, "Its fixed minimum") | `rules-extent-required` |
| 2 | Exactly one extent has no pattern. It is the one that holds every path that no pattern matches (section 12.1.4a, "The extent with no pattern"). | `catch-all-required` |
| 3 | Each name in an extent's `checks` is the `name` of a check in the field `checks` of the same act | `extent-check-unknown` |

*The `rules` update.* The send of `rules-wanted` is now the mark
`rules-update`, with empty clauses, in place of the written `relate`
of the row. It gives one `relate` to the sender, named `rules`, of
the item `rules`, in the state `current`. Its `detail` has six
members.

| Member | From |
|---|---|
| `approvals`, `ownerMayReview`, `labels` | The slots of those names |
| `checks` | The slot, when it is set. Before the first `publish` the member is left out: the lane's handler takes it as optional (the lane forms' section 18.9). |
| `extents` | For each extent of the rules, in their order: `name`, `approvals`, `approver`, `checks` and `class`. The patterns are left out: a lane reads no path. When the slot `extents` is unset, the extents are those of the first definition, as the next point says. |
| `singleControllerException` | The slot |

A rule is needed for two reasons. The member `extents` is a
projection of the slot, and no operand makes one. And a value of a
marked type is assignable to no written type, so a written `relate`
could not carry the slot. This answers ask 1 of the lane forms'
section 20.2.

*Before the first `publish`: the first definition is the default.*
The slot `extents` is unset until a `publish` sets it. A repository
has extents all the same. An observation of the rules, asked as
"rules", and the `rules` update each give the three extents of "The
first definition" of section 12.1.4a, computed from the values
`approvals` and `checks` as they then are: `rules` with 1 approval
and no check; `infrastructure` with the repository's `approvals` and
no check; and `source`, with no pattern, the repository's `approvals`
and the checks that are marked `required`. So no repository is judged
by one bar, and the `rules` extent holds from the first entry on. The
source's function `firstExtents` gives these three, and it is
confirmed as that default. The numbers are examples, and the proof
plan owns each (the delta EV12).
Stated in revision 26: this default was this note's reading of the
owner's direction on the request `42de9e34`, and revision 25 asked
the planner to confirm it. Decided by the planner (the act
`5a036318`): a repository has the three extents of the first
definition from before its first `publish`.

*What an observation of the rules then holds.* A `RulesContent` that
was asked as "rules" has two more members under this definition.

```ts
// Under `platform:rules@1`, as revision 25 states its rows:
//   { asked: "rules"; approvals; ownerMayReview; checks; labels;
//     extents: readonly Extent[];                 // 1 to 8, with their patterns
//     singleControllerException: boolean }
```

`singleControllerException` is in the contract's revision 19 (its
section 16.1). `extents` is asked of the contract: the type, and the
size of `content` with it. "The size of `extents`, counted", in
section 12.1.4a, has the numbers. Until the contract states the
member, no observation carries it, and the destination judges no
extent.

Changed in revision 27, from the day that a contract revision which
carries the form takes effect: the member is `extents: Digest`, and not
the list. The contract's revision 21 gives the reason: by its bounds the
list can pass the size of the entry that would hold the observation. The
digest is in the domain `artroom-rules-extents-1`, above. With both
members the largest `content` is 48,931 bytes, as the contract's sum.
What each reader of the rules then gets:

| The reader | What it gets |
|---|---|
| The destination's rule `judge` | The observation in `observed`, with the digest. And the list, as a retained value of its entry, under that domain and that digest. The rule reads the extents from those bytes. The row that observes the rules states `retains` for the domain (section 3.3). |
| A lane | The `rules` update, as before: five members of each extent, and no pattern. It holds no digest. |
| A reader of the destination's entry, and a replay | The entry, with the digest. The bytes, by a read of one retained value: the kind `value`, the domain and the digest. Without the bytes a replay is `incomplete`. |
| A reader of the rules scope | The item `rules`, with the slot `extents` whole |
| A scope that asks the rules scope for an observation as "rules" | The `RulesObservation` without `at`. Its `content.extents` is the digest, and the bytes of the list come beside the answer. An answer whose bytes are missing, are over the bound or do not hash to the digest is no answer. Its `revision` is read from the slot `published`: "The revision of the rules, and the answer to an observation", below. |

**The revision of the rules, and the answer to an observation (EQ8,
FB10). Decided in the second commit of revision 27.** A
`RulesObservation` states `revision`, the position of the latest
`publish` at the head that was read, and no slot held it: an item's own
revision counts its changes and is no position. So a rules scope could
answer no observation, and the destination's `judge` could have none.
Each row below uses a form of the adopted contract, and takes effect
with revision 27.

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| The slot | On the item `rules`: the reference `published` `{ type: "fact", kind: ["publish"], under: "platform:rules" }`. Not fixed. Not required. Unset until the first `publish`. |
| The effect | `publish` gains one written effect: `{ ref: { slot: "published", from: "self" } }`. The entry records `"self"`, and the fold reads it as the entry's own position, with its hash. Membership's `revoke-key` sets `revokedBy` in the same way. |
| The revision of the rules | The `seq` of `published`. While the slot is unset it is 0. |
| Before the first `publish` | The revision is 0. Position 0 is the genesis, and no `publish` can stand there. So 0 says one thing: no `publish` was made, and the rules are what the genesis gave, with the three extents of the first definition and the declaration false. |
| The answer to `{ of, asked: "rules" }` | `of`: this scope's reference, with its incarnation. `head`: its head. `revision`: as above. `content`: `approvals`, `ownerMayReview` and `labels` from their slots; `checks` from its slot, each with `checker` as the member ID of the slot's member reference; `singleControllerException` from its slot; and, when a contract revision that carries the member is adopted, `extents`, the digest of the list. `definition`: `platform:rules@1`. The answer holds no `at`. |
| The answer to `{ of, asked: "definitions" }` | The same `of`, `head`, `revision` and `definition`. `content.active`: the digest and the name of each item `definition` that is `active`, in the order of their IDs. |
| Who answers, and from what | The rules scope, as code of the version, from its folded state at its head. It writes no entry. A provisional rules scope answers none (section 12.1). |
| What a replay derives | It folds the history of the rules scope to `head`. It reads `published` in that state, and checks that its `seq` is the position of the last entry of the kind `publish` at or before `head`, or that the slot is unset and no such entry exists. It derives each member of `content` from the slots of that state, and the digest from the list. A difference is a `mismatch`. |

- *The sentence of the row `publish`.* "The revision of the rules is
  this entry's position" stands. The slot is where the folded state
  holds it.
- *A lane's `rules.source`* is unchanged: the relationship's revision is
  the position of the entry that sent the update.
- *What it gives the destination.* The rule `judge` has its rules
  observation. The text of `reason` has its `:r` and its `:h`: the
  revision, and the position of the head of the rules scope. And each
  `publication` update has the source of its member `rules`: the
  `revision` of the rules observation that the reservation's entry
  retains (the delta FA8).
- *The worker's suggestion is taken.* The I3 deltas note proposed this
  slot (its entry EQ8).

| Case | Input | What is written, or answered |
|---|---|---|
| f | `publish` whose `extents` has no extent named `rules`, or one that lacks a pattern of the four | Refused `guard-failed`, named `rules-extent-required`. The rules do not change. |
| g | `publish` whose `extents` has two extents with no pattern, or none | Refused, named `catch-all-required`. |
| h | `publish` whose extent names a check that the same act does not hold | Refused, named `extent-check-unknown`. |
| i | `publish` whose `extents` holds a name with an uppercase letter, or nine extents | Refused `bad-field`. |
| j | `publish` with no field `singleControllerException`, after one that declared it | Written. The value is false: the declaration is withdrawn. |
| k | `rules-wanted` before any `publish` | One `rules` update, with the three extents of the first definition and no member `checks`. |

#### 12.1.4a Extents

New in revision 22, for the planner's request `42de9e34`. The owner's
direction: a repository's layers must be distinguishable by rules
that a repository can change. A layer is, for example, its ignore
files, its infrastructure, its deployment configuration, or the
instruction files that an agent reads. This section is the design
side only. It says what the adopted texts already state, what an
extent is, and what is missing, with an owner for each missing form.
It changes no row of a lane and no lane digest. Nothing here is built
by adopting it: the rows of section 12.1.4 change only when the
missing forms exist.
Stated in revision 25: the rows of the forms 2, 3 and 14 are given,
in section 12.1.4. "Extents, decided in revision 25", at the end of
this section, says what else is decided.

**What the adopted texts already state.**

| Where | What it holds |
|---|---|
| The rules scope (section 12.1.4) | One `rules` item: `approvals`, a number; `ownerMayReview`; `checks`, at most 32, each with a name, a configuration, whether it is required and its checker; `labels`. `publish` sets them, under `rules.publish`. |
| The observation of the rules (section 3.3) | `content`, asked as "rules": those four values. |
| The `change` lane, as data | A copy of three of them, in its item `rules`: `approvals`, `checks` and `ownerMayReview`, with the revision. Its `merge` asks for that many approving reviews of the manifest, and for a passed job for each check that is required. Its `request-check` asks that the check be one of the rules. Nothing in the lane reads a path. |
| The destination, at the reservation (section 6.5) | It observes the rules itself, and counts from the complete statement: approvals by enough different members, each independent of the authors, and every required check. It reads the integration commit and its whole closure from the host. |

So one bar holds for a whole repository. A change to a workflow file
and a change to a comment meet the same one. No text names a part of
a tree.

**An extent.** An extent is a named part of a repository's tree, with
what a change to it must meet.

```ts
interface Extent {
  name: string;                      // at most 64 bytes; unique in the rules
  patterns: readonly string[];       // at most 32, each at most 256 bytes
  approvals: number;                 // approving reviews that count for this extent
  approver: string;                  // an action: a review counts only from a member who holds it
  checks: readonly string[];         // names of checks of the rules that are required for this extent
  class: "content" | "deployment" | "authority";
}
```

- *What it matches.* A path of the changed set, below. A path may
  match several extents, and then the change touches each. One
  extent, `source`, has no pattern: it holds every changed path that
  no other extent matches.
  Corrected in revision 25: the extent with no pattern is known by
  its empty list, and exactly one exists ("The extent with no
  pattern", below).
- *A pattern.* It is matched against a whole path from the root of
  the tree. A path is the names of its tree entries, joined by `/`,
  as bytes. `*` matches any bytes of one name. `**` matches any
  number of names, also none. Every other byte matches itself, and
  an ASCII letter matches in either case. Nothing else is folded: no
  Unicode form is changed.
  Two cases are made exact in revision 25 ("A pattern, in two
  cases", below).
- *`approver`.* An approving review counts for the extent only when
  its reviewer holds that action, by the observation that the
  destination reads for the reservation. One review may count for
  several extents. Changed in revision 25: a review counts for the
  one extent that it states ("Which reviews count for an extent",
  below). The rules of section 6.5 hold for each review as
  before: a different member, independent of the authors, and a key
  that is not compromised.
- *`class`.* A label of what a change to the extent does when it is
  published. `content`: it changes files. `deployment`: it can
  change what runs. `authority`: it can change who may do what, or
  what runs with a member's authority. The class is recorded and
  shown. It selects no rule in this revision. Changed in revision 23:
  the planner has decided what a class requires. "What the planner
  decided", below.

**The changed set.** The paths that a change touches, for the match.

- For each commit that the manifest newly brings, and for each parent
  of it: every path whose entry differs between that parent's tree
  and the commit's tree. And every path whose entry differs between
  the tree of the manifest's `base` and the tree of its
  `integration`. An entry differs when its mode or its object
  differs, or when one side has none.
- The commits that a manifest newly brings are the list F of its
  ancestry record, with the integration commit (section 6.2).
- So a rename is two paths, the old and the new. No rename is
  detected. A path that one commit adds and a later commit removes
  is in the set, although the two trees at the ends do not show it.
  A symbolic link is a path with its own mode: the link's path is in
  the set, and its target is not followed. Corrected in revision 25:
  the last clause is withdrawn. The planner decided a rule for links
  ("A symbolic link", below). A submodule's entry is a
  path.
- *Who computes it.* The runtime of the scope that judges, from the
  commits and trees that it reads by their IDs. Those objects do not
  change, so a replay reads the same ones and derives the same set.
  It is evidence of an outcome, and no judge of a commit computes
  it: a rule reads no repository.
- *From which retained input.* None holds it today. The ancestry
  record holds F and the snapshot of the staged refs, and no tree.
  The evidence of the destination's `judge` is "the read of the
  branch's head and of the integration commit's closure", and its
  body is not typed. That is the first missing form, below.
  Given in part in revision 25: the member `changes` ("The evidence
  of `judge`, for extents", below).

**How a change is judged.** At the destination, in the outcome of
`judge`, where the rules are already observed and the closure is
already read.

1. The runtime computes the changed set, and the extents that it
   touches under the rules that were observed for this reservation.
   The evidence holds the list of touched extents, each with one
   path that shows it.
   Corrected in revision 25: the evidence holds the changed set and
   the links, and the rule derives the touched extents.
2. The rule of the outcome checks, for each touched extent: enough
   approving reviews from members who hold its `approver`; and a
   passed job for each check that it names, as section 6.5 checks
   any required check.
3. The obligations of a mixed change are the union. Each touched
   extent must be met. Nothing is averaged, and the stricter extent
   does not replace the others.
4. An extent that is not met gives `not-reserved`, with the reason
   `rules-not-met` and the extent's name in the publication's
   `reason`.
   The exact text is stated in revision 25, below.
5. The class that is recorded for the change is the highest that it
   touches: `authority`, then `deployment`, then `content`.

A replay reads the commits again, derives the changed set and the
touched extents, and compares them with the evidence.

**How a repository changes its extents.** By `publish`, which sets
the rules. Its field `extents` is a list of at most 8 extents. The
grant is `rules.publish`, as for every value of the rules. No change
in a lane sets an extent, because the rules are in no file: they are
in the rules scope. So a change cannot lower the bar that judges it.
The rules that judge a reservation are those that the destination
observes for it, within ten seconds.

**The first definition.** Three extents. The numbers are examples,
and R4 owns each.

| Name | Patterns | Approvals, and from whom | Checks | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rules` | `**/AGENTS.md`, `**/CLAUDE.md`, `.github/workflows/**`, `.github/actions/**`, and what a repository adds | At least 1, from a member who holds `rules.publish`: the rules scope's controller | Those that the repository names | `authority` |
| `infrastructure` | `**/.gitignore`, `**/.gitattributes`, `.github/**`, and what a repository adds for its deployment configuration | The repository's `approvals`, from a member who holds `change.merge` | Those that the repository names | `deployment` |
| `source` | None: every other changed path | The repository's `approvals`, from a member who holds `change.review` | The checks that the rules mark `required` | `content` |

- *What the rules extent covers.* Four things, by the request. The
  rules definition and the activations are in the rules scope: they
  change only by `publish`, `keep-configuration`, `activate` and
  `retire-definition`, which already need `rules.publish` or
  `rules.activate`. Instruction files for agents, and the
  definitions of continuous integration and of automation, are files
  of the repository: they are the patterns of the row.
- *Its fixed minimum.* `publish` is refused, named
  `rules-extent-required`, unless `extents` holds an extent named
  `rules` with the four patterns of the row, at least 1 approval, the
  approver `rules.publish` and the class `authority`. A repository
  may add patterns to it. It may not remove one, lower its approvals
  or change its approver. That guard is one more mark of `publish`,
  at place 4.
- *"Met only with the rules scope's controller."* In this note's
  roles the controller of the rules scope is a member who holds
  `rules.publish`, which the role `admin` holds. Whether an
  installation has a narrower role is asked, below.
- *A `.github` path matches two extents.* A workflow file is in
  `rules` and in `infrastructure`. Both must be met. One review by an
  admin may count for both.
  Changed in revision 25: the admin signs one verdict for each
  extent.

**What the planner decided. Applied in revision 23.** Revision 22
asked the planner three questions: the missing forms 5, 6 and 7. The
planner answered each, in an assertion that rests on `4a1c97f2` and
`42de9e34`. The planner is the decider, and each answer is applied as
it stands.

*1. No self-review of a change to the rules.* "The rules extent's
obligation is met only by a controller other than the author, with a
stated single-controller exception recorded on every landing that
uses it."
Corrected in revision 24: those words are the builder's summary of
the decision. The planner's assertion,
`19cd4a03c32d29a83c9a553112b57f4fec8d8bac`, reads, as the builder
gave it for this revision: "No. The rules extent's obligation is met
only by a controller other than the author. An installation with one
controller may declare a stated exception in its rules, and every
landing that uses it records it." Revision 23 applied the summary,
and so lost the words "may declare" and "in its rules".

- *The rule.* A review counts for the `rules` extent only when its
  reviewer holds `rules.publish`, is independent of the authors as
  section 3.10 defines it, and is not the controller of an agent
  among the authors. For this extent `ownerMayReview` is read as
  false, whatever the repository set.
- *It agrees with section 3.10.* There an author never gives the
  counted review, whatever `ownerMayReview` says, and that value
  exempts only the relation of a controller to its agent. This rule
  removes that one exemption for the `rules` extent. It adds no way
  for an author to count.
- *The exception. Corrected in revision 24* (the verdict `546fa613`).
  Revision 23 let it hold whenever membership showed one controller.
  That made a count into a permission, and the planner gave none: an
  installation with one controller may declare the exception in its
  rules. So three things must all hold, at the reservation.
  1. *It is declared.* The rules that the destination observes for
     this reservation hold `singleControllerException: true`. The
     value is false by default, and a repository that never set it
     has no exception. The form of the value is not built: the
     missing form 14.
     Given as rows in revision 25 (section 12.1.4).
  2. *There is one controller.* Exactly one active member with an
     active key holds `rules.publish`, at the head of membership that
     the destination observes for this reservation. The form of that
     count is not built: the missing form 11.
  3. *That member cannot meet the ordinary bar.* The one controller
     is among the manifest's authors, or is the controller of an
     agent among them (section 3.10). Where the one controller is
     independent of the authors, the rule above holds as it stands:
     that member's review is asked, and no exception is used.
     Narrowed in revision 24: revision 23 did not say this.
     Reconciled in revision 25 with the planner's words: the one
     controller is the author. The clause on the controller of an
     agent is withdrawn ("The exception, in the planner's words",
     below).
     Restored in revision 26: that withdrawal is itself withdrawn.
     This condition stands as revision 24 wrote it above, with both
     clauses (the planner's act `5a036318`; "The exception, in the
     planner's words", below).

  Then the obligation of the `rules` extent is met when that member
  signed the `merge`. Every other obligation of the change stands:
  its other extents, its checks, and the reviews of the `source`
  extent, in which an author still does not count.
- *With no declaration. New in revision 24.* The exception is not
  available, whatever membership shows. The change is judged by the
  rule alone. With no counted review by an independent controller the
  publication ends `not-reserved`, with the reason `rules-not-met`
  and the extent's name, `rules`. That is the ordinary answer for an
  extent that is not met ("How a change is judged", step 4). No other
  reason is added. A count of one changes nothing by itself.
- *Which rules declare it. New in revision 24.* The rules in force
  before the change: those that the destination observes for the
  reservation. This note fixed that in revision 22, for every value
  of the rules, and revision 24 follows it. The rules are a value of
  the rules scope and are in no file, so "a change cannot lower the
  bar that judges it", and "the rules that judge a reservation are
  those that the destination observes for it" ("How a repository
  changes its extents", above). The declaration is one more value of
  those rules. Three things follow.
  - *A change cannot grant itself the exception.* Nothing that a
    manifest brings can set the value. Only `publish` sets it, and
    `publish` is an entry of the rules scope that is written before
    the observation that shows it.
  - *No change removes the declaration either.* It is withdrawn by a
    `publish` that sets the value to false, which is its own entry. A
    reservation whose observation was read before that entry may use
    the exception. A reservation whose observation was read after it
    may not. This is the order that section 6.5 gives a revocation:
    what the destination observed within ten seconds decides, and the
    entry records what that was.
  - *A reserved publication is not opened again* when the declaration
    is withdrawn after it (section 6.5).

  The reason for the rule: the bar that judges a change must be one
  that neither the change nor a later act of its author can move. The
  author's direction for revision 24 asked for the same rule. The
  note's model gave it already, so nothing new is decided here.
- *Who declares. New in revision 24.* A member who holds
  `rules.publish`, by `publish`, as for every value of the rules.
  `publish` is a signed entry of the rules scope, and this note has
  no review of a `publish`. So the one controller of a repository can
  declare the exception alone, which is what the planner permits.
  Where a repository has two controllers, either can publish the
  declaration, and it gives neither of them anything while both are
  controllers: the second condition fails. Whether a `publish` may
  declare the exception while more than one controller exists is not
  decided here. It is open, with the planner.
  Decided by the planner, and stated in revision 25: it may.
- *Its record. Corrected in revision 24.* A record shows that the
  exception was used. It does not make the use allowed: the three
  conditions do. The record is written by the destination, in the
  entry that reserves the publication: the outcome of `judge`. The
  entry states the extent, the words "single-controller", the member,
  the head of membership at which that member was the only
  controller, and the head and the revision of the rules that
  declared the exception. Both observations are in the entry's
  `observed`, as for every reservation. The `relate` update of the
  publication carries the same to the lane, in `reason`, so the
  lane's history shows it beside the merge. The receipt of the
  publication (section 6.10) repeats it. So every landing that used
  the exception says so in three histories. A replay derives the
  count again from membership's history at that head, and the
  declaration from the rules scope's history at that revision. An
  entry that claims the exception under a revision of the rules that
  does not declare it does not verify.
- *When a second controller exists.* The exception is not available.
  The destination judges the count at the head that it observed
  within ten seconds. Two controllers at that head mean that another
  must review. Making a second admin a non-admin is a signed act in
  membership, which the last-admin rules of section 12.1.3 bound, and
  it is in membership's history before any landing that uses the
  exception.
- *What is missing for it. Corrected in revision 24.* Two forms. The
  destination has no observation that counts the holders of an
  action: the missing form 11. The rules have no value for the
  declaration, `publish` has no field for it, and an observation of
  the rules does not carry it: the missing form 14. Until both exist
  no exception is declared or judged, and a change to the `rules`
  extent needs the review of a second controller.
  From revision 25: the declaration has its rows. The count is still
  the missing form 11.
  From revision 26: one more form is missing, for the second clause
  of the third condition: the missing form 15.

*2. What a class requires, beyond review.* "A declared destination
with its recovery custody; a standing grant on that destination for
the landing actor; a preview or dry-run witness where the destination
offers one; and the effect written as a replayable entry." These are
obligations of the classes `deployment` and `authority`. For a
landing on a repository's branch, records of this note already carry
each.

| The obligation | The record that carries it, for a landing on a branch | What is missing |
|---|---|---|
| A declared destination, with its recovery custody | The destination scope of that branch, which the `reserve` names and which is the branch's one writer. Its custody is its own history: the reservation, each attempt of the push with its outcome, `adopt-head`, `resend`, and the receipt (sections 6.5 to 6.10). | Nothing, for a branch. |
| A standing grant on that destination, for the landing actor | The merger's key holds `change.merge`, by an observation that the destination reads within ten seconds, and the grant's `within` covers the repository's scopes, of which the destination is one (sections 3.3 and 6.5). | Nothing, for a branch. Stated in revision 24: this grant covers every destination of the repository. The planner's words are "on that destination", and no grant of this note is narrower than a repository (section 3.3, `within`). Where a repository has more than one published branch, whether a grant on one destination alone is wanted is asked of the planner, with the missing form 12. Answered by the planner, and stated in revision 25: a grant that covers the one destination, which a grant on the repository satisfies only until `within` can name a destination ("The grant on one destination", below). |
| A preview or a dry-run witness, where the destination offers one | None. The destination of a branch offers no dry run. The checks that pass on the manifest's tree are the repository's own evidence, and are not a preview by the destination. | A form for a witness, when a destination offers one. The missing form 12. |
| The effect, written as a replayable entry | The reservation's outcome entry, the outcome entries of the push, and the receipt. A replay derives each (section 10). | Nothing, for a branch. |

  An effect that follows a landing and is not the branch itself, such
  as a deployment that a workflow then makes, has no destination
  scope in this note, no grant on one and no entry. So for such an
  effect none of the four is carried. That is the missing form 12,
  and it is not designed here. Until it exists the classes record and
  show, and the four obligations are met for the landing on the
  branch alone.
  Stated in revision 24: to record a class and to show it meets none
  of the four. This note does not claim that the planner's second
  decision is met for an effect beyond the branch, and nothing here
  permits such an effect. It reads "an effect class" as the classes
  `deployment` and `authority`, and not `content`.

**A symbolic link. Decided by the planner, and applied here.**
Revision 24 said of a link that "its target is not followed", and
listed the gap as the missing form 10. That sentence is withdrawn.
The rule has seven parts.

1. *A path is judged where it is and where it leads.* The extents of
   a path are judged by the path itself, and by every path that a
   link at it resolves to within the tree.
2. *A file is judged where it is and where it is linked from.* A
   change to a file is judged at its own path, and at the path of
   every link in the tree that resolves to it, through links to
   links. So where `AGENTS.md` is a link to `docs/agents.md`, a
   change to `docs/agents.md` is a change at `AGENTS.md`, and touches
   the `rules` extent.
3. *A change of target is judged at both targets.* A link whose
   target changes is a change in every extent that its own path, its
   old target and its new target fall in.
4. *Two things are refused.* Creating a link that leaves the tree or
   cannot be resolved, and giving an existing link such a target.
   Each is refused as a change to the `rules` extent: the change is
   not met, the extent `rules` is named as unmet, and no review meets
   it.
5. *Removing such a link is allowed.* It is judged as a change in
   the `rules` extent and in the extents of the link's own path.
6. *Replacing such a link is allowed.* With a regular file, or with
   a link that resolves inside the tree. It is judged in the `rules`
   extent, in the extents of the path and, for a new link, in the
   extents of the new target.
7. *A tree that already holds such a link is not blocked.* A change
   elsewhere is judged as if the link were not there. The link is
   never followed.

- *What "resolves" means.* A link's target is read as a path
  relative to the directory that holds the link. Each name is taken
  in turn; `.` stays and `..` goes up one name. Where a name on the
  way is itself a link, that link is resolved first. The link
  resolves to each path that it reaches on the way, and to its end.
  It *leaves the tree* when its target begins with `/`, when `..`
  would go above the root, or when a name on the way is a
  submodule's entry. It *cannot be resolved* when a name on the way
  is not in that tree, when a chain of links returns to a link that
  it passed, or when the chain is longer than 40 links. The number
  is an example, and the proof plan owns it.
- *In which tree.* A link of the tree that a change starts from is
  resolved in that tree, and a link of the tree that it makes is
  resolved in that one. For the changed set of "The changed set",
  above, that is each pair of trees that the set compares.
- *Who resolves.* The runtime that computes the changed set, from
  the same trees. The result is evidence: the rows `links` of "The
  evidence of `judge`, for extents", below. A rule reads the rows and
  no repository. A replay reads the trees again and compares.
- *A directory behind a link.* Where a link resolves to a directory,
  every changed path below that directory is judged at the link's
  path with the rest of the changed path, by part 2. A path below
  that directory which the change does not touch is not judged: it
  did not change.
- *Rules with no extent named `rules`.* None exists. The fixed
  minimum makes every published rules content hold one, and before
  the first `publish` the first definition holds one (section
  12.1.4). So parts 4 to 6 always have an extent to name.
- *What "refused" is read as.* The planner's words are "refused as a
  rules-extent change". This note reads them as part 4 states: not
  met, whatever the reviews. That is the stricter of two readings.
  The other is that such a link is judged as any change to the
  `rules` extent, and a controller's review meets it. The planner is
  asked to confirm the stricter one (the delta EV7, reading b).
  Decided, and stated in revision 26: the planner confirms the
  stricter one (the act `5a036318`). A link that leaves the tree is
  never met, by a review or by the exception. It is refused, and the
  way forward is to change the link.
- *What the source has.* `classify`, in
  `packages/platform/src/extents.ts`, judges by these seven parts,
  with the member `tree` of a link's row. It is confirmed as built.
  Its answer for rules with no extent `rules`, "unclassified", cannot
  arise under a published rules content.

**A pattern, in two cases that revision 24 left open (EV13).
Decided, as built.**

- *`**` inside a name.* `**` matches any number of names only when
  it is a whole name of the pattern. In any other name each `*`
  matches any bytes of one name, so `a**b` matches what `a*b`
  matches.
- *An empty name.* A pattern has none: the rule `extent-list`
  refuses a pattern that begins or ends with `/` or holds `//`
  (section 12.1.4). A path has none either, because a tree entry's
  name is never empty.
- *A path that is no text.* A changed path whose bytes are not
  well-formed UTF-8, or that holds a byte below 0x20 or the byte
  0x7F, cannot stand in the evidence as a text. Until IA says how
  the reader carries one, a change with such a path is treated as
  part 4 of the link rule treats a link that cannot be resolved: not
  met, with `rules` named. That fails closed. It is this note's
  reading, and IA and the planner may replace it.
  Decided, and stated in revision 26: the planner confirms it (the
  act `5a036318`). A changed path that is no text is not met, with
  `rules` named, until IA carries such a path's name.

**The extent with no pattern (EV14). Decided.** It is known by its
empty list of patterns, and not by the name `source`. The rule
`extents-hold` makes every published rules content hold exactly one
such extent (section 12.1.4, the refusal `catch-all-required`). So
every judged path is in at least one extent, and no path is
unclassified. No reason is added for an unclassified path, because
none can arise. Corrected: revision 24 said "One extent, `source`,
has no pattern". The first definition names its one such extent
`source`, and a repository may name it otherwise.

**The exception, in the planner's words (D1, D2). Reconciled.
Corrected in revision 26.**
Revision 24's third condition read "the one controller is among the
manifest's authors, or is the controller of an agent among them". The
planner's later words, in the assertion `7d7b6a78`, are "exactly one
controller who is the author". Revision 25 read those words as a
narrowing. It withdrew the second clause here, and told the source to
remove it. That was wrong, and the verdict `f456b67c` found it. The
planner's act `5a036318` settles the reading: "who is the author" was
shorthand, and no narrowing. The exception takes effect when the one
controller controls an agent among the authors, and revision 24's
condition stands: "among the manifest's authors, or the controller of
an agent among them". The planner's reason is the demonstration's own
case: one person who directs agents must be able to change the rules
without a commit written by hand.

The three conditions are these, at the reservation. Restated in
revision 26: they are those of revision 24, and the third is in its
words.

1. *It is declared.* The rules that the destination observes for
   this reservation hold `singleControllerException: true`. The value
   is false by default, and a repository that never set it has no
   exception.
2. *There is one controller.* Exactly one active member with an
   active key holds `rules.publish`, at the head of membership that
   the destination observes for this reservation. The count is
   observed, and a count alone permits nothing.
3. *That member cannot meet the ordinary bar.* The one controller is
   among the manifest's authors, or is the controller of an agent
   among them (section 3.10). Where the one controller is independent
   of the authors, the rule holds as it stands: that member's review
   is asked, and no exception is used.

Then the approvals of the `rules` extent are met when that member
signed the `merge`. Every other obligation of the change stands, as
revision 24 lists them: its other extents, its checks, and the
reviews of the `source` extent, in which an author still does not
count. The checks of the `rules` extent stand too (EV15), and so does
the merger's grant for a class (step 4 of the rule, below). No rule
of independence in section 3.10 changes.

- *An agent's change whose controller is the sole controller.* The
  agent is the author, and its controller is not. Condition 3 holds
  by its second clause. Where conditions 1 and 2 hold too, and that
  controller signed the `merge`, the exception takes effect: the
  approvals of the `rules` extent are met, and the landing records
  `single-controller`. The controller's review still does not count,
  because "The rule", above, counts no review by the controller of
  an agent among the authors. It is that member's signed `merge`
  that meets the extent, and only under the declaration.
  Corrected in revision 26: revision 25 said here that such a change
  is not reserved unless the one controller adds a commit of their
  own, and asked the planner. That is withdrawn. The change is
  refused as before in three cases, each `not-reserved`,
  `rules-not-met:rules`: the observed rules do not declare the
  exception; membership shows two controllers or none; or another
  member signed the `merge`.
- *What makes the relation replayable. New in revision 26.*
  Membership states who controls an agent. An agent is a member
  whose item `member` has the party `controller`. That party is
  fixed: `add-member` sets it when it opens the item, its guard asks
  that the controller is named and is an active person, and no row
  changes it (section 12.1.3, the rows `member` and `add-member`;
  section 3.1, the record "Controller"; section 3.7). Membership
  answers an observation from its head, and for an agent the answer
  carries that member as `controller`. For a member that is no agent
  the value is null (section 3.3, the types `Observation` and
  `MemberObservation`, and the row ED6). So "controls an agent" is a
  fact of membership's history. Because the party is fixed, every
  head that holds the agent gives the same controller. A replay
  derives it from that history, as it derives the count of condition
  2, and it takes no caller's word for it.
  - *What the destination retains of it.* Nothing, today. The outcome
    of `judge` retains an observation of the merger's key and of each
    key behind a counted verdict or result, and one observation of
    the rules (section 3.3, the table of nine rows; section 12.1.5,
    "The evidence of `judge`, and what the rule reads"). None is an
    observation of an author. The merger of this case is a person,
    whose `controller` is null. So no retained input of a reservation
    states who controls an agent among the authors.
  - *What is owed.* The missing form 15: one more row of what the
    outcome of `judge` retains in `observed`, so that the entry holds
    an observation of each authoring agent with its `controller`,
    read from membership for that reservation. The type exists. The
    row, its bound, and how the destination learns which authors are
    agents are owed. The owner is this note's next revision, with the
    contract for the bound on the foreign entries of one entry (G5)
    and R4 for the number. It is not designed here.
  - *Until it exists.* The second clause of condition 3 is shown for
    nobody. The exception is not judged for an agent's change: where
    the one controller is not among the manifest's authors, the
    change is `not-reserved`, `rules-not-met:rules`. That fails
    closed. The first clause needs no such record: it reads the
    manifest's authors and the merger's member.
  - *What this revision did not establish.* "The rule", above, and
