  Changed in revision 28: the row `mint` holds with one more condition.
  The slot is set only where the target is not closed. A mint for a
  receipt that is already final records its token and opens the
  revocation, and sets no slot ("A token whose write can no longer act,
  and who cleans it up", below).
- *The deciding read of a receipt's ref, and of a first head,* is judged
  by the column of its write, as revision 25 has it.
- *What is still open for a first head.* The way forward when its three
  attempts are used and the branch is still `empty`, at a founding with
  no import. It is carried (section 13.17).

**What `seen` decides for a push, with the item `receipt` and one read
for an operation.** The table of revision 25 stands, with three changes.

| Row of that table | Changed to |
|---|---|
| The publication's `integration`: `published` | It yields `{ state: "published" }`; `branch.slot` emptied; `branch.head`; the item `receipt`, opened with `publication` and `commit`; the `receipt` operation, its attempt 1 and that attempt's `mint`; the next `judge`; and the update `published`. It no longer sets a slot `receipt`. |
| "The base, otherwise", and "`failed`, in an outcome of a push" | A `read` operation is opened only when no outcome of this push operation has opened one. Otherwise the rule yields the state and the update, and no read. |
| "Any other commit" | Unchanged. It opens no read. |

- *Why one read for an operation (FA14, and row 4 of FC1).* Revision 25
  opened a read after each outcome of a push that decided nothing while
  no attempt was open, so a late answer could open another, and no
  number bounded them. A count that an item holds must be an upper bound
  of what the rules open. So a push operation, a `first-head` operation
  and a `receipt` operation each open at most one `read`. A rule knows
  it from the operations of its holder, which the folded state lists by
  item under `holds`. The read that `abort-if-behind` opens is beside
  those: one for a publication, because `aborting` is set once.
- *What that gives up.* A push whose one read has had its outcome, and
  showed another writer's commit, opens no further read when a late
  answer comes. The publication stays `unresolved`. That is the last row
  of revision 25's table already: an admin's `resend` or `adopt-head` is
  the way forward, and a `resend` adds one read.
- *The source must change.* It opens a read after each such outcome.

**A token whose write can no longer act, and who cleans it up. Decided
in revision 28** (the verdict `af0d0a5e` on revision 27, its first
finding; the adopted contract's revision 19, its section 6.6, "No effect
changes an item that was final before the entry", and its section 6.1,
the point on EJ11: an effect of an outcome's rule that a check would
refuse is a fault, and nothing is written). This block rests on the
adopted contract alone. It takes effect when this revision is adopted.
Where a row above and this block differ, this block is the rule.

*What was wrong.* Revision 27 let the rule `mint` set the slot `token`
whenever its own attempt had no outcome and the publication was not
`aborting`. It did not read whether the item that holds the slot was
already final. The verdict gives the case. A receipt is `owed`. Its
three attempts have `unknown` outcomes, and its deciding read is
pending. An admin signs `resend-receipt`, which opens a new operation,
its attempt and that attempt's mint. The old read then shows the
receipt's commit and makes the receipt `written`, which is final. The
new mint then confirms, and the rule gives `receipt.token`: an effect on
an item that was final before the entry. That is a fault of the rule.
Nothing is written, and the confirmed answer of the mint stays offered
with a live token that no entry records. In the other order the mint
confirms first, and the outcome of the new attempt later empties
`receipt.token` on a final receipt: the same fault, in the row of the
write.

*Three words.* The *target* of a write is the item whose slot `token`
the write uses. A target is *closed* when that write can no longer act
on it. The *holder of a mint* is the item that the mint's operation is
`for`: the holder of the write whose attempt it serves.

| The write | Its target | The slot | The target is closed when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `first-head` | The branch | `branch.token` | The branch is not `empty`: a first head, a read or an `adopt-head` made it `ready` |
| `push` | The publication | `publication.token` | The publication is final, which is `published`, `aborted` or `not-reserved`; or `aborting` is set |
| `receipt` | The item `receipt` | `receipt.token` | The receipt is final: `written` or `conflict` |

*The rules of a token.* Eight, and each says what it changes of revision
27.

| # | The entry | What the rule yields | Against revision 27 |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | A `confirmed` outcome of a `mint`, where its attempt has no outcome and the target is not closed | The slot `token` of the target is this operation's ID, and a publication that is `reserved` becomes `publishing`. The token is in use. | Changed: it read `aborting`, and no other way in which a target closes |
| T2 | A `confirmed` outcome of a `mint` otherwise: its attempt has an outcome, or the target is closed | The token's `revoke` operation with 3 attempts, and its attempt 1, `for` the holder of the mint. No slot of any item is set. The token was minted and is never used. | The same arm, for more cases |
| T3 | A `refused` or an `unknown` outcome of a `mint` | Nothing | Unchanged |
| T4 | The first outcome entry of an attempt of a write, where the slot `token` of its target names that attempt's own mint | The token's `revoke` operation and its attempt 1, `for` the holder of the write, which is the holder of the mint. Where the target was not final before the entry, the slot is emptied. Where it was final before the entry, nothing is set on it. | Changed: it emptied the slot in every case, and it read "the slot is set" |
| T5 | The entry of `compromised`, by the rule `abort-if-behind` | As revision 25: `aborting`, the revocation of the token that `publication.token` names, the slot emptied, and a read. The publication is `reserved`, `publishing` or `unresolved`, so it is not final. | Unchanged |
| T6 | Any entry that closes a target, and is not the entry of T4 or of T5 for the token that the slot names | Nothing on the slot `token`, and no revocation. This holds for an outcome of a read, a late answer of another attempt, an outcome of another operation, and an outcome of `adopt-read`. | New as a statement |
| T7 | The gateway, before it sends the request of an attempt of a write | It sends only where the slot `token` of the target names that attempt's own mint and the target is not closed, as the folded state has them when it sends. An attempt whose request it does not send gets the outcome `refused`, with `{ send: "not-sent", seen }`. | Changed: it waited for the mint's `confirmed` outcome alone |
| T8 | The function of a write's rule that says whether another attempt is allowed | Only while the target is not closed. For a push, as before: `seen` is the base and `aborting` is not set. | Stated for all three writes. It was stated for a push. |

- *The evidence is the mint's own.* In T1 and in T2 the outcome entry
  holds what the host answered: `{ token, ends }`, the host's ID of the
  credential and the time at which it ends. T2 writes that record whole
  and sets nothing of the target. No rule invents an outcome for the
  attempt that the mint serves, and none gives another attempt one. -
  *`not-sent` is the gateway's own answer.* It is written only for a
  request that the gateway did not send. A request that was sent gets
  its own answer, or `unknown` when the answer is lost, as before. So no
  evidence of a send is made up in either direction. - *Each token gets
  one revocation, and no token gets two.* A mint has one `confirmed`
  outcome at the most: its first outcome, or a late answer after
  `unknown`. That entry takes T1 or T2. With T2 the revocation is opened
  there, and the slot never names the mint, so T4 and T5 do not apply.
  With T1 the slot names the mint, and it stops naming it only by T4 or
  by T5, each of which opens the revocation. Where T5 did, the slot is
  empty and T4 yields nothing. Where another entry closed the target
  first, T6 leaves the slot as it is, and T4 opens the revocation in the
  first outcome of the attempt. An attempt has one first outcome, and
  every attempt gets one: its own answer, `unknown`, or `not-sent` by
  T7. - *The slot of an open target names one mint at the most.* One
  attempt of a write on one target is without an outcome at a time.
  Inside an operation the outcome entry of attempt n opens attempt n +
  1. A further operation is opened only by `resend` or by
  `resend-receipt`, whose guard `resend-due` asks that every attempt of
  every earlier operation for that target has an outcome. So when T1
  sets the slot of an open target, T4 or T5 has emptied it of every
  earlier mint. - *The slot on a final item is history.* After T6 the
  slot of a final publication or of a final receipt may still name a
  mint. No rule reads it but T4, once, for that mint's own attempt. T1
  never sets a slot of a closed target. - *No guard is added to
  `resend-receipt` or to `resend`.* Neither waits for an earlier read.
  So recovery is never held behind a read that does not answer, and no
  wait needs a bound. The earlier read stays pending and is judged when
  it answers. - *What stays as it was.* Every attempt that was admitted
  keeps its place and its outcomes. An attempt that is `unknown` stays
  `unknown`, and only its own answer follows it. Each mint and each
  write keeps the holder that the entry which opened it gave. Each token
  keeps the record of the mint that the host answered.

**Where the record of a token stands.** Not in a slot. The slot says
which token is in use, for the gateway and for `abort-if-behind`. The
record of a token is the ledger's, in the operations that are `for` the
holder of its mint.

| What | Where it stands |
|---|---|
| That a token was minted, with the host's ID of it and its end | The `confirmed` outcome entry of the `mint` operation: the body `{ token, ends }` |
| Which attempt of which write it serves | The entry that opened the mint. It opens one attempt of a write, and no more. |
| Which holder pays for it | The member `for` of the mint's `operation` effect |
| Whether it was put in use | Whether that outcome entry set a slot (T1) or opened the revocation (T2) |
| Its revocation | The one `revoke` operation whose opening entry is the mint's own outcome entry (T2), the first outcome entry of the attempt that it serves (T4), or the entry of `compromised` (T5). It is `for` the same holder, and its evidence `{ token }` holds the same ID. |

A replay derives each row from the history. An operator reads them in
one place:

```ts
/** Beside the read of a `publication` or of the `branch`. Derived from the history, so a replay derives the same. It is in no entry. */
interface Tokens {
  tokens: readonly {
    mint: OperationId;                                     // a `mint` operation that is `for` this holder, with a `confirmed` outcome
    serves: { operation: OperationId; attempt: number };   // the attempt of the write
    token: string;                                         // the host's ID of the credential. Never the secret.
    ends: Timestamp;                                       // when the host ends it
    used: boolean;                                         // true: T1. false: T2.
    revoke: OperationId | null;                            // null only between T1 and the entry of T4 or of T5
    revoked: "open" | "spent";                             // "spent": each attempt of the revocation has an outcome, and none is `confirmed`
  }[];                                                     // each such mint whose revocation is not `confirmed`
}
```

- *Its bound.* At most the mints that the holder's `holds` and the
  `adds` of its acts state: 6 for a publication and 6 for a branch, and
  1 more for each `resend`, `resend-receipt`, `add-room` or
  `add-branch-room`. - *Who may read it.* Whoever may read the item, as
  for `Stopped`. A final publication is still read, so the tokens of its
  receipt's attempts are found there. - *A revocation whose three
  attempts are used.* It stays a duty in the ledger and in this read, as
  revision 25 has it for every revocation. The token ends at the host at
  `ends`. No act opens a fourth attempt, and none is added here.

**One holder for each cleanup.** Revision 27 has two sentences. A
`revoke` is `for` the holder of the mint whose token it revokes. And a
rule of an outcome gives the holder of its own operation, with one
exception: the next `judge`. They disagree where an entry of one holder
would open the revocation of a token whose mint another holder holds.
That is the second order of the verdict's case: a read that a
publication holds closes the receipt while `receipt.token` names a mint
that the branch holds. From revision 28 no entry of one holder opens a
revocation for another, so the two sentences say one thing.

- In T2 the entry is the mint's own outcome. Its operation is `for` the
  holder of the mint. - In T4 the entry is an outcome of the write. Its
  operation is `for` the holder of the write, and a mint is `for` the
  holder of the write whose attempt it serves. So the two are one
  holder. - In T5 the entry is a delivery, and no outcome. It is on a
  publication, and `publication.token` names only a mint of a push of
  that publication. Each such mint is `for` that publication: by its
  `holds`, or by the `adds` of a `resend` on it. - By T6 no other entry
  opens a revocation.

So the revocation of a token is `for` the holder of its mint, and that
holder reserved it with the mint. The next `judge` stays the only
exception to the rule that an outcome gives the holder of its own
operation.

| The write | Opened by | Its mint and its token's revocation are `for` | Reserved by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `first-head`, attempts 1 to 3 | The genesis, or the delivery of `import` | The branch | The `holds` of the branch, at `establish` |
| `push`, attempts 1 to 3 | The outcome of `judge` that reserves | The publication | The `holds` of the publication, at the delivery of its `reserve` |
| `push`, by a `resend` | The act | The publication | The `adds` of that `resend` |
| `receipt` of a publication, attempts 1 to 3 | The entry that makes it `published` | The publication | The `holds` of the publication |
| `receipt` of the first head, attempts 1 to 3 | The entry that makes the branch `ready` by a first head | The branch | The `holds` of the branch |
| `receipt`, by a `resend-receipt` | The act | The branch | The `adds` of that `resend-receipt` |

Each `holds` and each `adds` states as many of `revoke` as of `mint`,
and a mint gets one revocation at the most. So no draw on `revoke`
passes a count, and no count of section 5.8 changes.

**The verdict's case, in both orders, as entries.** R is the receipt of
the publication P, which is `published`. Its `receipt` operation o1 is
`for` P. The three attempts of o1 have `unknown` outcomes, and its one
read, rd1, is `for` P and is pending. In each table the last column
names the holder on whose count the entry, or what it opens, is drawn.

*The first order: the old read, and then the new mint.*

| # | The entry | The rule, and its arm | The slot or state that changes | It opens | The holder that pays |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The act `resend-receipt`, for R | The written guard on `owed`; `resend-due`; `reopen-publish` | None. The act adds 1 `receipt`, 1 `mint`, 1 `revoke` and 1 `read` to the branch. | The `receipt` operation o2 with 1 attempt, its attempt 1, and that attempt's mint m2 | The act is new work. o2 and m2 are drawn on the branch. |
| 2 | The outcome of rd1, `confirmed`, with `seen` the commit of R | `deciding-read`, by the column of `receipt`; T6 | R is `written`. Nothing else. | Nothing | P: rd1 was drawn on P's count of `read` |
| 3 | The outcome of m2, `confirmed`, with `{ token, ends }` | `mint`, T2: R is closed | None | The `revoke` operation v2 for m2's token, and its attempt 1 | The branch: v2 is drawn on the `revoke` that entry 1 added |
| 4 | The outcome of attempt 1 of o2: `refused`, with `{ send: "not-sent", seen }`, by T7 | `receipt`. T4 does not apply: `receipt.token` does not name m2. R is final, so nothing follows. | None | Nothing | The branch |
| 5 | The outcomes of v2, to `confirmed` or to its third attempt | `revoke` | None | Its further attempts | The branch |

At entry 3 revision 27 gave `receipt.token`, on a final item. From
revision 28 the entry is written, the token is recorded in it, and its
revocation is opened in the same entry. The `read` that entry 1 added is
not drawn, and stays with the branch.

*The second order: the new mint, and then the old read.*

| # | The entry | The rule, and its arm | The slot or state that changes | It opens | The holder that pays |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The act `resend-receipt`, for R | As above | As above | o2, its attempt 1 and m2 | As above |
| 2 | The outcome of m2, `confirmed` | `mint`, T1: R is `owed`, and attempt 1 of o2 has no outcome | `receipt.token` is m2 | Nothing | The branch |
| 3 | The outcome of rd1, `confirmed`, with `seen` the commit of R | `deciding-read`; T6 | R is `written`. `receipt.token` is not touched, and still names m2. | Nothing. It opens no revocation of m2's token. | P |
| 4 | The first outcome of attempt 1 of o2. Where the request was sent before entry 3: its own answer, or `unknown`. Where it was not: `refused`, `not-sent`, by T7. | `receipt`, T4: the slot names this attempt's own mint, and R was final before the entry | None on R | v2 for m2's token, and its attempt 1 | The branch: this entry is of o2, which the branch holds |
| 5 | The outcomes of v2 | `revoke` | None | Its further attempts | The branch |

At entry 4 revision 27 emptied `receipt.token`, on a final item: the
same fault, in the row of the write. In both orders v2 is opened by an
entry of an operation that the branch holds, it is `for` the branch, and
the branch reserved it in entry 1. P pays for rd1 alone. The three
attempts of o1 stay `unknown`.

*The control: a mint that answers after its own attempt's outcome.* This
was safe in revision 27, and it is unchanged.

| # | The entry | The rule, and its arm | The slot or state that changes | It opens | The holder that pays |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | An entry opens attempt n of a write, with its mint m | The ledger, and the rule of the write | None | The attempt and m | The holder of the write |
| 2 | The answer of m is lost, so the gateway sends nothing (T7). The outcome of attempt n: `refused`, `not-sent`. | The rule of the write. T4 does not apply: the slot does not name m. | As the rule's table has it for `seen` | The next attempt with its mint, where T8 allows one | The same holder |
| 3 | The late answer of m: `confirmed` | `mint`, T2: its attempt has an outcome | None | The revocation of m's token | The same holder |

**The family of this fault, swept.** The verdict asks for every rule of
an outcome and every clause of a result in this section and in sections
12.1.1 and 12.1.2: each slot that it may set, and whether the item can
already be final, or the slot fixed, or the write unable to act, when
the outcome or the result arrives late. Late means after an abort, a
`withdraw`, a `compromised` notice, a read that decides, an
`adopt-head`, a `resend` or a retried attempt. Each row was read against
the rows of this note that it names. "Safe" means that the row already
yields nothing in that case, or that the case cannot arise, with the
reason.

| # | The rule or the clause | What it may set | Can it arrive late on a final item, a fixed slot or a closed target? | In revision 27 | From revision 28 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

The sweep has 30 rows. Six need a repair: rows 2, 3, 4, 6, 14 and 16.
Row 8 is stated and was not shown to be reachable. Rows 2 to 4, 6, 8 and
14 are repaired by the rules T1 to T8. Row 16 is repaired next. Each has
a case below and a row in section 14.

*Row 3, a push, as entries.* P is `unresolved`. The three attempts of
its push have `unknown` outcomes, and the read of that push is pending.
An admin signs `resend`, which opens a push with 1 attempt and its mint
m2, both `for` P. The old read shows the integration commit: P is
`published`, and by T6 `publication.token` is not touched. Where m2
confirms after that, T2 opens its revocation, `for` P, and sets nothing.
Where m2 confirmed before, T1 set `publication.token`, and the first
outcome of the new attempt opens the revocation by T4 and sets nothing
on P. P pays in both orders: the `resend` added the mint and the
revocation to P.

*Row 4, a first head.* The branch is `empty`, and attempt n of its first
head is open with its mint. An admin's `adopt-head` and its read make
the branch `ready`. A mint that confirms after that takes T2. One that
confirmed before took T1, and the attempt's first outcome opens the
revocation by T4 and empties `branch.token`: the branch is never final.
The branch pays in both orders.

*Row 16, the rule `adopt-read`, repaired.* The act `adopt-head` has two
guards: no publication is `reserved`, `publishing` or `unresolved`, and
`branch.slot` is unset. The rule reads both again at its outcome. Where
they hold and `seen` is the act's commit, it yields as before:
`branch.head`, `ready`, and the next `judge`. Where one does not hold,
it yields nothing. Its evidence `{ seen }` is in its outcome entry, and
the admin signs `adopt-head` again when the slot is free. It has no
token and opens no cleanup. Its one operation is `for` the branch, from
the `adds` of its act.

kind of sections 12.1.1, 12.1.2 and 12.1.5.

**The changed set, kept under a digest. Decided in the second commit of
revision 27.** Revision 25 put the changed set inside the evidence of
`judge`, as the member `changes`, and bounded it at 256 KiB as an
example. That is the size of a whole entry, so the outcome's entry could
not fit by its declared types (section 3.3). The adopted contract lets
an outcome keep evidence under a digest, apart from its entry, in a
domain that the effect's owner declares (its section 17.1, the table of
bytes). This definition declares one.

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| The domain | `artroom-changed-set-1`. A value in it is the canonical JSON of one `Changes` record of section 12.1.4a: `paths`, `links` and `unreadable`. |
| The bound on one value | 262,144 bytes, with at most 2,048 paths and 256 link rows, as revision 25 has them. Each number is an example for the proof plan. |
| The member of the evidence | `changes: Digest \| { over: "paths" \| "links" \| "bytes" } \| null`. The digest is of that value, in that domain. The other members of `JudgeEvidence` are as revision 25 has them. |
| Who gives the bytes | The runtime that read the host, beside the outcome. Bytes that do not hash to the digest, or that pass the bound, make the outcome `bad-input`. A changed set past a bound is given as `over`, as before, and the publication ends `not-reserved`, `evidence-too-large`. |
| What the rule reads | The value, as a retained input of its entry |
| What reserves it | The operation `judge`, for each of its 2 outcome entries, by the contract's row 5: what its owner declares. Under `holds` it is in `one(judge)`. |
| What a reader and a replay get | The entry, with the digest, and the bytes by a read of one retained value. Without the bytes a replay is `incomplete`. |

by a script. By the script of revision 28 it is 2,488 bytes, and 2,518
with its basis (section 3.3). The I3 source's type holds the changed set
inside the evidence, and no port gives one yet. It must change before
one does.

**A draw past a count: the read that shows it, and the way out.** The
contract makes it a fault of a rule to draw past a count that a holder
states (its section 17.2a, "Past a count"), and the planner confirmed it
(the act `1f8aba72`): the input is not judged, nothing is written, an
outcome stays offered, and no end state is forced. No entry holds the
fault. This note owes the read that shows it, and the act that ends it.

```ts
/** Beside an item of a platform scope, in the answer to a read of that item. The runtime derives it. It is in no entry. */
interface Stopped {
  holds: Held;                    // what the item still holds: the counts of the folded state
  waiting: readonly {             // each input that is offered for an operation or a request of this holder, and that a fault stops
    operation: OperationId | null;   // the operation whose outcome is offered; null for a result or a diagnosis
    kind: string | null;             // its kind
    rule: string;                    // the name of the rule that had the fault
    since: Timestamp;                // the observer's clock when the input was first offered
  }[];                            // at most 16, the oldest first
}
```

- *Who may read it.* Whoever may read the item: a read session of the
  repository (section 3.9). It is served with the read of a
  `publication`, of a `receipt` and of the `branch`.
- *What a replay can check of it.* `holds`, which it derives from the
  history. Not `waiting`: a fault writes nothing, so that an input is
  offered is the runtime's word. It is no entry, no update and no
  result, and nothing is judged on it.
- *What a member sees at the lane* is the lane forms' to state. No
  update can carry the fault, because no entry is written. So it reaches
  a lane by no message, and a page that shows it must read it from the
  destination.
- *The way out, by an act.* An admin signs `add-room` on the
  publication, or `add-branch-room` on the branch. The act is new work.
  It is admitted with room for what it adds, and it raises the counts.
  The outcome is offered again and is then judged.
- *The way out, by a definition.* A version whose rules stay inside the
  counts, or whose data states higher ones. How a scope comes under a
  later version is not designed here.
- *A final publication has no act.* The contract refuses an act with
  `adds` on a final holder, `final`. So when the fault is in an
  operation that is `for` a `published` publication, which is one of its
  receipt's, no act raises its counts. The way out is a definition, or a
  `resend-receipt` for the receipt, which opens a new operation `for`
  the branch and leaves the stopped outcome offered.
- *What the counts are for.* Section 5.8 derives each from the rules, so
  that no draw passes one in a definition whose rules are as this note
  states them. The read and the two acts are for a rule that is wrong.

**The index on `publication.operation`, and the selector
`publication-of`. Stated in revision 28**, in the form of the contract's
revision 23 at `3b3e394fc`, which is filed, in review and not adopted
(its section 17.2a, "An index that an item type declares" and "The
source of `bound.of`"; its rows D23-1 and D23-2; the planner's act
`2d3fa911`, answer 3: a binding selector must use an index). That
revision says that this note owes two rows, and these are the two. They
take effect only when a contract revision that carries `indexes`,
`index` and `key` is adopted, and this revision with it. Until then row
34 of section 12.1.8 stands as revision 26 has it.

| Where | What is stated |
|---|---|
| The item type `publication` | `indexes: ["operation"]`. The slot `operation` is a reference of the type `{ type: "fact", kind: ["merge"], under: "change" }`, fixed and required. A `fact` is one of the seven types that an index may be on, and this is 1 of the 4 that a type may state. |
| The mark `publication-of`, at place 2 of the handler `withdraw` | `{ code: "publication-of", row: "P15", item: "publication", index: "operation", key: "operation" }`. It is a binding selector. |
| Its key | The field `operation` of `withdraw`. It is required, and its type is `{ type: "fact", kind: ["merge"], under: "change" }`: the type of the slot, member for member. The contract's revision 23 did not find the field's type in the rows that it read. It is stated here. |

The handler `reserve` refuses a second publication for one operation, by its guard over all seven states, and the rule `open-withdrawn` opens one only where none is bound. So the contract's bound of 8 is not reached, and its fault for more than 8 cannot arise by these rows. |

#### 12.1.6 The inbox

One for each member. It holds that member's attention items, inside
the application (R2 section 10.6). No send leaves it.

| Item type | `many`, `max` | States (final in bold), `initial` | Parties | References | Values |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `inbox` | false, 1 | open; `open` | `owner` (fixed, required) | `membership` `{ type: "scope", kind: "membership" }` (fixed, required) | None |
| `notice` | true, 1000 | unread, read, **dismissed**; `unread` | None | None | `reason` `{ type: "text", max: 128 }` (fixed, required)<br>`at` `{ type: "time" }` (fixed, required)<br>`item` `{ type: "int", min: 0, max: 1000000000 }` (fixed)<br>`source` `{ type: "record", of: { scope: { type: "text", max: 64, required: true }, incarnation: { type: "text", max: 32, required: true }, seq: { type: "int", min: 0, max: 1000000000, required: true }, hash: { type: "digest", required: true } } }` (fixed, required) |

| Entry | Input, and who may | Opens or changes | Guards | Sends |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `establish` | Genesis, by membership's `create`. | Opens `inbox`, with its owner. | None. | None. |
| `notify`, twice: from `{ kind: "lane" }` and from `{ kind: "task" }` | A delivery of an advisory. `opens: "notice"`. | Opens `notice`, `unread`. `reason` and `item` from the message. `source` is the envelope's source fact (Code P22: no `fact` type names an entry of any definition). Corrected in revision 20: the data writes no effect on `source`. An effect mark stands there, and its rule gives one `value` effect: the record of the fact's scope ID, incarnation, position and hash. `at` is the commit time. | None. | None: a handler of class `advisory` sends nothing. |
| `mark-read` | An act. Grant `inbox.own`. | `{ state: "read" }` | `{ signer: ["owner"], of: "also.inbox" }`; `{ state: ["unread"] }` | None. |
| `dismiss` | An act. Grant `inbox.own`. | `{ state: "dismissed" }` | `{ signer: ["owner"], of: "also.inbox" }`; `{ state: ["unread", "read"] }` | None. |

- **How a notice finds its inbox.** A `notify` names members, and a
  member's inbox is a scope whose ID no sender can derive, because
  its seed's cause is the act that enrolled the member. So an
  attention send is addressed to the member. At dispatch, transport
  reads that member's `inbox` reference from the membership scope
  that the member reference names. The reference is set once and
  never changes. That read is bookkeeping of dispatch, as sending
  again is, and no judgment reads it. A notice to a member whose
  inbox is not confirmed yet is held and sent later. Code P23.
- **A notice grants nothing.** Opening one reads the item that it
  names with the member's present authority (R2 section 10.6).
- **A full inbox.** `max` bounds the notices that are not dismissed.
  A notice past it is not recorded. What the page then says is R2's,
  and the number is R4's.
- **A notice's `source` is a record, and its type is data. Stated in
  revision 20** (the I3 deltas note, entry E10; the contract's
  section 15.6n left it to this note). The slot is the record of four
  values that the item table gives. It is not a fact reference, which
  has three members, and it is not typed by code: the commit checks a
  value for it as it checks any record. What is code is the effect
  that sets it, because no operand builds a record from the parts of
  a reference. The four values are those of the delivery's `from`.
  Corrected in revision 22 (the I3 delta EJ9): the record has four
  members and no kind. Revision 20's sentence meant that the entry's
  own input holds `from` whole, and that `from` holds the kind of the
  sending scope. It read as if the record held it. A reader who
  needs the kind reads the entry that opened the notice. A data
  effect `{ value: { slot: "source", from: {
  source: "ref" } } }` validates, and the commit refuses its value.
  So no source writes that effect.
- **Nothing outside the application.** Section 9 stays a contract
  for a later version. This definition holds no subscription and
  sends nothing.
- No timed rule exists, and no entry starts a duty.

| Case | Input | What is written, or answered |
|---|---|---|
| a | A `notify` from a lane, for this member | One entry: a notice, `unread`, with the source fact. |
| b | The same advisory delivered again | Nothing. The envelope was recorded, and transport acknowledges it. |
| c | Another member signs `mark-read` on a notice here | Refused `guard-failed`: the signer is not the owner. |

#### 12.1.7 The task

One for each hosted task: one worker, one lane, one conversation. It
holds controls, the registration of the one instance that may save,
the checkpoints' receipts, the releases of exports and the private
streams. From revision 16 it also holds the record of a failed
recovery, with the decision on it. It does not hold the transcript, command output, files or
journals: those are private resources beside it (section 4.1). The
recovery design proposed where each of its records lives (its section
12.1), and this definition takes that proposal with the changes that
section 5.9 lists.

**The worker.** A task has a `worker` and a `controller`. For a
hosted agent the worker is the agent member, whose key the task
scope's signer holds, and the controller is the person fixed when the
agent was created. For a hold that a person holds, the worker and the
controller are that person, and the task has no signer: every act
below that the worker signs is signed by a device key of that person
(G9). Two actions are used. `task.control` is the controller's or an
admin's (section 4.1). `task.operate` is the worker's: new in
revision 14, in the table of section 3.2.

| Item type | `many`, `max` | States (final in bold), `initial` | Parties | References | Values |

- **The pointer** is `task.current`. **The registration** is the
  `registration` item that `task.registration` names. Both are local
  state that only a sealed entry changes, which is what the recovery
  design asks (its section 12.1).
- **A checkpoint item is the receipt.** It holds the checkpoint's ID,
  which is the digest of the manifest's head in the byte domain
  `artroom-checkpoint-1`, and the identity of section 5.1. The
  manifest, the payload and both journals stay private, and no
  replay of this scope reads them.
- **A cut item is the frozen cut.** It holds the journal cut and the
  attempt set of one save, and it is written before the manifest's
  head is built.
- **"Job" has two meanings.** In section 3.11 a job is a check job,
  an item of a change lane. In this definition `job` is the recovery
  design's word: one dispatch of work to an instance.
- **Three slots are new in revision 15** (review `14ad7c42`). A
  control has the final state `void`: it was never applied, because
  a `cancel` was applied first. A registration counts its restores
  in `restores`. A stream holds the `key` that opened it. The rows
  and the two blocks under the tables say how each is used.
- **One item type is new in revision 16** (review `60c940f3`): the
  `failure`. It is the record of one failed recovery, and `by` is the
  person who decided it. The final state `void` of a control now
  means that a stop was applied first: a `cancel` for any kind, or a
  `pause` for a `start` or a `resume`. No slot of another item type
  is added. The task definition has nine item types.
- **A failure is one at a time.** After every entry at most one
  `failure` is not final. An outcome opens one only when none is
  `undecided`, and it makes a `repair` one `lapsed` in the same
  entry. The `max` of 2 leaves room for that one entry, whatever the
  order of its two effects. So an outcome entry, which cannot be
  refused, never passes the `max`.

**Entries.** Every entry is one of four kinds, and the kind says
whose authority it rests on.

Each of the six named fields equals the failure's slot of that name. No guard reads the task's state, the queued controls or the worker's grant. | None. It opens no operation and sends nothing. |
| `open-read`, `continue-read`, `close-read` | Acts. A device key of the controller or of an admin. Grant `task.read-private`, on an observation within ten seconds (W3). | `open-read` opens `stream`: `reader` is the signer, `key` is the signing key (Code P14), `ends` is the commit time plus 70 seconds, and `checked` is the commit time. `continue-read` sets both times again. `close-read` sets `closed`, `reader`. | `continue-read`: `{ state: ["open"] }`; from revision 15, the signing key is the stream's `key` (Code P14); `{ before: { slot: "ends" } }`; `{ after: { slot: "checked" } }`, so a clock that has not moved passes no check. `close-read`: `{ state: ["open"] }`; `{ signer: ["reader"] }`. | None. |
| `start-export` | An act. A device key of the controller of the former holder, or of an admin. Grant `work.export` (W3). It presents the lane's `authorize-export` entry X. | Opens `pin`, `export-source`, on the checkpoint named, and empties that checkpoint's `expires`. | X is an `authorize-export` entry of `task.lane` that names this checkpoint's hold. | Code P16: opens the copy to the transfer stage. Its `confirmed` outcome opens `release`, `intent`, with X, the digest, the receiving hold and its instance. |
| `ask-license` | An act. The same signer and grant (W3). | `k` rises by 1 (Code P17). `licenseEnds` is the commit time plus 10 seconds (W5). | `{ state: ["intent"] }`; `k` is under 3; no dispatch of this release is unanswered. | `{ tell: { to: { slot: "lane" }, message: "export-license", fields: { export: { slot: "export" }, checkpoint: { slot: "digest" }, hold: { slot: "hold" }, instance: { slot: "instance" }, k: { slot: "k" } }, result: { applied: [ ... ], refused: [{ value: { slot: "refusedBy", from: { result: "reason" } } }] } } }`. The `applied` clause is the dispatch guard of section 4.2: `{ before: { slot: "licenseEnds" } }`, the license entry kept as `license`, and the authorizer's standing on an observation read for that commit (Code P19). When it holds: `{ state: "dispatched" }`, and it opens the release request as an operation with 1 attempt. |
| An outcome of a release request | An outcome entry. Basis `own-answer`: the storage's own answer. | `confirmed`: `{ state: "confirmed" }`, and the source pin is `released`. This entry is F. `refused`, nothing was made readable: back to `intent`. No answer: `{ state: "unknown" }`. | Section 4.2, "The states of the release". | On `confirmed`: `{ tell: { to: { slot: "lane" }, message: "export-settled", fields: { export: { slot: "export" }, final: { const: "confirmed" } }, result: {} } }`, and it opens the staged copy's deletion, at most 3 attempts. |
| `withhold` | An act. A device key of a holder of `work.export` for this task (W1). | `{ state: "withheld" }`, and the source pin is `released`. This entry is F. | `{ state: ["intent"] }`; no dispatch of this release is unanswered, and none is confirmed. | `export-settled`, with `final` `withheld`, and the staged copy's deletion. |
| `extend-retention` | An act. Grant `task.control` (W2). | Sets `expires` on a checkpoint to a later time. | `{ state: ["current", "kept"] }`; `{ set: "expires" }` | None. |
| `retry` | An act. Grant `ledger.retry`, or the worker's `task.operate` for a deletion. | None. | The operation's stated attempts are used, and it is not settled. It is a deletion, a host's destruction, or a push. From revision 19, one case more: the operation is a deletion whose outcome is `confirmed`, and the request carries the runtime's report that a key of that deletion is present again. The entry holds that report's digest. It is a trusted claim. | Code P16: opens one new operation of that kind, with 1 attempt (G3). |

| Timed rule | `on` | `states` | `deadline` | Effects |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `checkpoint-expiry` | `checkpoint` | `["current", "kept"]` | `expires` | `{ state: "expired" }` |
| `stream-end` | `stream` | `["open"]` | `ends` | `{ state: "closed" }`<br>`{ value: { slot: "reason", from: { const: "end-time" } } }` |

Revision 15 adds no timed rule. A queued stop is ended by its own
outcome. A restore is ended by its outcome, by the next `register`
or by `fence`. A stream of a revoked key is ended by `stream-end`.
Revision 16 adds none either. No time decides a failed recovery: an
`undecided` failure waits for a person.

**A restore before readiness. New in revision 15** (review
`14ad7c42`). Revision 14 asked for a `ready` registration before
every `intend`, and only a restore's outcome makes a registration
`ready`. So a fresh task, and a task whose restore failed, could
never open a restore. The rule is now this.

- *Which act opens a restore, and who signs it.* `intend` for a
  restore, signed by the worker's key, with `task.operate` on an
  observation within sixty seconds (W2). For an agent the observation
  carries `controllerActive`. No controller, no admin and no runtime
  opens a restore. A worker whose grant is gone opens none. From
  revision 16 the worker opens none while a failed recovery is
  `undecided`: "A failed recovery, and the person's decision",
  below.
- *What it is bound to.* The act names a hold, an epoch and an
  instance. They must equal those of the registration that
  `task.registration` names. `register` read them from the lane's own
  entry for the step `instance`, which the lane wrote on the holder's
  grant, observed within ten seconds, while the hold was held
  (section 5.7). So a restore is admitted only into the instance that
  the lane made current for that hold, at that epoch.
- *How many, and what bounds them.* Each restore is one operation
  with 1 attempt. One registration admits at most 3, and `restores`
  counts them. A replacement restore is a new operation and not a
  later attempt, so no `authorize-attempt` is used for it. After the
  third, or after a restore whose outcome is `unknown`, a further
  restore needs a new instance: the lane's step and a new `register`
  (section 5.9, steps 1 and 2). The number of registrations is
  bounded by the item type's `max`, which is R4's number. Changed in
  revision 16: the bound of 3 is an upper limit and no permission.
  After a failure for a fault of the checkpoint, a replacement also
  needs a person's decision, under this registration or under a new
  one.
- *What a restore restores.* The checkpoint that `task.current` names
  when the `intend` is admitted. A fresh task has none, and its first
  restore starts the environment from the hold's fork alone. What the
  environment then holds is the recovery design's subject.
- *The order that a replay follows.* `register`; `intend` for the
  restore; the restore's outcome; `ready`. Each is one sealed entry,
  and each guard reads only the items of this scope: the task's
  state, the queued controls, and the state and `restores` of the
  registration. From revision 16 the guard of a restore also reads
  the `failure` items.
- *What stays behind `ready`.* Every edit, command, commit
  preparation, dissociation and push, and every save. A restore
  opens no save and never moves the pointer.

| The registration that `task.registration` names | `register`, for a new instance | `intend` for a restore | Any other `intend`; the commit of a save |
|---|---|---|---|
| None yet: a fresh task | Admitted. It opens the first registration, `starting`, with `restores` 0. | Refused `guard-failed`: there is no registration to bind to. | Refused. |
| `starting`, with `restores` 0 | Admitted. This registration becomes `stale`. | Admitted: the first restore of this instance. `restores` is 1. From revision 16: refused `recovery-undecided` while a `failure` is `undecided`. | Refused. |
| `starting`, with `restores` 1 to 3: a restore is in flight, or its outcome is `unknown` | Admitted, as above. | Refused. A restore in flight has its own outcome. An `unknown` one is not replaced under this registration. | Refused. |
| `restore-failed`, with `restores` under 3 | Admitted, as above. | Changed in revision 16. Refused `recovery-undecided` while a `failure` is `undecided`. Admitted otherwise: a replacement. The registration is `starting` again, `restores` rises by 1, and a `failure` that is `repair` becomes `retried`. | Refused. |
| `restore-failed`, with `restores` 3 | Admitted, as above. | Refused. A new instance is needed, and it does not replace a decision. | Refused. |
| `ready` | Admitted, as above. | Refused. | Admitted, under the guards of its row. |
| `fenced` | Admitted, as above. | Refused. | Refused. |

Each `intend` in this table also needs the task to be `running`, no
`pause` or `cancel` to be `queued`, and the worker's grant.

**A failed recovery, and the person's decision. New in revision 16**
(review `60c940f3`). Under revision 15 a registration that was
`restore-failed` admitted the worker's next restore while `restores`
was under 3. Nothing recorded that a person had chosen to try again.
So after a first restore reported `checkpoint-corrupt`, an agent with
its own grant could sign a second at once. The adopted recovery
design keeps such a failure closed until a person's recorded decision
(its section 8.2). Section 5.9, "A recovery that failed", gives the
rule. These are its parts in this definition.

- *The record of the failure* is the `failure` item. A restore's
  `refused` outcome opens it, for the five reasons of the item's
  `reason`. Its fixed slots are the registration, the hold, the
  epoch, the instance, the restore's operation, the reason and the
  checkpoint. Nobody signs it: it rests on the restore's `intend`,
  as every outcome rests on its intent.
- *The record of the decision* is the entry of `decide-recovery`. It
  is signed by a device key of the controller or of an admin, with
  `task.control` (W2). It names the failure and repeats those six
  values, and each must equal the failure's. It sets the failure
  `repair` or `abandoned`, and `by`. The entry is kept with its
  signer, its observation and its fields, as every act is. The
  worker's grant `task.operate` does not admit it, and the role
  `agent` holds no `task.control` (section 3.2). For a hold that a
  person holds, that person is the worker and the controller, and
  signs both acts: the decision is still a person's.
- *What reads it.* The guard of `intend` for a restore: no `failure`
  is `undecided`. And its effect: a `failure` that is `repair`
  becomes `retried`. So one decision admits one replacement, for the
  failure that it names. After the replacement is opened, that
  decision admits nothing more. A second failure is a new item, and
  needs a new decision.
- *Abandonment has its own end.* The failure is `abandoned`, the
  pointer is empty, the abandoned checkpoint is `kept`, and the
  registration is `fenced`. The task keeps its state. The worker then
  takes the lane's step, `register` and a first restore, which starts
  from the hold's fork alone. The first save of the new chain has no
  prior. No checkpoint, pin, cut or operation of the abandoned chain
  is erased or settled.
- *Which failures need it.* The five reasons, and no other. A
  `refused` outcome with another reason opens no failure. A restore
  whose outcome is `unknown` opens none either, and needs a new
  instance. A first restore needs none.
- *Capacity.* The failure's item and the entry of its decision are
  reserved with the restore (section 5.8). So the decision is
  admitted at a scope with no free room. It is no control, so the
  bound on queued controls does not count it.

| The task's `failure` | `intend` for a restore, under any registration | `decide-recovery` |
|---|---|---|
| None, or every one is final: `retried`, `abandoned` or `lapsed` | As the table above. No decision is needed, and none is read. | Refused `guard-failed`: no failure is `undecided`. |
| `undecided` | Refused `recovery-undecided`. | Admitted, when it names the failure and its six values exactly. `repair`: the failure is `repair`. `abandon`: the failure is `abandoned`, the pointer is empty, and the registration is `fenced`. |
| `repair` | As the table above. When it is admitted, the failure is `retried`. | Refused `guard-failed`: this failure is decided. |
| `abandoned`, with the pointer empty | As the table above, after a new `register`: the restore starts from the hold's fork alone. | Refused `guard-failed`. |

**What ends a queued control. New in revision 15** (review
`14ad7c42`). An active admin could queue a `pause` or a `cancel`, and
only the worker's signed `apply` applied it. After the worker's key
was revoked, or its controller's standing was lost, no `apply` could
be signed. So a valid `cancel` could stay `queued` for ever, with the
task `running`. The rule is now this.

- *A stop is applied by its own outcome.* The entry of a `pause` or a
  `cancel` opens one operation of the task scope, the stop, with 1
  attempt, and reserves its outcome entry (section 5.8). The stop is
  addressed to the task scope's own supervisor, which is platform
  code of the scope and holds no key. Its outcome entry applies that
  one control. The task scope writes it as its next entry. It waits
  for no tool to finish, for no act of the worker, for no instance
  and for no observation.
- *New tools stop at the control's own entry.* From that entry on no
  `intend` is admitted, because a stop is `queued`. After the outcome
  none is admitted, because the task is not `running`. That is "the
  next tool boundary" of section 4.1. A tool that was already
  dispatched finishes, or is reconciled under its own identity, as
  section 4.3 says.
- *Why an outcome, and not a second act by an admin.* Two forms were
  open: an outcome that is bound to the control, or a narrow act by
  which an admin completes a control. The outcome is the simpler. An
  act needs a person to sign again, so an admitted control would
  still have no certain end. Its guard would also have to judge that
  the worker can no longer sign, which is an observation of another
  member's key (section 12.1.8, P19). An outcome needs neither. A
  replay reads it as it reads the outcome of a save: the entry names
  the control, the guard is that the control is `queued`, and the
  effects are fixed by the control's kind. Section 5.8 already
  reserved one entry for it, and section 4.1 already called it an
  outcome.
- *It revives nothing.* The outcome moves the task only toward a
  stop: `paused`, `cancelling` or `ended`. It opens no operation and
  sends nothing. It gives the worker no grant, and no `intend` is
  admitted by it. It applies no control of another kind.
- *A control of another kind* is an instruction to a worker: `start`,
  `steer`, `answer`, `resume`, `authorize-attempt` and
  `set-read-only`. It is applied by the worker's signed `apply`, as
  in revision 14. When the worker cannot sign, it waits and gives
  nothing, because no tool starts without an `intend`. It ends
  `void` in the outcome of the next `cancel`. Corrected in revision
  16: revision 15 said here that an admin can always sign that
  `cancel`. That was not so when 64 such controls were `queued`,
  because the `cancel` would have been the 65th item of its type.
  "Room for a stop", below, makes it so.
- *A stop ends an earlier order to run. New in revision 16.* A
  `start` or a `resume` that is still `queued` when a `pause` is
  applied becomes `void` in that outcome. So does every queued
  control when a `cancel` is applied. A `start` or a `resume` is not
  admitted while a stop is `queued`, so each one that a stop makes
  `void` was signed before that stop. A `steer`, an `answer`, an
  `authorize-attempt` and a `set-read-only` stay `queued` through a
  `pause`: none of them makes a task run. After a `pause` the task
  runs again only by a `resume` that is signed after it. Revision 15
  left the earlier `resume` `queued`, and the worker could apply it
  after the later `pause`.
- *The task's end.* A task that is `cancelling` becomes `ended` in
  the outcome entry that leaves none of its operations unsettled. An
  effect that stays `unknown` keeps it `cancelling`, which is what
  the page shows (section 4.3). No control is admitted in either
  state.

| Case | A queued `pause` or `cancel` is ended by | A queued control of another kind is ended by |
|---|---|---|
| The worker is present, with a `ready` instance | Its own outcome. A save of the instance is opened by the control's entry. | The worker's `apply`. From revision 16 a `start` or a `resume` is `void` in the outcome of a later `pause`. |
| The worker's key is revoked: an agent's key, or the last key of a person who is the worker | Its own outcome. No act of the worker is used. | No `apply` can be signed. It waits, and it is `void` in the outcome of a `cancel`. |
| The controller's standing is lost, so the agent's observation shows `controllerActive` false | Its own outcome. An admin can still sign the stop. The controller cannot: it has no active key. | The same. If a restored controller key signs `resume`, the worker can sign `apply` again, for that control and for the ones that waited. |
| The instance is `fenced` | Its own outcome. No save is opened, because no registration is `ready`. | The worker's `apply`, which reads no registration. |
| A restore is pending: no registration, or one that is `starting` or `restore-failed` | Its own outcome. No save is opened. A restore in flight keeps its own outcome. After a `pause`, a replacement restore waits for a `resume`. | The worker's `apply`, which reads no registration. |
| New in revision 16. 62 controls of the six other kinds are `queued`, and no worker can sign | Its own outcome. The stop is admitted as the 63rd or 64th item that is not final. | No further one is admitted: `controls-full`. Those that wait are `void` in the outcome of a `cancel`, and the `start` and `resume` among them in the outcome of a `pause`. |

So every admitted control has an end. A stop has one that no person
and no key can withhold. A control of another kind has the worker's
`apply`, or the next `cancel`. Corrected in revision 16: that last
clause holds only if the next `cancel` is admitted. Revision 15 did
not show that. The next block does.

**Room for a stop. New in revision 16** (review `60c940f3`). The
`control` type holds at most 64 items that are not final, and an
opening above that is refused `type-full` (R1 section 6.3). Under
revision 15 all 64 could be controls that only the worker applies.
With the worker's key revoked nothing applied them, an admin's
`cancel` was refused as the 65th, and only a `cancel` could make them
`void`. The rule is now this.

- *Two places are kept for stops.* A control of the six other kinds
  is admitted only while fewer than 62 of those kinds are `queued`.
  The refusal is `controls-full`. The act writes no entry, and the
  signer may send it again when the worker has applied some.
- *One stop of each kind at a time.* A `pause` is admitted only
  while no `pause` is `queued`, and a `cancel` only while no `cancel`
  is `queued`. The refusal is `stop-pending`: a stop of that kind is
  already admitted, and its outcome is reserved. The same signed
  bytes again are a repeat, and they are answered with the first
  entry (section 4.1). A `cancel` is admitted while a `pause` is
  `queued`, and a `pause` while a `cancel` is.
- *The count.* At every entry the `queued` controls are at most 62
  of the six other kinds, at most 1 `pause` and at most 1 `cancel`.
  That is at most 64, which is the type's `max`. So the type is never
  full for a stop, and `type-full` is never the answer to one.
- *The entries.* The task reserved the entry, the item, the outcome
  and the save of one `cancel` at its genesis, and of one `pause` at
  the `apply` that made it run (section 5.8). So a `cancel`, and a
  `pause` of a task that runs, are not refused `scope-full` either.
- *Why this form.* Three forms were open. A stop could be an item of
  a type of its own. Then every guard that reads a queued stop, the
  page's queue and the outcome would read two types, for no more
  than the count above gives. Or a stop could make the waiting
  controls `void` in its own entry. That does not help: the stop is
  still the 65th item when it opens. Keeping two places uses the one
  type, two `count` guards and one `none` guard, and no new state.
  A higher `max` alone would move the failure to that number.
- *Nothing is revived, erased or settled.* No worker's act is used.
  A control that becomes `void` stays an item in that final state,
  with its signer and its text. A `cancel` settles no outside effect:
  the task is `cancelling` until each effect has its own answer.

**That an authorized stop is always admitted, or is a repeat, with
one stated exception.** Take
any state of the task scope, and a `pause` or a `cancel` of kind K
that an active device key of the controller or of an admin signs,
with `task.control` on a fresh observation.

1. *The task is `cancelling` or `ended`.* A `cancel` was applied. The
   act is refused `guard-failed`, and nothing is left to stop: no
   `intend` is admitted in either state.
2. *A control of kind K is `queued`.* The act is refused
   `stop-pending`, or answered as a repeat. The one that is `queued`
   has a reserved outcome, which the scope writes with no key. So the
   stop that the signer asked for takes place.
3. *Otherwise.* The `queued` controls are at most 62 of the other
   six kinds and at most 1 of the other stop: at most 63. The new
   control is at most the 64th, and the type admits it. Its entries
   are reserved, apart from the one case below. No guard of the row reads the worker, a registration
   or a `failure`. So it is admitted, apart from that case.

One case stays new work: a `pause` while the task is `idle` or
`paused`, at a scope with no free room. It may be refused
`scope-full`. No tool can start in those states. The `apply` that
would make the task run needs the room of a `pause` and one entry
more, so it is refused wherever that `pause` is. A `cancel` is
admitted there.

Made exact in revision 17 (the approval `33787163`). Every sentence
of this note that says an authorized stop is always admitted is read
with this exception. Three things hold together, and none of them is
changed. A `cancel` holds its room from `establish`, in every state
before `cancelling`. A `pause` holds room only while the task is
`running` or `waiting`. And the `apply` that makes a task `running`
is admitted only with the room of the next `pause`. So the exception
never leaves a task that runs without a stop.

| The queue, before the act | A `steer`, or another of the six kinds | A `pause` | A `cancel` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fewer than 62 of the six kinds; no stop `queued` | Admitted. A `start` or a `resume` also needs its state. | Admitted. | Admitted. |
| 62 of the six kinds; no stop `queued` | Refused `controls-full`. | Admitted: the 63rd. | Admitted: the 63rd. |
| 62 of the six kinds; a `pause` `queued` | Refused `controls-full`. | Refused `stop-pending`, or a repeat. | Admitted: the 64th. |
| 62 of the six kinds; a `cancel` `queued` | Refused `controls-full`. | Admitted: the 64th. | Refused `stop-pending`, or a repeat. |
| 62 of the six kinds; a `pause` and a `cancel` `queued` | Refused `controls-full`. | Refused `stop-pending`, or a repeat. | Refused `stop-pending`, or a repeat. |
| Any; a stop `queued` | A `start` or a `resume` is refused `stop-pending`. Another kind is admitted under 62. | As its row above. | As its row above. |
| Any; the task is `cancelling` or `ended` | Refused `guard-failed`. | Refused `guard-failed`. | Refused `guard-failed`. |

**What a save and a restore reserve, and what a receipt is evidence
of. New in revision 17** (the contract's section 15.9, rows 6, 8 and
10, and its three readings; the recovery design's revision 4, section
12.1). The point "Reservations", below, gave the entries of a save
and of a restore in one sentence. This block gives each in the five
dimensions of the contract's section 17.1, and says what a
checkpoint's receipt shows. It decides this note's side only: the
records of the task definition, and their room. The runtime that
does the work is IA's. The stored bytes, and how they are checked,
are the recovery design's.

*A save.* It is opened by the entry that needs it: an `intend` for
an operation that changes the root, or the entry of a `pause` or a
`cancel` while a registration is `ready`. Its closure is at most 3
saves for one attempt set, because a `refused` commit in a surviving
instance opens one more.

| Dimension | One save | The closure: at most 3 saves | Reserved by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entries, for its two operations | 4. The first outcome and the late answer of the cut, and the same two of the commit (R1 section 17.2, row 5). | 12. | The entry that opens the first save. For a stop's save, the room of that stop (section 5.8). |
| Entries, for what a closed save deletes | 6. One deletion, with at most 3 attempts (G3). A save that commits may make its prior `expired`. A save that does not commit leaves stored bytes with no root. | 18. | The same entry. |
| Items | 1 `cut`, which the cut's outcome opens. 1 `checkpoint`, which a `confirmed` commit opens. | 3 `cut` and 1 `checkpoint`. Only one commit of a closure is `confirmed`. | The same entry. |
| Records | None. The task definition keeps its state in items. | None. | |
| Pending requests | None. A save sends no message. | None. | |
| Bytes | The bytes of those entries. No retained input: the manifest, the payload and both journals are private, and no entry names them under a digest. The cut's positions and its attempt set are values of the `cut` item, bounded by their declared types. The checkpoint's ID is one digest. | The bytes of 30 entries, each at most the bound on one entry. | The same entry. The number is R4's. |

- *The attempts of the set are not counted twice.* The `confirmed`
  outcome that a commit gives to an attempt of its cut is that
  attempt's own first outcome. The `intend` that opened the attempt
  reserved its entry (R1 section 17.2, row 5). Revisions 14 to 16
  said that a save reserves "one outcome for each attempt of its
  set, at most 8". Those are the same entries, and a save reserves
  none of them a second time. A runtime may hold more than this, and
  never less (the contract's decision D11-3).
- *An operation that may end `unknown`.* An `intend` for an
  operation whose class is not read-only also holds 1 `pin` item.
  Its `unknown` outcome opens that pin. Narrowed in revision 19: an
  operation that is confined to the root opens no pin, and its
  `intend` holds none. An `intend` that holds a pin also holds the
  7 entries of that pin's row in section 5.8.

*A restore.* It is opened by its `intend`, which is new work. A
registration reserves nothing for a restore that is not yet opened.
A replacement restore is a new `intend` and new work, also after
`repair`.

| Dimension | One restore | Reserved by |
|---|---|---|
| Entries | 9. The first outcome and the late answer of the restore: 2. The destruction of the old host, with at most 3 attempts (G3): 6. The entry of `decide-recovery`: 1. | The `intend` that opens it. |
| Items | 1 `failure`, which a `refused` outcome with one of the five reasons opens. | The same entry. |
| Records | None. | |
| Pending requests | None. | |
| Bytes | The bytes of those 9 entries. No retained input: a restore reads private storage, and no entry names what it read under a digest. | The same entry. |

- *A place in a type.* An item that an outcome entry opens needs a
  place under its type's `max`, as well as an item of the budget,
  because an outcome entry cannot be refused (R1 section 6.3). So
  the entry that reserves the item also holds the place: of `cut`,
  of `checkpoint`, of `pin` and of `failure`. An `intend` that
  cannot hold a place that it needs is refused `type-full`, and
  nothing is opened. A stop is never refused for a place. Made
  exact in revision 18 (review `545feb91`): its save is opened only
  with places for the save's whole remaining closure, which is 3 of
  `cut` and 1 of `checkpoint`, or when the stop's room already holds
  those places. One free place of each type is not enough: the
  table above reserves for the closure, and this sentence does not
  lower it. Otherwise the stop opens no save. The stop is applied by
  its own outcome either way. The `count` guards
  that keep those places are not written here. They are owed with
  the row P11 of section 12.1.8. Until they are written, no source
  may let an outcome entry open an item above a `max`. The approval
  `33787163` names this as owed, and it stays owed.
- *Counted, not measured.* 12 + 18 is 30, and 2 + 6 + 1 is 9. Each
  follows from a bound that this note already proposes. R4 owns
  every number.
- *Both counts are conditional. Stated in revision 18.* The 30 and
  the 9 are symbols for a sum, and not settled numbers. Each rests
  on a grouping that the recovery design has not confirmed: one
  deletion operation for each save or each root, and one destruction
  of an old host, each with the attempts that G3 states. That design
  counts them from its own storage and its own grouping of keys
  (point 3 of "Asked of the recovery design", below). Until it
  does, wherever this note says 30 or 9 it means "the sum above, at
  that grouping". A save's items compose with the `pin` of the
  operation that opened it, which that operation's own `intend`
  holds.
- *A stop that opens no save. Stated in revision 18.* The stop is
  applied, and the task is `paused`, `cancelling` or `ended` as its
  outcome says. Nothing else follows from it, and the page must show
  the difference between "stopped" and "stopped and saved".
  - The last good checkpoint stays as it is: `task.current` does not
    move, and no receipt is written.
  - Work that the instance holds and that no checkpoint covers is
    not saved by that stop. Each attempt that had exited keeps its
    record with no receipt, as "exited, not saved".
  - Each unknown duty keeps its own identity, its pin and its
    reservation. Custody of the unsaved work and of those duties
    stays where it was, under IA's runtime and the recovery design.
  - The stop proves no durable completion and no cleanup. It settles
    no outside effect, deletes nothing and releases no pin.
  - The recovery design's revision 5 is writing its side of this,
    under the request `d33a258e`. It is in progress, and it was not
    read. Stated in revision 24: that was so in revision 18. That
    design's revision 9 is adopted now (the opening, "The standing in
    force"), and it was not read for this point. What the instance
    may still do with unsaved work after
    such a stop is that design's and IA's to say.

*What a receipt is evidence of.* The first column is the recovery
design's record, in its revision 4. "Trust" is what a replay of the
task scope takes as the runtime's claim. A report labels each such
claim as trusted (R1 section 9.5).

| The recovery design's record | In the task scope | What a replay derives | What it takes on trust |
|---|---|---|---|
| The receipt of a checkpoint (its section 7.4) | The `checkpoint` item, which the `confirmed` outcome of a save's commit opens. The outcome's basis is `read`. Made exact in revision 19: every value that the head names was read back by its key and hashes to its digest, and the head was read back last and hashes to the ID. The basis names the evidence that the runtime had. It does not make the outcome derived. Its evidence is the checkpoint's ID, and nothing private. | The guards over this scope's own items. The registration's hold, epoch and instance equal the cut's. It is `ready`, or, from revision 20, it is `fenced` and the `save` that opened the save states `fenced: true` ("A save of a fenced root"). `task.current` is the cut's `prior`. Each attempt of the cut names that instance and has no outcome. And that the pointer moved one step, from that prior. | That the stored bytes exist and hash to the ID. That the head holds the cut's journal positions. That the cut agreed with the private journals when it was written. That the supervisor's report of jobs is true. |
| The receipt of each attempt of the frozen set | That attempt's `confirmed` outcome entry. Its evidence names the entry of the commit. | That the attempt is in the cut of that commit. | That the root held what the attempt did. |
| The frozen cut (its section 7.3) | The `cut` item, which the outcome of the cut opens before the head is built. | The cut's values, written once. | That they agree with the journals. |
| The pointer, and the registration | `task.current`, and the `registration` item. | Every change, each by one sealed entry. | Nothing. |
| The receipt of a restore (its section 8.1, step 8) | The `confirmed` outcome of the restore. Its basis is `own-answer`: the runtime's report that its steps 5 to 7 passed. Its evidence names the checkpoint and the instance. It makes the registration `ready`. | The registration, the count `restores`, and the guards on a `failure`. | That every byte was checked against the manifest, and that Git was checked. |
| A recovery failure (its section 8.2) | A `refused` outcome with one of the five reasons, and the `failure` item. | The item, and the person's decision on it. | The reason. |
| An interrupted attempt | An outcome `unknown`, with the basis `none`, and for a class that is not read-only its `pin`. | The outcome and the pin. | Nothing about the effect: it is unknown. |
| An expiry, with its tombstone (its section 10) | The `checkpoint` item in the state `expired`: by the timed rule `checkpoint-expiry`, or by the commit that replaced it. | The state, and the entry that set it. | Nothing. No byte is shown deleted by it. A deletion has its own outcome. |

- *The contract's first reading: the journal comparison is outside
  the judgment.* Confirmed. The comparison with the private journals
  is made before an outcome is offered. The `cut` item carries the
  cut, and the commit's guards read that item. No entry of the task
  scope is derived from a private journal, and a replay reads none.
- *Its second reading: a receipt's time may be clamped.* No rule of
  the task definition reads the commit time of a save's outcome.
  A `checkpoint` item holds no time of its own. `expires` is a slot
  that another entry sets from its own commit time: the outcome of a
  `pause`, an `apply`, or `extend-retention`. The two acts are judged
  on the commit clock, as every act is, and are never clamped. The
  outcome of a `pause` judges no time, so it may be written clamped,
  and a clock that is behind never delays a stop. The deadline that
  it sets is then later than the clock's reading would give. That
  lengthens retention and extends no authority, which is the rule of
  section 3.12. The expiry itself is a timed entry, and is never
  clamped.
- *Its third reading* is the recovery design's to give: that it has
  read the four changes of the contract's revision 11. Revision 4
  did not read the contract's sections 17 to 17.3 again.

*Asked of the recovery design.* Each is asked. None is claimed as
agreed.

1. That it read section 12.1.7 as the task definition. Its revision
   4 reads this note at revision 13, and lists the definition as
   owed.
2. That the basis of a save's `confirmed` outcome is `read`, and of
   a restore's `own-answer` (its seam 3 of section 12.1).
3. That the keys of one root, or of one save that did not commit,
   are deleted by one operation of the task scope, with at most 3
   attempts and then a `retry`. Its section 10 retries with a
   backoff and states no number. If it needs more operations, the
   18 entries above become that number times 6 for each save.
4. Whether its pin for an open job is an item that an entry opens.
   The `pin` type has the reason `open-job`, and no row of this
   definition opens one. If a row does, that entry holds the pin's
   place.
5. That it take the first two readings above as stated.
6. Its assumption A12 is contradicted by document for the host of
   its stage one. For stage two, IA says what separates a command
   from the supervisor, before a report cites the cut as more than a
   trusted claim.

What revision 16 asked of it stays asked (section 5.9).

*Answered in its revision 5, which is proposed.* That design's
revision 5, at `c254e207`, answers each of the six (its section
12.9). It reads this section as the task definition. It agrees to
the two bases, with what each covers. It groups deletions as point
3 asks, and counts 30 and 9 from its own steps. It says that the pin
of an open job is no item. It takes the two readings. It names IA's
duty for the supervisor. This note records those answers and rests
nothing on them: that revision is under review. If its verdict
changes one, the point is read again here. Stated in revision 24:
"proposed" and "under review" were the standing in revision 19. That
design's revision 9 is adopted now (the opening, "The standing in
force"). It was not read, so these answers were not read again in
it. Its third reading, of
the contract's revision 11, is still not given.

**The recovery design's ten asks. Answered in revision 19.** Its
revision 5 asks ten things back, B1 to B10 (its section 12.9). Each
is a request of a proposed text. Each is answered against the
adopted revision 18. An answer changes a row of this definition, or
is kept as a choice with its owner.

| # | Asked | Answer | Rows changed, or the owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | That the places of a stop's save be held with the stop's room: from `establish` for a `cancel`, and from the `apply` for a `pause`. | Agreed, as a rule. The room of a stop holds the places of its save's closure with the items. Revision 18 let a stop open its save when the room "already holds those places", and did not say that it does. It does. So a stop on its standing room always opens its save. That design asks for one place in `cut` and one in `checkpoint`. This note holds 3 and 1, as revision 18 has it. A failed cut is final, so one place of `cut` may be enough. Lowering it is for the form to decide. | The point "A place in a type". The form of a held place: the row P11, under `cc570904`. |
| B2 | An entry that opens a save alone. | Agreed. The act `save`. "A path that saves and does nothing else", below. | A new row, `save`. Section 5.8, one row. |
| B3 | That a pause's "compute stops" not end the host while the task is stopped but unsaved, and which entry opens the destruction of a host that no restore replaces. | Agreed. No stop ends a host. A host ends by a save that was cut after the stop and committed, or by `end-host`. "A host that is kept", below. | Section 4.3, two rows. New rows `end-host` and `extend-host`. The value `hostEnds`. The row of a stop's outcome, and of a commit's outcome. |
| B4 | That a `refused` cut count as one of the 3 saves and open the next. | Agreed. | The row "An outcome of a save's cut". |
| B5 | That `unknown`, basis `none`, also be written for an attempt whose instance was `fenced`. | Agreed. It is written once no save of that instance is open, because a save that was opened before the `fence` still has its own outcome. | The row "The outcome of any other operation". |
| B6 | That an interrupted operation that is confined to the root open no `pin`. | Agreed, and narrowed. That an operation is confined to the root is a trusted claim about the runtime's own tool, as that design says. | The same row; the point "An operation that may end `unknown`". |
| B7 | That the receipt's row say that every value is read back, and not the head alone. | Agreed. | The first row of the table of what a receipt is evidence of. |

| B9 | The reasons of a `refused` restore outside the five, with two rules of reporting. | Taken, as far as this definition goes. A `refused` restore carries one reason. The five are the values of `failure.reason`, and only they open a `failure`. Every other reason opens none, and bounds the replacements at 3 for one registration, as revision 16 has it. The two rules are taken as duties of the runtime: one of the five is reported before any other reason when both apply, and an error is never reported as an absence, nor an absence as an error. A replay derives neither. The names of the other reasons, and the order among the five, are that design's to own. This note lists no enum for them. | No row. Owner of the names: the recovery design, at its review. Owner of the reporting: IA. |
