The entry that releases the last `standing` pin on a checkpoint that is `kept` and has no `expires` sets it, to that entry's time plus 7 days. If that entry is clamped, the deadline is later, which lengthens retention and nothing else (section 3.12). | The row `decide-recovery`. The rows that release a pin: an operation's own answer, the final entry F of a release, and `withhold`. Section 5.8, two rows. |

**A path that saves and does nothing else. New in revision 19**
(B2; the request `837943bb`). Under revision 18 a save was opened
only by an operation that changes the root, or by a stop. So a task
that was stopped with unsaved work had no entry that could save it
when the stop's own save was not opened, or when its three saves had
failed. For a cancelled task there was none at all. The act `save`
is that entry.

- *What it opens.* One save of the registered instance: the cut,
  then store and commit. It opens no operation of the worker, so no
  tool, no command, no edit and no push starts by it. It writes
  nothing in the lane, and it reads no hold. So it cannot extend a
  hold, and it gives the worker no grant. A checkpoint that it makes
  after the hold has ended is private, as the last checkpoint of
  section 5.2 is.
- *Who signs it.* While the task runs, the worker, under
  `task.operate`. While the task is `paused` or `cancelling`, a
  person: a device key of the controller or of an admin, under
  `task.control`, on an observation within sixty seconds. The role
  `agent` holds no `task.control`, so an agent cannot open a save in
  a stopped task. The save itself needs no key: its outcomes rest on
  the registration, as a stop's save does.
- *In which states.* The registration is `ready`. Corrected in
  revision 20: revision 19 said here that a `fenced` instance cannot
  commit, so nothing saves it. A person can now save its root: "A
  save of a fenced root", below. No save is open: one
  at a time. The control that stopped the task was acknowledged by
  its own entry and applied by its own outcome before this, and
  `save` changes neither.
- *What it keeps.* Every rule of a save. The cut is taken with no
  writer. The whole cut is checked before the commit. The pointer
  moves one step, from the prior that the cut names. Each attempt of
  the cut is named by its operation, its attempt, its instance and
  its job, and gets its own outcome. No attempt is left out so that
  a cut fits. An effect that is unknown keeps its own identity and
  its pin.
- *How many, and what bounds them.* One `save` gives one closure: at
  most 3 saves. The task holds the room of one `save` while it is
  stopped (section 5.8). So after a stop whose own three saves
  failed, one more closure has its room. Corrected in revision 20:
  revision 19 said "is always admitted". Room is one condition of
  several. The `save` is admitted when the registration is `ready`
  or `fenced`, its host is not being destroyed, and no save is open.
  It then saves only if the supervisor can take the cut. "Where
  nothing can save", below, lists every state in which it cannot.
  A further `save` is new work. Four things bound repeated use: one is open at a time;
  each needs a signature under present authority; each beyond the
  first needs free room; and the host has an end time, below.
- *What it reserves.* 1 entry for the act. The closure of a save: at
  most 30 entries, 3 `cut` items and 1 `checkpoint` item, with their
  places. No record and no pending request. The bytes of 31 entries.
  The 30 is conditional, as section 12.1.7 says of it.
- *What it is not.* It resumes no tool. It makes no partial save. It
  calls nothing saved that is not in a committed checkpoint. It
  keeps no host by itself.

**A host that is kept, and the decision that ends it. New in
revision 19** (B3; the request `837943bb`). The host of an instance
holds the only copy of what no checkpoint holds.

- *When a task is stopped and not saved.* It is read from the
  records, and never from a belief about the root. The task is
  `paused` or `cancelling`. The registration that `task.registration`
  names is `ready` or `fenced`. And no `checkpoint` was opened by a
  save whose cut was opened after the stop's entry, under that
  registration. The field `unsaved` of `end-host` must equal this.
  Corrected in revision 20: the cut must also be `final`, and no
  destruction that its commit opened may have been `refused`. From
  revision 22: or left `unknown` (C3). A
  checkpoint from a cut that is not final leaves the task not saved,
  whenever it was made: "The final cut", below.
- *No stop ends a host.* The outcome of a stop destroys nothing.
  While the task is stopped and not saved, the runtime does not end
  the host, and does not let it sleep, on the strength of the stop.
- *A host ends in two ways, each recorded.* A save that was cut
  after the stop commits: its outcome makes the registration
  `fenced` and opens the host's destruction, because nothing is then
  unsaved. From revision 20 that holds for a final cut only. Or a
  person signs `end-host`. No timed rule, no outcome
  of a stop and no act of the worker opens the destruction of a host
  that holds unsaved work. A restore still destroys the host that it
  replaces, after the signed `register` and `intend` that section
  5.9 asks for.
- *`end-host` is the final decision.* A device key of the controller
  or of an admin signs it. It names the registration exactly, and it
  says `unsaved: true` when the records say so. So the entry shows
  who gave up which unsaved work. From it the registration is
  `fenced`, each attempt of that instance with no outcome is
  `unknown`, and the page shows each as interrupted. The destruction
  is an operation with its own outcome. A destruction whose answer
  is lost stays unknown, and the task stays `cancelling`.
- *How long, and who pays.* The outcome of a stop sets `hostEnds`,
  24 hours later. The page shows it. `extend-host` moves it to 24
  hours after its own entry. So each further day of a kept host has
  a person who signed for it. The `apply` of a `resume` empties
  `hostEnds`. The number is a proposal: R4 owns it,
  with IA for what a host costs and for how long the provider keeps
  one. The cost of the host is the deployment's, and the operator
  pays the provider. Inside the application the task's controller
  answers for it until `hostEnds`.
- *After `hostEnds`.* Nothing destroys the host. It is overdue. The
  page shows it so, to the controller and to every admin, and it is
  in the operator's record (G13). A `save`, an `extend-host`
  and an `end-host` are all still admitted. This is a choice, and
  its cost is stated: a host can outlast its end time until a person
  acts or the provider ends it. A rule that ended it by time alone
  would destroy unsaved work with no person's decision, and this note
  has none. Revision 19 asked the planner whether an installation
  may set a rule of its own. The planner answered, and the next point
  carries the answer.
- *An overdue host, ended by rule. New in revision 20.* The planner's
  answer, received 2026-10-05, is applied as it stands: "an
  installation may end an overdue stopped host by rule, but the
  end-host act is still signed by the installation's controller,
  names the rule it applies, follows a stated notice window in which
  the holder may restore or save, and the saved state is retained for
  restore for a stated period afterwards. The clock authorizes a
  controller to act; it never destroys by itself."
  - *The act.* It is `end-host`, and no other act. There is still no
    timed rule, and no outcome and no runtime event ends a host. A
    host that nobody signs for stays, overdue and shown, as before.
  - *Who signs.* The installation's controller, in the planner's
    words. In this note's roles that signer is a device key of an
    admin, under `task.control` on a sixty-second observation (W2),
    as for every `end-host`. The rule gives the task's own controller
    nothing that it lacks, and an agent cannot sign. Whether an
    installation has a narrower role for it is N5's.
  - *What the act names.* Everything that an `end-host` names, and
    `rule`: the name of the installation's rule. The entry holds it.
    So the history shows who ended which host, under which rule, and
    whether work was unsaved. That the installation has set a rule of
    that name is the signer's statement. No guard of the task scope
    reads the installation's configuration, and the name is a trusted
    claim until N5 says where an installation states its rules.
  - *The notice window.* It starts at `hostEnds`, when the host
    becomes overdue and the page shows it so to the controller and to
    every admin. An `end-host` that names a rule is admitted only
    when the commit time is later than `hostEnds` plus the notice
    window. Inside the window the holder may save, by `save`; may
    keep the host, by `extend-host`, which moves `hostEnds` and so
    starts the window again; or may restore, after a `resume`. Each
    is admitted as before. The page shows the time from which the
    rule may be applied.
  - *The retention period.* The saved state of the task is the
    checkpoint that `task.current` names. After an `end-host` that
    names a rule it is kept for a restore until the commit time plus
    the retention period, at least. A checkpoint with a `standing`
    pin gets no deadline at all, and is kept while the pin stands
    (the answer to B12).
  - *When the work was unsaved.* Nothing is invented. What no
    checkpoint holds is lost when the host is destroyed. The act must
    say `unsaved: true` when the records say so, as revision 19
    requires, and it is refused otherwise. What is kept is the last
    checkpoint that committed. When `task.current` names none,
    nothing is kept, and the entry shows both facts.
  - *The two values.* The notice window and the retention period are
    values of this definition's version, on the task scope's commit
    clock, like the 24 hours of `hostEnds`. No number is proposed
    here: the proof plan R4 owns both, with IA for what a host costs.
    A restart changes neither, because `hostEnds` and `expires` are
    stored slots. With the clock behind no act is written, so the
    rule fails closed.
  - *What stays as it was.* An `end-host` that names no rule is the
    decision of revision 19: the controller or an admin signs it at
    any time while the task is stopped. Each guard of `end-host`
    holds for both: the task is stopped, the registration is named
    exactly, no save is open, and `unsaved` equals the records. So a
    rule never ends a host during a save. Both use the one entry that
    `register` reserved.
  - *Two forms that are owed.* No form compares the clock with a slot
    plus a duration, and none sets a time only when the slot holds an
    earlier one. Each is one more place of platform code in this row,
    and section 12.1.8 has no row for either. A second time slot, set
    with `hostEnds`, would need no code for the first. The choice is
    IA's, with the recovery design.
- *A host that is lost.* The provider can end a host by its own
  event, and the task scope cannot tell that from a host that it
  cannot reach. What is then true: the pointer names the last
  checkpoint that committed. A save whose values were all stored and
  read back may still commit, because the commit is the controller's
  side's. A save that was cut and not stored whole does not commit,
  in any part: its outcome is `refused` or `unknown`, and its stored
  bytes are deleted as bytes with no root. What is shown: "not
  saved", the time of the last checkpoint, each attempt with no
  receipt, and the host as not answering. What is recoverable: the
  last checkpoint, by a restore after a `resume`; the journals and
  the results; and an edit's recorded content, as a new attempt.
  What is not: files that a command wrote, and a prepared commit's
  objects. The record that closes it is still a person's `end-host`,
  or the `register` of a new instance. Its destruction is then
  answered "no such host".
- *The room.* `register` reserves the entry of one `end-host` and
  the host's destruction (section 5.8). So a person can end a host
  at a scope with no free room. `extend-host` is new work.

**The final cut. New in revision 20** (the verdict `d2068c05`, its
second finding). Revision 19 ended a host when a save that was cut
after a stop committed, "because nothing is then unsaved". That does
not follow. The adopted recovery design thaws a declared background
job after the cut is read and checked (its section 6, step 5), and
says that what a thawed process writes is not in the checkpoint. Its
own table shows such an append after the commit (its table 14.8, row
5). So a checkpoint proves what its cut held. It proves nothing
about the root afterwards.

- *What a final cut is.* A cut is final when, by the supervisor's
  report, every process of the instance but the supervisor's own was
  ended or frozen before the read, and none was thawed after it: the
  thaw of step 5 was not made. The item `cut` holds this as `final`.
  It is the runtime's evidence, a trusted claim, labelled as the
  cut's agreement with the journals is.
- *When a cut is asked to be final.* Every cut that is opened while
  the task is `paused` or `cancelling`, and every cut of a fenced
  root. A task that is stopped runs no command, so nothing is lost
  by leaving a background job frozen. A cut of a task that runs is
  never final: its jobs are thawed, as that design says. Made exact
  in revision 21: that last sentence is of a `ready` instance. The
  cut of a fenced root is asked to be final in every state of the
  task, also while the task runs, because a fenced instance runs
  nothing. This weakens nothing: until the supervisor's side is
  agreed, no cut is final.
- *The freeze is held.* After a final cut the supervisor keeps every
  unit frozen until one of two things: the `apply` of a `resume`,
  which thaws them, or the destruction of the host. It thaws nothing
  on the strength of the commit.
- *The destruction names its cut.* The destruction that a commit
  opens is asked for that cut. The supervisor carries it out only if
  nothing was thawed and no process ran since that cut. Otherwise it
  answers `refused`, and the host stays. That refusal makes the task
  "not saved" again, by the rule above. From revision 22 (the
  recovery design's ask C3): the entry that opens such a destruction
  is the commit's own outcome, which holds the cut and the
  checkpoint, and the destruction's request names the cut, the
  save's job and the checkpoint. An attempt of it that is `unknown`
  makes the task "not saved" as a `refused` one does: a host that
  did not answer has not shown that its freeze held.
- *When this cannot be established.* A host on which the supervisor
  cannot hold a freeze, or cannot say that it did, gives no final
  cut. Its saves still commit, and each checkpoint is good for what
  it holds. No commit ends that host. The task stays "stopped and
  not saved", the host is kept with its end time, and it ends by a
  later save whose cut is final, or by a person's signed `end-host`
  that says `unsaved: true`.
- *What a receipt may be shown as.* A checkpoint is shown with the
  time of its cut: "saved as of" that time. It is never shown, and
  never read by a guard, as proof that the present root holds
  nothing more. Only a final cut whose freeze was held, in a task
  that has not been resumed since, says that.
- *What is asked, and not decided.* The supervisor's side is the
  recovery design's and IA's. Asked of the recovery design: that the
  thaw of its step 5 is not made for a cut that is asked to be
  final; that a frozen unit stays frozen until a resume or the
  destruction; and that its section 7.4 and its table 14.8 follow.
  Asked of IA: that the supervisor reports `final`, holds the
  freeze, and refuses a destruction after any thaw, with what its
  host can and cannot establish. None is claimed as agreed. Until
  they answer, this note's rule is the conservative one: no cut is
  final, and no commit ends a host.

**A save of a fenced root. New in revision 20** (the verdict
`d2068c05`, its first finding). Under revision 19 a `fenced`
registration could not be saved by anyone. The verdict's case: the
task is `cancelling`, its `ready` host holds a dirty root, all three
saves of the stop were refused, and no save is open. An authorized
`fence` then leaves a fenced instance with unsaved work, and the
person's reserved `save` is refused. A `register` and a restore
replace the root, and `end-host` records its loss. Recording a known
loss is not recovery. The repair is one narrow case of `save`.

| | A save of a fenced root |
|---|---|
| Who signs | A person: a device key of the controller or of an admin, under `task.control`, on a sixty-second observation (W2). Never the worker's key, in any state of the task, so never an agent. |
| The act | `save`, with `fenced: true`. No other act and no outcome opens such a save. |
| The registration | The one that `task.registration` names, and it is `fenced`. It stays `fenced` through the save and after it. No entry of the save changes its state. |
| The host | No destruction of it is open or `confirmed`. |
| The attempts | Every attempt that names that instance has an outcome. The `unknown` outcomes of a fenced instance are written first (the row "The outcome of any other operation"), or the act is refused, named `attempts-open`. So the cut's set of attempts is empty. |
| One at a time | No save of the task is open. |
| The cut | It is asked to be final. The supervisor freezes or ends every process, takes the census, reads the whole root and thaws nothing. A root that it cannot make quiescent is not saved: the cut is `refused`, `not-quiescent`. |
| The commit | The recovery design's guards 1 to 8, with one change: the registration is `fenced`, and the opening `save` says so. Its hold, epoch and instance equal the cut's. `task.current` is the cut's `prior`. The whole stored head is read back. A cut that was not stored whole does not commit, in any part. |
| The room | While the task is stopped, the room that the task holds for one `save` (section 5.8). Otherwise it is new work. |
| After it | The checkpoint is `current`, and private. Made exact in revision 21: the commit opens the host's destruction only in the branch of the commit's own row, which is a task that is `paused` or `cancelling` and a cut that is final. While the task runs, a save of a fenced root ends no host: the host is kept, fenced, until the task is stopped or a person signs. |

- *What it does not give.* No tool: an `intend` needs a `ready`
  registration, and this one stays `fenced`. No write: the save
  reads the root and changes nothing in it. Nothing under the old
  hold: the save reads no lane and writes none, and a hold that has
  ended stays ended. No push and no export: each needs its own act,
  its own grant and a `ready` registration or a lane's entry, as
  before. No partial root: the closure is whole or nothing.
- *What it does not settle.* Its cut names no attempt. So it writes
  no outcome for any attempt, it settles no `unknown` effect, and it
  releases no pin. An attempt that was `unknown` before it is
  `unknown` after it, with its pin, and the prior checkpoint is
  `kept` when a pin stands on it, by the commit's own clause.
- *What is trusted.* That the root which was read is the root of
  that instance, unchanged since it was fenced but for what its own
  processes wrote, is the supervisor's evidence. It is labelled so,
  like every comparison of the root with the private journals.
- *What is asked, and not decided.* The recovery design's section
  7.4 has the guard that an instance is `ready`. Asked: that it take
  this one case. Asked of IA: that the supervisor takes a cut of a
  fenced instance, which runs nothing and may still be read. None is
  claimed as agreed.

**Where nothing can save. New in revision 20.** These are the states
in which a root may hold work that no checkpoint holds, and no entry
can save it. In each, what remains is an `end-host` that says
`unsaved: true`, or the provider's own end of the host. Each is a
limit of this design, stated so that no page and no source claims
more.

| # | The state | Why nothing saves it | What would close it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The host is lost, or does not answer | No cut can be taken. Revision 19 says what is then shown and what is recoverable. | Nothing in this design. Only the provider's keeping of a stopped host. |
| 2 | The root cannot be made quiescent: a process in no recorded unit, or a unit that cannot be frozen or ended | The cut is refused `not-quiescent`, each time. The recovery design marks such an instance, and takes no save from it. | A host that can make the root unwritable, or copy it atomically (that design's RU-4). |
| 3 | The host's destruction is open, by an `end-host` or by a commit | A save is refused while a destruction is open or `confirmed`. | Nothing. The decision was recorded before it. |
| 4 | A save is refused by the store or by the read-back, three times, and the standing room is used | A further `save` is new work, and at a full scope it is refused `scope-full`. | The composition of section 5.8, with a second standing room or free places. |
| 5 | The task runs, its registration is `fenced` and the scope is full | A save of a fenced root is new work while the task runs. | The same. Or a stop first: a stopped task holds the room. |
| 6 | The task runs, and the worker signs `register` over a `fenced` registration that holds unsaved work | The old registration is `stale`, and the restore destroys its host. The worker may be an agent. Revision 19 states this, and it is not changed. Closed in revision 22: `register` and a restore's `intend` are refused `unsaved-undecided` in that state (C1). The row is kept for a history that reached it before. | A guard on `register`: no registration over a fenced one that is not saved, without a person's decision. Added in revision 22. |
| 7 | No cut is final on this host | Saves commit, and no commit ends the host. Nothing is lost by a rule, and the host is kept until a person signs. | The supervisor's side of "The final cut". |
| 8 | The registration is `starting` or `restore-failed` | Its root is a restore that did not finish, and no cut of it is taken. It holds no work of the task that a checkpoint lacks. | Nothing is needed. |
| 9 | New in revision 22 (C4). A `fenced` root that the store refuses by a rule of the recovery design's section 5.3: Git storage that it borrows, a damaged closure, a special file, or a limit | A fenced instance admits no operation, so nothing can dissociate the root or repair it. The save is refused each time. | An operation of the supervisor alone that makes such a root storable, with no tool of the worker. It is the recovery design's and IA's to state. |
| 10 | New in revision 22. A save's commit is `unknown`: the store did not answer | One save is open at a time, and that one is not settled. No stop and no person opens another until it has its answer. | The read that decides a save: its basis is `read`, so a read-back of the stored head settles it as `confirmed` or `refused`. |

Rows 1 to 6 are states with dirty work that nobody can save. Rows 7
and 8 are listed so that the table is whole: in 7 nothing is lost,
and in 8 nothing is unsaved. From revision 22: row 6 is closed for
new histories, and rows 9 and 10 are added. Row 9 is a seventh state
with dirty work that nobody can save. Row 10 lasts until one read
answers.

**Two questions of the recovery design's revision 6: B11 and B12.**

| # | Asked | Answer | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| B11 | Whether the places of a `cancel`'s save, of a `pause`'s save and of an operation's own save are held side by side | Not decided, and stated as unproved. Three closures hold 9 places of `cut` against a `max` of 8, and the standing `save` holds 3 more. No guard of this note keeps places, and none is invented. | Section 5.8, "How many closures are open at once". Owners: the capacity work `cc570904`, R4, IA and that design. |
| B12 | Whether the deadline that the outcome of a `pause` sets can expire a checkpoint that a standing pin keeps | Under revision 19, yes: the timed rule `checkpoint-expiry` reads `expires` alone, opening a pin empties it, and a later `pause` set it again. That was a fault. From revision 20 no entry sets `expires` on a checkpoint while a pin on it is `standing`: the outcome of a `pause`, the `apply` of a wait, `abandon`, `extend-retention` and an `end-host` that names a rule. So a pinned checkpoint holds no deadline, and the timed rule cannot expire it. The rule itself is unchanged: a timed rule's effects are total. | The row "The outcome of a `pause` or a `cancel`"; this table. |

**One save at a time, and the places of a save. Decided in revision
22.** This is a finding about revision 20, and its repair.

*The finding.* A task that runs holds the room of a `cancel` and the
room of a `pause`, and from revision 19 the room of one `save`.
Section 5.8 gave each "3 `cut` items and 1 `checkpoint` item, with
their places", and said that the standing room is "beside the room of
each stop". The `max` of `cut` is 8. Read as written, the rooms add:
3 and 3 and 3 is 9. The `apply` of a `start` is admitted only with
the room of a `pause`. So it would be refused, and no task could run.
An operation that changes the root needs 3 more. Revision 20 called
this unproved. It is worse than unproved: as the rows stood, it did
not fit.

*What the rows already hold.* A `cut` is `frozen` from its own outcome
to the outcome of its commit, and then it is `committed` or `failed`,
which are final. A final item has left its place under `max`. A save
has at most 3 cuts, and each later one is opened by the outcome that
ends the one before. So one save has one `frozen` cut at a time. And
the act `save` is refused while a save is open.

*The rule, which is now of every entry that opens a save.* At most
one save of a task is open. A save is open from the entry that opens
its cut until its last outcome is `confirmed` or `refused`.

| The entry | When no save is open | When a save is open |
|---|---|---|
| An `intend` for an operation that changes the root | It opens that operation's save. Refused `cut-full` when 8 such attempts already have no outcome. | Refused `save-open`. Corrected in revision 23: revision 22 admitted it while no `cut` was `frozen`. |
| The entry of a `pause` or a `cancel` | It opens the stop's save, when the registration is `ready`. | It opens none. If the open save's cut is opened after the stop's entry, that save is the stop's. Otherwise the outcome that ends the open save opens the stop's save, in that same entry. |
| A person's `save`, also of a fenced root | It opens one save. | Refused, as before. |
| The outcome that ends one save of a closure as `refused` | Not applicable. | It opens the next save of the same closure, at most 3, as before. The cut before it is `failed` in that entry. With a stop that waits, see "The attempts of one cut", below: one successor is opened, and never two. |

*The attempts of one cut. Decided in revision 23* (the verdict
`6f9cc0c7`, its finding). A `cut` names at most 8 attempts. Revision
22 let an `intend` join an open save "while no cut is frozen" and
promised that the save's cut would name it. Nine such `intend`s met
the rule, and the cut holds eight. The repair is a bound at the
admission, and no partition.

- *Which attempts a cut names.* Every attempt of an operation that
  changes the root, that names the registered instance and that has
  no outcome. It names all of them, or the save is refused. It never
  names a part: so no committed cut covers part of a dirty root, and
  no checkpoint from a part can mark the root saved or end a host.
- *One operation that changes the root at a time.* Its `intend` opens
  the operation and its save in one entry, and no further such
  `intend` is admitted until that save has ended. This is the adopted
  recovery design's rule, "mutations are serialized": no edit, no
  command and no commit preparation is dispatched while a save job is
  open. The task definition now refuses at the admission what the
  supervisor would not dispatch. So nothing is admitted that could
  miss the open save's cut.
- *How more than one attempt comes to be unsaved.* Only by a closure
  that failed. A save has at most 3 tries for one set. When the third
  is `refused`, the closure has ended, its attempts still have no
  outcome, and the root still holds what they wrote. The next
  `intend` then opens a save whose cut names those attempts and its
  own.
- *The bound.* At most 8 attempts are unsaved at once. It is a state
  bound, held at its opening, as the contract's section 6.1 asks of
  an entry that cannot be refused: the outcome of a cut cannot be
  refused, and its list holds 8. The opening is the `intend` for an
  operation that changes the root. It is refused, named `cut-full`,
  when 8 such attempts already have no outcome.
- *The count.* For a task that runs, with an instance on which every
  save is refused: a script counted the unsaved attempts after each
  act.

  | The act | Before it: unsaved, and a save open | The answer | After it: unsaved |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `intend` 1 | 0, none | Admitted. It opens save S1, whose cut names 1 attempt. | 1 |
  | `intend` 2, while S1 is open | 1, S1 | Refused `save-open`. | 1 |
  | S1's three tries are `refused` | 1, S1 | The closure ends. | 1 |
  | `intend` 2 | 1, none | Admitted. Its save's cut names 2. | 2 |
  | And so on, to `intend` 8, each after the closure before it has failed | 7, none | Admitted. Its save's cut names 8. | 8 |
  | `intend` 9, after that closure has failed | 8, none | Refused `cut-full`. | 8 |
  | A `pause`, a `cancel` or a person's `save` | 8, none | Admitted. Its save's cut names all 8. | 8, or 0 when it commits |

  So at most 8 attempts are unsaved at once, and the next `intend`
  for an operation that changes the root is refused `cut-full`. A
  save by a stop or by a person is still admitted, and its cut holds
  them all. When any save commits, each of its attempts gets its own
  `confirmed` outcome, and the count is 0.
- *What a refused `intend` leaves.* Nothing: no entry, no operation
  and no attempt. So no admitted attempt is ever outside every cut.
  An operation that does not change the root opens no save and is in
  no cut, and neither refusal applies to it.
- *What the reservation says.* A closure is counted for a cut of at
  most 8 attempts: each attempt's own outcome is one of its entries
  (section 5.8). That count is section 12.1.7's, as "What a save and
  a restore reserve" has it, and it was not made again here.
- *A stop that waits, and a retry.* Made exact in revision 23, as the
  verdict asks. An outcome that ends one save may find two reasons to
  open the next: its closure has a try left, and a stop is waiting
  for a save of its own. It opens one save, never two.

  | The outcome that ends a save | A stop waits | What it opens, in that entry |
  |---|---|---|
  | `refused`, and the closure has a try left | No | The closure's next try, for the same set. |
  | `refused`, and the closure has a try left | Yes | The closure's next try, and no other. Its cut is opened after the stop's entry, so it is also the stop's save. The stop's own room is not used yet. |
  | `refused`, and it was the closure's third | No | Nothing. The attempts stay unsaved. |
  | `refused`, and it was the closure's third | Yes | The stop's save: the first try of a new closure, on the stop's room. Its cut names the same attempts. |
  | `confirmed`, from a cut that was opened before the stop's entry | Yes | The stop's save, on the stop's room. Its cut names no attempt, unless one was admitted since, which the rule above excludes. |
  | `confirmed`, from a cut that was opened after the stop's entry | Yes | Nothing. That save was the stop's. |

  The retry comes first, because it is the same closure and holds its
  own entries. The stop's closure begins only when the closure before
  it has ended. With two stops that wait, a `pause` and then a
  `cancel`, one save serves both when its cut is opened after both
  entries.
- *What is kept.* A receipt's identity, the binding of a cut to its
  prior, its checkpoint and its journal positions, the three tries,
  the `unknown` outcome of an attempt whose instance was fenced or
  replaced, and every rule of "The final cut". None is changed.
- *What each note owns.* This note owns the admission: `save-open`,
  `cut-full`, which attempts a cut names, and which entry opens which
  save. The recovery design owns the supervisor: that one mutating
  operation runs at a time, that nothing is dispatched during a save
  job, and how a cut is taken. Its sentence "a root with more unsaved
  attempts needs more than one save" stays true and has no case: no
  root has more than 8. Asked of it, and of IA: to take the two
  refusals and the rule that a cut names every unsaved attempt, in
  its revision that is under review or the next. None is claimed as
  agreed.
  Stated in revision 24: that revision, 9, is adopted now (the
  opening, "The standing in force"). This note did not read it. So
  whether it holds the two refusals and the rule is not known here,
  and they stay asked of that design, in its next revision if
  revision 9 does not hold them.

*What follows for the places.*

- *`cut`.* A task has at most one `frozen` cut. So all its saves
  need one place of `cut`, of 8, and the task holds that one place
  from `establish`. The "3 `cut` items" of a closure are three items
  in turn, and never three places.
- *`checkpoint`.* A save that commits opens one checkpoint. Its prior
  is `expired` in the same entry, or stays `kept` when a pin stands
  on it. So each save that may commit and cannot be refused holds
  one place. A `cancel` holds one, from `establish`. A `pause` holds
  one, from the `apply` of a `start` or a `resume`. The standing
  `save` holds none of its own: it is there for a stop whose saves
  did not commit, and then that stop's place is still free.
- *An operation's own save* can be refused, at its `intend`. It needs
  one free place of `checkpoint` beyond those that the stops hold,
  or the `intend` is refused `type-full`.
- *A further `save` by a person, after a stop's save committed,* is
  new work for its place. At a type that is full it is refused, and
  that is row 4 of "Where nothing can save".

*The arithmetic.* A script added up the places, for a task with u
checkpoints in use.

| The state | `cut`, as revision 20's rows add | `cut`, with one save at a time | `checkpoint` held, as the rows add | `checkpoint` held, with one save at a time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Established and idle | 6 of 8 | 1 of 8 | 2 | 1 |
| Running | 9 of 8: it does not fit | 1 of 8 | 3 | 2 |
| Running, with one operation in flight and its save open | 12 of 8: it does not fit | 1 of 8 | 4 | 3 |

So a task can be established, started and run with an operation in
flight, when u is at most 61. The recovery design's example has 62 in
use, by 61 pinned checkpoints, and 2 held: 64. There the task runs,
and an operation that changes the root is refused `type-full` until
a pin is released. That is the bound of `checkpoint`, and R4 owns the
number.

*What this does not decide.* The entries and the bytes of the
closures: they are used one after another, each room keeps its own,
and their sum is a budget, which R4 and the capacity work under
`cc570904` own. The form of a held place, which is the row P11. And
the other dimensions of section 5.8's point. No second mechanism is
added: a place is held as `max` and the reservations of section 5.8
already hold one.

*What is asked.* Of the recovery design and IA: that the supervisor
runs one save of an instance at a time, which a cut with no writer
already needs. Of R2: the reason `save-open`, for a page.

**The recovery design's asks C1 to C5. Answered in revision 22** (its
revision 7 at `e865fd05`, section 12.9).

| # | Asked | Answer | The rows that change |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | That `register`, and `intend` for a restore, be refused while the registration that the task names is `fenced`, unsaved and undecided, or while a save of it is open | Agreed, and added. The guard is named `unsaved-undecided`. A fenced registration is undecided while no save of it that was opened by a person's `save` with `fenced: true` has committed, and no destruction of its host is open or `confirmed`. It is decided by such a save, or by an `end-host`, which says `unsaved: true` when the records say so. "Unsaved" is read conservatively: a fenced registration with no such save is unsaved, whatever an earlier checkpoint holds. | The rows `register` and `intend`, for a restore. Row 6 of "Where nothing can save". |
| C2 | A deciding act and an end time for an old host whose registration is already `stale`, with its destruction withheld | Agreed. `end-host` may also name a registration that is `stale`, when no destruction of its host is open or `confirmed`. Nothing can save a stale root, so the act says `unsaved: true`, and is refused otherwise. Its end time is not a slot: such a host is overdue from the entry that made its registration `stale`. The notice window of an installation's rule is counted from that entry's time. `extend-host` does not apply to it. | The row `end-host`, by this answer. It uses new room, because `register` reserved one `end-host` for each registration, and that one is the stale registration's own. |
| C3 | That a destruction which a commit opens carry its cut, the save's job and the checkpoint; and that a read-back with no answer leave the task "not saved" | Agreed, both. | "The final cut", the point "The destruction names its cut". "When a task is stopped and not saved". |
| C4 | That "Where nothing can save" list a fenced root that fails a refusal of the store | Agreed. It is row 9, a seventh state with dirty work that nobody can save. | "Where nothing can save" |
| C5 | That the answer to B12 be kept: no deadline on a pinned checkpoint | Kept. It is adopted with revision 20, and nothing of it changes. | None |

*What this note asks back of the recovery design.* Each is asked,
and none is claimed as agreed.

1. That its section 7.6 take the acts `save`, `end-host` and
   `extend-host`, and its table "Which entry can open a save" with
   them. Its cells "none" then have an entry.
2. That it say what a host costs for each day that it is kept, and
   the longest that its provider keeps one, with IA.
3. That it confirm the 7 entries that a pin, and an abandonment, now
   reserve for a `kept` checkpoint: one expiry and one deletion
   group.
4. That its destruction of a host that no restore replaces is one
   operation with at most 3 attempts, as for a restore.
5. The names of the reasons outside the five, and the order among
   the five, as its own.
6. Whether one cut may name more than 8 attempts. This definition
   bounds a cut at 8, and that design says that a root with more
   needs more than one save.

**What I2 and IA read.**

- **The release, and its final entry F.** The lane's guard `settled`
  reads the source entry of `export-settled` (the contract's
  companion file, note N12). F is that source entry: the outcome
  entry that makes the release `confirmed`, or the act `withhold`. In
  both, F's own effects set the `release` item to its final state,
  and F's message names the export and that state. So the guard
  reads three parts of one fetched entry: the state that it set, the
  export and the final value. It reads no other entry of the task
  scope.
- **A control.** The `control` item, from `queued` to `applied` or
  `void`. The page's "accepted, queued, applied" are the control's
  entry, its place among the queued controls, and the entry that
  applies it: the control's own outcome for a `pause` or a `cancel`,
  and the worker's `apply` for another kind.
- **The journal.** The intent of an operation is an entry here, and
  holds a digest of its private record. The command journal and the
  conversation journal are not entries. A `cut` item holds the
  positions that one checkpoint covers.
- **Recovery.** The registration, the checkpoint items with their
  chain of `prior`, the pointer, and the outcome of each operation.
  A restore is an operation that `intend` opens, under a registration
  that is not yet `ready`, and it never moves the pointer. From
  revision 16: the `failure` item, which is the page's "recovery
  failed" with its reason, and the entry of `decide-recovery`, which
  is the person's decision.
- **A durable conversation is private activity.** Nothing that an
  agent says in it is a work outcome. A work outcome is an entry of a
  lane: a report, a manifest, a comment, a judgment. No entry of a
  task scope stands in for one, and no lane reads a task scope's
  history apart from the one entry F.

**How this differs from the base, and why.** The contract lets only
an act, a delivery of a request, a genesis and an outcome send a
message (R1 section 7.5), and it gives a timed entry and a delivery
of a result no signer and no observation of their own. Four things
follow. Each keeps the base's bound and its promise.

1. *A private stream's check is signed.* The base had the task scope
   check a stream every sixty seconds by itself. Here the reader's
   device signs `continue-read`, on an observation read for that
   commit. The end time is still seventy seconds after the last
   check that passed, and the bound of eighty seconds is unchanged
   (section 4.2). A check that is refused moves nothing. The runtime
   sends nothing more on a stream whose check was refused. From
   revision 15 the device that signs is the one that opened the
   stream: the stream holds that key, and `continue-read` is guarded
   on it.
2. *Each license request is signed.* The base had the task scope ask
   again by itself. Here the authorizer's device signs `ask-license`.
   A license that lapsed, or a restart, is followed by another signed
   request, up to three.
3. *A withheld release is closed by a signed act.* The delivery of a
   refused license cannot send `export-settled`, so F is then the act
   `withhold`. Until someone who holds `work.export` signs it, the
   lane's `export` item stays `authorized`, and nothing is released.
4. *The mark `fenced` is a record, and not the fence.* The fence is
   the lane's answer to each check, and the worker's grant, without
   which no `intend` is admitted (section 5.2). When the worker's
   grant is gone, the worker can sign no act, so `fenced` is written
   by the controller or an admin, or the registration becomes `stale`
   at the next `register`. A save that was opened before the grant
   was lost can still commit, because an outcome entry needs no
   grant: that is the last checkpoint that section 5.2 asks for.
   From revision 15 the same holds for a stop: the outcome of a
   `pause` or a `cancel` needs no grant of the worker.

One thing is owed to the contract: an entry that is no act and that
retains an observation read for it, which the `applied` clause of a
license and the destination's reservation both need (P19).

- **Reservations, from revision 19.** The room of one `save` while
  the task is stopped; the entry of one `end-host`, and a host's
  destruction, with each registration; and 7 entries with each pin
  and with each restore that may be abandoned (section 5.8).
- **Reservations.** Revision 17 gives a save and a restore in all
  five dimensions: "What a save and a restore reserve", above. As
  section 5.8, and added here: a save reserves
  the outcome of its cut, the outcome of its commit, and one outcome
  for each attempt of its set, at most 8; a restore reserves its
  outcome and the destruction of the old host, at most 3 attempts;
  each `intend` for a restore is new work, so a registration reserves
  nothing for a restore that is not yet opened; a `pause` or a
  `cancel` reserves 1 entry for its outcome, and a control that
  becomes `void` uses none; from revision 16 a restore also reserves
  1 item for a `failure` and 1 entry for its `decide-recovery`, and a
  task reserves the room of its stops before they are signed, as
  section 5.8 says;
  a stream reserves 1 entry for its timed end; a checkpoint with a
  time in `expires` reserves 1 entry for its expiry. Each chain of
  timed rules is 1.
- **Who may declare a command read-only** (the recovery design's
  RU-10): the controller, by `set-read-only`. The declaration is a
  trusted claim of the controller. With no list, every interrupted
  command needs an `authorize-attempt`.
- **A pin for an unsettled effect** (RU-11) is released only by that
  effect's own answer, as section 5.6 says. A restore from a named
  older checkpoint (RU-12) is not offered: no control asks for one,
  and a restore that cannot be made fails closed. From revision 16
  the decision that follows is `decide-recovery`, and it offers no
  older checkpoint: `repair` tries the same one again, and `abandon`
  starts from the hold's fork.

Its `confirmed` outcome makes the registration `ready`. An `intend` for a command before that outcome is refused `guard-failed`. The `cancel` is `applied`. The 62 are `void`, and each stays as an item with its signer and its text. The task is `cancelling`, and `ended` when no operation is unsettled. - *The questions of the three deltas, answered.* EM6: a longer list,
  and all 34 names (section 3.2). EM7: `member-of` is a rule of
  version 1, at place 5, under the row P26, and the field `handle`
  stays a text. EM8: `handle-form` is a rule of version 1, at place
  4, under the row P27, and its refusal is named `bad-handle` beside
  the answer `bad-field`.
- *One thing that was not checked.* The contract's operand
  `{ const }` holds a `FieldValue`, which may be a list. So once the
  contract's bound holds 34, the role table might be written as data,
  as five effects from constants, with no rule. Whether the source's
  validator takes such a constant was not read. Until someone checks
  it, `role-table` is a rule.

### 12.2 Two decisions: a first commit, and a report with no commit

New in revision 14. Gap G12 left both to "R0 and R2", and R4 asks
both of this note (its section 13). Each has one part that is this
note's own subject, which is decided here as a proposal, and one part
that a sibling owns, which is named.

**Founding writes a first commit.** A repository that the register
has just created is empty. Its branch has no head. Three rules of
this note need a head: a fork's seed from the destination's head
(section 5.2), the published history that an ancestry check stops at
(section 6.2), and a manifest's base, which is the first parent of
its integration commit (section 6.5). So the destination gives its
branch a first head before it reserves anything, and it is the only
writer of that head, as it is of every later one (decision D3-1;
H4).

| | A founding with no import | A founding by import, which is R0's step 1 |
|---|---|---|
| The first head | The **founding commit**. Its tree is the empty tree. It has no parent. Its author and committer are a fixed platform identity that names G's scope ID. Both times are the time of G's genesis entry. Its message is a fixed sentence and the claim's fact. So its ID is the same on every attempt. | The head of the imported history. The directory's import copies the objects into the canonical repository under `refs/artroom/import/<digest of the claim's fact>`, and writes no branch. Its `confirmed` outcome sends the commit to G (section 12.1.2). |
| What opens G's write | The entry of G that records the directory's `confirm`. | The delivery of the directory's `import` update, state `done`. |
| The write | One operation of G, `first-head`: create the branch ref only if it is absent, pointing at that commit. It has its own attempts, at most 3, its own grant at the gateway, and its own token and duties, exactly as section 6.6. | The same. Before the write G checks, by a read of the host, that the commit and its whole closure are in the canonical repository, as it does for an integration commit (section 6.5). |
| What decides | A read of the branch. It holds that commit: G's head is set and the branch is `ready`. It is absent: the same create is sent again, as a new attempt. It holds anything else: another writer (section 6.9). | The same. |
| The receipt | One, named by the digest of the operation's fact. It holds G's final fact for the operation, the claim's fact and the commit. | The same. |

Stated in revision 27: each part of the founding commit, and of the
receipt, is stated byte for byte in section 12.1.5, with the two ref
names. "Digest of the claim's fact" and "digest of the operation's fact"
in this table are the 64 hexadecimal characters of the fact's `hash`.
The receipt of the first head has an item, `receipt`, as a publication's
has.

- **Before the first head.** The branch is `empty`. A `reserve` that
  arrives is recorded and stays `queued`. Nothing is judged and
  nothing is sent to the host for it. When an import fails for good,
  the branch stays `empty`, and the ways forward are an admin's
  `retry-import` or a new founding.
- **The seed of a fork.** A seed `from: destination-head` is read
  from the host for that creation. If the read shows no branch, the
  `fork` record becomes `failed`, with the name `no-head`, and no
  creation attempt is opened. The hold has no fork, the page says so,
  and the holder may release it and take another once the branch has
  a head. No fork is ever created from an empty repository. The first
  head is published history: a seed from it adds no author (section
  5.2).
- **Staging.** No rule of section 6.2 gets a special case. The first
  head is reachable from itself, so it is a stop at the branch and is
  never listed. Every integration commit has a first parent, which is
  its manifest's base. A commit with no parent that is offered as an
  integration commit is not reserved: `integration-invalid` (section
  6.5). A first change to an empty tree adds its files on top of the
  founding commit.
- **An unknown attempt.** An attempt of `first-head` whose answer was
  lost stays `unknown` under its own identity. The read shows the
  effect and gives that attempt no outcome (G1). Each attempt is the
  same create, so a late one is refused by the host once the ref
  exists, under H1.
- **What it rests on.** H1, for a ref that is expected to be absent.
  That is the same use as the receipt's (section 6.10), and R4's case
  HS7 is its witness.
- **Owners.** This note, for the destination and the directory. R0 is
  asked for nothing in its step 1: the demonstration founds by
  import, and its record "default branch at the imported commit" is
  the second column. R0 is asked only to say, where it describes a
  founding with no import, that the repository starts with one empty
  commit. R2 is asked for no form: the seed `destination-head` is in
  its adopted text.

| Case | What happens | G's branch | A hold taken then |
|---|---|---|---|
| A founding with no import | G creates the branch at the founding commit, and a read shows it. | `ready`, with that head | Its fork is seeded there. |
| The create's reply is lost, and the read shows the ref absent | Attempt 2 sends the same create. Attempt 1 stays `unknown`. | `empty`, until a read shows the commit | `fork` is `failed`, `no-head`. |
| A founding by import; the copy is confirmed | The directory's update arrives. G checks the closure and creates the branch. | `ready`, at the imported head | Seeded at the imported head. |
| The import's three attempts are refused | The directory sends `failed`. | `empty` | No fork. An admin may sign `retry-import`. |
| A manifest whose integration commit has no parent | Not reserved: `integration-invalid`. | Unchanged | Not a case. |

**A report names a commit.** R4 asks whether staging is skipped for a
report with no commit. In the texts in force it does not arise. R0
revision 4 has each concern report "an exact commit and tree" (its
step 8). R2 revision 14 has `commit` and `tree` as fixed, required
values of a `report`, with the guards `staged` and `ancestry` on the
act. So the decision for the first version is: a report names a
commit and a tree, and every report is staged and checked as section
6.2 says. Staging is never skipped.

R4's proof plan still lists "a result with no commit" as a wanted
witness, and says that it must not be met by forcing a commit into
every lane. That is a matter of R2's form. So this note states now
what its own side would be, so that no later revision has to invent
it. It is a proposal that waits on R2, and it changes nothing until
R2's `report` row changes.

| If R2 lets a `report` name no commit and no tree | This note's rule |
|---|---|
| Preparation | None. No step `stage` and no step `check` is asked. No root, no pin, no token and no ancestry record exists for it. |
| The hold | Not needed. The commitment and the performer are needed, as for the reuse of a staged root (section 6.2). |
| The grant | The act's own grant, in its ordinary window (W1). No outside write follows, so the ten-second kind does not apply. |
| The guards `staged` and `ancestry` | Not evaluated, because the field that they read is absent. A report that names a commit and no tree, or a tree and no commit, is refused `bad-field`. |
| A fork's seed | Never. The seed rule takes a report whose staged root is `live`, and this report has none (section 5.2). |
| A manifest's selection | Never. A selection names a commit that must be an ancestor of the integration commit (section 6.5). |
| `use-input` | Allowed. Its authors enter the commitment's attribution. Nothing is fetched or staged. |
| What it reserves | Nothing beyond the act. |

- **Owners.** R2, for whether the `report` item and act take that
  form. R0, for whether the demonstration needs it: revision 4 does
  not. R4, to keep its row conditional until R2 answers, or to drop
  it.

written they did not agree by one. From revision 15 the contract
agrees: its revision 12, which is adopted, counts the index row. The
case is the one that all three use: 32 links are `set`, and an issue
lane staged the merged manifest.

**Where the three notes agree.**

- 33 requests leave the entry, and 33 results return: 32 from the
  issue lanes and 1 from the staging lane. R1 section 17.2, R2
  sections 13.5 and 13.6, and R4's row F23 all say 33.
- A merge that is asked for reserves that entry, 33 pending requests
  and 66 more entries: 67 entries in all (R1 section 17.2; R2 section
  13.6).
- The order of an entry's sends: the written forms in order, a
  fan-out's sends in its own order, and then the platform's one
  result (R1 section 6.6). So the ordinals follow from the row.
- The bound: at most 104 sends for the delivery of a request (R1
  section 7.5). The count is inside it.
- The destination's side: one final update, answered once. The
  destination matches that result by its own entry and its own
  send's ordinal. It reads no ordinal of the lane's entry.

**Where one changed.** R2's adopted row has the index send, so that
the directory's row shows a merge (its sections 11.3 and 13.5). R1's

Revision 14 of this note asked R1 to count the index row. R1's
revision 12 does so, in its section 7.5, its witness 18.6 and its
decision D12-5, and it is adopted. R4's row F23 states both counts
and asserts the one that is adopted when it is built.

like the rest of revision 15.

| Asked | Answer | Where |
|---|---|---|
| R1-48: the genesis act of each platform definition | Stated. `install` for `platform:register@1`. `establish` for each of the other six: `platform:directory@1`, `platform:membership@1`, `platform:rules@1`, `platform:destination@1`, `platform:inbox@1` and `platform:task@1`. A genesis entry of a platform scope records that name as its `kind`. | Section 12.1, the table of names, column "Genesis act"; the first row of each table of entries in sections 12.1.1 to 12.1.7. |
| R1-49: whether the rules of `hold@1` add anything to an entry that uses only its item form | Confirmed: nothing is added, and the contract's section 6.8 stands. One difference in this note's own text is stated below, and narrowed. | Section 5.7; below. |
| A scripted capability in test support (the contract's section 6.11; I2 delta DJ14), and the answer `unsupported-definition` for a capability form with no code (its section 6.1) | Confirmed, both. A scripted capability is a labelled stand-in, and it is evidence only about what a definition's rows do after a capability has answered. | Below. |

**The genesis acts, in detail.**

- Each of the seven tables of entries has exactly one genesis row,
  and it is the row named above. None was added in revision 15.
- For the register two values are spelled alike. The installer's
  founding intent has the kind `install`, and the register's genesis
  act is `install`. The contract keeps the two apart (its section
  4.1). The `kind` of the genesis entry is the genesis act.
- For the directory they differ: the founder's intent is a `found`,
  which is an act of the register, and the directory's genesis act is
  `establish`.
- One fact type of section 12.1 names a platform genesis by its kind:
  the register's slot `genesis`, of kind `establish` under
  `platform:directory` (section 12.1.1). It needs the genesis entry
  to state its kind, which the contract's revision 12 decides and
  the source still owes (its section 11.10, row 10). The `claim`
  slots name `found`, and a lane's `rules.source` names `publish`.
  Both are acts and not a genesis.

**The item form of `hold@1`, in detail.**

- *What is confirmed.* An entry of a definition that uses only the
  item form holds what the hold type and the `hold` effect derive, as
  the contract's section 6.8 states them. This note's rules add no
  record and no effect to it. A runtime that derives the item form
  writes such an entry whole.
- *The difference, exactly.* Section 5.7, as revisions 10 to 14 wrote
  it, has three things happen in entries that the item form also
  writes. The entry that opens a hold makes the `fork` record, and
  opens the fork's creation or the read for its seed. The entry that
  ends a hold makes the `instance` record `past`. The entry that
  ends a token's use opens its revocation. Each is a record or an
  operation of the capability's own.
- *How they stand together.* None of the three is part of the item
  form, and none is derived for a definition that uses only the item
  form. A hold of such a definition has no fork, no token and no
  instance. Its entries stay as they were written, and no entry that
  exists gains a record. A hold has a workspace only under a
  definition whose rows use the workspace forms. A runtime that lacks
  their code answers `unsupported-definition` for that scope, by the
  contract's section 6.1.
- *What was owed, and is decided in revision 17.* Revision 15 left
  open how a row states that it uses the workspace forms. No row
  states it, and no form is added. The definition states it by what
  it uses: its holds have a workspace exactly when it uses at least
  one guard or effect of `hold@1` (section 5.7, "When a hold has a
  workspace"). Every hold row of both lanes was read for this, as
  data: each writes the `hold` effect alone, and each definition
  uses the capability's guards and effects on other rows. The
  sentence of revision 15 stands: no source derives the three
  records from the `hold` effect alone. They are derived from the
  `hold` effect and the predicate together. R1 is asked for no form,
  and R2 for no row.

**A scripted capability, and what I3 owes instead.**

- *What is confirmed.* A test may supply a scripted capability
  through test support that the production entry does not import, and
  it is labelled a stand-in wherever a result with it is cited. Such
  a result shows which guard refuses, which effects and sends follow,
  and what an entry then holds, after a capability has answered. It
  proves nothing about a real hold, a Git read, a pin, a license or a
  provider. It is evidence for no rule of sections 3.11, 4.2, 5.1 to
  5.7 and 6.2 of this note.
- *Real evidence for `hold@1`.* The records `fork`, `token`,
  `instance`, `root`, `pin`, `check` and `receiver-pin`, derived by
  the capability's own code from sealed entries on real storage, and
  derived again by a replay that has that code and no script. The
  steps `instance`, `token` and `stage` as `preparation` entries.
  Each outside effect of the evidence table of section 5.7 against a
  real Git host, by the basis that the table names: a fork's
  creation, a token's mint and its revocation by ID, a staged ref's
  creation and deletion with the read that decides, and a push to a
  hold's fork. An attempt whose own answer was lost stays `unknown`.
  The lane's answer to a fence check, from its own state and clock
  (section 5.2). A pin in both orders (section 6.2), and a bound
  license request that is decided once at a lane with no free room
  (section 4.2).
- *Real evidence for `git-read@1`.* The ancestry record from a real
  read of the canonical repository's objects, with the staged refs
  that it read kept, and the `too-large` record of a read that was
  cut short (section 6.2). The step `job-read`: a real read token for
  a job, and the snapshot repository of a filtered check (section
  3.11). The checks of the retained Git reader (section 11.1).
- These are the rows that sections 11.1 and 11.2 already give I3, at
  the boundaries that R4 names. This list adds no gate, no suite and
  no number of runs. None of it establishes H1 to H6.

None of the four stops a step of I3. The task scope's rows are IA's.
I3's part is the lane's side of an export, which reads the digest.

The planner wants a member's `withdraw` of their own pending request settled from what the publication holds, whatever is decided (the act `1f8aba72`, answer 3). | The verdict on the contract's revision 22 | Three things. `decisions: { withdraw: 1 }` on the `holds` of `publication`. `bound: { of: "also.publication", where: [...] }` on the handler `withdraw`, with the mark `publication-of` as the binding selector: it states `code`, `row` and `item`, and no other member.
